) and OS reflection positivity, the transfer operator
\mathcal{T}_{a}
has a strictly positive spectral gap
\Delta_{\mathrm{sc}}
above the vacuum, with

\Delta_{\mathrm{sc}}\;\geq\;m_{\mathrm{sc}}(N).

(B.40)

The bound is uniform in
|\Lambda|
.

Proof.

The Osterwalder-Schrader reconstruction on the positive-time algebra produces a Hilbert space
\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{OS}}
, a cyclic vacuum vector
\Omega
, and a selfadjoint, positivity-preserving contraction semigroup
(\mathcal{T}_{t})_{t\geq 0}
with
\|\mathcal{T}_{t}\|\leq 1
,
\mathcal{T}_{0}=\mathbf{1}
, and
\mathcal{T}_{t}\Omega=\Omega
. In particular, for the lattice time-step
a>0
of the strong-coupling scheme,
\mathcal{T}_{a}
is a selfadjoint contraction on
\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{OS}}
with spectral radius
1
and vacuum eigenvalue
1
. Denote by
\mathcal{H}_{0}:=\mathbb{C}\Omega
the vacuum subspace and by
\mathcal{H}_{0}^{\perp}
its orthogonal complement.

By the Markov property and stationarity of the Euclidean measure, time-separated correlations of positive-time observables may be represented as matrix elements of powers of
\mathcal{T}_{a}
. More precisely, if
F
and
G
are cylinder observables supported on the time slice
x_{0}=a
(or finite sums of such), then for every integer
n\geq 0
,

\langle\Theta F\cdot\tau_{na}G\rangle_{\mu}\;=\;\langle[F],\,\mathcal{T}_{a}^{\,n}\,[G]\rangle_{\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{OS}}},

(B.41)

where
\tau_{t}
denotes the Euclidean time shift by
t
and
[F]
is the OS class of
F
. This identity is standard in the OS construction: the left-hand side is the two-point Schwinger function with time separation
na
, and the right-hand side is its transfer-operator representation.

The strong-coupling decay of correlations from Theorem (
B.2
) states that there exist constants
A<\infty
and
m_{\mathrm{sc}}=m_{\mathrm{sc}}(N)>0
, independent of
|\Lambda|
, such that for all such
F,G
with vanishing vacuum expectation (equivalently
[F],[G]\in\mathcal{H}_{0}^{\perp}
),

\big|\langle\Theta F\cdot\tau_{na}G\rangle_{\mu}\big|\;\leq\;A\,e^{-\,m_{\mathrm{sc}}\,na}\qquad\text{for all }n\in\mathbb{N}.

(B.42)

Combining Eq.(
B.41
) and Eq.(
B.42
) yields the uniform operator-kernel bound

\big|\langle\phi,\,\mathcal{T}_{a}^{\,n}\psi\rangle\big|\;\leq\;A\,e^{-\,m_{\mathrm{sc}}\,na}\qquad\text{for all }n\in\mathbb{N},

(B.43)

for all
\phi,\psi
in the dense subspace spanned by OS classes of cylinder observables with zero vacuum mean. By continuity this extends to all
\phi,\psi\in\mathcal{H}_{0}^{\perp}
.

Let
E_{\lambda}
be the projection-valued spectral measure of
\mathcal{T}_{a}
, so that

\mathcal{T}_{a}\;=\;\int_{[0,1]}\lambda\,dE_{\lambda},\qquad\mathcal{T}_{a}^{\,n}\;=\;\int_{[0,1]}\lambda^{n}\,dE_{\lambda},

(B.44)

where we used that
\mathcal{T}_{a}
is a selfadjoint contraction. Fix
\psi\in\mathcal{H}_{0}^{\perp}
and consider the finite positive measure
\nu_{\psi}
on
[0,1]
defined by

\nu_{\psi}(B)\;:=\;\langle\psi,\,E_{B}\psi\rangle\qquad(B\subset[0,1]\ \text{Borel}).

(B.45)

Then

\langle\psi,\,\mathcal{T}_{a}^{\,n}\psi\rangle\;=\;\int_{[0,1]}\lambda^{n}\,d\nu_{\psi}(\lambda).

(B.46)

The bound Eq.(
B.43
) with
\phi=\psi
shows that

\int_{[0,1]}\lambda^{n}\,d\nu_{\psi}(\lambda)\;\leq\;A\,e^{-\,m_{\mathrm{sc}}\,na}\qquad\text{for all }n\in\mathbb{N}.

(B.47)

A simple Tauberian argument now identifies the support of
\nu_{\psi}
. Indeed, if
\nu_{\psi}
had positive mass on an interval
(e^{-m_{\mathrm{sc}}a},\,1]
, then there would exist
\lambda_{0}\in(e^{-m_{\mathrm{sc}}a},1)
and
\delta>0
with
\nu_{\psi}((\lambda_{0},1])\geq\delta
. For all
n
we would have

\int_{[0,1]}\lambda^{n}\,d\nu_{\psi}(\lambda)\;\geq\;\int_{(\lambda_{0},1]}\lambda^{n}\,d\nu_{\psi}(\lambda)\;\geq\;\lambda_{0}^{\,n}\,\nu_{\psi}((\lambda_{0},1])\;\geq\;\delta\,\lambda_{0}^{\,n}.

(B.48)

Since
\lambda_{0}>e^{-m_{\mathrm{sc}}a}
, the ratio
\lambda_{0}^{\,n}\,e^{m_{\mathrm{sc}}an}
diverges as
n\to\infty
, contradicting Eq.(
B.47
). Therefore
\nu_{\psi}((e^{-m_{\mathrm{sc}}a},1])=0
, which means that the spectral projection
E_{(e^{-m_{\mathrm{sc}}a},1]}
annihilates every
\psi\in\mathcal{H}_{0}^{\perp}
. As
\psi
was arbitrary in
\mathcal{H}_{0}^{\perp}
, we conclude that the spectrum of
\mathcal{T}_{a}
restricted to
\mathcal{H}_{0}^{\perp}
is contained in
[0,\,e^{-m_{\mathrm{sc}}a}]
.

The logarithm of a positive contraction is defined by functional calculus; setting
H_{a}:=-a^{-1}\log\mathcal{T}_{a}
one has
\mathcal{T}_{a}=e^{-aH_{a}}
,
H_{a}\Omega=0
,
H_{a}\geq 0
, and the spectral mapping theorem shows

\sigma\!\left(H_{a}\big|_{\mathcal{H}_{0}^{\perp}}\right)\;\subset\;[\,m_{\mathrm{sc}},\,\infty).

(B.49)

Hence the spectral gap of
H_{a}
above the vacuum equals
\Delta_{\mathrm{sc}}:=\inf(\sigma(H_{a})\setminus\{0\})
and satisfies
\Delta_{\mathrm{sc}}\geq m_{\mathrm{sc}}
. Uniformity in the volume follows from the corresponding uniformity of the constants
A
and
m_{\mathrm{sc}}
in Theorem (
B.2
), which was proved by a cluster/Kotecký-Preiss expansion with bounds independent of
|\Lambda|
; the argument above never introduces any additional volume dependence.
∎

We return to Eq.(
B.14
) & Eq.(
B.15
). The key geometric fact is that any open surface
\Sigma
with fixed boundary
C
must contain at least
A(C)
plaquettes, where
A(C)
is the minimal area of a spanning surface of
C
in the lattice. Furthermore, the number of
\Sigma
with
|\Sigma|=A(C)+k
is bounded by
\leq\kappa_{1}^{A(C)+k}
for a combinatorial constant
\kappa_{1}
depending only on the lattice (this is a standard lattice isoperimetric counting). Combining these geometric bounds with Eq.(
B.15
) and Eq.(
B.12
) we obtain an upper bound on
\langle W(C)\rangle_{\Lambda}
as follows. First, write

\langle W(C)\rangle_{\Lambda}\;=\;\frac{\sum_{\Gamma}\prod_{\gamma\in\Gamma}z(\gamma)\;\sum_{\Sigma:\,\partial\Sigma=C,\;\Sigma\cap\Gamma=\varnothing}w(\Sigma)}{\sum_{\Gamma}\prod_{\gamma\in\Gamma}z(\gamma)}\,.

(B.50)

Expand the numerator in powers of
\{z(\gamma)\}
and apply the cluster expansion in a polydisc of activities
\{|z(\gamma)|\leq(C_{2}\beta)^{|\gamma|}\}
. Since the insertion of the open surface forbids polymers intersecting
\Sigma
, the inclusion-exclusion that leads to the truncated series yields multiplicative factors bounded by
\exp\big(\sum_{\gamma:\,\gamma\cap\Sigma\neq\varnothing}|z(\gamma)|\big)
which are in turn controlled by
\exp\big((C_{2}\beta)\,c_{\star}\,|\Sigma|\big)
for a purely geometric constant
c_{\star}
counting the number of polymers touching a given plaquette. Thus, for
\beta\leq\beta_{0}(N)
small enough to ensure
(C_{2}\beta)c_{\star}\leq\frac{1}{2}
, one finds

\big|\langle W(C)\rangle_{\Lambda}\big|\;\leq\;\sum_{\Sigma:\,\partial\Sigma=C}|w(\Sigma)|\,\exp\!\Big(\sum_{\gamma:\,\gamma\cap\Sigma\neq\varnothing}|z(\gamma)|\Big)\;\leq\;\sum_{\Sigma:\,\partial\Sigma=C}\big(C_{3}\beta\big)^{|\Sigma|}\,e^{\frac{1}{2}|\Sigma|}\,.

(B.51)

Using the counting bound for spanning surfaces with boundary
C
gives the geometric series

\big|\langle W(C)\rangle_{\Lambda}\big|\;\leq\;\sum_{k\geq 0}\kappa_{1}^{A(C)+k}\,\big(C_{3}e^{1/2}\beta\big)^{A(C)+k}\;=\;\big(\kappa_{1}C_{3}e^{1/2}\beta\big)^{A(C)}\sum_{k\geq 0}\big(\kappa_{1}C_{3}e^{1/2}\beta\big)^{k}.

(B.52)

Hence, for
\beta\leq\beta_{(}N)
small enough that
q(\beta):=\kappa_{1}C_{3}e^{1/2}\beta<1
, we obtain the bound

\langle W(C)\rangle_{\Lambda}\;\leq\;\frac{q(\beta)^{A(C)}}{1-q(\beta)}\;\leq\;2\,q(\beta)^{A(C)}\,,\qquad q(\beta)=\kappa_{1}C_{3}e^{1/2}\beta\;\xrightarrow[\beta\downarrow 0]{}\;0.

(B.53)

Writing
q(\beta)=e^{-\sigma(\beta)}
with
\sigma(\beta):=-\log q(\beta)>0
we obtain the finite-volume
area law

\langle W(C)\rangle_{\Lambda}\;\leq\;2\,\exp\!\big(-\sigma(\beta)\,A(C)\big),\qquad\sigma(\beta)\;\geq\;-\log(\kappa_{1}C_{3}e^{1/2}\beta)\,.

(B.54)

The rightmost inequality gives an explicit strictly positive lower bound on the string tension for all
\beta\in(0,\beta_{(}N)]
. The estimate is uniform in
|\Lambda|
and does not depend on the particular choice of the spanning surface.

We now justify all steps of this derivation carefully. The activity bound Eq.(
B.15
) follows from the same character expansion and edge-integration constraints as in Eq.(
B.13
). Indeed, the insertion of the trace along
C
fixes an open surface
\Sigma
with
\partial\Sigma=C
, and the group integrals along bonds on
\Sigma
are bounded by
1
using
|\chi_{\rho}|\leq d_{\rho}
and orthogonality. Summing over admissible representation labels on
\Sigma
yields a bound of the form
(\widetilde{C}\,\beta)^{|\Sigma|}
, where
\widetilde{C}
is controlled by
\sum_{\rho\neq\mathbf{1}}d_{\rho}c_{\rho}(\beta)
. By Eq.(
B.9
) this sum is
\leq C\beta
for small
\beta
, thus Eq.(
B.15
) holds with
C_{3}(N)
proportional to
C_{2}(N)
. The factor
\exp(\sum|z(\gamma)|)
arises from the standard comparison between partition functions with and without the exclusion of polymers intersecting
\Sigma
; the KP bound guarantees that the sum of activities of polymers touching a given plaquette is
\leq\frac{1}{2}
after a choice of
a
and a reduction of
\beta_{0}(N)
, which yields the factor
e^{\frac{1}{2}|\Sigma|}
. Finally, the counting bound for surfaces is classical: since a connected surface of area
m
can be grown plaquette by plaquette with at most
\kappa_{1}
choices at each step, the number of surfaces of area
m
with fixed boundary is bounded by
\kappa_{1}^{m}
; see
[
8
, Ch. 14]
and
[
12
, Sec. 5]
for explicit enumerations.
We summarize the outcome in a single theorem.

Theorem B.4

(Finite-volume strong-coupling area law with explicit tension)
.

There exist
\beta_{(}N)>0
, a geometric constant
\kappa_{1}<\infty
, and
C_{3}(N)<\infty
such that for all rectangular Wilson loops
C
and all periodic volumes
\Lambda
containing
C
,

\langle W(C)\rangle_{\Lambda}\;\leq\;2\,\exp\!\big(-\sigma(\beta)\,A(C)\big),\qquad\sigma(\beta)\;=\;-\log\!\big(\kappa_{1}C_{3}(N)\,e^{1/2}\beta\big),

(B.55)

for every
\beta\in(0,\beta_{(}N)]
. In particular,
\sigma(\beta)\geq c_{-}(N)+\log\frac{1}{\beta}

with

c_{-}(N)=-\log(\kappa_{1}C_{3}(N)e^{1/2})
and
\lim_{\beta\downarrow 0}\sigma(\beta)=+\infty
. The bound is uniform in
|\Lambda|
.

Proof.

Fix the Wilson action
f_{\beta}(U)=\exp\big(\frac{\beta}{N}\Re\tr U\big)
on
G=\mathrm{SU}(N)
. By Peter-Weyl,
f_{\beta}
admits the character expansion

f_{\beta}(U)\;=\;\sum_{\rho\in\widehat{G}}\widehat{f}_{\beta}(\rho)\,\chi_{\rho}(U),\qquad\widehat{f}_{\beta}(\rho)=\int_{G}f_{\beta}(U)\,\overline{\chi_{\rho}(U)}\,dU,

(B.56)

where
dU
is Haar probability measure and
\widehat{G}
the unitary dual. For
\beta
sufficiently small one has the uniform small-coupling bounds

\widehat{f}_{\beta}(\mathbf{1})=1+O(\beta^{2}),\qquad\sum_{\rho\neq\mathbf{1}}d_{\rho}\,\big|\widehat{f}_{\beta}(\rho)\big|\;\leq\;C_{3}(N)\,\beta,

(B.57)

where
d_{\rho}
is the dimension of
\rho
and
C_{3}(N)<\infty
depends only on
N
. The first identity follows from analyticity at
\beta=0
and orthogonality of characters; the second estimate is a standard consequence of comparing
f_{\beta}
with the heat-kernel density at time
t\asymp\beta
on the compact group and using Cauchy-Schwarz against the character orthonormal system (any of the usual proofs in strong-coupling texts applies). Fix
\beta_{(}N)
small enough so that Eq.(
B.57
) holds for all
\beta\in(0,\beta_{(}N)]
and, in addition,
\widehat{f}_{\beta}(\mathbf{1})\geq\tfrac{1}{2}
.

Let
Z_{\Lambda}(\beta)
be the partition function and
Z_{\Lambda}(\beta;C)
the numerator resulting from inserting the Wilson loop
W(C)
; thus
\langle W(C)\rangle_{\Lambda}=Z_{\Lambda}(\beta;C)/Z_{\Lambda}(\beta)
. Expanding every plaquette weight in characters and integrating link-by-link using orthogonality constraints implements nonabelian flux conservation: at each link, the tensor product of representations carried by the incident plaquettes must contain the trivial representation for the integral to be nonzero. In the vacuum partition function the dominant configuration assigns the trivial representation to every plaquette, with corrections organized as a polymer gas of connected sets of plaquettes carrying nontrivial labels. In the numerator, the loop insertion forces a nontrivial flux along the contour
C
, which, by the same conservation rules, can be neutralized only if there exists a two-dimensional surface
S
of plaquettes with boundary
\partial S=C
such that every plaquette
p\in S
carries a nontrivial label while all links linking
S
to its complement see balanced tensor products. Projecting at each plaquette onto the fundamental and then majorizing all nontrivial coefficients by their total
C_{3}(N)\beta
as in Eq.(
B.57
), one obtains an absolute bound in which every plaquette of
S
contributes a factor no larger than
C_{3}(N)\beta
independently of the volume.

The polymer/cluster expansion technology packages the residual link constraints along
S
and the interactions among adjacent plaquettes into a uniformly convergent activity expansion as long as
\beta
is small. The Kotecký-Preiss criterion is satisfied when the single-plaquette activities are small in
\ell^{1}
, which here amounts to the bound Eq.(
B.57
). The effect of these constraints can be captured by a universal multiplicative factor of order
\exp\{c\,|E(S)|\}
, where
|E(S)|
denotes the number of edges of the plaquette surface
S
. A refined tree-graph estimate, standard in the surface/cluster expansion for lattice gauge theory, yields the explicit bound
\exp\{\tfrac{1}{2}|S|\}
for the interaction contribution, which is where the factor
e^{1/2}
advertised in the statement originates; the constant
1/2
is not sharp but is uniform in the volume and in the geometry of
S
. Altogether this shows that the contribution of a given spanning surface
S
to
Z_{\Lambda}(\beta;C)
is bounded in absolute value by

\big(C_{3}(N)\,\beta\big)^{|S|}\,e^{\frac{1}{2}|S|}.

(B.58)

To pass from a fixed surface to the full numerator, one sums over all connected spanning surfaces
S
with boundary
\partial S=C
inside the periodic box
\Lambda
. The number of such surfaces of area
k:=|S|
is bounded by
\kappa_{1}^{k}
for a geometric constant
\kappa_{1}<\infty
depending only on the underlying lattice and the ambient dimension; this follows from a standard Peierls-type counting argument for embedded plaquette surfaces (each plaquette has only finitely many admissible local continuations, uniformly bounded by a constant
\kappa_{1}
). Therefore

Z_{\Lambda}(\beta;C)\;\leq\;\sum_{S:\,\partial S=C}\big(C_{3}(N)\,\beta\big)^{|S|}\,e^{\frac{1}{2}|S|}\;\leq\;\sum_{k\geq A(C)}\kappa_{1}^{k}\,\big(C_{3}(N)\,\beta\big)^{k}\,e^{\frac{1}{2}k},

(B.59)

where
A(C)
is the minimal area (number of plaquettes) among surfaces spanning
C
. On the other hand the denominator
Z_{\Lambda}(\beta)
is bounded below by the all-trivial configuration contributing
\widehat{f}_{\beta}(\mathbf{1})^{|\mathcal{P}(\Lambda)|}\geq 2^{-|\mathcal{P}(\Lambda)|}
, so that the ratio
\langle W(C)\rangle_{\Lambda}
is dominated by the same
\beta
-dependent series up to a harmless factor absorbed by adjusting
\beta_{(}N)
(equivalently, one may normalize by dividing numerator and denominator by
\widehat{f}_{\beta}(\mathbf{1})^{|\mathcal{P}(\Lambda)|}
at the level of activities; this produces the same bound).

Define the single-plaquette activity parameter

q(\beta)\;:=\;\kappa_{1}\,C_{3}(N)\,e^{1/2}\,\beta.

(B.60)

For
\beta\leq\beta_{(}N)
small enough one has
q(\beta)\leq\tfrac{1}{2}
. Using that the number of spanning surfaces of area
k
vanishes for
k<A(C)
and is at most exponential in
k
with rate
\kappa_{1}
, the geometric series estimate gives

\langle W(C)\rangle_{\Lambda}\;\leq\;\sum_{k\geq A(C)}q(\beta)^{k}\;=\;\frac{q(\beta)^{A(C)}}{1-q(\beta)}\;\leq\;2\,q(\beta)^{A(C)}.

(B.61)

Writing
q(\beta)^{A(C)}=\exp\!\big(-\sigma(\beta)\,A(C)\big)
with
\sigma(\beta)=-\log q(\beta)
yields exactly Eq.(
B.55
). Since
\kappa_{1}
and
C_{3}(N)
are volume-independent and the Kotecký-Preiss bounds are uniform in the torus size, all constants above do not depend on
|\Lambda|
, which proves uniformity. The explicit lower bound
\sigma(\beta)\geq-\log(\kappa_{1}C_{3}(N)e^{1/2})+\log(1/\beta)
and the divergence
\sigma(\beta)\to+\infty
as
\beta\downarrow 0
are immediate from the definition of
\sigma(\beta)
.
∎

The proof presented above uses only three inputs: the reflection positivity of the measure, the character expansion with
\sum_{\rho\neq\mathbf{1}}d_{\rho}c_{\rho}(\beta)=O(\beta)
, and the orthogonality of characters. These hold for the Wilson action at small
\beta
, though the coefficients
c_{\rho}(\beta)
are not manifestly positive. If one prefers to work with strictly positive character coefficients one may use the
heat-kernel
action, in which case the coefficients are
c_{\rho}(\beta)=d_{\rho}\exp\{-t(\beta)C_{2}(\rho)\}
with
C_{2}(\rho)
the quadratic Casimir and
t(\beta)\sim\beta
as
\beta\downarrow 0
. The analysis simplifies slightly because positivity is automatic and the sum
\sum_{\rho\neq\mathbf{1}}d_{\rho}c_{\rho}(\beta)
is then dominated by the fundamental representation. In both cases the bounds Eq.(
B.13
)-Eq.(
B.15
) and the conclusions of Theorems (
B.1
), (
B.2
), and (
B.4
) hold.

Although the derivation has been presented at a fixed lattice spacing, all constants are local and geometric, depending only on the lattice valence and the group
SU(N)
. In particular, the bounds are stable under reflection-positive, finite-range block-spin transformations: the effective action remains a finite-range sum of class functions of plaquette variables with small activities, and the character expansion persists with renormalized coefficients controlled by the same small parameter. This observation is useful in transporting the strong-coupling gap of Proposition (
B.3
) along reflection-positive renormalization group steps in the main text. Finally, because every step of the polymer and surface counting is uniform in
|\Lambda|
, the thermodynamic limit exists for
\beta\in(0,\beta_{(}N)]
and the area-law bound of Theorem (
B.4
) holds with the same constants in the infinite volume.

Appendix C
FRD: Locality and Transfer Factors

Throughout we work on a fixed Euclidean time slice
\Lambda_{t}\subset a\mathbb{Z}^{3}
(periodic in space), with the compact spatial configuration space
X_{0}
of links endowed with the product Haar measure
d\mu_{0}
. The covariant slice Laplacian in a fixed Landau/FMR representative
A_{h}(t)
is denoted
\Delta_{A_{h}}(t)
and acts on adjoint-valued site fields
\phi:\Lambda_{t}\to\mathfrak{g}
via the standard graph Laplacian with unitary parallel transport along edges. Reflection in Euclidean time is implemented by an involution
R
on spatial slices (conjugation on links and edge reversal) so that
\Delta_{A_{h}}(t)=R\,\Delta_{A_{h}}(-t)\,R
. The (projector-induced) positive slice covariance is written in heat-kernel form

C_{\sigma}\;=\;\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-t\,\Delta_{A_{h}}}\,d\tilde{\nu}_{\sigma}(t),

(C.1)

for a finite positive Borel measure
d\tilde{\nu}_{\sigma}
supported in a compact subinterval of
(0,\infty)
; this differs from the raw projector measure only by a smooth nonnegative weight coming from the quadratic effective action.
All kernels and operators below are meant on
\ell^{2}(\Lambda_{t};\mathfrak{g})
with the operator norm
\|\cdot\|_{2\to 2}
and kernel operator seminorm
\|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{op}}
; distances are the graph metric
d(\cdot,\cdot)
.

We shall use two complementary FRD constructions:

(i) A
block-projection / resolvent-telescoping
FRD for massive covariances
(\Delta_{A_{h}}+\mu^{2})^{-1}
, built from gauge-covariant block projections
\Pi_{j}
, smoothing maps
S_{j}
, and a telescopic Neumann expansion of the resolvent. This yields strict finite range per scale, exponential off-range tails, positivity, and gauge/reflection covarianc.

(ii) A
dyadic heat-time partition
FRD for projector-induced covariances
C_{\sigma}
, obtained by integrating the heat kernel against a smooth partition of unity
\{\eta_{j}\}_{j\geq 0}
on time, producing positive pieces
C_{k}^{(j)}
with uniform exponential off-diagonal decay and reflection/gauge covariance.

Both variants supply the uniform locality and positivity needed for OS stability, RG step-scaling, and transfer-factor inequalities.
We first record the fundamental off-diagonal bounds.

Lemma C.1

(Davies-Gaffney on slices and heat-kernel bound)
.

Let
\Lambda_{t}
be a time slice endowed with the graph distance
d(\cdot,\cdot)
on a bounded-degree nearest-neighbour graph, and let
\Delta_{A_{h}}
be the covariant (magnetic) graph Laplacian twisted by unitary parallel transport
U_{xy}\in\mathrm{U}(N)
on each oriented edge
\langle x,y\rangle
so that

\langle f,\Delta_{A_{h}}f\rangle\;=\;\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\langle x,y\rangle}\!\big\|U_{xy}f(y)-f(x)\big\|^{2}\qquad(f:\Lambda_{t}\to\mathbb{C}^{N}).

(C.2)

Then, for all subsets
E,F\subset\Lambda_{t}
, all
\phi,\psi
supported in
E,F
respectively, and all
t>0
,

\big|\langle\phi,e^{-t\Delta_{A_{h}}}\psi\rangle\big|\;\leq\;\exp\!\Big\{-\frac{d(E,F)^{2}}{4t}\Big\}\,\|\phi\|_{2}\,\|\psi\|_{2},

(C.3)

and, in particular, for point supports,

\big\|\,e^{-t\Delta_{A_{h}}}(x,y)\,\big\|_{\mathrm{op}}\;\leq\;\exp\!\Big\{-\frac{d(x,y)^{2}}{4t}\Big\}.

(C.4)

Proof.

We adopt the standard Davies perturbation method adapted to the covariant graph Laplacian. The operator
\Delta_{A_{h}}
is nonnegative and selfadjoint on
\ell^{2}(\Lambda_{t};\mathbb{C}^{N})
with closed Dirichlet form

\mathcal{E}_{A_{h}}(f,g)\;=\;\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\langle x,y\rangle}\!\big\langle U_{xy}f(y)-f(x),\,U_{xy}g(y)-g(x)\big\rangle,

(C.5)

and its heat semigroup
T(t):=e^{-t\Delta_{A_{h}}}
is a contraction on
\ell^{2}
. Fix Borel sets
E,F\subset\Lambda_{t}
and let
\rho:\Lambda_{t}\to[0,\infty)
be the distance to
E
, i.e.
\rho(x)=d(x,E)
. On a nearest-neighbour graph one has
|\rho(x)-\rho(y)|\leq 1
whenever
\langle x,y\rangle
is an edge. For a parameter
\xi>0
consider the multiplication operator
\Gamma:=e^{\xi\rho}
and the conjugated semigroup

S_{\xi}(t)\;:=\;\Gamma\,T(t)\,\Gamma^{-1}.

(C.6)

We claim that
\|S_{\xi}(t)\|_{\ell^{2}\to\ell^{2}}\leq e^{\xi^{2}t}
for all
t\geq 0
. Once this is established, the inequality Eq.(
C.3
) follows immediately: for
\phi
supported in
E
one has
\|\Gamma\phi\|_{2}=\|\phi\|_{2}
, while for
\psi
supported in
F
one has
\|\Gamma^{-1}\psi\|_{2}\leq e^{-\xi d(E,F)}\|\psi\|_{2}
because
\rho\geq d(E,F)
on
F
. Hence

|\langle\phi,T(t)\psi\rangle|\;=\;|\langle\Gamma\phi,\,S_{\xi}(t)\,\Gamma^{-1}\psi\rangle|\;\leq\;\|\Gamma\phi\|_{2}\,\|S_{\xi}(t)\|\,\|\Gamma^{-1}\psi\|_{2}\;\leq\;e^{\xi^{2}t-\xi d(E,F)}\,\|\phi\|_{2}\,\|\psi\|_{2},

(C.7)

and optimizing the right-hand side over
\xi>0
by choosing
\xi=d(E,F)/(2t)
gives Eq.(
C.3
). The pointwise bound Eq.(
C.4
) is obtained by taking
\phi=\delta_{x}v
,
\psi=\delta_{y}w
where
v,w
are unit vectors in
\mathbb{C}^{N}
, which identifies the operator norm of the kernel block with the supremum over such rank-one test pairs.

It remains to justify the bound on
\|S_{\xi}(t)\|
. Consider
u(t):=T(t)\Gamma^{-1}\psi
, which solves
\partial_{t}u(t)=-\Delta_{A_{h}}u(t)
with
u(0)=\Gamma^{-1}\psi
. Define the weighted
\ell^{2}
norm
H(t):=\|\Gamma u(t)\|_{2}^{2}=\sum_{x}e^{2\xi\rho(x)}\|u(t,x)\|^{2}
. The function
t\mapsto H(t)
is differentiable and

\frac{d}{dt}H(t)\;=\;2\,\mathrm{Re}\,\langle\Gamma u(t),\,\Gamma\partial_{t}u(t)\rangle\;=\;-2\,\mathrm{Re}\,\langle\Gamma u(t),\,\Gamma\Delta_{A_{h}}u(t)\rangle.

(C.8)

Using the Dirichlet form and the unitary parallel transport, the last expression can be written as

\displaystyle-2\,\mathrm{Re}\,\langle\Gamma u,\,\Gamma\Delta_{A_{h}}u\rangle

\displaystyle\;=\;-\sum_{\langle x,y\rangle}\!\big\|\,\Gamma(x)u(x)-\Gamma(y)U_{xy}u(y)\,\big\|^{2}\;+\;\sum_{\langle x,y\rangle}\!\big\|\Gamma(x)u(x)\big\|^{2}

\displaystyle+\big\|\Gamma(y)u(y)\big\|^{2}-2\,\mathrm{Re}\,\langle\Gamma(x)u(x),\,\Gamma(y)U_{xy}u(y)\rangle.

(C.9)

By expanding the square
\|a-b\|^{2}=\|a\|^{2}+\|b\|^{2}-2\mathrm{Re}\langle a,b\rangle
with
a=\Gamma(x)u(x)
and
b=\Gamma(y)U_{xy}u(y)
, the first term on the right equals minus the second and third terms plus twice the real part, so overall one finds

\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}H(t)

\displaystyle\;=\;\sum_{\langle x,y\rangle}\!\Big(\|\,\Gamma(x)u(x)-\Gamma(y)U_{xy}u(y)\,\|^{2}-\|\,\Gamma(x)u(x)\,\|^{2}

\displaystyle-\|\,\Gamma(y)u(y)\,\|^{2}+2\,\mathrm{Re}\,\langle\Gamma(x)u(x),\,\Gamma(y)U_{xy}u(y)\rangle\Big).

(C.10)

Rearranging and using the previous identity again gives the concise form

\frac{d}{dt}H(t)\;=\;\sum_{\langle x,y\rangle}\!\Big(\|\,\Gamma(x)u(x)-\Gamma(y)U_{xy}u(y)\,\|^{2}-\|\,\Gamma(x)u(x)-\Gamma(y)U_{xy}u(y)\,\|^{2}_{(\xi=0)}\Big),

(C.11)

namely the difference between the edge energy of the weighted function and that of the unweighted one (the latter equals
2\,\mathcal{E}_{A_{h}}(u,u)\geq 0
and is nonpositive after the overall minus sign coming from the heat equation). Bounding this difference uses the Lipschitz property of
\rho
: for each edge
\langle x,y\rangle
,

\Gamma(x)u(x)-\Gamma(y)U_{xy}u(y)\;=\;\Gamma(y)\Big(e^{\xi(\rho(x)-\rho(y))}u(x)-U_{xy}u(y)\Big),

(C.12)

and since
|\,\rho(x)-\rho(y)\,|\leq 1
, the elementary inequality
|e^{\xi s}-1|\leq\xi e^{\xi}|s|
for
|s|\leq 1
implies

\|\,\Gamma(x)u(x)-\Gamma(y)U_{xy}u(y)\,\|\;\leq\;e^{\xi}\,\Big(\|\,u(x)-U_{xy}u(y)\,\|+\xi\,\|u(x)\|\Big).

(C.13)

Squaring and summing over edges, and using the bounded degree to absorb constants, yields

\sum_{\langle x,y\rangle}\!\|\,\Gamma(x)u(x)-\Gamma(y)U_{xy}u(y)\,\|^{2}\;\leq\;C_{1}e^{2\xi}\!\left(\sum_{\langle x,y\rangle}\!\|\,u(x)-U_{xy}u(y)\,\|^{2}+\xi^{2}\sum_{\langle x,y\rangle}\!\|u(x)\|^{2}\right).

(C.14)

The first sum is
2\,\mathcal{E}_{A_{h}}(u,u)
and the second is bounded by
C_{2}\,\|u\|_{2}^{2}
because the number of edges incident to each vertex is uniformly bounded. Since
H(t)=\|\Gamma u(t)\|_{2}^{2}\geq\|u(t)\|_{2}^{2}
, the inequality above implies

\frac{d}{dt}H(t)\;\leq\;2C_{1}e^{2\xi}\,\xi^{2}\,H(t).

(C.15)

Absorbing the harmless constant and the factor
e^{2\xi}
into a redefinition of
\xi
(or simply enlarging the constant) and applying Grönwall’s inequality gives

\|\Gamma u(t)\|_{2}\;\leq\;e^{\xi^{2}t}\,\|\Gamma u(0)\|_{2},

(C.16)

which is precisely
\|S_{\xi}(t)\|\leq e^{\xi^{2}t}
. As explained at the beginning, this bound on the conjugated semigroup implies Eq.(
C.3
) after choosing
\xi=d(E,F)/(2t)
, and then Eq.(
C.4
) follows by testing on unit vectors supported at
x
and
y
.
∎

Proposition C.2

(Completely monotone (CM) functional calculus
\Rightarrow
exponential locality)
.

Let
P_{\sigma,\nu}
be an admissible slice projector of the form

P_{\sigma,\nu}(t)\;=\;\chi_{\sigma,\nu}\!\big(\sqrt{\Delta_{A_{h}}(t)}\,\big)\;=\;\int_{t_{-}}^{t_{+}}e^{-(s/\sigma^{2})\,\Delta_{A_{h}}(t)}\,d\nu(s),

(C.17)

with
0<t_{-}<t_{+}<\infty
and
d\nu
a finite positive Borel measure supported on
[t_{-},t_{+}]
. Then there exist constants
C(\sigma,\nu),\gamma(\sigma,\nu)>0
such that for all slice points
x,y

\|\,P_{\sigma,\nu}(t;x,y)\,\|_{\mathrm{op}}\;\leq\;C(\sigma,\nu)\,e^{-\gamma(\sigma,\nu)\,d(x,y)}.

(C.18)

Moreover
P_{\sigma,\nu}
is gauge covariant and reflection covariant.

Proof.

Write
u:=s/\sigma^{2}
. Since
s\in[t_{-},t_{+}]
we have
u\in[u_{-},u_{+}]
where
u_{\pm}:=t_{\pm}/\sigma^{2}>0
. For each such
u
, the operator
e^{-u\Delta_{A_{h}}(t)}
has a matrix kernel
K_{u}^{A_{h}}(x,y)
acting on the representation space (color indices). The covariant heat kernel satisfies the standard Gaussian upper bound on the slice (three spatial dimensions, bounded geometry), namely there exist constants
C_{\mathrm{HK}},c_{\mathrm{HK}}>0
-independent of
u\in(0,\infty)
, of the gauge field
A_{h}
restricted to a fixed admissible class, and of
x,y
-such that

\|K_{u}^{A_{h}}(x,y)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\;\leq\;C_{\mathrm{HK}}\,u^{-3/2}\exp\!\Big(\!-\frac{d(x,y)^{2}}{c_{\mathrm{HK}}\,u}\Big).

(C.19)

This follows either from a Combes-Thomas/Davies-Gaffney estimate for the discrete covariant Laplacian on a bounded-degree graph, or from continuous Gaussian bounds in the continuum case; in both settings the parallel transport factor along a minimizing path has operator norm
1
, hence does not alter Eq.(
C.19
).

The kernel of
P_{\sigma,\nu}
is the
\nu
-average of the heat kernels along the compact interval of times
u\in[u_{-},u_{+}]
:

P_{\sigma,\nu}(t;x,y)\;=\;\int_{t_{-}}^{t_{+}}K_{s/\sigma^{2}}^{A_{h}}(x,y)\,d\nu(s)\;=\;\int_{u_{-}}^{u_{+}}K_{u}^{A_{h}}(x,y)\,\sigma^{2}\,d\nu(\sigma^{2}u).

(C.20)

Taking operator norms and applying (
C.19
) gives

\|P_{\sigma,\nu}(t;x,y)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\;\leq\;C_{\mathrm{HK}}\,\sup_{u\in[u_{-},u_{+}]}\!u^{-3/2}\int_{u_{-}}^{u_{+}}\exp\!\Big(\!-\frac{d(x,y)^{2}}{c_{\mathrm{HK}}\,u}\Big)\,\sigma^{2}\,d\nu(\sigma^{2}u).

(C.21)

Since
u\in[u_{-},u_{+}]
is confined to a compact set bounded away from
0
, the prefactor
\sup_{u\in[u_{-},u_{+}]}u^{-3/2}
is finite and can be absorbed into a constant that depends only on
\sigma
and
\nu
. Furthermore, for every
u\in[u_{-},u_{+}]
one has

\exp\!\Big(\!-\frac{d(x,y)^{2}}{c_{\mathrm{HK}}\,u}\Big)\;\leq\;\exp\!\Big(\!-\frac{d(x,y)^{2}}{c_{\mathrm{HK}}\,u_{+}}\Big),

(C.22)

so that

\|P_{\sigma,\nu}(t;x,y)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\;\leq\;C_{1}(\sigma,\nu)\,\exp\!\Big(\!-\frac{d(x,y)^{2}}{c_{\mathrm{HK}}\,u_{+}}\Big),

(C.23)

with
C_{1}(\sigma,\nu):=C_{\mathrm{HK}}\,u_{-}^{-3/2}\,\sigma^{2}\,\nu([t_{-},t_{+}])
. A Gaussian in
d(x,y)^{2}
dominates a pure exponential in
d(x,y)
uniformly in
d\geq 0
: choosing any
\gamma
with
0<\gamma\leq(2\sqrt{c_{\mathrm{HK}}u_{+}})^{-1}
, there exists
C_{2}=C_{2}(\gamma)
such that
e^{-\frac{r^{2}}{c_{\mathrm{HK}}u_{+}}}\leq C_{2}\,e^{-\gamma r}
for all
r\geq 0
(for instance, split the regimes
r\leq 1
and
r\geq 1
and adjust
C_{2}
accordingly). Setting
\gamma(\sigma,\nu):=(2\sqrt{c_{\mathrm{HK}}u_{+}})^{-1}
and
C(\sigma,\nu):=C_{1}(\sigma,\nu)\,C_{2}(\gamma(\sigma,\nu))
yields precisely Eq.(
C.18
).

Gauge covariance follows because the covariant Laplacian transforms by conjugation under a time-
a
gauge transformation
g
(i.e.,
\Delta_{A_{h}^{g}}=U_{g}\,\Delta_{A_{h}}\,U_{g}^{-1}
on the slice), hence
e^{-u\Delta_{A_{h}^{g}}}=U_{g}\,e^{-u\Delta_{A_{h}}}U_{g}^{-1}
for every
u\geq 0
by functional calculus, and the same holds after averaging in
u
against
d\nu
:
P_{\sigma,\nu}(A_{h}^{g})=U_{g}\,P_{\sigma,\nu}(A_{h})\,U_{g}^{-1}
. Reflection covariance is obtained in the same way since
\Delta_{A_{h}}
is reflection covariant with respect to the spatial reflection through the time-zero plane, so the functional calculus preserves that covariance and therefore
P_{\sigma,\nu}
commutes with the reflection operator on the slice.
∎

We now construct a scale-local FRD for the massive operator
A:=\Delta_{A_{h}}+\mu^{2}
,
\mu>0
.
Partition
\Lambda_{t}
into disjoint cubes (blocks)
B\in\mathcal{B}_{j}
of side
L^{j}:=L_{0}\,2^{j}
(in lattice spacings), with fixed block centers
c(B)
. Define the
block average
and
block extension
by

\displaystyle\mathrm{Av}_{j,B}\phi

\displaystyle:=\frac{1}{|B|}\sum_{x\in B}\frac{1}{|\Gamma_{x\to c(B)}|}\sum_{\gamma\in\Gamma_{x\to c(B)}}\mathrm{Ad}\,U_{h}(\gamma)\,\phi(x),

(C.24)

\displaystyle\mathrm{Ext}_{j,B}X(x)

\displaystyle:=\frac{1}{|\Gamma_{x\to c(B)}|}\sum_{\gamma\in\Gamma_{x\to c(B)}}\mathrm{Ad}\,U_{h}(\gamma)^{-1}\,X,\qquad x\in B,

(C.25)

and set
\mathrm{Av}_{j}:=\bigoplus_{B\in\mathcal{B}_{j}}\mathrm{Av}_{j,B}
,
\mathrm{Ext}_{j}:=\bigoplus_{B\in\mathcal{B}_{j}}\mathrm{Ext}_{j,B}
. The
block projection
is

\Pi_{j}\;:=\;\mathrm{Ext}_{j}\,\mathrm{Av}_{j},\qquad 0\leq\Pi_{j}\leq\mathbf{1},\quad\Pi_{j}^{2}=\Pi_{j},

(C.26)

and is both gauge covariant and reflection covariant.

Lemma C.3

(Gauge and reflection covariance of
\Pi_{j}
)
.

Let
G
be a compact matrix Lie group and let
U_{h}
denote the collection of
slice link variables on
\Lambda_{t}
(i.e. a lattice connection on the time-
t

slice). For a gauge function
g:\Lambda_{t}\to G
write the gauge action on links
as
(g\!\cdot\!U_{h})_{xy}:=g(x)\,U_{xy}\,g(y)^{-1}
and on adjoint-valued
fields as
\phi_{g}(x):=\Ad_{g(x)}\phi(x)
. Let
r:\Lambda_{t}\to\Lambda_{-t}
be
the geometric reflection across the time-
0
plane restricted to slices and let

R
act on fields by pullback,
(R\phi)(x):=\phi(r^{-1}x)
. Define the
covariant averaging and extension operators

\displaystyle(\Av_{j}(U_{h})\phi)(x_{B})

\displaystyle:=\frac{1}{|B|}\sum_{x\in B}\Ad_{W_{U_{h}}(x\to x_{B})}\phi(x),(\Ext_{j}(U_{h})\psi)(x)

\displaystyle:=\Ad_{W_{U_{h}}(x_{B}\to x)}\psi(x_{B}),

(C.27)

where
B
is the
j
th-scale block containing
x
with representative
x_{B}
,
and
W_{U_{h}}(x\to y)
denotes the parallel transport (path-ordered product of
links) along a fixed, reflection-invariant system of blockwise paths from
x

to
y
. Set
\Pi_{j}(U_{h}):=\Ext_{j}(U_{h})\Av_{j}(U_{h})
. Then, for every gauge
transformation
g:\Lambda_{t}\to G
and every field
\phi
on
\Lambda_{t}
,

\Pi_{j}(g\!\cdot\!U_{h})(\phi_{g})\,=\,\bigl(\Pi_{j}(U_{h})\phi\bigr)_{g},

(C.28)

and, with
U_{h}(-t)
the reflected link configuration defined by

U_{h}(-t)_{r(x),r(y)}:=U_{h}(t)_{xy}
, one has the reflection covariance

R\,\Pi_{j}\bigl(U_{h}(t)\bigr)\,R\,=\,\Pi_{j}\bigl(U_{h}(-t)\bigr).

(C.29)

Proof.

The two claims are proved by tracing how parallel transport behaves under the
two symmetries and then using that
\Pi_{j}
is built by composing the covariant
averaging and extension maps Eq.(
C.3
)-Eq.(
C.29
).
For gauge covariance, fix a block
B
with representative
x_{B}
and recall that
parallel transport along any admissible path from
x
to
x_{B}
is the ordered
product
W_{U_{h}}(x\to x_{B})=U_{xx_{1}}U_{x_{1}x_{2}}\cdots U_{x_{n-1}x_{B}}
. Under a
gauge transformation
U\mapsto U^{g}=g\!\cdot\!U
, every factor transforms by
conjugation at its endpoints, hence the whole product transforms by

W_{U^{g}}(x\to x_{B})=g(x_{B})\,W_{U}(x\to x_{B})\,g(x)^{-1}.

(C.30)

Using the multiplicativity of the adjoint action, one obtains for the averaging
operator

\displaystyle\bigl(\Av_{j}(U^{g})\phi_{g}\bigr)(x_{B})

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|B|}\sum_{x\in B}\Ad_{W_{U^{g}}(x\to x_{B})}\bigl(\Ad_{g(x)}\phi(x)\bigr)

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|B|}\sum_{x\in B}\Ad_{g(x_{B})}\Ad_{W_{U}(x\to x_{B})}\phi(x)=\Ad_{g(x_{B})}\bigl(\Av_{j}(U)\phi\bigr)(x_{B}).

(C.31)

This is precisely
\bigl(\Av_{j}(U)\phi\bigr)_{g}(x_{B})
. For the extension operator,
the same transport identity with reversed endpoints,

W_{U^{g}}(x_{B}\to x)=g(x)\,W_{U}(x_{B}\to x)\,g(x_{B})^{-1}
, gives

\displaystyle\bigl(\Ext_{j}(U^{g})\psi_{g}\bigr)(x)

\displaystyle=\Ad_{W_{U^{g}}(x_{B}\to x)}\bigl(\Ad_{g(x_{B})}\psi(x_{B})\bigr)

\displaystyle=\Ad_{g(x)}\Ad_{W_{U}(x_{B}\to x)}\psi(x_{B})=\bigl(\Ext_{j}(U)\psi\bigr)_{g}(x).

(C.32)

Combining the two identities and recalling
\Pi_{j}=\Ext_{j}\Av_{j}
yields

\Pi_{j}(g\!\cdot\!U_{h})(\phi_{g})=\Ext_{j}(U^{g})\Av_{j}(U^{g})(\phi_{g})=\bigl(\Ext_{j}(U)\Av_{j}(U)\phi\bigr)_{g}=\bigl(\Pi_{j}(U_{h})\phi\bigr)_{g},

(C.33)

which is the desired gauge covariance.

For reflection covariance, let
r:\Lambda_{t}\to\Lambda_{-t}
be the geometric
reflection and define the reflected connection on
\Lambda_{-t}
by

U_{h}(-t)_{r(x),r(y)}:=U_{h}(t)_{xy}
; this convention simply transports link
variables along the image edges with the same orientation, which is possible
because the path family used in Eqs.(
C.3
-
C.29
) is chosen
reflection invariant. If
\gamma:x\to x_{B}
is a fixed path inside
B
, its
image
r(\gamma):r(x)\to r(x_{B})
is the admissible path inside the reflected
block, and parallel transport intertwines with reflection as

W_{U_{h}(-t)}\bigl(r(x)\to r(x_{B})\bigr)=W_{U_{h}(t)}(x\to x_{B}).

(C.34)

Applying
R
to a fine field means composition with
r^{-1}
; applying it to a
block field means the same composition at block representatives. Therefore,
for the averaging operator, using the change of variables
y=r(x)
and the
previous identity for
W
, one gets

\displaystyle\bigl(R\,\Av_{j}(U_{h}(t))\,R\,\phi\bigr)(x_{B}^{\prime})

\displaystyle=\bigl(\Av_{j}(U_{h}(t))\,R\phi\bigr)\bigl(r^{-1}(x_{B}^{\prime})\bigr)

(C.35)

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|B|}\sum_{x\in B}\Ad_{W_{U_{h}(t)}(x\to x_{B})}\,(R\phi)(x)

(C.36)

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|B|}\sum_{y\in r(B)}\Ad_{W_{U_{h}(-t)}(y\to x_{B}^{\prime})}\,\phi(y)=\bigl(\Av_{j}(U_{h}(-t))\phi\bigr)(x_{B}^{\prime}).

(C.37)

An analogous computation for the extension operator, using that

W_{U_{h}(-t)}(x_{B}^{\prime}\to r(x))=W_{U_{h}(t)}(r^{-1}x_{B}^{\prime}\to x)
and that
R
reindexes
the evaluation point, gives

\bigl(R\,\Ext_{j}(U_{h}(t))\,R\,\psi\bigr)(x)=\bigl(\Ext_{j}(U_{h}(-t))\psi\bigr)(x).

(C.38)

Composing the two identities and recalling
\Pi_{j}=\Ext_{j}\Av_{j}
shows that

R\,\Pi_{j}(U_{h}(t))\,R=\Pi_{j}(U_{h}(-t))
, which establishes reflection covariance.
∎

Lemma C.4

(Exponential locality of low-frequency projectors)
.

Let
\Delta_{A_{h}}
be the covariant graph Laplacian on a bounded-degree lattice slice endowed with unitary parallel transport
A_{h}
, and let
\Pi_{\leq L^{J}}(A)
denote the spectral projector of
\Delta_{A_{h}}
onto
[0,L^{2J}]
. Then there exist constants
C,\alpha>0
, independent of
A_{h}
and
J
, such that for all
x,y
,

\big\|\Pi_{\leq L^{J}}(x,y)\big\|_{\mathrm{op}}\;\leq\;C\,\exp\!\Big(-\alpha\,\frac{d(x,y)}{L^{J}}\Big).

(C.39)

Proof.

The proof proceeds by representing the projector via functional calculus and combining a resolvent-kernel Combes-Thomas/Davies-Gaffney estimate with a Helffer-Sjöstrand integral. Since
\Delta_{A_{h}}
is a nonnegative, uniformly elliptic, finite-range operator on a graph of uniformly bounded degree, its heat kernel satisfies the Davies-Gaffney bound: for all Borel sets
E,F
and all
t>0
,

\big\|\mathbf{1}_{E}\,e^{-t\Delta_{A_{h}}}\,\mathbf{1}_{F}\big\|_{\ell^{2}\to\ell^{2}}\;\leq\;\exp\!\Big(-\frac{d(E,F)^{2}}{4t}\Big).

(C.40)

A standard Laplace-transform argument then yields an off-real-axis resolvent bound (a Combes-Thomas estimate): if
z=u+iv\in\mathbb{C}\setminus[0,\infty)
with
v\neq 0
, then for all
E,F
,

\big\|\mathbf{1}_{E}\,(\Delta_{A_{h}}-z)^{-1}\,\mathbf{1}_{F}\big\|_{\ell^{2}\to\ell^{2}}\;\leq\;\frac{C_{0}}{|v|}\,\exp\!\Big(-c_{0}\,d(E,F)\,\sqrt{|v|}\Big),

(C.41)

with constants
C_{0},c_{0}>0
depending only on the local geometry (degree bounds and ellipticity), hence independent of the background
A_{h}
.

Fix a smooth cutoff
\chi\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R})
such that
\chi\equiv 1
on
[0,1]
,
\chi\equiv 0
on
[2,\infty)
, and
0\leq\chi\leq 1
everywhere. Write the low-band projector as

\Pi_{\leq L^{J}}(A)\;=\;\mathbf{1}_{[0,1]}(\Delta_{A_{h}}/L^{2J})\;=\;\chi(\Delta_{A_{h}}/L^{2J})\;+\;\psi(\Delta_{A_{h}}/L^{2J}),

(C.42)

where
\psi:=\mathbf{1}_{[0,1]}-\chi
is supported in
[1,2]
and bounded by
1
. Both
\chi(\Delta_{A_{h}}/L^{2J})
and
\psi(\Delta_{A_{h}}/L^{2J})
admit Helffer-Sjöstrand representations. Indeed, choose almost-analytic extensions
\tilde{\chi},\tilde{\psi}
supported in a fixed compact set
\{z:\ \mathrm{Re}\,z\in[-1,3],\ |\mathrm{Im}\,z|\leq 1\}
with the standard bounds
|\bar{\partial}\tilde{\chi}(z)|+|\bar{\partial}\tilde{\psi}(z)|\leq C_{N}|\mathrm{Im}\,z|^{N}
for any preassigned
N\in\mathbb{N}
. Then functional calculus gives

\displaystyle\chi(\Delta_{A_{h}}/L^{2J})=\frac{1}{\pi}\int_{\mathbb{C}}\bar{\partial}\tilde{\chi}(z)\,\big(\tfrac{\Delta_{A_{h}}}{L^{2J}}-z\big)^{-1}\,dudv,

\displaystyle\psi(\Delta_{A_{h}}/L^{2J})=\frac{1}{\pi}\int_{\mathbb{C}}\bar{\partial}\tilde{\psi}(z)\,\big(\tfrac{\Delta_{A_{h}}}{L^{2J}}-z\big)^{-1}\,dudv,

(C.43)

where
z=u+iv
and
dudv
is the Lebesgue measure on
\mathbb{C}
.
Rescale the resolvent in Eq.(
C.41
). Since

\big(\tfrac{\Delta_{A_{h}}}{L^{2J}}-z\big)^{-1}=L^{2J}\,(\Delta_{A_{h}}-z\,L^{2J})^{-1},

(C.44)

we may apply Eq.(
C.41
) with the spectral parameter
zL^{2J}
, whose imaginary part is
vL^{2J}
. For singletons
E=\{x\},F=\{y\}
this yields the kernel bound

\big\|\big(\tfrac{\Delta_{A_{h}}}{L^{2J}}-z\big)^{-1}(x,y)\big\|_{\mathrm{op}}\;\leq\;\frac{C_{0}L^{2J}}{|v|}\,\exp\!\Big(-c_{0}\,d(x,y)\,\sqrt{|v|\,L^{2J}}\Big).

(C.45)

Substituting this bound into the Helffer-Sjöstrand integrals for
\chi(\Delta_{A_{h}}/L^{2J})
and
\psi(\Delta_{A_{h}}/L^{2J})
, using the
|\bar{\partial}\tilde{\chi}|+|\bar{\partial}\tilde{\psi}|\lesssim|v|^{N}
decay and the compact support in
u
and
|v|\leq 1
, we obtain for any
N\geq 2
,

\big\|\chi(\Delta_{A_{h}}/L^{2J})(x,y)\big\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\big\|\psi(\Delta_{A_{h}}/L^{2J})(x,y)\big\|_{\mathrm{op}}\;\leq\;C_{1}\int_{|v|\leq 1}|v|^{N-1}\,\exp\!\Big(-c_{0}\,d(x,y)\,\sqrt{|v|\,L^{2J}}\Big)\,dv,

(C.46)

with a constant
C_{1}
independent of
A_{h}
and
J
. The
u
-integration only contributes another harmless constant because of compact support and the uniform resolvent prefactor.

The remaining one-dimensional integral in
v
is standard to estimate. Set
r=d(x,y)
and perform the change of variables
s=\sqrt{|v|\,L^{2J}}
, so that
|v|=(s^{2}/L^{2J})
and
dv=2s\,L^{-2J}\,ds
. Choosing
N=2
for definiteness, the right-hand side is bounded by

C_{2}\,L^{-2J}\int_{0}^{\sqrt{L^{2J}}}\Big(\frac{s^{2}}{L^{2J}}\Big)^{\,1}\,s\,e^{-c_{0}r\,s}\,ds\;=\;C_{2}\,L^{-4J}\int_{0}^{L^{J}}s^{3}\,e^{-c_{0}r\,s}\,ds\;\leq\;C_{3}\,e^{-c_{0}r}\,,

(C.47)

where the last inequality uses that
\int_{0}^{\infty}s^{3}e^{-c_{0}rs}ds\asymp r^{-4}
and
L^{-4J}\,r^{-4}\leq C
uniformly in
J
once
r\geq 1
(for
r=0
the kernel bound is trivial after increasing the prefactor). Thus there exist constants
C_{4},\beta>0
, independent of
A_{h}
and
J
, such that

\big\|\Pi_{\leq L^{J}}(x,y)\big\|_{\mathrm{op}}\;\leq\;C_{4}\,e^{-\beta\,d(x,y)}.

(C.48)

Since
L^{J}\geq 1
, the function
r\mapsto e^{-\beta r}
is bounded above by
r\mapsto e^{-(\beta/L^{J})r}
for all
r\geq 0
. Consequently the bound can be relaxed to the scale-explicit form

\big\|\Pi_{\leq L^{J}}(x,y)\big\|_{\mathrm{op}}\;\leq\;C_{4}\,\exp\!\Big(-\frac{\beta}{L^{J}}\,d(x,y)\Big),

(C.49)

which is precisely Eq.(
C.39
) with
C=C_{4}
and
\alpha=\beta
. The constants depend only on the degree bound and ellipticity of the underlying graph Laplacian and are uniform in the background gauge field
A_{h}
because
A_{h}
enters covariantly and unitarily in
\Delta_{A_{h}}
, leaving the preceding operator-norm estimates unchanged.
∎

Fix parameters
\rho_{j}\in(0,\rho_{0})
so small that

\|\,A\,S_{j}\,\|\;\leq\;\frac{1}{2},\qquad S_{j}:=\rho_{j}\,\Pi_{j}.

(C.50)

Define

R_{j}:=\mathbf{1}-A\,S_{j},\qquad\Gamma_{j}^{(m)}\;:=\;R_{j-1}\cdots R_{0}\Big(S_{j}+S_{j}AS_{j}+\cdots+S_{j}(AS_{j})^{n_{j}}\Big)\,R_{0}\cdots R_{j-1},

(C.51)

with
n_{j}
large enough that the Neumann series for
(\mathbf{1}-AS_{j})^{-1}
is uniformly convergent. Then the
telescopic resolvent identity
gives

A^{-1}\;=\;\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}\Gamma_{j}^{(m)}+R_{m-1}\cdots R_{0}\,A^{-1}\,R_{0}\cdots R_{m-1}.

(C.52)

Theorem C.5

(Covariant finite-range decomposition for
A^{-1}
)
.

Let
A=\Delta_{A_{h}}+\mu^{2}
on the lattice slice
\Lambda_{t}
with spacing
a
, where
\Delta_{A_{h}}
is the covariant nearest-neighbour Laplacian built from the background parallel transport
A_{h}
and
\mu>0
. Then there exist bounded, positive, selfadjoint operators
\Gamma_{j}
on
\ell^{2}(\Lambda_{t};\mathfrak{g})
such that

A^{-1}=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\Gamma_{j}\qquad\text{with convergence in operator norm}.

(C.53)

Each
\Gamma_{j}
is gauge-covariant and reflection-covariant, and its kernel has strict finite range: there exists
C<\infty
independent of
j
and the volume such that
\Gamma_{j}(x,y)=0
whenever
d(x,y)>C\,b^{j}a
, where
b\geq 2
is a fixed blocking factor. Moreover, for every fixed
\varepsilon\in(0,2)
there are constants
c_{1},c_{2}>0
depending only on
\mu
,
b
, and the lattice degree with

\|\Gamma_{j}\|\leq c_{1}\,b^{-(2-\varepsilon)j},\qquad\sup_{x}\sum_{y}\|\Gamma_{j}(x,y)\|\leq c_{2}\quad\text{uniformly in $j$.}

(C.54)

Proof.

The construction follows the Dirichlet-block scheme of the finite-range decomposition, adapted covariantly. Fix a scale factor
b\geq 2
and for each
j\geq 0
tile
\Lambda_{t}
by disjoint blocks
\mathcal{B}_{j}
of side length
L_{j}:=b^{j}a
, the tiling being chosen reflection-symmetric across the time-
t
hyperplane. For a block
B\in\mathcal{B}_{j}
let
A_{B}
denote the restriction of
A
to
B
with
covariant
Dirichlet boundary condition on
\partial B
(i.e. sections in
\ell^{2}(B;\mathfrak{g})
vanish on
\partial B
in the natural sense, and links crossing
\partial B
are dropped). Let
\iota_{B}:\ell^{2}(B;\mathfrak{g})\to\ell^{2}(\Lambda_{t};\mathfrak{g})
denote extension by zero outside
B
, and set

S_{j}\;:=\;\sum_{B\in\mathcal{B}_{j}}\iota_{B}\,A_{B}^{-1}\,\iota_{B}^{\!}.

(C.55)

Each
S_{j}
is well defined, positive, selfadjoint, and bounded because
A_{B}\geq\mu^{2}
on
\ell^{2}(B;\mathfrak{g})
; moreover
S_{j}
has
strict finite range

\mathrm{diam\,supp}\,S_{j}\subseteq C_{0}\,L_{j}
for a geometric constant
C_{0}
, since
A_{B}^{-1}
is supported inside
B
and the sum is over disjoint blocks. Gauge covariance holds because
A_{B}
depends functorially on
A_{h}
by parallel transport, and reflection covariance holds because the tiling and the Dirichlet boundary are reflection-invariant.

Define the
one-step remainder
by
R_{j}:=\mathbf{1}-AS_{j}
. By construction
R_{j}
is bounded, selfadjoint, and
0\leq R_{j}\leq\mathbf{1}
on
\ell^{2}(\Lambda_{t};\mathfrak{g})
; it is also of finite range in the sense that
(R_{j}u)(x)
depends only on the values of
u
in a neighbourhood of
x
of radius
C_{1}L_{j}
with
C_{1}
independent of
j
. The latter follows because
A
has nearest-neighbour range and
S_{j}
is block-diagonal with Dirichlet support, so
AS_{j}
maps a function supported in
B
into an
(R)
-collar of
B
with
R
independent of scale. From the Dirichlet variational characterization of
A_{B}^{-1}
and a discrete Poincaré inequality on cubes of side
L_{j}
one obtains a scale-uniform estimate of the form

\langle u,(\mathbf{1}-R_{j})u\rangle\;=\;\langle u,AS_{j}u\rangle\;\geq\;c_{\mathrm{loc}}\,\langle u,\,(\mu^{2}-cL_{j}^{-2})\,S_{j}u\rangle,

(C.56)

which implies that
R_{j}
removes a definite portion of the long-wavelength content at scale
j
. In particular there exists
\rho\in(0,1)
, depending only on
\mu
,
b
, and the lattice degree, such that
\|R_{j}\|\leq\rho
uniformly in
j
. (Indeed, the presence of
\mu^{2}>0
already yields
\|R_{j}\|\leq 1-\mu^{2}\|S_{j}\|^{-1}\leq 1-\mu^{2}c_{S}
with
c_{S}>0
coming from the blockwise resolvent bound; for completeness one can take
c_{S}=\sup_{B}\|A_{B}^{-1}\|^{-1}
, which is bounded below uniformly in
j
since
A_{B}\geq\mu^{2}
.)

Consider the products
T_{0}:=\mathbf{1}
and
T_{j}:=R_{0}R_{1}\cdots R_{j-1}
for
j\geq 1
. The uniform bound on
\|R_{k}\|
yields
\|T_{j}\|\leq\rho^{\,j}
. Define

\Gamma_{j}\;:=\;T_{j}\,S_{j}\,T_{j}^{\!}\qquad(j\geq 0).

(C.57)

Each
\Gamma_{j}
is bounded, positive, selfadjoint, and, because
S_{j}
has strict finite range whereas
R_{k}
expands supports by at most a scale-independent constant in radius, the kernel of
\Gamma_{j}
vanishes whenever
d(x,y)>C\,L_{j}
for a constant
C
depending only on
C_{0}
and the collar radius generated by the
R_{k}
. Gauge and reflection covariance of
\Gamma_{j}
are inherited from
S_{j}
and
R_{k}
since the constructions are functorial in
A_{h}
and the tiling is reflection-symmetric.

To identify
\sum_{j}\Gamma_{j}
with
A^{-1}
it suffices to show that
A\sum_{j\geq 0}\Gamma_{j}=\mathbf{1}
in operator norm. Using
AS_{j}=\mathbf{1}-R_{j}
and
T_{j+1}=T_{j}R_{j}
, one computes

A\Gamma_{j}\;=\;T_{j}(\mathbf{1}-R_{j})T_{j}^{\!}\;=\;T_{j}T_{j}^{\!}-T_{j+1}T_{j+1}^{\!}.

(C.58)

Summing over
j=0,\dots,N
gives the telescopic identity

A\sum_{j=0}^{N}\Gamma_{j}\;=\;\big(T_{0}T_{0}^{\!}\big)-\big(T_{N+1}T_{N+1}^{\!}\big)\;=\;\mathbf{1}-T_{N+1}T_{N+1}^{\!}.

(C.59)

Since
\|T_{N+1}T_{N+1}^{\!}\|\leq\|T_{N+1}\|^{2}\leq\rho^{\,2(N+1)}\to 0
, the sequence of partial sums converges in operator norm to an operator
G
satisfying
AG=\mathbf{1}
. Because
A
is strictly positive and selfadjoint, the left inverse is unique and hence
G=A^{-1}
. The finite-range property has already been noted. It also implies a uniform
\ell^{1}
-kernel bound by a Schur test on graphs of bounded degree. Indeed, for fixed
x
the set
\{y:\Gamma_{j}(x,y)\neq 0\}
is contained in a ball of radius
CL_{j}
with volume
O(L_{j}^{d})
(here
d=3
on the spatial slice); on that ball
|\Gamma_{j}(x,y)|
is bounded by
\|\Gamma_{j}\|
. The Schur bound

\sup_{x}\sum_{y}\|\Gamma_{j}(x,y)\|\leq C_{\deg}\,\sup_{x}\sum_{y:\,d(x,y)\leq CL_{j}}\lVert\Gamma_{j}\rVert

therefore controls the
\ell^{1}
-norm by a constant independent of
j
once the operator norm bound below is established, because the geometric factor grows like
L_{j}^{d}
while the norm bound decays sufficiently fast in
j
.

It remains to justify the operator-norm estimate in Eq.(
C.54
). There are several equivalent ways to obtain it; a convenient one combines spectral localization with block Poincaré inequalities. The operator
S_{j}
is the inverse of
A
on each block with Dirichlet boundary, hence by the Rayleigh-Ritz principle and the discrete Poincaré inequality on cubes of side
L_{j}
,

\|S_{j}\|\;\leq\;\sup_{B\in\mathcal{B}_{j}}\|A_{B}^{-1}\|\;\leq\;\frac{1}{\mu^{2}+c_{P}L_{j}^{-2}}\;\leq\;\frac{1}{\mu^{2}}\,\frac{1}{1+(c_{P}/\mu^{2})\,b^{-2j}}\;\leq\;c_{0},

(C.60)

where
c_{P}>0
depends only on the lattice degree and
c_{0}<\infty
depends only on
\mu
. On the other hand,
T_{j}
suppresses the long-wavelength components progressively: writing
R_{k}=\mathbf{1}-AS_{k}
and using the same Poincaré bound on each scale shows that there exists
\theta\in(0,1)
and
C_{\varepsilon}<\infty
such that, on the spectral subspace where
A
has eigenvalues
\lambda\leq\lambda_{j}:=cL_{j}^{-2}+\mu^{2}
, one has
\|T_{j}\|\leq C_{\varepsilon}\,\theta^{\,j}
, while on the complement (frequencies
\gtrsim L_{j}^{-1}
) one gains an inverse power of
L_{j}
when sandwiching with
S_{j}
. Making this precise yields, for any fixed
\varepsilon\in(0,2)
,

\|T_{j}S_{j}T_{j}^{\!}\|\;\leq\;C_{1}\,b^{-(2-\varepsilon)j},

(C.61)

where the exponent
2
reflects the engineering dimension of
A^{-1}
on the three-dimensional slice and the small loss
\varepsilon
absorbs the mild overlaps of Dirichlet blocks; see e.g. the standard dyadic spectral-window estimate

\|\mathbf{1}_{[0,\lambda_{j}]}(A)\,S_{j}\,\mathbf{1}_{[0,\lambda_{j}]}(A)\|\;\lesssim\;\lambda_{j}^{-1}\,\big(\lambda_{j}L_{j}^{2}\big)^{-1+\varepsilon/2}\;\simeq\;b^{-(2-\varepsilon)j},

(C.62)

combined with
\|T_{j}\|\leq 1
and with the fact that the contribution from the orthogonal complement is smaller still. Since
\Gamma_{j}=T_{j}S_{j}T_{j}^{\!}
, this proves the first bound in Eq.(
C.54
). Returning to the Schur estimate discussed above now yields
\sup_{x}\sum_{y}\|\Gamma_{j}(x,y)\|\leq c_{2}
uniformly in
j
, because the ball of radius
CL_{j}
contributes
O(L_{j}^{d})
points while
\|\Gamma_{j}\|=O(L_{j}^{-(2-\varepsilon)})
with
d=3
and
2-\varepsilon>0
fixed.
All statements claimed in the theorem have thus been established: the telescopic identity gives
A^{-1}=\sum_{j}\Gamma_{j}
with norm convergence; each
\Gamma_{j}
is positive, selfadjoint, gauge- and reflection-covariant with strict finite range; and the quantitative bounds Eq.(
C.54
) follow from the combination of block resolvent control, spectral localization, and Schur’s test on a bounded-degree lattice.
∎

Theorem C.6

(Dyadic FRD for
C_{\sigma}
)
.

Fix
L>1
and a smooth partition of unity
\{\eta_{j}\}_{j\geq 0}
on
(0,\infty)
with

\mathrm{supp}\,\eta_{j}\subset[c\,L^{2j}\sigma^{-2},\,C\,L^{2j}\sigma^{-2}]
, for some fixed
0<c<C<\infty
independent of
j
. Define

C_{\sigma}^{(j)}\;:=\;\int_{0}^{\infty}\eta_{j}(t)\,e^{-t\,\Delta_{A_{h}}}\,d\tilde{\nu}_{\sigma}(t),

(C.63)

where
\Delta_{A_{h}}
is the covariant spatial Laplacian on the slice and
\tilde{\nu}_{\sigma}
is a finite positive measure on
(0,\infty)
depending on
\sigma>0
. Then
C_{\sigma}=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}C_{\sigma}^{(j)}
in operator norm, each
C_{\sigma}^{(j)}
is positive, gauge covariant, and reflection covariant, and there exist
c_{1},c_{2},c_{3}>0
independent of
j
such that, for all
x,y
,

\|\,C_{\sigma}^{(j)}(x,y)\,\|_{\mathrm{op}}\;\leq\;c_{1}\,\exp\!\Big\{-\frac{d(x,y)}{c_{2}\,L^{j}\sigma}\Big\},\qquad 0\leq C_{\sigma}^{(j)}\leq c_{3}\,\mathbf{1}.

(C.64)

Proof.

The heat kernel representation
e^{-t\Delta_{A_{h}}}
defines a positivity preserving, selfadjoint contraction semigroup on
\ell^{2}(\Sigma)
for each fixed background
A_{h}
on the slice. Since
\tilde{\nu}_{\sigma}
is a finite positive measure and
\eta_{j}\geq 0
, the Bochner integral Eq.(
C.63
) converges in the strong operator topology and yields a bounded selfadjoint operator. Positivity of
C_{\sigma}^{(j)}
follows immediately because it is a positive linear combination (integral) of positive operators; precisely, for any
\psi
,
\langle\psi,C_{\sigma}^{(j)}\psi\rangle=\int_{0}^{\infty}\eta_{j}(t)\langle\psi,e^{-t\Delta_{A_{h}}}\psi\rangle\,d\tilde{\nu}_{\sigma}(t)\geq 0
. Gauge covariance is inherited from the semigroup: for any gauge transformation
g
, one has
U_{g}\Delta_{A_{h}}U_{g}^{-1}=\Delta_{A_{h}^{g}}
and hence
U_{g}e^{-t\Delta_{A_{h}}}U_{g}^{-1}=e^{-t\Delta_{A_{h}^{g}}}
; since
\eta_{j}
is scalar and the measure is gauge-invariant by construction,
U_{g}C_{\sigma}^{(j)}U_{g}^{-1}=C_{\sigma}^{(j)}[A_{h}^{g}]
. Reflection covariance across the time plane is identical:
\Delta_{A_{h}}
commutes with the spatial part of the Euclidean reflection and so does
e^{-t\Delta_{A_{h}}}
, therefore
C_{\sigma}^{(j)}
is reflection covariant.

To obtain the pointwise decay bound, invoke a standard off-diagonal estimate for the covariant heat kernel (Combes-Thomas or Davies-Gaffney): there exist constants
a_{1},a_{2}>0
, independent of
A_{h}
, such that for all
t>0
,

\big\|e^{-t\Delta_{A_{h}}}(x,y)\big\|_{\mathrm{op}}\;\leq\;a_{1}\,\exp\!\Big\{-\frac{d(x,y)^{2}}{a_{2}\,t}\Big\}.

(C.65)

On the support of
\eta_{j}
we have
t\in[c\,L^{2j}\sigma^{-2},\,C\,L^{2j}\sigma^{-2}]
, so
t^{-1/2}\asymp\sigma\,L^{-j}
uniformly in
t
there. Using the elementary inequality
\frac{r^{2}}{\alpha}\geq\frac{r}{\sqrt{\alpha}}
with
r=d(x,y)
and
\alpha=a_{2}t
, one deduces from Eq.(
C.65
) that

\big\|e^{-t\Delta_{A_{h}}}(x,y)\big\|_{\mathrm{op}}\;\leq\;a_{1}\,\exp\!\Big\{-\frac{d(x,y)}{\sqrt{a_{2}t}}\Big\}\;\leq\;a_{1}\,\exp\!\Big\{-\frac{d(x,y)}{\sqrt{a_{2}C}\,L^{j}\sigma^{-1}}\Big\}\;=\;a_{1}\,\exp\!\Big\{-\frac{d(x,y)}{c_{2}\,L^{j}\sigma}\Big\},

(C.66)

with
c_{2}:=\sqrt{a_{2}C}
. Integrating this bound against
\eta_{j}(t)\,d\tilde{\nu}_{\sigma}(t)
produces

\|C_{\sigma}^{(j)}(x,y)\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\Big\|\int\eta_{j}(t)\,e^{-t\Delta_{A_{h}}}(x,y)\,d\tilde{\nu}_{\sigma}(t)\Big\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\exp\!\Big\{-\frac{d(x,y)}{c_{2}\,L^{j}\sigma}\Big\}\,a_{1}\,\tilde{\nu}_{\sigma}\!\big([0,\infty)\big).

(C.67)

Thus Eq.(
C.64
) holds with
c_{1}:=a_{1}\,\tilde{\nu}_{\sigma}([0,\infty))
and the displayed
c_{2}
; the finiteness of
c_{1}
is part of the hypotheses.
The uniform operator bound
0\leq C_{\sigma}^{(j)}\leq c_{3}\,\mathbf{1}
follows from the contractivity of the semigroup together with the finiteness of the measure. Indeed, for every
\psi
with
\|\psi\|=1
,

\langle\psi,C_{\sigma}^{(j)}\psi\rangle=\int_{0}^{\infty}\eta_{j}(t)\,\langle\psi,e^{-t\Delta_{A_{h}}}\psi\rangle\,d\tilde{\nu}_{\sigma}(t)\leq\int_{0}^{\infty}\eta_{j}(t)\,d\tilde{\nu}_{\sigma}(t)\leq\tilde{\nu}_{\sigma}\!\big([0,\infty)\big),

(C.68)

so
\|C_{\sigma}^{(j)}\|\leq c_{3}
with
c_{3}:=\tilde{\nu}_{\sigma}([0,\infty))
, independent of
j
.

Finally, to show that
C_{\sigma}=\sum_{j\geq 0}C_{\sigma}^{(j)}
in operator norm, observe that the partition of unity implies
\sum_{j=0}^{N}\eta_{j}(t)\uparrow\mathbf{1}_{(0,\infty)}(t)
pointwise and monotonically as
N\to\infty
. Therefore,

\sum_{j=0}^{N}C_{\sigma}^{(j)}=\int_{0}^{\infty}\Big(\sum_{j=0}^{N}\eta_{j}(t)\Big)\,e^{-t\Delta_{A_{h}}}\,d\tilde{\nu}_{\sigma}(t)\;\xrightarrow[N\to\infty]{\ \ \text{s.o.t.}\ \ }\;\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-t\Delta_{A_{h}}}\,d\tilde{\nu}_{\sigma}(t)\;=\;C_{\sigma},

(C.69)

by monotone convergence in the strong operator topology. The convergence is in fact in operator norm because the tails are dominated uniformly: using
\|e^{-t\Delta_{A_{h}}}\|\leq 1
and
\sum_{j>N}\eta_{j}\leq 1
one gets

\Big\|\,C_{\sigma}-\sum_{j=0}^{N}C_{\sigma}^{(j)}\Big\|\leq\int_{0}^{\infty}\Big(1-\sum_{j=0}^{N}\eta_{j}(t)\Big)\,d\tilde{\nu}_{\sigma}(t)\;\xrightarrow[N\to\infty]{}\;0,

(C.70)

where the right-hand side is just the
\tilde{\nu}_{\sigma}
-mass of the complement of the union of supports, which tends to zero because
\{\eta_{j}\}
is a partition of unity with locally finite overlap. This proves the norm convergence and completes the proof of all stated properties with constants
c_{1},c_{2},c_{3}
independent of
j
.
∎

We pass from slice covariances to the
one-slab
and
one-step
transfer kernels. Let
K_{k}
be the positive one-slab kernel on the
k
-th scale and
V_{k}
the vacuum-preserving coarse-grain contraction mapping fine to coarse boundary fields; let
K_{k+1}
be the corresponding coarse kernel. FRD-localization implies a block-decomposition of
K_{k+1}
by connected unions of coarse blocks
X
,

\tilde{K}_{k+1}\;:=\sum_{X}K_{k+1}^{(X)},\qquad K_{k+1}\;=\;\tilde{K}_{k+1}\;+\;R^{\rm tail}_{k+1},\quad R^{\rm tail}_{k+1}\geq 0,

(C.71)

with a
trace-class
tail bound

\|R^{\rm tail}_{k+1}\|_{1}\;\leq\;\varepsilon^{\rm slab}_{k},\qquad\sum_{k\geq 0}\varepsilon^{\rm slab}_{k}<\infty,

(C.72)

coming from the exponentially small FRD pieces whose range overflows the slab interface.

Lemma C.7

(Block decoupling under
V_{k}
)
.

Pointwise on boundary fields, one has
\tilde{K}_{k+1}\;\preceq\;V_{k}\,K_{k}\,V_{k}
. Hence there exists a positive trace-class operator
E^{\rm slab}_{k}\geq 0
with
\|E^{\rm slab}_{k}\|_{1}\leq\varepsilon^{\rm slab}_{k}
such that

K_{k+1}\;\preceq\;V_{k}\,K_{k}\,V_{k}\;+\;E^{\rm slab}_{k}.

(C.73)

Proof.

Let
\mathscr{H}_{k}
denote the boundary Hilbert space of complex
L^{2}
-functions of the fine boundary field at time
x_{0}=a
on scale
k
, and let
K_{k}
be the positive transfer kernel acting on
\mathscr{H}_{k}
. By Osterwalder-Schrader reflection positivity and the Markov property on the time-slice, we may write
K_{k}=G_{k}{\,}G_{k}
for a bounded operator
G_{k}:\mathscr{H}_{k}\to\mathcal{K}_{k}
, where
\mathcal{K}_{k}
is the positive-time bulk Hilbert space (this is the standard Gram representation coming from the conditional expectation of the slab weight given the boundary data). The coarse-to-fine lift
V_{k}:\mathscr{H}_{k+1}\to\mathscr{H}_{k}
is the reflection-positive, boundary-local partial isometry that embeds a coarse boundary configuration into a fine one by the admissible FRD-covariant block extension; in particular
V_{k}V_{k}=\mathbf{1}
on
\mathscr{H}_{k+1}
.

Consider the
\sigma
-algebra
\mathcal{F}^{\rm blk}
on the slab generated by the disjoint coarse blocks
X
that abut the time-
a
slice at scale
k
together with their fixed boundary collars of thickness
O(1)
in lattice units. Let
P_{k}:\mathcal{K}_{k}\to\mathcal{K}_{k}
denote the orthogonal conditional expectation onto
\mathcal{F}^{\rm blk}
-measurable vectors, i.e.
(P_{k}\Psi)(\cdot)=\mathbb{E}(\Psi\mid\mathcal{F}^{\rm blk})(\cdot)
in the
L^{2}
-sense. The operator
P_{k}
is a contraction,
0\leq P_{k}\leq\mathbf{1}
, and is block-diagonal across the coarse blocks. By construction of the one-step block RG on the slab, the lifted coarse kernel
\tilde{K}_{k+1}
is precisely the Gram operator obtained after integrating out, within each block
X
, the fine FRD-localized activities against the conditional law with the exterior held fixed; in the present notation this means

\tilde{K}_{k+1}\;=\;(P_{k}\,G_{k}\,V_{k})\,(P_{k}\,G_{k}\,V_{k}).

(C.74)

Since
P_{k}
is a contraction and
V_{k}
is an isometry on its domain, the operator inequality

(P_{k}\,G_{k}\,V_{k})\,(P_{k}\,G_{k}\,V_{k})\;\preceq\;(G_{k}\,V_{k})\,(G_{k}\,V_{k})\;=\;V_{k}\,K_{k}\,V_{k}

(C.75)

holds in the sense of quadratic forms. Explicitly, for every
\varphi\in\mathscr{H}_{k+1}
,

\langle\varphi,\,(V_{k}K_{k}V_{k}-\tilde{K}_{k+1})\,\varphi\rangle\;=\;\big\|(\mathbf{1}-P_{k})\,G_{k}\,V_{k}\,\varphi\big\|_{\mathcal{K}_{k}}^{\,2}\;\geq\;0,

(C.76)

which proves the pointwise decoupling
\tilde{K}_{k+1}\preceq V_{k}K_{k}V_{k}
.

It remains to compare the actual coarse kernel
K_{k+1}
with the lifted, block-decoupled kernel
\tilde{K}_{k+1}
. By finite-range decomposition locality on the slab, the difference consists solely of cross-block contributions carried by FRD tails that traverse the collars beyond the block-diagonal
\sigma
-algebra. More precisely, there exists a positive operator
R^{\rm tail}_{k+1}\geq 0
on
\mathscr{H}_{k+1}
, supported on boundary configurations that are coupled through collars of thickness at least
b_{k}
(the slab blocking factor), such that

K_{k+1}\;=\;\tilde{K}_{k+1}\;+\;R^{\rm tail}_{k+1}.

(C.77)

Positivity follows from the same Gram-type representation: the interpolation that switches on the cross-block collar couplings along a BKAR forest parameter produces a derivative of the coarse Gram map that is itself a positive quadratic form, and integration of these positive forms over the interpolation parameter yields
R^{\rm tail}_{k+1}\geq 0
. Exponential FRD locality implies that the integral kernel of
R^{\rm tail}_{k+1}
decays at least like
\exp(-c\,b_{k})
across distinct blocks, uniformly in the transverse boundary coordinates. Summing these tails over the finite number of collars meeting a given boundary site and using Schur’s test shows that
R^{\rm tail}_{k+1}
is trace-class with

\|R^{\rm tail}_{k+1}\|_{1}\;\leq\;C\,e^{-c\,b_{k}}\;=:\;\varepsilon^{\rm slab}_{k},

(C.78)

for some constants
C,c>0
independent of
k
(the trace is computed on
\mathscr{H}_{k+1}
; bounded boundary degree and uniform collar thickness give finiteness). Defining
E_{k}^{\rm slab}:=R^{\rm tail}_{k+1}
we obtain

K_{k+1}\;=\;\tilde{K}_{k+1}\;+\;E^{\rm slab}_{k}\;\preceq\;V_{k}K_{k}V_{k}\;+\;E^{\rm slab}_{k},

(C.79)

which is Eq.(
C.73
) together with the stated positivity and trace-norm bound on
E^{\rm slab}_{k}
.
∎

Composing the finitely many slab kernels that make up one transfer step, one obtains the
one-step interlacing

K_{k+1}^{\;\text{(step)}}\;\preceq\;V_{k}\,K_{k}{\;\text{(step)}}\,V_{k}\;+\;E_{k},\qquad\|E_{k}\|_{1}\;\leq\;C\,\varepsilon^{\rm slab}_{k},\qquad\sum_{k}\|E_{k}\|_{1}<\infty,

(C.80)

with
E_{k}\geq 0
positive trace class. The summability follows from the exponential FRD tail bound per scale:

\|{\mathcal{C}}_{k,j}\|\;\leq\;C_{2}\,e^{-\alpha L^{j}},\qquad\|R^{\rm tail}_{k+1}\|_{1}\;\leq\;\sum_{j>j_{0}}C_{3}\,e^{-\alpha L^{j}}\;=\;\varepsilon^{\rm slab}_{k},\quad\sum_{k}\varepsilon^{\rm slab}_{k}<\infty,

(C.81)

for a fixed
j_{0}
and constants independent of
k
; (see also the Wilson-loop surgery bounds Eqs.(
6.37
)-(
6.39
))
We now quantify the dependence of the one-step kernel and transfer operator on the admissible parameters: the projector
(\sigma,\nu)
and the blocking
B
.

Proposition C.8

(Projector-Lipschitz stability)
.

Fix an admissible blocking
B
. There exists
C=C(B)>0
such that for every pair of admissible parameters
(\sigma,\nu)
and
(\sigma^{\prime},\nu^{\prime})
one has

\big\|K_{\sigma,\nu;B}-K_{\sigma^{\prime},\nu^{\prime};B}\big\|_{L^{1}(\mu_{0}\otimes\mu_{0})}\;\leq\;C\Big(|\sigma-\sigma^{\prime}|+W_{1}(\nu,\nu^{\prime})\Big),

(C.82)

and consequently

\big\|T_{\sigma,\nu;B}-T_{\sigma^{\prime},\nu^{\prime};B}\big\|_{B(L^{2})}\;\leq\;C\Big(|\sigma-\sigma^{\prime}|+W_{1}(\nu,\nu^{\prime})\Big).

(C.83)

Proof.

The slab transfer kernel for a single blocking cell decomposes into a product of three factors: spatial Wilson weights attached to the entrance and exit faces of the slab, the time-mixed plaquette weight through the interior of the slab, and the two one-slice factors obtained by applying the horizon projector on the slices
t=0
and
t=a
. The first two factors do not depend on
(\sigma,\nu)
; all the dependence on
(\sigma,\nu)
is contained in the slice factors. By admissibility, each such slice factor is a completely monotone functional of the covariant slice generator
\mathcal{D}_{\Sigma}(A_{h})
with a compactly supported Laplace measure, and, more concretely, it can be written in the form

\Pi_{\sigma,\nu}\;=\;f_{\sigma,\nu}(\mathcal{D}_{\Sigma})\qquad\text{with}\qquad f_{\sigma,\nu}(\lambda)\;=\;\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-t\lambda}\,d\mu_{\sigma,\nu}(t),

(C.84)

where
\mu_{\sigma,\nu}
is the pushforward of
\nu
by the dilation
s\mapsto\sigma s
; explicitly,

\int\phi(t)\,d\mu_{\sigma,\nu}(t)\;=\;\int\phi(\sigma s)\,d\nu(s)\quad\text{for all bounded Lipschitz }\phi.

(C.85)

This is the standard normalization for admissible projectors and reflects that the parameter
\sigma
is the slice-time scale while
\nu
determines the profile of the completely monotone mixture. In particular, the supports of
\nu
and
\nu^{\prime}
are uniformly contained in
[0,S_{B}]
, and hence the supports of
\mu_{\sigma,\nu}
and
\mu_{\sigma^{\prime},\nu^{\prime}}
are contained in
[0,\sigma_{\max}S_{B}]
, with
\sigma,\sigma^{\prime}
ranging in a fixed compact interval by admissibility. Denote by
K_{t}(\cdot,\cdot)
the kernel of
e^{-t\mathcal{D}_{\Sigma}}
on the slice endowed with the reference measure
\mu_{0}
(this is the marginal of the gauge-invariant Euclidean measure on the slice), by
K_{\sigma,\nu}^{\rm slice}
the kernel of
\Pi_{\sigma,\nu}
, and by
K_{\sigma,\nu;B}
the full slab kernel after inserting the two slice factors at the ends. Since the other slab factors are independent of
(\sigma,\nu)
and are uniformly bounded in absolute value by a constant depending only on
B
, it suffices to establish Eq.(
C.82
) for the slice kernels; the general bound follows by multiplying with the same harmless constant.

We first show that the map
t\mapsto K_{t}
is Lipschitz as a function into
L^{1}(\mu_{0}\otimes\mu_{0})
with a constant depending only on
B
. The slice generator
\mathcal{D}_{\Sigma}
is a nonnegative, finite-range, uniformly elliptic operator on a bounded-degree graph (the blocked slice), hence the heat kernels
K_{t}
satisfy the Davies-Gaffney estimate and are strongly differentiable in
t>0
with
\partial_{t}K_{t}=-(\mathcal{D}_{\Sigma}e^{-t\mathcal{D}_{\Sigma}})(\cdot,\cdot)
. Since
\mathcal{D}_{\Sigma}
is finite range and bounded on
L^{1}\to L^{1}
uniformly on the blocked slice, while
e^{-t\mathcal{D}_{\Sigma}}
is a positivity preserving contraction on
L^{1}
for every
t\geq 0
, there exists
C_{1}=C_{1}(B)
such that

\big\|\partial_{t}K_{t}\big\|_{L^{1}(\mu_{0}\otimes\mu_{0})}\;=\;\big\|\mathcal{D}_{\Sigma}e^{-t\mathcal{D}_{\Sigma}}\big\|_{L^{1}\to L^{1}}\;\leq\;C_{1}\qquad\text{for all }t\in[0,\sigma_{\max}S_{B}].

(C.86)

Integrating this bound in
t
shows that for any
t,s\in[0,\sigma_{\max}S_{B}]
,

\big\|K_{t}-K_{s}\big\|_{L^{1}(\mu_{0}\otimes\mu_{0})}\;\leq\;C_{1}\,|t-s|.

(C.87)

In particular, for every
L^{1}
-Lipschitz function
\Phi:[0,\sigma_{\max}S_{B}]\to L^{1}(\mu_{0}\otimes\mu_{0})
with Lipschitz constant
\mathrm{Lip}(\Phi)\leq C_{1}
, the Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality for the
1
-Wasserstein distance gives

\Big\|\int\Phi(t)\,d\eta(t)-\int\Phi(t)\,d\eta^{\prime}(t)\Big\|_{L^{1}(\mu_{0}\otimes\mu_{0})}\;\leq\;\mathrm{Lip}(\Phi)\,W_{1}(\eta,\eta^{\prime})

(C.88)

(
for any probability measures
\eta,\eta^{\prime}
) supported in
[0,\sigma_{\max}S_{B}]
. Applying this to
\Phi(t)=K_{t}
and
\eta=\mu_{\sigma,\nu}
,
\eta^{\prime}=\mu_{\sigma^{\prime},\nu^{\prime}}
yields

\big\|K_{\sigma,\nu}^{\rm slice}-K_{\sigma^{\prime},\nu^{\prime}}^{\rm slice}\big\|_{L^{1}(\mu_{0}\otimes\mu_{0})}\;\leq\;C_{1}\,W_{1}(\mu_{\sigma,\nu},\mu_{\sigma^{\prime},\nu^{\prime}}).

(C.89)

It remains to relate the Wasserstein distance of the pushed measures to the parameter distance
|\sigma-\sigma^{\prime}|+W_{1}(\nu,\nu^{\prime})
. If
\phi
is a
1
-Lipschitz function on
[0,\sigma_{\max}S_{B}]
, then
s\mapsto\phi(\sigma s)
is
\sigma_{\max}
-Lipschitz on
[0,S_{B}]
, and similarly for
\sigma^{\prime}
. Writing

\int\phi\,d\mu_{\sigma,\nu}-\int\phi\,d\mu_{\sigma^{\prime},\nu^{\prime}}\;=\;\int\phi(\sigma s)\,d\nu(s)-\int\phi(\sigma^{\prime}s)\,d\nu^{\prime}(s)

(C.90)

and adding and subtracting
\int\phi(\sigma s)\,d\nu^{\prime}(s)
gives

\bigg|\int\phi\,d\mu_{\sigma,\nu}-\int\phi\,d\mu_{\sigma^{\prime},\nu^{\prime}}\bigg|\;\leq\;\bigg|\int\big[\phi(\sigma s)-\phi(\sigma^{\prime}s)\big]\,d\nu^{\prime}(s)\bigg|\;+\;\bigg|\int\phi(\sigma s)\,d(\nu-\nu^{\prime})(s)\bigg|.

(C.91)

The first term is bounded by
\|\phi\|_{\mathrm{Lip}}\,|\sigma-\sigma^{\prime}|\,\int s\,d\nu^{\prime}(s)
, and the second by
\sigma_{\max}\,\|\phi\|_{\mathrm{Lip}}\,W_{1}(\nu,\nu^{\prime})
by Kantorovich-Rubinstein on
[0,S_{B}]
. Admissibility gives a uniform bound on the first moment
\int s\,d\nu^{\prime}(s)\leq S_{B}
, and
\|\phi\|_{\mathrm{Lip}}\leq 1
. Taking the supremum over
1
-Lipschitz
\phi
therefore shows that

W_{1}(\mu_{\sigma,\nu},\mu_{\sigma^{\prime},\nu^{\prime}})\;\leq\;S_{B}\,|\sigma-\sigma^{\prime}|\;+\;\sigma_{\max}\,W_{1}(\nu,\nu^{\prime}).

(C.92)

Combining this with Eq.(
C.89
) yields

\big\|K_{\sigma,\nu}^{\rm slice}-K_{\sigma^{\prime},\nu^{\prime}}^{\rm slice}\big\|_{L^{1}(\mu_{0}\otimes\mu_{0})}\;\leq\;C_{1}\,(S_{B}\,|\sigma-\sigma^{\prime}|+\sigma_{\max}W_{1}(\nu,\nu^{\prime})),

(C.93)

and, since
K_{\sigma,\nu;B}
differs from
K_{\sigma,\nu}^{\rm slice}
only by multiplication with the fixed, bounded slab factors, the same estimate holds for
K_{\sigma,\nu;B}
with a possibly larger constant
C
depending only on
B
.
To pass from the
L^{1}
-bound on kernels to the operator bound Eq.(
C.83
), recall that
T_{\sigma,\nu;B}
is the integral operator on
L^{2}(\mu_{0})
with kernel
K_{\sigma,\nu;B}
. Schur’s test gives

\displaystyle\big\|T_{\sigma,\nu;B}-T_{\sigma^{\prime},\nu^{\prime};B}\big\|_{B(L^{2})}\;\leq\;

\displaystyle\max\Big\{\sup_{y}\int|K_{\sigma,\nu;B}-K_{\sigma^{\prime},\nu^{\prime};B}|(x,y)\,\mu_{0}(dx),\ \sup_{x}\int|K_{\sigma,\nu;B}-K_{\sigma^{\prime},\nu^{\prime};B}|(x,y)\,\mu_{0}(dy)\Big\}.

(C.94)

Both suprema are bounded by
\|K_{\sigma,\nu;B}-K_{\sigma^{\prime},\nu^{\prime};B}\|_{L^{1}(\mu_{0}\otimes\mu_{0})}
, hence Eq.(
C.83
) follows immediately from Eq.(
C.82
) with the same constant (after enlarging
C
by a universal factor if desired).
∎

Proposition C.9

(Blocking-Lipschitz stability)
.

If
\|B-B^{\prime}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\delta
in the polymer-activity Banach norm, then

\|K_{B}-K_{B^{\prime}}\|_{L^{1}(\mu_{0}\otimes\mu_{0})}\;\leq\;C\,\delta,\qquad\|T_{B}-T_{B^{\prime}}\|_{B(L^{2})}\;\leq\;C^{\prime}\,\delta,

(C.95)

with constants
C,C^{\prime}>0
depending only on the uniform FRD locality data (range parameters, decay exponents, and degree bounds), but not on
B,B^{\prime}
or the volume.

Proof.

The transfer kernel at a given scale admits the standard FRD/cluster representation

K_{B}(x,y)\;=\;\sum_{\Gamma\ni x,y}\,\Phi_{\Gamma}(B)\;k_{\Gamma}(x,y),

(C.96)

where the sum is over connected polymers
\Gamma
intersecting the two-slice collar that contains the points
x
and
y
, the coefficient
\Phi_{\Gamma}(B)
is the renormalized activity obtained by applying the blocking map
B
to the local degrees of freedom supported on
\Gamma
, and the geometric kernel
k_{\Gamma}(x,y)
depends only on the FRD scheme (block geometry, collar width, and finite-range Dirichlet problems). Uniform locality guarantees exponential summability of the family
\{k_{\Gamma}\}
in the
L^{1}(\mu_{0}\otimes\mu_{0})
norm, namely

\sum_{\Gamma\ni x,y}\|k_{\Gamma}\|_{L^{1}(\mu_{0}\otimes\mu_{0})}\;w(\Gamma)\;\leq\;C_{\mathrm{FRD}},\qquad w(\Gamma):=e^{\alpha|\Gamma|},

(C.97)

for some
\alpha>0
and a constant
C_{\mathrm{FRD}}<\infty
fixed by the FRD data, and the same bound holds uniformly in
x,y
by translation invariance or bounded geometry of the partition. The Banach norm
\|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{op}}
on activities is chosen so that the map
B\mapsto\Phi_{\Gamma}(B)
is locally Lipschitz with weight
w(\Gamma)
; concretely there exists
L>0
(independent of
\Gamma
and of the volume) such that

|\Phi_{\Gamma}(B)-\Phi_{\Gamma}(B^{\prime})|\;\leq\;L\,\delta\,w(\Gamma)^{-1}.

(C.98)

This is the usual consequence of writing
\Phi_{\Gamma}
as a convergent cluster power series in the elementary block variables and estimating the Fréchet derivative with respect to the operator-norm metric on
B
, together with the exponential polymer weights built into
\|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{op}}
.

With these two inputs, the
L^{1}
-difference of kernels factorizes into a coefficient-difference and a geometric part:

\|K_{B}-K_{B^{\prime}}\|_{L^{1}(\mu_{0}\otimes\mu_{0})}\;\leq\;\sum_{\Gamma}\,|\Phi_{\Gamma}(B)-\Phi_{\Gamma}(B^{\prime})|\,\|k_{\Gamma}\|_{L^{1}(\mu_{0}\otimes\mu_{0})}.

(C.99)

Inserting Eq.(
C.98
) and summing with Eq.(
C.97
) gives

\|K_{B}-K_{B^{\prime}}\|_{L^{1}(\mu_{0}\otimes\mu_{0})}\;\leq\;L\,\delta\;\sum_{\Gamma}w(\Gamma)^{-1}\,\|k_{\Gamma}\|_{L^{1}(\mu_{0}\otimes\mu_{0})}\;\leq\;L\,\delta\,C_{\mathrm{FRD}},

(C.100)

and the first inequality in Eq.(
C.95
) follows with
C:=L\,C_{\mathrm{FRD}}
.
To pass from the
L^{1}
-bound to an operator-norm bound on
L^{2}
, apply the Schur test in its
L^{1}
-
L^{\infty}
form. FRD locality yields, in addition to Eq.(
C.97
), uniform one-sided Schur bounds

\sup_{x}\int|K_{B}(x,y)|\,d\mu_{0}(y)\;\leq\;C_{0},\qquad\sup_{y}\int|K_{B}(x,y)|\,d\mu_{0}(x)\;\leq\;C_{0},

(C.101)

with the same constant
C_{0}
for all admissible
B
, because each
K_{B}
is obtained by summing absolutely convergent local contributions supported in a fixed-width collar. The same uniform bounds hold for
K_{B^{\prime}}
. For the difference we write

\sup_{x}\int|K_{B}(x,y)-K_{B^{\prime}}(x,y)|\,d\mu_{0}(y)\;\leq\;\sup_{x}\sum_{\Gamma\ni x}\,|\Phi_{\Gamma}(B)-\Phi_{\Gamma}(B^{\prime})|\int|k_{\Gamma}(x,y)|\,d\mu_{0}(y)

(C.102)

and estimate exactly as above to obtain

\sup_{x}\int|K_{B}-K_{B^{\prime}}|(x,y)\,d\mu_{0}(y)\;\leq\;\widetilde{C}\,\delta,\qquad\sup_{y}\int|K_{B}-K_{B^{\prime}}|(x,y)\,d\mu_{0}(x)\;\leq\;\widetilde{C}\,\delta,

(C.103)

with
\widetilde{C}
depending only on the FRD locality constants. The Schur test then gives

\displaystyle\|T_{B}-T_{B^{\prime}}\|_{B(L^{2})}\;\leq\;

\displaystyle\sqrt{\Big(\sup_{x}\!\int|K_{B}-K_{B^{\prime}}|(x,y)\,d\mu_{0}(y)\Big)\Big(\sup_{y}\!\int|K_{B}-K_{B^{\prime}}|(x,y)\,d\mu_{0}(x)\Big)}\;\leq\;\widetilde{C}\,\delta,

(C.104)

which proves the second inequality in Eq.(
C.95
) with
C^{\prime}:=\widetilde{C}
. Both constants
C
and
C^{\prime}
depend only on the polymer weights and the geometric
L^{1}
-summability of the FRD kernels, hence only on the uniform FRD locality bounds.
∎

Lemma C.10

(Telescoping in time)
.

Let
(\Sigma,\mu_{0})
be a probability space and let
K_{\theta}
and
K_{\theta^{\prime}}
be (measurable) Markov kernels on
\Sigma
with densities
K_{\theta}(x,y),K_{\theta^{\prime}}(x,y)\geq 0
with respect to
\mu_{0}
, normalized in the sense that

\int_{\Sigma}K_{\theta}(x,y)\,d\mu_{0}(y)=1\quad\text{for $\mu_{0}$-a.e.\ $x$,}\qquad\int_{\Sigma}K_{\theta^{\prime}}(x,y)\,d\mu_{0}(y)=1\quad\text{for $\mu_{0}$-a.e.\ $x$,}

(C.105)

and such that
\mu_{0}
is invariant:

\int_{\Sigma}K_{\theta}(x,y)\,d\mu_{0}(x)=1=\int_{\Sigma}K_{\theta^{\prime}}(x,y)\,d\mu_{0}(x)

for
\mu_{0}
-a.e.
y
. Denote by
K_{\theta}^{(n)}
the
n
-fold time-convolution kernel and by
T_{\theta}
the corresponding
L^{2}(\mu_{0})\to L^{2}(\mu_{0})
integral operator:

\displaystyle K_{\theta}^{(n)}(x,y):=\int_{\Sigma^{n-1}}\prod_{j=0}^{n-2}K_{\theta}(x_{j},x_{j+1})\,K_{\theta}(x_{n-1},y)\,d\mu_{0}(x_{1})\cdots d\mu_{0}(x_{n-1}),

\displaystyle(T_{\theta}f)(x):=\int_{\Sigma}K_{\theta}(x,y)\,f(y)\,d\mu_{0}(y).

(C.106)

Then for every
n\in\mathbb{N}
,

\displaystyle\big\|K_{\theta}^{(n)}-K_{\theta^{\prime}}^{(n)}\big\|_{L^{1}(\mu_{0}\otimes\mu_{0})}\;\leq\;n\,\|K_{\theta}-K_{\theta^{\prime}}\|_{L^{1}(\mu_{0}\otimes\mu_{0})},

\displaystyle\|T_{\theta}^{n}-T_{\theta^{\prime}}^{n}\|_{B(L^{2})}\;\leq\;n\,\|K_{\theta}-K_{\theta^{\prime}}\|_{L^{1}(\mu_{0}\otimes\mu_{0})}.

(C.107)

Proof.

The algebraic identity
A^{n}-B^{n}=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}B^{\,j}(A-B)A^{\,n-1-j}
holds in any associative algebra. Applying it to the convolution algebra of kernels (with convolution
(AB)(x,y):=\int_{\Sigma}A(x,z)B(z,y)\,d\mu_{0}(z)
) gives

K_{\theta}^{(n)}-K_{\theta^{\prime}}^{(n)}\;=\;\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}K_{\theta^{\prime}}^{(j)}\big(K_{\theta}-K_{\theta^{\prime}}\big)K_{\theta}^{(n-1-j)}.

(C.108)

Taking absolute values and integrating over
(x,y)
with respect to
\mu_{0}\otimes\mu_{0}
, Tonelli’s theorem yields

\big\|K_{\theta}^{(n)}-K_{\theta^{\prime}}^{(n)}\big\|_{L^{1}}\;\leq\;\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\big\|K_{\theta^{\prime}}^{(j)}(K_{\theta}-K_{\theta^{\prime}})K_{\theta}^{(n-1-j)}\big\|_{L^{1}}.

(C.109)

To bound each term, write out the
L^{1}
-norm of a triple convolution and use the Markov normalizations on the left and right factors:

\displaystyle\big\|AHB\big\|_{L^{1}}

\displaystyle=\int_{\Sigma}\!\!\int_{\Sigma}\Big|\int_{\Sigma}\!\!\int_{\Sigma}A(x,u)\,H(u,v)\,B(v,y)\,d\mu_{0}(u)\,d\mu_{0}(v)\Big|\,d\mu_{0}(x)\,d\mu_{0}(y)

(C.110)

\displaystyle\leq\int_{\Sigma}\!\!\int_{\Sigma}\!\!\int_{\Sigma}\!\!\int_{\Sigma}A(x,u)\,|H(u,v)|\,B(v,y)\,d\mu_{0}(u)\,d\mu_{0}(v)\,d\mu_{0}(x)\,d\mu_{0}(y)

\displaystyle=\int_{\Sigma}\!\!\int_{\Sigma}\Big(\int_{\Sigma}A(x,u)\,d\mu_{0}(x)\Big)\,|H(u,v)|\,\Big(\int_{\Sigma}B(v,y)\,d\mu_{0}(y)\Big)\,d\mu_{0}(u)\,d\mu_{0}(v).

If
A
and
B
are Markov kernels with invariant
\mu_{0}
then
\int_{\Sigma}A(x,u)\,d\mu_{0}(x)=1
for
\mu_{0}
-a.e.
u
and
\int_{\Sigma}B(v,y)\,d\mu_{0}(y)=1
for
\mu_{0}
-a.e.
v
, hence the right-hand side collapses to
\int_{\Sigma}\!\!\int_{\Sigma}|H(u,v)|\,d\mu_{0}(u)\,d\mu_{0}(v)=\|H\|_{L^{1}}
. Applying this bound with
A=K_{\theta^{\prime}}^{(j)}
and
B=K_{\theta}^{(n-1-j)}
gives

\big\|K_{\theta^{\prime}}^{(j)}(K_{\theta}-K_{\theta^{\prime}})K_{\theta}^{(n-1-j)}\big\|_{L^{1}}\;\leq\;\|K_{\theta}-K_{\theta^{\prime}}\|_{L^{1}},

(C.111)

and summing over
j=0,\dots,n-1
proves the first inequality in Eq.(
C.10
).

For the operator bound on
L^{2}(\mu_{0})
, use the same telescoping identity at the operator level,

T_{\theta}^{n}-T_{\theta^{\prime}}^{n}\;=\;\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}T_{\theta^{\prime}}^{\,j}\,\big(T_{\theta}-T_{\theta^{\prime}}\big)\,T_{\theta}^{\,n-1-j},

(C.112)

and estimate the operator norm of each term. By the Schur test, if
H
is any kernel then

\|T_{H}\|_{B(L^{2})}\;\leq\;\max\Big\{\ \sup_{x}\int_{\Sigma}|H(x,y)|\,d\mu_{0}(y),\ \sup_{y}\int_{\Sigma}|H(x,y)|\,d\mu_{0}(x)\ \Big\}\ \leq\ \|H\|_{L^{1}(\mu_{0}\otimes\mu_{0})}.

(C.113)

In particular,
\|T_{\theta}-T_{\theta^{\prime}}\|_{B(L^{2})}\leq\|K_{\theta}-K_{\theta^{\prime}}\|_{L^{1}}
. Moreover, the Schur test with the Markov normalizations shows
\|T_{\theta}\|_{B(L^{2})}\leq 1
and
\|T_{\theta^{\prime}}\|_{B(L^{2})}\leq 1
, hence
\|T_{\theta^{\prime}}^{\,j}\|\leq 1
and
\|T_{\theta}^{\,n-1-j}\|\leq 1
for every
j
. Consequently,

\big\|T_{\theta^{\prime}}^{\,j}\,(T_{\theta}-T_{\theta^{\prime}})\,T_{\theta}^{\,n-1-j}\big\|_{B(L^{2})}\;\leq\;\|T_{\theta}-T_{\theta^{\prime}}\|_{B(L^{2})}\;\leq\;\|K_{\theta}-K_{\theta^{\prime}}\|_{L^{1}},

(C.114)

and summing the
n
identical bounds yields the second inequality in Eq.(
C.10
). In particular, the transfer maps are nonexpansive on the weighted diameter seminorm used in Appendix (
F
), so that composition with
T_{\theta}
and
T_{\theta^{\prime}}
does not increase
\|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{diam},\mu}
.
∎

Let
K_{k}^{\text{(step)}}
be the one-step kernel obtained by composing the finitely many slab kernels in a time step. From Lemma (
C.7
), composition preserves positivity and trace-class control of the remainder, yielding Eq.(
C.80
). Passing to transfer operators on
L^{2}(X_{0},\mu_{0})
,

T_{k+1}\;\preceq\;V_{k}\,T_{k}\,V_{k}\;+\;E_{k},\qquad E_{k}\geq 0,\quad\sum_{k}\|E_{k}\|_{1}<\infty,

(C.115)

(which is the form used in the spectral step-scaling argument for persistence of the gap Section (
5
)) iterating the defect inequality shows
\rho_{k}:=\|Q_{k}T_{k}Q_{k}\|
remains strictly below
1
, hence the transfer gap
\gamma_{k}=1-\rho_{k}
