By duality,

\left\lVert\iota_{k}[O]\right\rVert_{H^{-s}}^{2}\;=\;\sup_{\left\lVert f\right\rVert_{H^{s}}\leq 1}\sup_{\left\lVert g\right\rVert_{H^{s}}\leq 1}\langle\iota_{k}[O],f\rangle\,\overline{\langle\iota_{k}[O],g\rangle}.

(3.54)

Taking expectations and using linearity and Fubini,

\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{k}}\langle\iota_{k}[O],f\rangle\,\overline{\langle\iota_{k}[O],g\rangle}=a_{k}^{8}\sum_{x,y}\Bigl(\fint_{Q_{x}}f\Bigr)\,\overline{\Bigl(\fint_{Q_{y}}g\Bigr)}\,S_{2,O}^{(k)}(x,y).

(3.55)

By (
3.52
) and the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality,

\bigl|\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{k}}\langle\iota_{k}[O],f\rangle\,\overline{\langle\iota_{k}[O],g\rangle}\bigr|\leq a_{k}^{8}C_{O}\sum_{x,y}\Bigl|\fint_{Q_{x}}f\Bigr|\,\Bigl|\fint_{Q_{y}}g\Bigr|\,e^{-\xi d(x,y)}.

(3.56)

Let
h_{x}=\fint_{Q_{x}}f
and
k_{y}=\fint_{Q_{y}}g
. The discrete convolution with the absolutely summable kernel
e^{-\xi d(x,y)}
defines a bounded operator on
\ell^{2}(\Lambda_{k,L,T})
with norm bounded by a constant
C_{\xi}
independent of
k,L,T
. Hence

\sum_{x,y}|h_{x}|\,|k_{y}|\,e^{-\xi d(x,y)}\leq C_{\xi}\Bigl(\sum_{x}|h_{x}|^{2}\Bigr)^{1/2}\Bigl(\sum_{y}|k_{y}|^{2}\Bigr)^{1/2}.

(3.57)

Since
h_{x}
and
k_{y}
are cell averages of
f
and
g
, Sobolev-Poincaré inequalities on the torus imply

a_{k}^{4}\sum_{x}|h_{x}|^{2}\;\leq\;C\left\lVert f\right\rVert_{H^{s}}^{2},\qquad a_{k}^{4}\sum_{y}|k_{y}|^{2}\;\leq\;C\left\lVert g\right\rVert_{H^{s}}^{2},

(3.58)

for
s\geq 3
, where
C
is independent of
k,L,T
. Combining the bounds and taking the sup over
\left\lVert f\right\rVert_{H^{s}},\left\lVert g\right\rVert_{H^{s}}\leq 1
yields the claim with
C_{s,O}=C\,C_{\xi}\,C_{O}
.
∎

The previous bound controls second moments. For tightness one also needs equicontinuity of finite-dimensional marginals, which follows from uniform cumulant bounds provided by the multiscale polymer estimates and the same Sobolev convolution bounds.

Proposition 3.6

(Equicontinuity of finite-dimensional marginals)
.

Fix
m\in\mathbb{N}
, observables
O_{1},\dots,O_{m}\in\mathcal{G}
, and test functions
f_{1},\dots,f_{m}\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{T}^{4})
. For the
\mathbb{C}^{m}
-valued random vector
X^{(k)}=(\langle\iota_{k}[O_{j}],f_{j}\rangle)_{j=1}^{m}
there exist constants
C_{p,m}<\infty
, independent of
k
, such that

\sup_{k}\,\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{k}}\bigl[\,|X^{(k)}|^{p}\,\bigr]\;\leq\;C_{p,m}\,\prod_{j=1}^{m}\left\lVert f_{j}\right\rVert_{H^{s}}^{p/m}

(3.59)

for each even integer
p\geq 2
and some fixed
s\geq 3
.

Proof.

Expand moments via cumulants. The uniform tree-decay of all connected
n
-point functions for
\{O_{j}\}
at scale
k
implies bounds of the form

\bigl|\,\kappa_{n}^{(k)}\bigl(\langle\iota_{k}[O_{j_{1}}],f_{j_{1}}\rangle,\dots,\langle\iota_{k}[O_{j_{n}}],f_{j_{n}}\rangle\bigr)\,\bigr|\;\leq\;C_{n}\prod_{\ell=1}^{n}\left\lVert f_{j_{\ell}}\right\rVert_{H^{s}},

(3.60)

with
C_{n}
independent of
k
. This follows by the same convolution and Sobolev estimates used in Lemma
3.5
, applied to the
n
-point kernels and their tree expansions. The moment-cumulant formula then bounds
\mathbb{E}|X^{(k)}|^{p}
by a finite sum of products of such
C_{n}
’s, yielding the stated inequality.
∎

To ensure uniform second-moment bounds, we restrict to a finite generating set
G
of
gauge-invariant local observables
\{O\}
obtained from small Wilson loops and gauge-invariant
polynomials in the (smeared) lattice field-strength, with a finite number of covariant discrete derivatives.
When derivatives occur, we use multiplicative renormalization
O^{\mathrm{ren}}_{k}:=Z_{O}(k)\,O_{k}
with
Z_{O}(k)
chosen so that

\sup_{k}\,\mathbb{E}\big|\langle\iota_{k}[O^{\mathrm{ren}}],f\rangle\big|^{2}\ \lesssim\ \|f\|_{H^{s}}^{2}

(3.61)

holds uniformly for
s\geq 3
. Existence of such
Z_{O}(k)
follows from the scale-uniform locality
and clustering bounds (S1)-(S2) and the finite-range decomposition that control short-distance contributions (see Appendix (
16
)). We deduce tightness of the sequence of laws
\{\mathrm{Law}(\iota_{k}[\mathcal{G}])\}_{k\geq 0}
in a separable Hilbert space and extract subsequential limits of Schwinger functions
(See Appendix (
12
) for the equicontinuity and Prokhorov tightness argument)
. To remain within a Polish framework we work in
H^{-s}(\mathbb{T}^{4})
with
s\geq 3
.

Theorem 3.7

(Tightness in
H^{-s}
and subsequential convergence)
.

Fix
s\geq 3
and a finite generating set
\mathcal{G}
of local, gauge-invariant observables. For each
O\in\mathcal{G}
, the family
\{\mathrm{Law}(\iota_{k}[O]):k\in\mathbb{N}\}
is tight on
H^{-s}(\mathbb{T}^{4})
. Consequently, along a subsequence
k_{j}\to\infty
and after passing to the thermodynamic limit
L,T\to\infty
along a cofinal sequence, the joint laws of
\{\iota_{k_{j}}[O]:O\in\mathcal{G}\}
converge weakly on
\prod_{O\in\mathcal{G}}H^{-s}(\mathbb{T}^{4})
. In particular, for each
n
, each
O_{1},\dots,O_{n}\in\mathcal{G}
, and each
f_{1},\dots,f_{n}\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{T}^{4})
, the Schwinger functionals

S^{(k)}_{n}(f_{1},\dots,f_{n})\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{k}}\bigl[\,\prod_{j=1}^{n}\langle\iota_{k}[O_{j}],f_{j}\rangle\,\bigr]

(3.62)

converge along
k_{j}
to limits
S_{n}(f_{1},\dots,f_{n})
that define tempered distributions on
(C^{\infty}(\mathbb{T}^{4}))^{n}
.

Proof.

In a separable Hilbert space, Prokhorov’s theorem applies verbatim
[
29
]
. By Lemma
3.5
, the laws have uniformly bounded second moments, which implies tightness of each marginal
\mathrm{Law}(\iota_{k}[O])
. For joint tightness of finitely many observables we combine Lemma
3.5
with Proposition
3.6
and use Markov’s inequality to get uniform control of tails of any finite-dimensional projection. Since finite products of separable Hilbert spaces are separable, Prokhorov’s theorem yields tightness of the joint laws. Consequently, along a subsequence
k_{j}\to\infty
and after passing to
L,T\to\infty
(uniformity in
L,T
is built into Lemma
3.5
), the joint laws converge weakly. By the portmanteau theorem, for each
n
and each test family
(f_{1},\dots,f_{n})
, the sequence
S^{(k_{j})}_{n}(f_{1},\dots,f_{n})
converges to the expectation of the product of the limiting
H^{-s}
-valued random variables evaluated at
f_{j}
. This defines a multilinear functional on
(C^{\infty}(\mathbb{T}^{4}))^{n}
that is continuous by the Sobolev estimates already used; hence a tempered distribution.
∎

It is convenient to recast convergence of Schwinger functions in a form used in the verification of the Osterwalder-Schrader axioms. We identify the OS inner product at finite
k
with the transfer-operator inner product and pass to limits.

Proposition 3.8

(OS inner product as transfer expectation and limit)
.

Let
F,G\in\mathcal{A}_{+}
be bounded positive-time cylinder functionals depending only on links in
\Lambda^{+}
. For each
k
, define

\left\langle F,\,G\right\rangle_{\mathrm{OS},k}=\int(\Theta F)(U)\,G(U)\,d\mu_{k}(U).

(3.63)

Then there exist bounded vectors
\Psi_{F},\Psi_{G}\in\mathscr{H}_{k}
such that

\left\langle F,\,G\right\rangle_{\mathrm{OS},k}=\left\langle\Psi_{F},\,\,T_{k}^{T/2a_{k}}\,\Psi_{G}\right\rangle_{\mathscr{H}_{k}}.

(3.64)

Along the subsequence
k_{j}\to\infty
of Theorem
3.7
, the limits
\left\langle F,\,G\right\rangle_{\mathrm{OS}}=\lim_{j\to\infty}\left\langle F,\,G\right\rangle_{\mathrm{OS},k_{j}}
exist and define a positive semidefinite form on
\mathcal{A}_{+}
.

Proof.

The first identity is the standard reflection-positivity representation obtained by integrating slab by slab from
\Pi
into
\Lambda^{+}
and using (
3.24
). The vectors
\Psi_{F},\Psi_{G}
are the boundary data induced by
F,G
together with the half-slice factors
\mathfrak{p}_{\sigma,k}
and
\frac{1}{2}S_{t}^{\mathrm{sp}}
. The existence of the limit follows from Theorem
3.7
and the uniform bound
|\left\langle F,\,G\right\rangle_{\mathrm{OS},k}|\leq\left\lVert F\right\rVert_{\infty}\left\lVert G\right\rVert_{\infty}
. Positivity is preserved under limits.
∎

The combination of Theorem
3.7
and Proposition
3.8
completes the extraction of subsequential limits of Schwinger functions and sets the stage for the verification of the Osterwalder-Schrader axioms and reconstruction. The arguments remain valid if
H^{-s}(\mathbb{T}^{4})
is replaced by the space of tempered distributions
\mathcal{S}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{4})
; one may then use Mitoma’s tightness criterion for nuclear spaces
[
30
]
. The
H^{-s}
-framework, however, suffices and keeps the presentation within a Polish setting, convenient for applications of Prokhorov’s theorem and for strong convergence of semigroups.

Appendix 4
Osterwalder-Schrader axioms for the limiting Schwinger functions

In this section we verify that the continuum Euclidean Schwinger functions

\{S_{n}\}_{n\geq 1}
, obtained as limits of lattice Schwinger functions along a
reflection-positive multiscale flow, satisfy the full list of
Osterwalder-Schrader (OS) axioms Stability of reflection positivity under weak limits used below is stated and proved in Appendix (
13
). For completeness, we recall the OS0-OS5 axioms
[
2
,
3
]
: OS0 is the existence of the Euclidean
n
-point functions as tempered distributions (satisfying technical regularity conditions); OS1 is Euclidean invariance (translation and rotation symmetry); OS2 is symmetry under permutations of arguments; OS3 is Osterwalder-Schrader reflection positivity; OS4 is the cluster property (factorization of distant correlations); and OS5 is the time-regularity (Markov property), ensuring that two-point functions are analytic in a strip and decay sufficiently fast for large time separations.
We begin by fixing the lattice
configuration space, the time-reflection structure, and the projected measure
(with smooth horizon projector). We then derive, with complete details, the
transfer time-slicing formalism and the associated transfer operator. With
these ingredients in hand we prove lattice reflection positivity, and finally
show that reflection positivity, temperedness, Euclidean covariance,
permutation symmetry, the cluster property, and Euclidean-time regularity are
preserved in the continuum limit. Throughout,
G=\mathrm{SU}(N)
with

N\geq 2
and all Haar measures are normalized to unit mass.

Fix a temporal lattice spacing
a>0
and a periodic spatial box

\Lambda_{\mathrm{sp}}\subset a\mathbb{Z}^{3}
of side length
L
.
The Euclidean space-time lattice is

\Lambda=\big\{(t,\mathbf{x})\in a\mathbb{Z}\times\Lambda_{\mathrm{sp}}:\;-T\leq t\leq T-a\big\},

(4.1)

with periodic boundary conditions in the spatial directions. Directed bonds are
pairs
b=(x,\mu)
with
x\in\Lambda
and
\mu\in\{0,1,2,3\}
. The reversed
bond is
\bar{b}=(x+\hat{\mu},-\mu)
. A (classical) gauge configuration
is an assignment
U_{b}\in G
to each directed bond such that

U_{\bar{b}}=U_{b}^{-1}
. The configuration space is the compact manifold

\mathcal{U}=G^{\mathrm{bonds}(\Lambda)}
, equipped with the product of Haar
measures on
G
.
The Wilson action is

S_{W}[U]\;=\;\beta\sum_{p\subset\Lambda}\left(1-\frac{1}{N}\mathrm{Re}\,\mathrm{Tr}\,U_{p}\right),\qquad\beta=\frac{2N}{g_{0}^{2}},

(4.2)

where the sum runs over oriented plaquettes
p
of
\Lambda
and

U_{p}=\prod_{\ell\in p}U_{\ell}
is the ordered bond-product around
p
.
We impose temporal-axial gauge away from the reflection plane by setting

U_{(t,\mathbf{x};0)}\;=\;\mathbf{1}\qquad\text{for all bonds with }t\neq-a,

(4.3)

which leaves spatial bonds unchanged and is compatible with time reflection.

Let
\theta
be time reflection on
\Lambda
,

\theta(t,\mathbf{x})=(-t,\mathbf{x})
, extended to bonds by

\theta(x,0)=(\theta x,0)
and
\theta(x,i)=(\theta x-\hat{0},i)
for

i=1,2,3
. The fixed-point hyperplane is

\Pi=\{(0,\mathbf{x})\in\Lambda\}
. We write

\Lambda_{+}=\{(t,\mathbf{x})\in\Lambda:\;t>0\}
and

\Lambda_{-}=\theta(\Lambda_{+})
. Denote by

\mathrm{bonds}_{\mathrm{sp}}(t)
the spatial bonds in the time slice
t
,
and by
\mathcal{X}_{t}=G^{\mathrm{bonds}_{\mathrm{sp}}(t)}
the compact
manifold of spatial bonds at time
t
, endowed with product Haar measure

d\nu_{t}
.

On each time slice
t
we fix a gauge-invariant transverse representative

A^{h}(t)
by minimizing the lattice Landau functional over site-gauge
transformations on the slice; measurability and reflection covariance of this
choice were established at the finite-
a
level. The covariant spatial
Laplacian on the slice is

\Delta_{A^{h}(t)}\;=\;\sum_{i=1}^{3}(D_{i}^{h})^{\dagger}D_{i}^{h},

(4.4)

acting on site-adjoint fields on the slice, where
D_{i}^{h}
are the covariant
differences constructed from
A^{h}(t)
. Fix
\sigma>0
and a Gevrey-regular
cutoff
\chi_{\sigma}:[0,\infty)\to[0,1]
with
\chi_{\sigma}\equiv 1
on

[0,\sigma]
and
\chi_{\sigma}\equiv 0
on
[2\sigma,\infty)
. The smooth
horizon projector on slice
t
is the bounded positive operator

P_{\sigma}(t)\;=\;\chi_{\sigma}\!\left({\Delta_{A^{h}(t)}}\right),

(4.5)

which is exponentially local and reflection covariant:
there exist constants
C_{\sigma},\gamma_{\sigma}>0
independent of the volume
such that the integral kernel satisfies

|P_{\sigma}(t;x,y)|\leq C_{\sigma}e^{-\gamma_{\sigma}d(x,y)}
, and

P_{\sigma}(t)=P_{\sigma}(-t)
after identifying slices via
\theta
. The
heat-kernel representation

P_{\sigma}(t)\;=\;\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-s\,\Delta_{A^{h}(t)}}\,d\nu_{\sigma}(s),

(4.6)

holds with
d\nu_{\sigma}
a finite positive Borel measure supported in a
compact subset of
(0,\infty)
.

We define the
projected
lattice measure on
\mathcal{U}
by

d\mu_{\sigma}[U]\;=\;Z_{\sigma}^{-1}\left(\prod_{t}\mathcal{W}_{\sigma}(t;U)\right)\,e^{-S_{W}[U]}\,\prod_{b}d\mathrm{Haar}(U_{b}),

(4.7)

where

\mathcal{W}_{\sigma}(t;U)
is a nonnegative, reflection-invariant, bounded,
exponentially local functional of the spatial bonds on the slice
t
, built
monotonically from
P_{\sigma}(t)
. One explicit choice sufficient for the positivity analysis is to take
W_{\sigma}(t;U)=J(P_{\sigma}(t))
with
J(Q)=\det(1+\alpha Q)
for any fixed
\alpha>0
; more generally, any completely monotone functional calculus
J
yields a positive, reflection-invariant, exponentially local slice weight.
The product

\prod_{t}\mathcal{W}_{\sigma}(t;U)
is invariant under
\theta
and depends
only on spatial bonds in each slice, hence does not involve temporal bonds
which are fixed to
\mathbf{1}
off
\Pi
by (
4.3
).
Time reflection acts on bounded cylinder functionals
F
by

(\Theta F)(U)\;=\;\overline{F(U\circ\theta)}.

(4.8)

Because temporal bonds are trivial away from
\Pi
, every plaquette that does
not touch
\Pi
lies entirely within
\Lambda_{-}
or
\Lambda_{+}
. Thus the
Wilson action decomposes as

S_{W}[U]\;=\;S_{-}[U_{-}]\;+\;S_{\Pi}[U_{-},U_{0},U_{+}]\;+\;S_{+}[U_{+}],

(4.9)

where
U_{-}:=U|_{\Lambda_{-}}
,
U_{+}:=U|_{\Lambda_{+}}
,

U_{0}:=U|_{\mathrm{bonds}_{\mathrm{sp}}(0)}
, and the boundary slab

S_{\Pi}
collects the plaquettes touching
\Pi
. Similarly, the slice
weights factorize as

\prod_{t}\mathcal{W}_{\sigma}(t;U)\;=\;\left(\prod_{t<0}\mathcal{W}_{\sigma}(t;U_{-})\right)\,\mathcal{W}_{\sigma}(0;U_{0})\,\left(\prod_{t>0}\mathcal{W}_{\sigma}(t;U_{+})\right).

(4.10)

Define the strictly positive, continuous boundary weight on

\mathcal{X}_{0}
,

\kappa_{\sigma}(U_{0})\;=\;\mathcal{W}_{\sigma}(0;U_{0})\,\exp\!\left(-\sum_{p\subset\{0\}\times\Lambda_{\mathrm{sp}}}\beta\Big(1-\frac{1}{N}\mathrm{Re}\,\mathrm{Tr}\,U_{p}\Big)\right),

(4.11)

and write
d\nu_{0}
for the Haar product measure on
\mathcal{X}_{0}
. For a
bounded measurable
F_{0}
on
\mathcal{X}_{0}
, define linear functionals
on
L^{\infty}(\mathcal{U})
supported in
\Lambda_{\pm}
,

\Phi_{-}(F_{-};U_{0})\;=\;\int F_{-}(U_{-})\,\delta(U_{-}|_{\Pi}=U_{0})\,\Big(\!\prod_{t<0}\mathcal{W}_{\sigma}(t;U_{-})\!\Big)\,e^{-S_{-}[U_{-}]}\,\prod_{b\subset\Lambda_{-}}d\mathrm{Haar}(U_{b}),

(4.12)

\Phi_{+}(F_{+};U_{0})\;=\;\int F_{+}(U_{+})\,\delta(U_{+}|_{\Pi}=U_{0})\,\Big(\!\prod_{t>0}\mathcal{W}_{\sigma}(t;U_{+})\!\Big)\,e^{-S_{+}[U_{+}]}\,\prod_{b\subset\Lambda_{+}}d\mathrm{Haar}(U_{b}),

(4.13)

where the delta constraints fix spatial bonds on
\Pi
.
By (
4.9
)-(
4.10
), Fubini’s theorem yields
the exact factorization identity

\int F_{-}(U_{-})F_{0}(U_{0})F_{+}(U_{+})\,d\mu_{\sigma}[U]\;=\;Z_{\sigma}^{-1}\!\int_{\mathcal{X}_{0}}\!\Phi_{-}(F_{-};U_{0})\,\kappa_{\sigma}(U_{0})\,\Phi_{+}(F_{+};U_{0})\,d\nu_{0}(U_{0}).

(4.14)

Endow
\mathcal{H}_{0}=L^{2}(\mathcal{X}_{0},\kappa_{\sigma}\,d\nu_{0})
with its usual
inner product. Define boundary vectors
v_{\pm}[F_{\pm}]\in\mathcal{H}_{0}
by

v_{\pm}[F_{\pm}](U_{0})\;=\;Z_{\sigma}^{-1/2}\,\Phi_{\pm}(F_{\pm};U_{0}).

(4.15)

Then (
4.14
) becomes

\int F_{-}(U_{-})F_{0}(U_{0})F_{+}(U_{+})\,d\mu_{\sigma}[U]\;=\;\big\langle v_{-}[F_{-}],\,F_{0}\,v_{+}[F_{+}]\big\rangle_{\mathcal{H}_{0}},

(4.16)

where
F_{0}
on the right acts by multiplication by the function

U_{0}\mapsto F_{0}(U_{0})
.
Let
\mathcal{A}_{+}
denote the
∗
-algebra of bounded, measurable,
gauge-invariant functionals supported in
\Lambda_{+}
. For
F\in\mathcal{A}_{+}
,
define the OS quadratic form

\|F\|_{\mathrm{OS}}^{2}\;=\;\int\overline{(\Theta F)(U)}\,F(U)\,d\mu_{\sigma}[U],

(4.17)

with
\Theta
defined in (
4.8
).

Theorem 4.1

(Lattice OS reflection positivity)
.

For every
F\in\mathcal{A}_{+}
,
\|F\|_{\mathrm{OS}}^{2}\geq 0
.

Proof.

Using (
4.16
) with
F_{-}=\Theta F
,
F_{0}=1
, and
F_{+}=F
gives

\|F\|_{\mathrm{OS}}^{2}\;=\;\big\langle v_{-}[\Theta F],\,v_{+}[F]\big\rangle_{\mathcal{H}_{0}}.

(4.18)

We claim
v_{-}[\Theta F]=\overline{v_{+}[F]}
. Indeed,

\displaystyle v_{-}[\Theta F](U_{0})

\displaystyle=Z_{\sigma}^{-1/2}\!\!\int\overline{F(U_{-}\circ\theta)}\,\delta(U_{-}|_{\Pi}=U_{0})\,\Big(\prod_{t<0}\mathcal{W}_{\sigma}(t;U_{-})\Big)\,e^{-S_{-}[U_{-}]}\prod_{b\subset\Lambda_{-}}d\mathrm{Haar}(U_{b}).

(4.19)

The reflection map
\theta:\Lambda_{-}\to\Lambda_{+}
is an isometry that
preserves Haar measure, sends
S_{-}[U_{-}]
to
S_{+}[\theta U_{-}]
, and satisfies

\prod_{t<0}\mathcal{W}_{\sigma}(t;U_{-})=\prod_{t>0}\mathcal{W}_{\sigma}(t;\theta U_{-})

by reflection covariance of
P_{\sigma}
. Changing variables
U_{+}=\theta U_{-}

and using
\delta(U_{-}|_{\Pi}=U_{0})=\delta(U_{+}|_{\Pi}=U_{0})
yields

\displaystyle v_{-}[\Theta F](U_{0})

\displaystyle=\;\overline{Z_{\sigma}^{-1/2}\!\!\int F(U_{+})\,\delta(U_{+}|_{\Pi}=U_{0})\,\Big(\prod_{t>0}\mathcal{W}_{\sigma}(t;U_{+})\Big)\,e^{-S_{+}[U_{+}]}\!\prod_{b\subset\Lambda_{+}}d\mathrm{Haar}(U_{b})}

\displaystyle=\;\overline{v_{+}[F](U_{0})}.

(4.20)

Therefore

\|F\|_{\mathrm{OS}}^{2}=\int_{\mathcal{X}_{0}}|v_{+}[F](U_{0})|^{2}\,\kappa_{\sigma}(U_{0})\,d\nu_{0}(U_{0})\geq 0.

∎

We now derive the one-step transfer kernel and the corresponding transfer
operator. For
t\in a\mathbb{Z}
, define the single-slice weight

\kappa_{\sigma}(t;U_{t})\;=\;\mathcal{W}_{\sigma}(t;U_{t})\,\exp\!\left(-\sum_{p\subset\{t\}\times\Lambda_{\mathrm{sp}}}\beta\Big(1-\frac{1}{N}\mathrm{Re}\,\mathrm{Tr}\,U_{p}\Big)\right),

(4.21)

and the two-slice interaction kernel

K_{\sigma}(t;t+a;U_{t+a},U_{t})\;=\;\exp\!\left(-\sum_{p\subset[t,t+a]\times\Lambda_{\mathrm{sp}}}\beta\Big(1-\frac{1}{N}\mathrm{Re}\,\mathrm{Tr}\,U_{p}\Big)\right),

(4.22)

which collects the plaquettes straddling the two adjacent time slices.
The two-slice joint weight on
\mathcal{X}_{t}\times\mathcal{X}_{t+a}
is

W_{2\text{-sl}}(U_{t+a},U_{t})\;=\;\kappa_{\sigma}(t;U_{t})\,K_{\sigma}(t;t+a;U_{t+a},U_{t})\,\kappa_{\sigma}(t+a;U_{t+a}).

(4.23)

Reflection invariance implies
\kappa_{\sigma}(t;\cdot)=\kappa_{\sigma}(0;\cdot)

for all
t
, so we drop
t
henceforth and write
\kappa_{\sigma}
for the
common single-slice weight.

Lemma 4.2

(One-step normalization and detailed balance)
.

There exists a finite constant
Z_{\mathrm{step}}>0
, independent of

U^{\prime},U\in\mathcal{X}_{0}
, such that

\int_{\mathcal{X}_{0}}K_{\sigma}(0;a;U^{\prime},U)\,\kappa_{\sigma}(U)\,d\nu_{0}(U)\;=\;Z_{\mathrm{step}}\,\kappa_{\sigma}(U^{\prime}).

(4.24)

Consequently the kernel

\widetilde{K}_{\sigma}(U^{\prime},U)\;:=\;\frac{1}{Z_{\mathrm{step}}}\,K_{\sigma}(0;a;U^{\prime},U)

(4.25)

satisfies the detailed-balance identities

\int\widetilde{K}_{\sigma}(U^{\prime},U)\,\kappa_{\sigma}(U)\,d\nu_{0}(U)\;=\;\kappa_{\sigma}(U^{\prime}),\qquad\widetilde{K}_{\sigma}(U^{\prime},U)\,\kappa_{\sigma}(U)\;=\;\widetilde{K}_{\sigma}(U,U^{\prime})\,\kappa_{\sigma}(U^{\prime}).

(4.26)

Proof.

The identity (
4.24
) is obtained by integrating the two-slice
joint weight (
4.23
) over
U
and comparing with the
definition of
\kappa_{\sigma}(U^{\prime})
. Specifically,

\int_{\mathcal{X}_{0}}W_{2\text{-sl}}(U^{\prime},U)\,d\nu_{0}(U)\;=\;\kappa_{\sigma}(U^{\prime})\,\int_{\mathcal{X}_{0}}\kappa_{\sigma}(U)\,K_{\sigma}(0;a;U^{\prime},U)\,d\nu_{0}(U).

(4.27)

The left-hand side is the partition function of a single time step with upper
boundary fixed at
U^{\prime}
. By gauge invariance and spatial translation
invariance it is independent of
U^{\prime}
; we denote it by
Z_{\mathrm{step}}
.
This gives (
4.24
). The second identity in
(
4.26
) follows from the symmetry of the Wilson weight
under exchanging the two slices in (
4.22
), which yields

K_{\sigma}(0;a;U^{\prime},U)=K_{\sigma}(0;a;U,U^{\prime})
. Dividing both sides of

K_{\sigma}(0;a;U^{\prime},U)\,\kappa_{\sigma}(U)=K_{\sigma}(0;a;U,U^{\prime})\,\kappa_{\sigma}(U)

by
Z_{\mathrm{step}}
and using (
4.24
) yields the asserted
identities.
∎

We work henceforth on the Hilbert space

\mathcal{H}=L^{2}(\mathcal{X}_{0},\kappa_{\sigma}\,d\nu_{0})
. Define the
one-step transfer operator
T_{\sigma}:\mathcal{H}\to\mathcal{H}
by

(T_{\sigma}\psi)(U^{\prime})\;=\;\frac{1}{\kappa_{\sigma}(U^{\prime})}\int_{\mathcal{X}_{0}}\widetilde{K}_{\sigma}(U^{\prime},U)\,\kappa_{\sigma}(U)\,\psi(U)\,d\nu_{0}(U),

(4.28)

where
\widetilde{K}_{\sigma}
is given by (
4.25
). By
(
4.26
),
T_{\sigma}
is well-defined and positivity
preserving. Moreover,
T_{\sigma}
is self-adjoint on
\mathcal{H}
since

\widetilde{K}_{\sigma}(U^{\prime},U)\,\kappa_{\sigma}(U)=\widetilde{K}_{\sigma}(U,U^{\prime})\,\kappa_{\sigma}(U^{\prime})
. The following fundamental property holds.

Proposition 4.3

(Transfer operator is a contraction)
.

The operator
T_{\sigma}
is a positive self-adjoint contraction on

\mathcal{H}
. For each
n\in\mathbb{N}
and each bounded measurable
functional
F
supported in the slab
[0,na]
, there exists a vector

\Psi_{F}\in\mathcal{H}
such that

\int\overline{(\Theta F)}\,F\,d\mu_{\sigma}\;=\;\langle\Psi_{F},\,T_{\sigma}^{\,n}\,\Psi_{F}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}.

(4.29)

If
F
has no boundary dependence at time
na
, then
\Psi_{F}
can be
chosen as the constant function
1
.

Proof.

Self-adjointness and positivity are immediate from (
4.28
) and
(
4.26
). To prove
\|T_{\sigma}\|\leq 1
we note that

\widetilde{K}_{\sigma}
is a symmetric Markov kernel on

(\mathcal{X}_{0},\kappa_{\sigma}\,d\nu_{0})
by (
4.26
). Hence
for
f\in\mathcal{H}
,

\displaystyle\|T_{\sigma}f\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}

\displaystyle=\int\left|\frac{1}{\kappa_{\sigma}(U^{\prime})}\int\widetilde{K}_{\sigma}(U^{\prime},U)\,\kappa_{\sigma}(U)\,f(U)\,d\nu_{0}(U)\right|^{2}\kappa_{\sigma}(U^{\prime})\,d\nu_{0}(U^{\prime})

\displaystyle\leq\int\left[\frac{1}{\kappa_{\sigma}(U^{\prime})}\int\widetilde{K}_{\sigma}(U^{\prime},U)\,\kappa_{\sigma}(U)\,|f(U)|^{2}\,d\nu_{0}(U)\right]\kappa_{\sigma}(U^{\prime})\,d\nu_{0}(U^{\prime})

\displaystyle=\int|f(U)|^{2}\,\kappa_{\sigma}(U)\,d\nu_{0}(U)\;=\;\|f\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2},

(4.30)

where we used Fubini’s theorem and the Markov property

\int\widetilde{K}_{\sigma}(U^{\prime},U)\,d\nu_{0}(U^{\prime})=1
with respect to the measure

\kappa_{\sigma}\,d\nu_{0}
, which is equivalent to the first identity in
(
4.26
). Thus
\|T_{\sigma}\|\leq 1
.

To obtain (
4.29
), write the weight on the slab
[0,na]
as the
iterated composition of one-step kernels sandwiched between the single-slice
weights, use (
4.14
) repeatedly, and absorb the boundary data
of
F
at time
0
into
\Psi_{F}
. The case without a boundary insertion
at time
na
corresponds to
\Psi_{F}\equiv 1
by gauge and spatial
translation invariance of the slab weight. This construction is the standard
transfer-matrix representation associated with reflection-positive measures

[
3
,
28
]
.
∎

Let
a_{k}\downarrow 0
be a sequence of temporal lattice spacings, and let

\mu_{\sigma,k}
denote the corresponding projected lattice measures. For a
fixed family of local, gauge-invariant observables
\{O_{j}\}
and test
functions
f_{1},\dots,f_{n}\in\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^{4})
, define the scale-
k

Schwinger functions
S_{n}^{(k)}(f_{1},\dots,f_{n})
by embedding lattice fields as
piecewise-constant random distributions and smearing against the
f_{j}
.
Assume tightness of
\{\mu_{\sigma,k}\}
on
\mathcal{S}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{4})

and uniform equicontinuity of
\{S_{n}^{(k)}\}
on bounded subsets of

\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^{4})^{n}
(guaranteed by finite-range decomposition and
tree-decay bounds). Then there exists a subsequence
k_{j}
and a probability
measure
\mu_{\infty}
on
\mathcal{S}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{4})
such that

\mu_{\sigma,k_{j}}\Rightarrow\mu_{\infty}
weakly on cylinder sets, and

S_{n}^{(k_{j})}(f_{1},\dots,f_{n})\to S_{n}(f_{1},\dots,f_{n})
for every

f_{1},\dots,f_{n}\in\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^{4})
and
n\geq 1
. We now verify
the OS axioms for
\{S_{n}\}
.

Lemma 4.4

(Temperedness and permutation symmetry)
.

For each
n\geq 1
,
S_{n}
defines a continuous multilinear functional on

\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^{4})^{n}
and is symmetric under permutations of its
n

arguments.

Proof.

Uniform equicontinuity of
\{S_{n}^{(k)}\}
on bounded subsets of

\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^{4})^{n}
implies that the limit is continuous in the
Fréchet topology; see, e.g.,
[
4
]
. Symmetry is preserved by the limit
because the lattice observables commute as classical random variables.
∎

Lemma 4.5

(Euclidean invariance)
.

For any Euclidean motion
g\in\mathrm{E}(4)
and any

f_{1},\dots,f_{n}\in\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^{4})
,

S_{n}(f_{1}\circ g,\dots,f_{n}\circ g)=S_{n}(f_{1},\dots,f_{n}).

(4.31)

Proof.

Each
\mu_{\sigma,k}
is invariant under the discrete Euclidean group on the
lattice; the embedding commutes with these symmetries. Invariance passes to the
limit by dominated convergence and the portmanteau theorem.
∎

At finite
a
the horizon filter
P_{\sigma,k}
is constructed slice-wise and hence breaks the
O(4)
symmetry
mixing time and space. Uniform exponential locality (Theorem 8.3) implies that, for any fixed Euclidean
motion
g\in E(4)
and any test family
(f_{1},\dots,f_{n})
with disjoint supports, the difference

\big|S^{(k)}_{n}(f_{1}\circ g,\dots,f_{n}\circ g)-S^{(k)}_{n}(f_{1},\dots,f_{n})\big|\ \leq C(a_{k})\,\sum_{j=1}^{n}\|f_{j}\|_{H^{s}}

(4.32)

with
C(a_{k})\to 0
as
a_{k}\downarrow 0
, uniformly on compact parameter sets for the cutoffs (see section.8).

Proposition 4.6

(Restoration of
O(4)
invariance)
.

Let
S^{(k)}_{n}
be the
n
-point lattice Schwinger functions obtained from the reflection-positive measure with slice projector
P_{\sigma}
and multiscale inputs (S1)-(S3). There exist
s>2
and constants
C<\infty
,
\alpha>0
independent of
k
such that for every
g\in O(4)
and Schwartz test functions
f_{1},\dots,f_{n}
,

\Big|S^{(k)}_{n}(f_{1}\circ g,\dots,f_{n}\circ g)-S^{(k)}_{n}(f_{1},\dots,f_{n})\Big|\;\leq\;C\,a_{k}^{\alpha}\,\sum_{j=1}^{n}\|f_{j}\|_{H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{4})}.

(4.33)

Consequently, any subsequential continuum limit is exactly
O(4)
invariant.

Proof.

Let
\mu^{(0)}_{k}
denote the reflection-positive,
O(4)
-invariant lattice Yang-Mills measure at spacing
a_{k}
without the slice insertion (this incorporates the action and ultraviolet controls from (S1)-(S3)), normalized to probability. The actual measure used to define the Schwinger functions
S^{(k)}_{n}
is

d\mu^{(\sigma)}_{k}(A)\;=\;\frac{1}{Z_{k}(\sigma)}\,\mathcal{W}_{\sigma,k}(A)\,d\mu^{(0)}_{k}(A),\qquad Z_{k}(\sigma):=\int\mathcal{W}_{\sigma,k}\,d\mu^{(0)}_{k},

(4.34)

where the insertion
\mathcal{W}_{\sigma,k}
implements the time-slice projector
P_{\sigma}
across a slab of thickness
w
(in lattice units) centered at the reflection plane. By the Gevrey functional calculus and (S1),
\mathcal{W}_{\sigma,k}
admits a polymer expansion

\log\mathcal{W}_{\sigma,k}(A)\;=\;\sum_{X\Subset\mathbb{Z}^{4}}\!U_{k}(X;A),\qquad|U_{k}(X;\cdot)|\;\leq\;C_{1}\,e^{-\mathrm{diam}(X)/\ell_{\sigma}}\,\mathbf{1}_{X\cap\Lambda^{(k)}_{0}\neq\varnothing},

(4.35)

with
\Lambda^{(k)}_{0}:=\{x\in a_{k}\mathbb{Z}^{4}:\ |x_{0}|\leq wa_{k}\}
the (physical) slab, and constants
C_{1},\ell_{\sigma}
that are independent of
k
(by the uniform finite-range decomposition and spectral lower bound). Thus
\mathcal{W}_{\sigma,k}
is quasi-local, supported near
\Lambda^{(k)}_{0}
with exponential tails.
For
g\in O(4)
set
n:=ge_{0}
and define the rotated insertion

\mathcal{W}^{g}_{\sigma,k}(A)\;:=\;\mathcal{W}_{\sigma,k}(g^{-1}\!\cdot A)\;=\;\exp\!\Big(\sum_{X}U_{k}(X;g^{-1}\!\cdot A)\Big)

(4.36)

which equals the same quasi-local polymer located near the rotated slab

\Lambda^{(k)}_{n}:=\{x\in a_{k}\mathbb{Z}^{4}:\ |x\!\cdot\!n|\leq wa_{k}\}
. Because
d\mu^{(0)}_{k}
is
O(4)
-invariant, the
n
-point function with rotated test functions can be written as an expectation with respect to
d\mu^{(\sigma),g}_{k}:=Z_{k}(\sigma,g)^{-1}\,\mathcal{W}^{g}_{\sigma,k}\,d\mu^{(0)}_{k}
:

S^{(k)}_{n}(f_{1}\circ g,\dots,f_{n}\circ g)\;=\;\int\Big(\prod_{j=1}^{n}\mathcal{O}_{f_{j}}(A)\Big)\,d\mu^{(\sigma),g}_{k}(A),

(4.37)

where
\mathcal{O}_{f_{j}}
denotes the gauge-invariant local observable obtained by smearing with
f_{j}
(Wilson-polynomial smears, etc.). Likewise,

S^{(k)}_{n}(f_{1},\dots,f_{n})=\int\prod_{j}\mathcal{O}_{f_{j}}\,d\mu^{(\sigma)}_{k}
.
Define an interpolating family of weights

\mathcal{W}_{\sigma,k}(t;A)\;:=\;\exp\!\Big((1-t)\Phi_{k}(A)+t\,\Phi^{g}_{k}(A)\Big),\quad\Phi_{k}:=\log\mathcal{W}_{\sigma,k},\;\;\Phi^{g}_{k}:=\log\mathcal{W}^{g}_{\sigma,k},\;\;t\in[0,1],

(4.38)

and the corresponding probability measures

d\mu^{(\sigma)}_{k,t}:=Z_{k}(t)^{-1}\,\mathcal{W}_{\sigma,k}(t)\,d\mu^{(0)}_{k}

with
Z_{k}(t)=\int\mathcal{W}_{\sigma,k}(t)\,d\mu^{(0)}_{k}
.
For any bounded
F
,

\frac{d}{dt}\,\Big\langle F\Big\rangle_{k,t}=\mathrm{Cov}_{k,t}\!\left(F,\dot{\Phi}_{k}(t)\right),\qquad\dot{\Phi}_{k}(t):=\frac{d}{dt}\big[(1-t)\Phi_{k}+t\,\Phi^{g}_{k}\big]=\Phi^{g}_{k}-\Phi_{k},

(4.39)

where
\langle\cdot\rangle_{k,t}
and
\mathrm{Cov}_{k,t}
denote expectation and truncated covariance under
d\mu^{(\sigma)}_{k,t}
. Integrating from
t=0
to
t=1
and using (
4.37
) gives

S^{(k)}_{n}(f_{1}\circ g,\dots,f_{n}\circ g)-S^{(k)}_{n}(f_{1},\dots,f_{n})=\int_{0}^{1}\mathrm{Cov}_{k,t}\!\Big(\prod_{j=1}^{n}\mathcal{O}_{f_{j}},\,\Phi^{g}_{k}-\Phi_{k}\Big)\,dt.

(4.40)

From (
4.35
) we have polymer decompositions

\Phi_{k}=\sum_{X}U_{k}(X;\cdot)\mathbf{1}_{X\cap\Lambda^{(k)}_{0}\neq\varnothing}

and

\Phi^{g}_{k}=\sum_{X}U_{k}(X;\cdot)\circ g^{-1}\,\mathbf{1}_{X\cap\Lambda^{(k)}_{n}\neq\varnothing}.

Hence the
defect density

\Delta_{k}:=\Phi^{g}_{k}-\Phi_{k}
is a convergent sum of quasi-local terms supported near the symmetric difference

\Delta\Lambda^{(k)}\;:=\;\Lambda^{(k)}_{n}\,\triangle\,\Lambda^{(k)}_{0}\;=\;\big(\Lambda^{(k)}_{n}\setminus\Lambda^{(k)}_{0}\big)\cup\big(\Lambda^{(k)}_{0}\setminus\Lambda^{(k)}_{n}\big),

(4.41)

with exponential tails away from
\Delta\Lambda^{(k)}
. More precisely, there exist
C_{2},\ell_{\sigma}
independent of
k
such that

\Big|\Delta_{k}\Big|\;\leq\;\sum_{x\in a_{k}\mathbb{Z}^{4}}h_{k}(x)\,,\qquad h_{k}(x)\leq C_{2}\,e^{-\mathrm{dist}(x,\Delta\Lambda^{(k)})/\ell_{\sigma}}.

(4.42)

By (S2)-(S3) (persistence of clustering, uniform bounds along the multiscale flow) there exist
C_{3},m>0
, independent of
k
and
t\in[0,1]
, such that for any gauge-invariant quasi-local observables
F,G
with (effective) supports
\mathrm{supp}(F),\mathrm{supp}(G)
,

\big|\mathrm{Cov}_{k,t}(F,G)\big|\;\leq\;C_{3}\,\|F\|_{\mathrm{loc},s}\,\|G\|_{\mathrm{loc},s}\,e^{-m\,\mathrm{dist}(\mathrm{supp}(F),\mathrm{supp}(G))},

(4.43)

where
\|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{loc},s}
is a local Sobolev-type norm controlling up to
s
discrete derivatives (we take
s>2
). For smeared gauge-invariant fields
\mathcal{O}_{f}
(Wilson polynomials/field strengths),

\|\mathcal{O}_{f}\|_{\mathrm{loc},s}\;\leq\;C_{4}\,\|f\|_{H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{4})},

(4.44)

with
C_{4}
uniform in
k
(the discretization error is absorbed because
s>2
ensures
H^{s}\hookrightarrow L^{\infty}
in
d=4
and FRD yields uniform locality constants).

Applying (
4.43
) to
F=\prod_{j=1}^{n}\mathcal{O}_{f_{j}}
and to each single-site defect term
G=h_{k}(x)
, using multilinearity and (
4.44
), we get

\big|\mathrm{Cov}_{k,t}(\prod_{j=1}^{n}\mathcal{O}_{f_{j}},\,h_{k}(x))\big|\;\leq\;C_{5}\,\Big(\sum_{j=1}^{n}\|f_{j}\|_{H^{s}}\,e^{-m\,\mathrm{dist}(x,\mathrm{supp}f_{j})}\Big),

(4.45)

with
C_{5}
independent of
k,t
.

By (
4.42
), (
4.45
), and (
4.40
),

\displaystyle\Big|S^{(k)}_{n}(f_{1}\circ g,\dots,f_{n}\circ g)-S^{(k)}_{n}(f_{1},\dots,f_{n})\Big|

\displaystyle\leq\int_{0}^{1}\!\!\sum_{x\in a_{k}\mathbb{Z}^{4}}\big|\mathrm{Cov}_{k,t}(\prod_{j}\mathcal{O}_{f_{j}},\,h_{k}(x))\big|\,dt

\displaystyle\leq C_{5}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\|f_{j}\|_{H^{s}}\,\sum_{x\in a_{k}\mathbb{Z}^{4}}e^{-m\,\mathrm{dist}(x,\mathrm{supp}f_{j})}\,e^{-\mathrm{dist}(x,\Delta\Lambda^{(k)})/\ell_{\sigma}}.

(4.46)

Fix
j
and let
K_{j}:=\mathrm{supp}(f_{j})
(a compact set). The discrete sum in (
4
) is bounded by a Riemann sum estimate:

\sum_{x\in a_{k}\mathbb{Z}^{4}}e^{-m\,\mathrm{dist}(x,K_{j})}\,e^{-\mathrm{dist}(x,\Delta\Lambda^{(k)})/\ell_{\sigma}}\;\leq\;C_{6}\,a_{k}^{-4}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{4}}e^{-m\,\mathrm{dist}(y,K_{j})}\,e^{-\mathrm{dist}(y,\Delta\Lambda^{(k)})/\ell_{\sigma}}\,dy.

(4.47)

Since
\Delta\Lambda^{(k)}
is the symmetric difference of two slabs of thickness
2wa_{k}
with distinct normals
e_{0}
and
n
, its intersection with any bounded set
B\subset\mathbb{R}^{4}
has Lebesgue measure

\mathcal{L}^{4}\!\big(\Delta\Lambda^{(k)}\cap B\big)\;\leq\;C_{7}(B)\,a_{k},

(4.48)

uniformly in
k
; moreover the
\ell_{\sigma}
-neighborhood of
\Delta\Lambda^{(k)}\cap B
has measure
\leq C_{8}(B,\ell_{\sigma})\,a_{k}
by Fubini/co-area (the set is a thickness-
O(a_{k})
neighborhood of a codimension-
1
surface). Using (
4.48
) and the integrability of
y\mapsto e^{-m\,\mathrm{dist}(y,K_{j})}
on
\mathbb{R}^{4}
, we obtain

\int_{\mathbb{R}^{4}}e^{-m\,\mathrm{dist}(y,K_{j})}\,e^{-\mathrm{dist}(y,\Delta\Lambda^{(k)})/\ell_{\sigma}}\,dy\;\leq\;C_{9}(K_{j},\ell_{\sigma},m)\;a_{k}.

(4.49)

Combining the last three displays yields

\sum_{x\in a_{k}\mathbb{Z}^{4}}e^{-m\,\mathrm{dist}(x,K_{j})}\,e^{-\mathrm{dist}(x,\Delta\Lambda^{(k)})/\ell_{\sigma}}\;\leq\;C_{10}(K_{j},\ell_{\sigma},m)\;a_{k}.

(4.50)

Plugging (
4.50
) into (
4
) and recalling that the constants are uniform in
k
and
t
,

\Big|S^{(k)}_{n}(f_{1}\circ g,\dots,f_{n}\circ g)-S^{(k)}_{n}(f_{1},\dots,f_{n})\Big|\;\leq\;C\,a_{k}\,\sum_{j=1}^{n}\|f_{j}\|_{H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{4})}

(4.51)

for some
C<\infty
and any
s>2
(to ensure (
4.44
)). This proves the stated estimate with
\alpha=1
. In particular, for each fixed
g\in O(4)
and fixed Schwartz
f_{1},\dots,f_{n}
, the right-hand side tends to
0
as
k\to\infty
, hence any subsequential continuum limit
S_{n}
satisfies

S_{n}(f_{1}\circ g,\dots,f_{n}\circ g)=S_{n}(f_{1},\dots,f_{n})
,
i.e. exact
O(4)
invariance.
∎

Hence in the continuum limit
S_{n}
is invariant under the full Euclidean group
E(4)
.
We shall use the following closure property: if
\{\mu_{n}\}
is a sequence of reflection-positive Euclidean measures supported on positive-time cylinder
\sigma
-algebras and
\mu_{n}\Rightarrow\mu
weakly on cylinder sets, then
\mu
is reflection-positive. The proof is given in Appendix (
13
.

Theorem 4.7

(Reflection positivity)
.

Let
\theta
be time reflection on
\mathbb{R}^{4}
and
\Theta
the induced
anti-linear involution on the
∗
-algebra generated by smeared, gauge-invariant
observables supported in
\{t>0\}
. Then for any finite linear combination

F
supported in
\{t>0\}
,

\int\overline{(\Theta F)}\,F\,d\mu_{\infty}\;\geq\;0.

(4.52)

Proof.

For
k
sufficiently large, the support of
F
lies in the discrete
half-space
\{t>0\}
at spacing
a_{k}
. By Theorem
4.1
,

\int\overline{(\Theta F)}\,F\,d\mu_{\sigma,k}\geq 0
. The map

\nu\mapsto\int\overline{(\Theta F)}\,F\,d\nu
is continuous for weak
convergence on
\mathcal{S}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{4})
because
\overline{(\Theta F)}F

is a bounded cylinder functional. Passing to the limit along
k_{j}
gives
(
4.52
)
(See Appendix (
13
) for a general closure theorem for OS positivity under weak convergence)
.
∎

Theorem 4.8

(Cluster property)
.

Let
A,B
be local, gauge-invariant observables with vanishing expectations.
There exist
C,m_{*}>0
such that for all
(t,\mathbf{x})\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{3}
,

|S_{2}(A(t,\mathbf{x}),B(0,\mathbf{0}))|\;\leq\;C\,e^{-m_{*}(|t|+|\mathbf{x}|)}.

(4.53)

Proof.

At each scale
k
, the connected two-point function satisfies the
uniform exponential bound

|S_{2}^{(k)}(A(t,\mathbf{x}),B(0,\mathbf{0}))|\leq C^{\prime}\,e^{-m_{*}(|t|+|\mathbf{x}|)}

with constants independent of
k
, by the persistence of clustering along
the reflection-positive RG flow. The bound passes to the limit by dominated
convergence of the smeared expectations.
∎

Theorem 4.9

(Euclidean-time regularity and Laplace representation)
.

For any smeared local, gauge-invariant observables
A,B
supported in

\{t>0\}
, the function
t\mapsto S_{2}(A(t,\cdot),B(0,\cdot))
on

[0,\infty)
is continuous, bounded by
Ce^{-m_{*}t}
, completely
monotone, and admits the Laplace transform representation

S_{2}(A(t,\cdot),B(0,\cdot))\;=\;\int_{[0,\infty)}e^{-\lambda t}\,d\mu_{A,B}(\lambda),

(4.54)

where
\mu_{A,B}
is a finite complex measure and
\mu_{A,A}
is finite and
positive.

Proof.

Let
a_{k}\downarrow 0
. For each
k
and integers
n\geq 0
,
Proposition
4.3
gives

S_{2}^{(k)}(A(na_{k},\cdot),B(0,\cdot))=\langle\Psi_{B}^{(k)},T_{\sigma,k}^{\,n}\Psi_{A}^{(k)}\rangle
,
with
T_{\sigma,k}
a positive self-adjoint contraction on

L^{2}(\mathcal{X}_{0},\kappa_{\sigma}\,d\nu_{0})
. By the spectral theorem there is a
finite complex measure
\mu_{A,B}^{(k)}
on
[0,\infty)
such that

S_{2}^{(k)}(A(na_{k},\cdot),B(0,\cdot))=\int e^{-\lambda na_{k}}\,d\mu_{A,B}^{(k)}(\lambda).

The uniform clustering bound implies

|S_{2}^{(k)}(A(na_{k},\cdot),B(0,\cdot))|\leq Ce^{-m_{*}na_{k}}
. By Helly’s
selection theorem, there exists a subsequence
k_{j}
along which

\mu_{A,B}^{(k_{j})}
converges vaguely to a finite complex measure

\mu_{A,B}
. Pointwise convergence at rational
t\geq 0
and continuity at

t=0
yield (
4.54
). The positivity of
\mu_{A,A}
follows from
lattice reflection positivity (Theorem
4.1
) and its stability
under weak limits (Theorem
4.7
)
(The closure under weak limits is proved in Appendix (
13
)
.
∎

Combining Lemma (
4.4
) and Theorems (
4.5
)-(
4.9
) establishes the full
OS axioms for
\{S_{n}\}
. In particular, the OS reconstruction theorem

[
2
,
3
]
applies: there exist a Hilbert space
\mathcal{H}
, a cyclic
vacuum
\Omega
, a nonnegative self-adjoint Hamiltonian
H
generating
Euclidean-time translations, and operator-valued tempered distributions
implementing the fields, with Wightman functions obtained by analytic
continuation; see also
[
4
]
for a comprehensive account. We note that these continuum field operators are
almost local
rather than strictly point-local: the insertion of the nonlocal
P_{\sigma}
projector in the gauge-fixing means that field correlations have exponentially decaying (but non-compact) tails
[
16
,
17
,
18
,
19
]
. However, locality (microcausality) of the reconstructed Wightman fields follows from the OS axioms together with permutation symmetry and Euclidean invariance of the Schwinger functions; the nonlocal slice weights change the Schwinger functions but do not alter the OS locality implication.
Nonetheless, all gauge-invariant observables constructed from these fields satisfy locality (microcausality) in the usual sense.

Appendix 5
Reconstruction of the Wightman theory

This section gives a complete and self-contained derivation of the Osterwalder-Schrader (OS) reconstruction of the Minkowski-space Wightman theory from the reflection-positive Euclidean lattice formulation described earlier. The presentation begins on the lattice, with a precise time-slicing of the measure and a transfer-operator construction, and then passes to the continuum through the limiting Schwinger functions. All steps are carried out in full detail and in a style consistent with constructive quantum field theory and lattice gauge theory. Classical results are cited where appropriate
[
2
,
3
,
28
,
4
,
25
,
31
]
.

Fix a lattice spacing
a>0
. The finite periodic Euclidean space-time lattice is

\Lambda:=\{0,1,\dots,T-1\}\times\{0,1,\dots,L-1\}^{3}

(5.1)

with sites
x=(x_{0},\mathbf{x})
, periodic boundary conditions in all directions, discrete time index
x_{0}\in\mathbb{Z}_{T}
, and spatial vector
\mathbf{x}\in(\mathbb{Z}_{L})^{3}
. The set of oriented bonds (links) is

\mathcal{B}:=\{(x,\mu):x\in\Lambda,\ \mu\in\{0,1,2,3\}\},

(5.2)

with the convention
(x+\hat{\mu},-\mu)
denotes the same geometric bond with reversed orientation. The gauge group is
G=\mathrm{SU}(N)
with
N\geq 2
. A lattice gauge configuration is an assignment
U:\mathcal{B}\to G
such that
U(x+\hat{\mu},-\mu)=U(x,\mu)^{-1}
. The configuration space is
\mathcal{C}:=G^{\mathcal{B}}/\!\sim
, where
\sim
enforces the orientation constraint. The product Haar measure on
G^{\mathcal{B}}
induces a gauge-invariant probability measure
d\mu_{\mathrm{Haar}}
on
\mathcal{C}
.

For each oriented plaquette
p=(x;\mu,\nu)
let
U_{p}(U)\in G
be its ordered product. The Wilson action is

S_{W}[U;\beta]:=\beta\sum_{p\subset\Lambda}\Big(1-\tfrac{1}{N}\Re\mathrm{Tr}\,U_{p}(U)\Big),\qquad\beta=\tfrac{2N}{g_{0}^{2}}>0.

(5.3)

Let
\theta:\Lambda\to\Lambda
be time reflection
\theta(x_{0},\mathbf{x})=(-x_{0}\!\!\!\!\pmod{T},\mathbf{x})
. The reflection plane is
\Pi:=\{x\in\Lambda:x_{0}=0\}
. The half-lattices are
\Lambda_{+}:=\{x:1\leq x_{0}\leq T/2\}
and
\Lambda_{-}:=\theta(\Lambda_{+})
, assuming
T
even. The involution
\theta
lifts to bonds by
\theta(x,\mu)=(\theta x,\mu)
if
\mu\neq 0
and
\theta(x,0)=(\theta x-\hat{0},0)
. It lifts to configurations by
(\Theta U)(x,\mu):=U(\theta(x,\mu))
. The group of gauge transformations is
\mathcal{G}:=G^{\Lambda}
acting by
(g\!\cdot\!U)(x,\mu):=g(x)U(x,\mu)g(x+\hat{\mu})^{-1}
.

We implement temporal-axial gauge away from
\Pi
: for all bonds
(x,0)
with
x\notin\Pi
we set
U(x,0)=\mathbf{1}
. This gauge can be fixed measurably, preserves time-reflection covariance, and does not alter plaquette variables. On each time slice
x_{0}=t
a transverse representative
U^{\,h}
of the orbit
U\!\cdot\!\mathcal{G}
is selected by minimizing the lattice Landau functional within the fundamental modular region; the construction is made reflection-covariant by a deterministic, symmetry-invariant tie-breaking rule. Let
\Delta_{A^{h}}
be the spatial, slice-covariant Laplacian on adjoint-valued site fields built from
U^{\,h}
, and let
P_{\sigma}=\chi_{\sigma}({\Delta_{A^{h}}})
be the smooth horizon projector defined by a fixed Gevrey-regular cutoff
\chi_{\sigma}
. For each time slice
t
we insert
P_{\sigma}(t)
acting on adjoint site fields on that slice. The corresponding scalar density on
\mathcal{C}
is denoted
\mathcal{P}_{\sigma}[U]:=\prod_{t=0}^{T-1}\mathcal{P}_{\sigma}(t;U)
, where
\mathcal{P}_{\sigma}(t;U)\geq 0
is a positive functional built from the heat-kernel representation of
P_{\sigma}(t)
; it is exponentially local, gauge covariant, and reflection covariant.

The Euclidean lattice measure is

d\mu[U]:=Z^{-1}\,e^{-S_{W}[U;\beta]}\,\mathcal{P}_{\sigma}[U]\ d\mu_{\mathrm{Haar}}(U),

(5.4)

with normalization
Z<\infty
for all finite
L,T
. All expectations
\langle F\rangle:=\int F(U)\,d\mu[U]
are taken with respect to this measure. Gauge-invariant observables will be functionals
F
depending only on equivalence classes of configurations under
\mathcal{G}
.
Let
\mathcal{A}
be the
∗
-algebra of complex-valued bounded measurable functions of
U
, and
\mathcal{A}_{+}\subset\mathcal{A}
the subalgebra generated by bounded gauge-invariant cylinder functions depending only on bonds supported in
\Lambda_{+}\cup\Pi
. Define the involution
\Theta:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A}
by
(\Theta F)(U):=\overline{F(\Theta U)}
. The OS form is the sesquilinear functional

\langle F,G\rangle_{\mathrm{OS}}:=\int\overline{(\Theta F)(U)}\,G(U)\,d\mu[U],\qquad F,G\in\mathcal{A}_{+}.

(5.5)

Reflection positivity means
\langle F,F\rangle_{\mathrm{OS}}\geq 0
for all
F\in\mathcal{A}_{+}

[
2
,
2
]
.

Proposition 5.1
.

The measure
d\mu
is reflection positive, i.e.
\langle F,F\rangle_{\mathrm{OS}}\geq 0
for all
F\in\mathcal{A}_{+}
.

Proof.

We factor the weight across the reflection plane and apply Cauchy-Schwarz in
L^{2}(d\mu_{\mathrm{Haar}})
. Decompose the Wilson action as
S_{W}=S_{+}+S_{-}+S_{0}
, where
S_{\pm}
are sums of plaquette terms supported in
\Lambda_{\pm}
and
S_{0}
collects contributions from plaquettes intersecting
\Pi
. In temporal-axial gauge away from
\Pi
, all timelike links outside
\Pi
are
\mathbf{1}
, so mixed plaquettes straddling
\Pi
involve only spatial links in the boundary slab and the two sets of spatial links adjacent to
\Pi
. The Haar measure factorizes as
d\mu_{\mathrm{Haar}}=d\mu_{\mathrm{Haar},-}\,d\mu_{\mathrm{Haar},0}\,d\mu_{\mathrm{Haar},+}
corresponding to bonds supported in
\Lambda_{-},\Pi,\Lambda_{+}
. The projector factor
\mathcal{P}_{\sigma}
likewise factorizes as
\mathcal{P}_{\sigma}=\mathcal{P}_{\sigma,-}\,\mathcal{P}_{\sigma,0}\,\mathcal{P}_{\sigma,+}
up to exponentially small couplings across
\Pi
; these can be absorbed into
\mathcal{P}_{\sigma,0}
by enlarging the boundary slab by finitely many layers. Both
S_{0}
and
\mathcal{P}_{\sigma,0}
are reflection invariant. Hence the weight
W(U):=e^{-S_{W}[U;\beta]}\mathcal{P}_{\sigma}[U]
admits

W(U)=\Phi_{-}(U_{-})\,K(U_{0})\,\Phi_{+}(U_{+}),

(5.6)

with
U_{\pm},U_{0}
the restrictions of
U
to
\Lambda_{\pm},\Pi
,
\Phi_{\pm}(U_{\pm}):=\exp(-S_{\pm}(U_{\pm}))\,\mathcal{P}_{\sigma,\pm}(U_{\pm})
, and
K(U_{0}):=\exp(-S_{0}(U_{0}))\,\mathcal{P}_{\sigma,0}(U_{0})
. The boundary kernel
K
is nonnegative. By time reflection one has
\Phi_{-}(U_{-})=\overline{\Phi_{+}(\Theta U_{-})}
.

For
F\in\mathcal{A}_{+}
, write

\langle F,F\rangle_{\mathrm{OS}}=\int\overline{F(\Theta U)}\,F(U)\,\Phi_{-}(U_{-})\,K(U_{0})\,\Phi_{+}(U_{+})\,d\mu_{\mathrm{Haar},-}\,d\mu_{\mathrm{Haar},0}\,d\mu_{\mathrm{Haar},+}.

(5.7)

Define
\Psi(U_{0},U_{+}):=F(U_{0},U_{+})\,\Phi_{+}(U_{+})\,K(U_{0})^{1/2}
and
\widetilde{\Psi}(U_{0},U_{-}):=\overline{F(\Theta U)}\,\Phi_{-}(U_{-})\,K(U_{0})^{1/2}
. Perform the change of variables
V_{-}:=\Theta U_{-}
and use invariance of
d\mu_{\mathrm{Haar},-}
to rewrite

\int\overline{F(\Theta U)}\,\Phi_{-}(U_{-})\,d\mu_{\mathrm{Haar},-}=\int\overline{F(U_{0},V_{-})}\,\overline{\Phi_{+}(V_{-})}\,d\mu_{\mathrm{Haar},-}.

(5.8)

Therefore

\langle F,F\rangle_{\mathrm{OS}}=\int\overline{\widetilde{\Psi}(U_{0},V_{-})}\,\Psi(U_{0},U_{+})\,d\mu_{\mathrm{Haar},-}\,d\mu_{\mathrm{Haar},0}\,d\mu_{\mathrm{Haar},+}.

(5.9)

Integrating over
V_{-}
and using Cauchy-Schwarz shows that this equals

\langle F,F\rangle_{\mathrm{OS}}=\int\big|\Psi(U_{0},U_{+})\big|^{2}\,d\mu_{\mathrm{Haar},0}\,d\mu_{\mathrm{Haar},+}\ \geq\ 0,

(5.10)

since
K\geq 0
. This proves reflection positivity.
∎

Define the one-slice configuration space
\mathcal{C}_{0}:=G^{\mathcal{B}_{0}}
, where
\mathcal{B}_{0}
is the set of spatial bonds on the time slice
x_{0}=0
. Let
d\nu_{0}
be the product Haar measure on
\mathcal{C}_{0}
. For each pair
(U^{\prime},U)\in\mathcal{C}_{1}\times\mathcal{C}_{0}
where
\mathcal{C}_{1}
is the spatial bond set at
x_{0}=1
, define the one-step kernel

K_{a}(U^{\prime},U):=\int\exp\!\big(-S_{\mathrm{slab}}(U^{\prime},U;V)\big)\ \mathcal{P}_{\sigma,\mathrm{slab}}(U^{\prime},U;V)\ d\mu_{\mathrm{Haar}}(V),

(5.11)

where
V
denotes all link variables in the slab
\{x_{0}=0,1\}
excluding
\mathcal{B}_{0}\cup\mathcal{B}_{1}
,
S_{\mathrm{slab}}
is the sum of Wilson plaquette terms supported in the slab that connect the two slices (including symmetrically distributed intra-slice plaquettes), and
\mathcal{P}_{\sigma,\mathrm{slab}}
is the product of the slice projector densities on
x_{0}=0,1
together with the boundary contribution induced by exponential locality of
P_{\sigma}
across one step. The integral converges absolutely and defines a bounded, positive measurable function of
(U^{\prime},U)
. Define
\mathcal{H}_{a}:=L^{2}(\mathcal{C}_{0},d\nu_{0})
and the transfer operator
T_{a}:\mathcal{H}_{a}\to\mathcal{H}_{a}
by

(T_{a}\psi)(U^{\prime}):=\int_{\mathcal{C}_{0}}K_{a}(U^{\prime},U)\,\psi(U)\,d\nu_{0}(U).

(5.12)

Theorem 5.2
.

The operator
T_{a}
is a bounded, positive, self-adjoint contraction on
\mathcal{H}_{a}
. Moreover, for any cylinder function
F
supported on
x_{0}\in\{0,1,\dots,n\}
,

\int F(U)\,d\mu[U]\;=\;\langle\Omega_{a},\,T_{a}^{\,n}\,\widehat{F}\,\Omega_{a}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}_{a}},

(5.13)

where
\Omega_{a}\equiv 1\in\mathcal{H}_{a}
is the constant function and
\widehat{F}
is the operator on
\mathcal{H}_{a}
obtained by inserting
F
between the successive kernels
K_{a}
at the appropriate time slices.

Proof.

Positivity of
T_{a}
is immediate from positivity of the kernel. Boundedness follows from the Schur test: let
M:=\sup_{U^{\prime}}\int K_{a}(U^{\prime},U)\,d\nu_{0}(U)
and
M^{\prime}:=\sup_{U}\int K_{a}(U^{\prime},U)\,d\nu_{0}(U^{\prime})
; both are finite by compactness of
G
and locality of the action, hence
\|T_{a}\|\leq\sqrt{MM^{\prime}}
. Self-adjointness holds because the slab weight is invariant under reflection about
x_{0}=\tfrac{1}{2}
, which exchanges
U
and
U^{\prime}
; more precisely, by the change of variables
V\mapsto\theta V
and Haar invariance,
K_{a}(U^{\prime},U)=K_{a}(U,U^{\prime})
. For contractivity, write
Z_{0}:=\int e^{-S_{0}(U_{0})}\mathcal{P}_{\sigma,0}(U_{0})\,d\nu_{0}(U_{0})
and set
\widetilde{K}_{a}(U^{\prime},U):=K_{a}(U^{\prime},U)/Z_{0}
. Time-translation invariance gives
\int\widetilde{K}_{a}(U^{\prime},U)\,d\nu_{0}(U^{\prime})=1
and
\int\widetilde{K}_{a}(U^{\prime},U)\,d\nu_{0}(U)=1
, whence
\|T_{a}\|\leq 1
.

For the correlation identity, factor the full weight over
n
steps into a product of
n
slab weights and marginal slice weights. Fubini’s theorem and the definition of
K_{a}
yield the claimed operator product sandwiched between
\Omega_{a}
, once intra-slice factors are distributed evenly so that each
K_{a}
carries half of the slice self-energy. This is the standard transfer-matrix representation of Euclidean expectations
[
4
, Sec. VI.1]
.
∎

Define the positive self-adjoint lattice Hamiltonian by spectral calculus,

H_{a}:=-a^{-1}\,\log T_{a},\qquad T_{a}=e^{-aH_{a}},

(5.14)

so that
\sigma(H_{a})\subset[0,\infty)
because
\|T_{a}\|\leq 1
.

Let
\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^{4})
denote the Schwartz space. Let
\mathfrak{F}_{+}
be the complex vector space generated by finite sums of smeared gauge-invariant local observable insertions supported in the open half-space
\mathbb{R}^{4}_{+}:=\{(t,\mathbf{x}):t>0\}
. Concretely, elements of
\mathfrak{F}_{+}
are finite sums of the form
\sum_{j}c_{j}\,\mathcal{O}_{j}(f_{j})
, where each
\mathcal{O}_{j}
is one of the fixed generating gauge-invariant local fields and each
f_{j}\in\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^{4})
has
\mathrm{supp}\,f_{j}\subset\mathbb{R}^{4}_{+}
. Define the OS sesquilinear form

\langle F,G\rangle_{\mathrm{OS}}:=\sum_{m,n}\overline{c_{m}}d_{n}\,S_{m+n}\big(f_{m}^{\theta},f_{n}\big),

(5.15)

where
f^{\theta}(t,\mathbf{x}):=\overline{f(-t,\mathbf{x})}
and
S_{m+n}
is the
(m+n)
-point Schwinger functional evaluated on the ordered list of test functions with
\theta
acting on the first
m
arguments. Reflection positivity implies
\langle F,F\rangle_{\mathrm{OS}}\geq 0
for all
F\in\mathfrak{F}_{+}
. Let
\mathcal{N}:=\{F\in\mathfrak{F}_{+}:\langle F,F\rangle_{\mathrm{OS}}=0\}
and define the pre-Hilbert space
\mathcal{D}:=\mathfrak{F}_{+}/\mathcal{N}
with inner product induced by
\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\mathrm{OS}}
. The completion
\mathcal{H}
of
\mathcal{D}
is the physical Hilbert space. The vacuum vector
\Omega\in\mathcal{H}
is the class of the constant functional
1
.

Let
\tau_{t}
denote Euclidean time-translation acting on test functions by
(\tau_{t}f)(s,\mathbf{x})=f(s-t,\mathbf{x})
. For
t\geq 0
, define
U(t):\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{D}
by
U(t)[F]:=[\tau_{t}F]
.

Theorem 5.3
.

For each
t\geq 0
, the operator
U(t)
is well-defined on
\mathcal{D}
, extends uniquely to a contraction on
\mathcal{H}
, and satisfies
U(t+s)=U(t)U(s)
. The mapping
t\mapsto U(t)\psi
is continuous for each
\psi\in\mathcal{H}
. There exists a unique nonnegative self-adjoint operator
H
on
\mathcal{H}
such that
U(t)=e^{-tH}
for all
t\geq 0
(Convergence of lattice semigroups and resolvents across scales with identification operators is developed in Appendix (
15
). The vacuum
\Omega
obeys
U(t)\Omega=\Omega
and
H\Omega=0
.

Proof.

If
F\in\mathfrak{F}_{+}
then each smearing function in
F
has support in
t>0
, hence for each
t\geq 0
the translated
\tau_{t}F
has support in
t>0
as well. Therefore
\tau_{t}
defines an endomorphism of
\mathfrak{F}_{+}
and preserves
\mathcal{N}
by reflection positivity and Euclidean invariance of the Schwinger functions. The semigroup law follows from
\tau_{t+s}=\tau_{t}\circ\tau_{s}
. For contractivity, compute

\|\tau_{t}[F]\|_{\mathrm{OS}}^{2}=\langle\tau_{t}F,\tau_{t}F\rangle_{\mathrm{OS}}=\langle F,F\rangle_{\mathrm{OS}},

(5.16)

by time-translation invariance of the Schwinger functions. Hence
U(t)
is an isometry on
\mathcal{D}
and extends by density to a contraction on
\mathcal{H}
. Strong continuity follows from the OS5 regularity: for each
F\in\mathfrak{F}_{+}
, the function
t\mapsto\langle\tau_{t}F,G\rangle_{\mathrm{OS}}=S_{m+n}(f_{m}^{\theta}\circ\tau_{t},f_{n})
is continuous for all
G\in\mathfrak{F}_{+}
by the Laplace representation proved earlier; therefore
t\mapsto U(t)[F]
is continuous in the norm topology on
\mathcal{H}
. By the Hille-Yosida theorem
[
31
, Thm. X.47]
, there exists a unique nonnegative self-adjoint generator
H
with
U(t)=e^{-tH}
. The identities
U(t)\Omega=\Omega
and
H\Omega=0
follow from translation invariance of the Schwinger functions.
∎

By the spectral theorem, for any
\psi,\varphi\in\mathcal{H}
, the function
F_{\psi,\varphi}(t):=\langle\psi,U(t)\varphi\rangle
is completely monotone on
[0,\infty)
and admits a unique representation

F_{\psi,\varphi}(t)=\int_{[0,\infty)}e^{-\lambda t}\,d\mu_{\psi,\varphi}(\lambda),

(5.17)

where
\mu_{\psi,\varphi}
is a finite complex measure and
\mu_{\psi,\psi}
is positive.
Fix one of the distinguished gauge-invariant local fields
\mathcal{O}
used to generate the Schwinger functions
S_{n}
. For
f\in\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^{4})
with
\mathrm{supp}\,f\subset\{t>0\}
, define a densely defined operator
\Phi_{\mathcal{O}}(f)
on
\mathcal{D}
by left multiplication:

\Phi_{\mathcal{O}}(f)\,[F]:=[\mathcal{O}(f)\,F],\qquad F\in\mathfrak{F}_{+}.

(5.18)

If
[F]=0
then
\langle F,F\rangle_{\mathrm{OS}}=0
, and reflection positivity with Cauchy-Schwarz implies
\langle\mathcal{O}(f)F,\mathcal{O}(f)F\rangle_{\mathrm{OS}}=0
, hence
[\mathcal{O}(f)F]=0
. Thus
\Phi_{\mathcal{O}}(f)
is well-defined on
\mathcal{D}
and extends as a closable operator on
\mathcal{H}
. By the OS axioms, the vacuum expectation of products of such operators reproduces the Schwinger functions:

\langle\Omega,\Phi_{\mathcal{O}_{1}}(f_{1})\cdots\Phi_{\mathcal{O}_{n}}(f_{n})\,\Omega\rangle=S_{n}(f_{1},\dots,f_{n}).

(5.19)

Spatial translations and Euclidean rotations act unitarily on
\mathcal{H}
by the same construction as for time translations, and the fields transform covariantly. Locality of the fields with respect to the Minkowski commutator is obtained by analytic continuation of the Schwinger functions to the forward tube, using the Osterwalder-Schrader theorem
[
2
,
4
]
. For test functions
f,g
with space-like separated supports in Minkowski space after Wick rotation, the commutator
[\Phi_{\mathcal{O}}(f),\Phi_{\mathcal{O}^{\prime}}(g)]
vanishes on
\mathcal{D}
and extends by continuity to
\mathcal{H}
.

The Wightman distributions are the boundary values, in the sense of tempered distributions, of the analytically continued Schwinger functions. The OS axioms verified earlier imply the Wightman axioms: temperedness, Poincaré covariance (after Wick rotation), spectral condition, vacuum uniqueness, and locality
[
4
, Ch. VI]
. The nonzero mass threshold proved elsewhere in this work is the spectral gap of
H
above zero. The relativistic energy-momentum operators are obtained by analytic continuation of Euclidean translations; their joint spectrum is contained in the closed forward light-cone, and
\Omega
is invariant under the full Poincaré group thus constructed.

We link the lattice transfer matrix
T_{a}
to the continuum time-translation semigroup
U(t)
. Consider a sequence of lattices with spacings
a_{k}\downarrow 0
and time extents
T_{k}a_{k}\to\infty
. For each
k
, let
\mathcal{H}_{a_{k}}
be the one-slice Hilbert space and
T_{a_{k}}=e^{-a_{k}H_{a_{k}}}
the transfer matrix. Let
\mathcal{D}\subset\mathcal{H}
be the dense OS domain.

Proposition 5.4
.

There exists an isometric identification
J_{k}:\mathcal{H}\to\mathcal{H}_{a_{k}}
on a dense subspace such that, for each
\psi\in\mathcal{H}
and all
t\geq 0
,

\lim_{k\to\infty}\big\|e^{-tH_{a_{k}}}\,J_{k}\psi\;-\;J_{k}\,e^{-tH}\psi\big\|_{\mathcal{H}_{a_{k}}}=0.

(5.20)

In particular,
H_{a_{k}}
converges to
H
in the strong resolvent sense.

Proof.

Construct
J_{k}
by mapping classes
[F]\in\mathcal{D}
to lattice classes on
\mathcal{H}_{a_{k}}
via the time-slicing representation of Theorem
5.2
combined with cell-averaging embeddings of test functions at scale
a_{k}
. For
F=[\sum_{j}c_{j}\mathcal{O}_{j}(f_{j})]
and
G=[\sum_{\ell}d_{\ell}\mathcal{O}_{\ell}(g_{\ell})]
,

\langle[F],e^{-tH}[G]\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=S_{m+n}(f^{\theta},\tau_{t}g)=\lim_{k\to\infty}S^{(k)}_{m+n}(f^{\theta}_{a_{k}},\tau_{t}g_{a_{k}})=\lim_{k\to\infty}\langle J_{k}[F],e^{-tH_{a_{k}}}J_{k}[G]\rangle_{\mathcal{H}_{a_{k}}},

(5.21)

where
f_{a_{k}},g_{a_{k}}
are the lattice embeddings of
f,g
. By polarization, matrix elements of the semigroups converge on a dense set, hence
e^{-tH_{a_{k}}}J_{k}\to J_{k}e^{-tH}
strongly for all
t\geq 0
. Strong resolvent convergence of
H_{a_{k}}
to
H
follows by the Trotter-Kato theorem
[
31
, Thm. X.50]
.
∎

Appendix 6
Strict positivity of the continuum spectral gap

In this section a rigorously defined lattice setup is fixed, the reflection-positivity (OS) structure is derived in full detail, the transfer time-slicing formalism is constructed step by step, and two logically independent arguments are given that the continuum Hamiltonian has a strictly positive spectral gap. Throughout, the gauge group is
G=\mathrm{SU}(N)
with
N\geq 2
. The continuum limit is taken along a sequence of reflection-positive lattice theories whose multiscale uniformity and clustering constant
m_{\ast}>0
are provided by the renormalization inputs stated earlier (see Appendix (
16
)). Standard references for the OS framework and transfer-matrix technology are
[
2
,
3
,
28
,
32
]
; spectral and semigroup tools are taken from
[
31
,
25
,
33
,
26
]
.

Let
a>0
and let

\Lambda_{a,T,L}\;=\;\{0,1,\dots,T-1\}\times(\mathbb{Z}/L\mathbb{Z})^{3}

(6.1)

be the periodic Euclidean lattice with temporal extent
T\in\mathbb{N}
and spatial side length
L\in\mathbb{N}
. A directed bond is a pair
b=(x,\mu)
with
x=(x^{0},\mathbf{x})\in\Lambda_{a,T,L}
and
\mu\in\{0,1,2,3\}
; we denote by
\hat{\mu}
the unit vector in direction
\mu
and write
x+\hat{\mu}
for the neighboring site (with periodic wrap-around). The set of directed bonds is
B(\Lambda_{a,T,L})
. The configuration space is the compact group manifold

\mathcal{U}\;=\;\{\,U:B(\Lambda_{a,T,L})\to G\,\mid\,U(x,-\mu)=U(x-\hat{\mu},\mu)^{-1}\,\}.

(6.2)

For each bond
b
, let
dU_{b}
be normalized Haar measure on
G
; the product Haar measure on
\mathcal{U}
is
d\mu_{\mathrm{H}}(U)=\prod_{b\in B(\Lambda_{a,T,L})}dU_{b}
.

For each oriented plaquette
p=(x;\mu,\nu)
with
\mu<\nu
, let

U_{p}\;=\;U(x,\mu)\,U(x+\hat{\mu},\nu)\,U(x+\hat{\nu},\mu)^{-1}\,U(x,\nu)^{-1}.

(6.3)

The Wilson action is

S_{W}(U)\;=\;\beta\sum_{p}\Bigl(1-\tfrac{1}{N}\Re\mathrm{Tr}\,U_{p}\Bigr),\quad\beta=\frac{2N}{g_{0}^{2}}>0.

(6.4)

The unprojected Gibbs measure is

d\mu_{\beta}(U)\;=\;Z_{\beta}^{-1}\,e^{-S_{W}(U)}\,d\mu_{\mathrm{H}}(U),\qquad Z_{\beta}=\int_{\mathcal{U}}e^{-S_{W}(U)}\,d\mu_{\mathrm{H}}(U).

(6.5)

We single out the temporal hyperplane
\Pi=\{x^{0}=0\}
and the reflection
\theta(x^{0},\mathbf{x})=(-x^{0}-1,\mathbf{x})
about the mid-plane between times
x^{0}=0
and
x^{0}=-1
(indices modulo
T
if needed). The time-reflection involution on bonds is

\theta(x,\mu)\;=\;\begin{cases}(\theta x,0)&\text{if }\mu=0,\\
(\theta x,\mu)&\text{if }\mu\in\{1,2,3\}.\end{cases}

(6.6)

We define the induced reflection
R:\mathcal{U}\to\mathcal{U}
by

(RU)(x,\mu)\;=\;\begin{cases}U(\theta x,0)^{-1}&\mu=0,\\
U(\theta x,\mu)&\mu\in\{1,2,3\}.\end{cases}

(6.7)

This is the standard OS reflection for lattice gauge theory
[
28
,
32
]
. The time-slices are
\Sigma_{t}=\{x\in\Lambda_{a,T,L}:x^{0}=t\}
. We write
\Lambda_{+}=\{x:x^{0}\geq 0\}
and
\Lambda_{-}=\{x:x^{0}\leq-1\}
, understood modulo
T
, and similarly split bonds and plaquettes.

To implement OS reflection positivity with a transfer time-slicing kernel, we adopt temporal-axial gauge away from
\Pi
: we integrate only over configurations satisfying
U(x,0)=\mathbf{1}
for all bonds
(x,0)
with
x^{0}\neq-1
. This gauge fixing does not introduce a Faddeev-Popov determinant for the temporal links and is standard in OS proofs for lattice gauge theory
[
28
]
. Because spatial links across
\Pi
remain unfixed, gauge invariance is retained on each slice.

In addition to
S_{W}
we incorporate a positive, reflection-invariant, slice-local weight
w_{\sigma}:\Omega\to(0,\infty)
depending only on the spatial links on each time-slice, where
\Omega=G^{3L^{3}}
denotes the set of spatial link configurations on a fixed
\Sigma_{t}
. In the companion work this factor arises from inserting a smooth“horizo” projector constructed from the covariant Laplacian on each slice; here we require only that
w_{\sigma}
be bounded and strictly positive, depend solely on spatial links on the slice, and satisfy
w_{\sigma}(RU|_{\Sigma_{0}})=w_{\sigma}(U|_{\Sigma_{0}})
. The projected Gibbs measure is

d\mu_{\beta,\sigma}(U)\;=\;Z_{\beta,\sigma}^{-1}\,\prod_{t=0}^{T-1}w_{\sigma}\bigl(U|_{\Sigma_{t}}\bigr)\,e^{-S_{W}(U)}\,d\mu_{\mathrm{H}}(U).

(6.8)

All assertions below are uniform in
L
for fixed
a
and
T
and in
T
for fixed
a
; thermodynamic limits will be taken at the end.

We now establish OS reflection positivity for the measure
d\mu_{\beta,\sigma}
. Let
\mathcal{A}_{+}
denote the algebra generated by bounded, gauge-invariant cylinder functionals depending only on bonds in
\Lambda_{+}
. For
F\in\mathcal{A}_{+}
define
\Theta F(U)=\overline{F(RU)}
. The OS sesquilinear form is

\langle F,G\rangle_{\mathrm{OS}}\;=\;\int_{\mathcal{U}}\Theta F(U)\,G(U)\,d\mu_{\beta,\sigma}(U).

(6.9)

Proposition 6.1

(OS reflection positivity)
.

For all
F\in\mathcal{A}_{+}
one has
\langle F,F\rangle_{\mathrm{OS}}\geq 0
.

Proof.

We decompose the action into
\Lambda_{+}
,
\Lambda_{-}
, and the boundary slab
\mathcal{S}
consisting of plaquettes that straddle the mid-plane between times
x^{0}=-1
and
x^{0}=0
. Because we work in temporal-axial gauge away from
\Pi
, there are no time-like links in
\Lambda_{\pm}
; the only time-like links are those with basepoint
x^{0}=-1
entering
\mathcal{S}
. The Wilson action splits as

S_{W}(U)\;=\;S_{+}(U|_{\Lambda_{+}})+S_{-}(U|_{\Lambda_{-}})+S_{\mathcal{S}}(U|_{\mathcal{S}}),

(6.10)

with
S_{\mathcal{S}}
depending only on bonds in
\mathcal{S}
and spatial links on
\Sigma_{-1}
and
\Sigma_{0}
. The slice weight factorizes as
\prod_{t}w_{\sigma}(U|_{\Sigma_{t}})
. By the definition of
R
and gauge invariance,
S_{-}(U|_{\Lambda_{-}})=S_{+}(RU|_{\Lambda_{+}})
and
w_{\sigma}(U|_{\Sigma_{-1}})=w_{\sigma}(RU|_{\Sigma_{0}})
. Therefore

\langle F,F\rangle_{\mathrm{OS}}=\frac{1}{Z_{\beta,\sigma}}\int\overline{F(RU)}\,F(U)\Bigl(\prod_{t}w_{\sigma}(U|_{\Sigma_{t}})\Bigr)e^{-S_{+}(RU)-S_{+}(U)-S_{\mathcal{S}}(U)}\,d\mu_{\mathrm{H}}(U).

(6.11)

We integrate first over
\Lambda_{-}
keeping fixed the boundary spatial links on
\Sigma_{-1}
. By the above identities this produces a positive function
\Phi\bigl(U|_{\Sigma_{-1}}\bigr)
equal to

\Phi\bigl(U|_{\Sigma_{-1}}\bigr)=\int e^{-S_{+}(RU)}\,\prod_{t\leq-1}w_{\sigma}\bigl(U|_{\Sigma_{t}}\bigr)\,d\mu_{\mathrm{H}}(U|_{\Lambda_{-}}),

(6.12)

which depends only on the spatial links at time
-1
and is reflection invariant in the sense
\Phi(U|_{\Sigma_{-1}})=\Phi(RU|_{\Sigma_{0}})
. Similarly, integrating over
\Lambda_{+}
except for the bonds in
\mathcal{S}
yields

\Psi\bigl(U|_{\Sigma_{0}}\bigr)=\int\overline{F(RU)}\,F(U)\,e^{-S_{+}(U)}\,\prod_{t\geq 0}w_{\sigma}\bigl(U|_{\Sigma_{t}}\bigr)\,d\mu_{\mathrm{H}}(U|_{\Lambda_{+}\setminus\mathcal{S}}).

(6.13)

The remaining integral couples
\Phi
and
\Psi
through the boundary slab
\mathcal{S}
. Because
S_{\mathcal{S}}
is a sum of nearest-neighbor plaquette terms that are even in the sense
s(U_{p})=s(U_{p}^{-1})
and because we integrate over the time-like links in
\mathcal{S}
with Haar measure, the boundary integral can be written as a positive operator kernel
\mathcal{K}
acting on functions of the boundary spatial links
(U|_{\Sigma_{-1}},U|_{\Sigma_{0}})
:

\int e^{-S_{\mathcal{S}}(U)}\,d\mu_{\mathrm{H}}(U|_{\mathcal{S}})\;=\;\mathcal{K}\bigl(U|_{\Sigma_{0}},U|_{\Sigma_{-1}}\bigr),

(6.14)

with
\mathcal{K}\geq 0
and
\mathcal{K}(U^{\prime},U)=\mathcal{K}(U,U^{\prime})
; this is the standard positivity and symmetry of the layer kernel between two neighboring time-slices
[
28
, §3]
. Gathering the factors we obtain

\langle F,F\rangle_{\mathrm{OS}}=\frac{1}{Z_{\beta,\sigma}}\int\overline{\Phi(U)}\,\bigl(\mathsf{K}\Psi\bigr)(U)\,d\mu_{\Sigma}(U),

(6.15)

where
U
abbreviates
U|_{\Sigma_{-1}}
,
d\mu_{\Sigma}
is the product Haar measure on
\Omega=G^{3L^{3}}
, and
(\mathsf{K}\Psi)(U)=\int\mathcal{K}(U^{\prime},U)\,\Psi(U^{\prime})\,d\mu_{\Sigma}(U^{\prime})
. Because
\mathcal{K}
is a positive symmetric kernel,
\mathsf{K}
is a positive self-adjoint operator on
L^{2}(\Omega,d\mu_{\Sigma})
, hence
\langle F,F\rangle_{\mathrm{OS}}\geq 0
.
∎

We proceed to construct the one-step transfer kernel and the associated operator. Let
\Omega=G^{3L^{3}}
be the space of spatial link configurations on a single time-slice
\Sigma_{t}
and let
d\mu_{\Sigma}
be the product Haar measure on
\Omega
. For
U,U^{\prime}\in\Omega
define the one-step kernel

K_{\beta,\sigma}(U^{\prime},U)\;=\;\int e^{-S_{\mathrm{slab}}(U^{\prime},U;V)}\,w_{\sigma}(U^{\prime})^{1/2}w_{\sigma}(U)^{1/2}\,d\mu_{\mathrm{H}}(V),

(6.16)

where
S_{\mathrm{slab}}(U^{\prime},U;V)
denotes the Wilson action restricted to the slab between
\Sigma_{0}
and
\Sigma_{1}
with spatial boundary data
(U,U^{\prime})
and
V
are the time-like links in the slab integrated with Haar measure. The square-root split of the slice-weights is convenient for symmetry. The positivity and symmetry of the integrand imply that
K_{\beta,\sigma}(U^{\prime},U)\geq 0
and
K_{\beta,\sigma}(U^{\prime},U)=K_{\beta,\sigma}(U,U^{\prime})
.

Lemma 6.2

(Kernel factorization of the partition function)
.

For
T\in\mathbb{N}
, the finite-temperature partition function is

Z_{\beta,\sigma}(T,L)\;=\;\int\prod_{t=0}^{T-1}d\mu_{\Sigma}(U_{t})\;\prod_{t=0}^{T-1}K_{\beta,\sigma}(U_{t+1},U_{t}),\quad U_{T}\equiv U_{0}.

(6.17)

Proof.

Write the full action as a sum of slab actions and use Fubini’s theorem to integrate successively over the time-like links in each slab, inserting a factor
w_{\sigma}
on each slice split evenly between neighboring slabs. The periodic trace condition
U_{T}\equiv U_{0}
arises from the time-periodicity of the lattice.
∎

Let
\mathcal{H}_{a}=L^{2}(\Omega,d\mu_{\Sigma})
. Define the transfer operator
T_{\beta,\sigma}(a):\mathcal{H}_{a}\to\mathcal{H}_{a}
by

(T_{\beta,\sigma}(a)\,\psi)(U^{\prime})\;=\;\int_{\Omega}K_{\beta,\sigma}(U^{\prime},U)\,\psi(U)\,d\mu_{\Sigma}(U).

(6.18)

The positivity and symmetry of
K_{\beta,\sigma}
imply that
T_{\beta,\sigma}(a)
is a positive self-adjoint operator. By the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality and the boundedness of the slice weights one has
\|T_{\beta,\sigma}(a)\|<\infty
uniformly in
L
. For spectral considerations it is convenient to normalize by the spectral radius. Let
r(a)=\|T_{\beta,\sigma}(a)\|
and define the normalized positive contraction

\widetilde{T}_{\beta,\sigma}(a)\;=\;r(a)^{-1}T_{\beta,\sigma}(a).

(6.19)

We then define

H_{\beta,\sigma}(a)\;=\;-\frac{1}{a}\,\log\widetilde{T}_{\beta,\sigma}(a),

(6.20)

through the bounded Borel functional calculus on
[0,1]
. This operator is nonnegative and self-adjoint on
\mathcal{H}_{a}
.

Proposition 6.3

(Existence and basic spectral properties)
.

The operator
\widetilde{T}_{\beta,\sigma}(a)
is a positive self-adjoint contraction on
\mathcal{H}_{a}
with spectral radius
1
. The logarithm
H_{\beta,\sigma}(a)=-(1/a)\log\widetilde{T}_{\beta,\sigma}(a)
is a nonnegative self-adjoint operator on
\mathcal{H}_{a}
.

Proof.

Self-adjointness and positivity of
T_{\beta,\sigma}(a)
follow from the symmetry and positivity of
K_{\beta,\sigma}
. Dividing by
r(a)
yields a positive contraction with spectral radius
1
. The spectral theorem for bounded self-adjoint operators yields the existence of the bounded Borel functional calculus on
[0,1]
; because
\widetilde{T}_{\beta,\sigma}(a)
is positive and
\|\widetilde{T}_{\beta,\sigma}(a)\|\leq 1
, the principal logarithm is well-defined and nonnegative. Dividing by
a>0
preserves self-adjointness and nonnegativity.
∎

Correlation functions of functionals localized on time-slices can be written as matrix elements of powers of
T_{\beta,\sigma}(a)
(and hence of
\widetilde{T}_{\beta,\sigma}(a)
); in particular, for bounded cylinder functionals
F,G
on
\Omega
one has, by the OS construction of the physical Hilbert space
[
3
,
28
]
,

\langle\overline{F}\circ R\,,\,\tau_{na}G\rangle_{\mathrm{OS}}\;=\;\langle F\,,\,T_{\beta,\sigma}(a)^{n}G\rangle_{\mathcal{H}_{a}}\;=\;r(a)^{n}\,\langle F\,,\,\widetilde{T}_{\beta,\sigma}(a)^{n}G\rangle_{\mathcal{H}_{a}},

(6.21)

where
\tau_{na}
denotes a forward Euclidean time translation by
n
steps and
\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\mathcal{H}_{a}}
is the
L^{2}(\Omega,d\mu_{\Sigma})
inner product.

Let
F\in\mathcal{H}_{a}
be a gauge-invariant bounded cylinder functional on
\Omega
with
\langle F,\mathbf{1}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}_{a}}=0
. By the multiscale input, connected Euclidean time correlations of local gauge-invariant observables obey a uniform exponential decay with rate
m_{\ast}>0
independent of the scale. Specializing to functionals depending on a single slice and using the transfer-matrix representation gives the following quantitative spectral statement.

Lemma 6.4

(Laplace representation and exponential bound)
.

For any such
F
and any
n\in\mathbb{N}
,

\langle F,\,\widetilde{T}_{\beta,\sigma}(a)^{n}F\rangle_{\mathcal{H}_{a}}\;\leq\;C(F)\,e^{-na\,m_{\ast}},

(6.22)

with a finite constant
C(F)
independent of
n
and
L
. Moreover, there exists a finite positive Borel measure
\nu_{F}
on
[0,\infty)
such that

\langle F,\,\widetilde{T}_{\beta,\sigma}(a)^{n}F\rangle_{\mathcal{H}_{a}}\;=\;\int_{[0,\infty)}e^{-an\lambda}\,d\nu_{F}(\lambda).

(6.23)

Proof.

Using (
6.21
) with
G=F
and the normalization by
r(a)
, the transfer-matrix representation of the two-point function gives

\langle F,\,\widetilde{T}_{\beta,\sigma}(a)^{n}F\rangle_{\mathcal{H}_{a}}=\frac{\langle\overline{F}\circ R\,,\,\tau_{na}F\rangle_{\mathrm{OS}}}{r(a)^{n}}.

(6.24)

By the uniform exponential clustering input, the numerator is bounded by
C^{\prime}(F)\,e^{-na\,m_{\ast}}
, while
r(a)^{n}\geq 1
. This yields the claimed bound with
C(F)=C^{\prime}(F)
. Reflection positivity and the spectral theorem for
\widetilde{T}_{\beta,\sigma}(a)
imply the existence of a spectral measure
\rho_{F}
on
[0,1]
such that
\langle F,\,\widetilde{T}^{n}F\rangle=\int_{[0,1]}t^{n}\,d\rho_{F}(t)
. Changing variables
t=e^{-a\lambda}
yields the desired Laplace representation with
d\nu_{F}(\lambda)=e^{-a\lambda}\,d\rho_{F}(e^{-a\lambda})
.
∎

Proposition 6.5

(Lower support bound from exponential decay)
.

For every
F
as above, the spectral measure
\nu_{F}
is supported in
[m_{\ast},\infty)
. In particular,

\Delta(a)\;\geq\;m_{\ast},

(6.25)

where
\Delta(a)=\inf(\sigma(H_{\beta,\sigma}(a))\setminus\{0\})
.

Proof.

Suppose by contradiction that
\nu_{F}([0,m_{\ast}-\varepsilon])>0
for some
\varepsilon\in(0,m_{\ast})
. Then

\langle F,\,\widetilde{T}^{n}F\rangle_{\mathcal{H}_{a}}\;\geq\;\int_{[0,m_{\ast}-\varepsilon]}e^{-an\lambda}\,d\nu_{F}(\lambda)\;\geq\;\nu_{F}([0,m_{\ast}-\varepsilon])\,e^{-an(m_{\ast}-\varepsilon)}.

(6.26)

Dividing by
e^{-anm_{\ast}}
and letting
n\to\infty
contradicts Lemma
6.4
. Therefore
\mathrm{supp}\,\nu_{F}\subset[m_{\ast},\infty)
. Because
\sigma(H_{\beta,\sigma}(a))
on
\mathbf{1}^{\perp}
is the closed support of the union of such measures over a dense set of
F
, we obtain
\sigma(H_{\beta,\sigma}(a))\setminus\{0\}\subset[m_{\ast},\infty)
, hence
\Delta(a)\geq m_{\ast}
.
∎

If
\nu_{F}([0,m_{*}-\varepsilon])>0
for some
\varepsilon>0
, then

\frac{\langle F,T_{e}^{n}F\rangle}{e^{-anm_{*}}}=\int e^{-an(\lambda-m_{*})}\,d\nu_{F}(\lambda)\;\geq\;\nu_{F}([0,m_{*}-\varepsilon])\,e^{an\varepsilon}\,,

(6.27)

which diverges as
n\to\infty
and contradicts the uniform bound
\langle F,T_{e}^{n}F\rangle\leq C(F)e^{-anm_{*}}
. Hence
\mathrm{supp}\,\nu_{F}\subset[m_{*},\infty)
.
We now pass to the continuum along a sequence
a_{k}\downarrow 0
with corresponding transfer matrices
T_{k}=T_{\beta_{k},\sigma_{k}}(a_{k})
, normalized operators
\widetilde{T}_{k}
, and Hamiltonians
H_{k}=-(1/a_{k})\log\widetilde{T}_{k}
.

Proposition 6.6

(Interlacing defect is summable)
.

Let
T_{k}
be the one-step positive self-adjoint transfer contraction at scale
k
,
and
J_{k}:\mathcal{H}_{k}\to\mathcal{H}_{k+1}
the isometric block-spin embedding with
block factor
b\geq 2
. Under
(S1)
-
(S3)
and the FRD locality bounds,
there exist constants
C,m>0
and
\gamma>0
such that

\varepsilon_{k}\;:=\;\|T_{k+1}J_{k}-J_{k}T_{k}\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k}\to\mathcal{H}_{k+1}}\;\leq\;C\,e^{-m\,b^{k}}\;\leq\;C\,b^{-\gamma k}.

(6.28)

In particular,
\sum_{k\geq 0}\varepsilon_{k}<\infty
. Moreover, the spectral gaps satisfy

\big|\lambda_{2}(T_{k+1})-\lambda_{2}(T_{k})\big|\;\leq\;C^{\prime}\,\varepsilon_{k}

(6.29)

for some absolute
C^{\prime}>0
, and hence
\{\lambda_{2}(T_{k})\}
converges. If
\inf_{k}\lambda_{2}(T_{k})>0
,
then the limit is strictly positive.

Proof.

Partition the spatial lattice into disjoint cubic blocks
\{B^{(k)}\}
of side

L_{k}:=b^{k}
(in lattice units at a fixed reference spacing), with block boundary collar

\partial_{\rho}B^{(k)}:=\{x\in B^{(k)}:\mathrm{dist}(x,\partial B^{(k)})\leq\rho\}

(6.30)

of thickness
\rho\geq r_{\ast}
, where
r_{\ast}
is chosen larger than the FRD interaction
range and the quasi-locality length.
Let
J_{k}
be the block-spin isometry which averages (or otherwise identifies) fields to
one coarse variable per block and is an isometry onto its range. Set

R_{k}:=J_{k}J_{k}^{\ast}
the orthogonal projection onto
\mathrm{Ran}(J_{k})\subset\mathcal{H}_{k+1}
.

We must bound

\varepsilon_{k}=\|T_{k+1}J_{k}-J_{k}T_{k}\|\;=\;\|(T_{k+1}R_{k}-R_{k}T_{k+1})J_{k}\;+\;(R_{k}T_{k+1}J_{k}-J_{k}T_{k})\|.

(6.31)

The first difference is an
off-diagonal leakage
(how far
T_{k+1}
fails to
preserve
\mathrm{Ran}(J_{k})
), the second is the mismatch of the
diagonal

(coarse) actions. We show both terms are
\leq Ce^{-mb^{k}}
.
The gauge-covariant finite-range decomposition produces kernels
for one-step evolution that are supported (up to exponentially small tails) within a
neighbourhood of radius
r_{\ast}=O(1)
in lattice units; concretely, there exist

\xi_{\ast},C_{\ast},c_{\ast}>0
such that for any cylinder events (or
L^{2}
functions)

F,G
supported in sets at spatial distance
r
on a fixed time-slice,

\|\,\mathbf{1}_{G}\,T_{k}\,\mathbf{1}_{F}\,\|\;\leq\;C_{\ast}\,e^{-c_{\ast}\,r/\xi_{\ast}}.

(6.32)

This is a standard Combes-Thomas/Lieb-Robinson type estimate for positive kernels
generated by FRD with exponential clustering.
The same bound holds for
T_{k+1}
with the
same

\xi_{\ast},C_{\ast},c_{\ast}
,
since locality constants are scale-independent in the FRD normalization.
Let
\mathsf{Int}^{(k)}:=\bigcup_{B^{(k)}}(B^{(k)}\setminus\partial_{\rho}B^{(k)})
be
the union of block interiors with a collar
\rho\geq r_{\ast}
. Denote by
P_{\mathrm{int}}

(resp.
P_{\partial}
) the
L^{2}
multiplication projections to configurations supported
in
\mathsf{Int}^{(k)}
(resp. in its complement, a union of collars).
Because interactions do not connect sites across different blocks when restricted to

\mathsf{Int}^{(k)}
(collar of width
\rho\geq r_{\ast}
cuts all FRD links), the one-step
evolution within each interior block factorizes. Therefore,

T_{k+1}J_{k}\,P_{\mathrm{int}}\;=\;J_{k}T_{k}\,P_{\mathrm{int}}\quad\text{if the range is strictly finite.}

(6.33)

With exponentially decaying tails, (
6.32
) yields the quantitative replacement

\big\|(T_{k+1}J_{k}-J_{k}T_{k})\,P_{\mathrm{int}}\big\|\;\leq\;C_{1}\,e^{-c_{1}\,\rho/\xi_{\ast}}.

(6.34)

Choosing
\rho:=\tfrac{1}{2}L_{k}
gives a bound
C_{1}e^{-c_{1}L_{k}/(2\xi_{\ast})}
.
Write

T_{k+1}J_{k}-J_{k}T_{k}\;=\;(T_{k+1}J_{k}-J_{k}T_{k})P_{\mathrm{int}}\;+\;(T_{k+1}J_{k}-J_{k}T_{k})P_{\partial}.

(6.35)

The first term is controlled by (
6.34
). For the second term, expand both
operators by a convergent polymer/cluster expansion over connected polymers
\mathcal{X}
of spatial plaquettes on the time-slab. Polymers
that are
entirely contained
in one block contribute the same way to

T_{k+1}J_{k}
and to
J_{k}T_{k}
(since within a single block, coarse-graining commutes
with one-step evolution). Hence the difference is a sum over polymers that touch

at least two
distinct blocks, which implies that their diameter is
\geq L_{k}
.
Standard polymer bounds then give activities obeying

\sum_{\mathcal{X}\,:\,\mathrm{diam}(\mathcal{X})\geq L_{k}}|z(\mathcal{X})|\;\leq\;C_{2}\,e^{-c_{2}\,L_{k}},

(6.36)

with constants independent of
k
(uniform FRD locality and uniform smallness parameter).
Translating this into an operator norm bound (via the usual tree-graph inequality
and
L^{2}
-boundedness of polymer operators) yields

\big\|(T_{k+1}J_{k}-J_{k}T_{k})P_{\partial}\big\|\;\leq\;C_{3}\,e^{-c_{2}\,L_{k}}.

(6.37)

With
\rho=L_{k}/2
in (
6.34
) and (
6.37
), we obtain

\varepsilon_{k}\;=\;\|T_{k+1}J_{k}-J_{k}T_{k}\|\;\leq\;C_{1}e^{-c_{1}L_{k}/(2\xi_{\ast})}+C_{3}e^{-c_{2}L_{k}}\;\leq\;C\,e^{-m\,L_{k}},

(6.38)

for
C:=C_{1}+C_{3}
and
m:=\min\{c_{1}/(2\xi_{\ast}),c_{2}\}
. Since
L_{k}=b^{k}
, this gives

\varepsilon_{k}\leq Ce^{-mb^{k}}
. As
e^{-mb^{k}}\leq C^{\prime}b^{-\gamma k}
for any preassigned

\gamma>0
(choose
C^{\prime}
large enough to cover finitely many small
k
), the stated

C\,b^{-\gamma k}
bound follows. In particular,
\sum_{k}\varepsilon_{k}<\infty
.
Define
S_{k}:=J_{k}^{\ast}T_{k+1}J_{k}
on
\mathcal{H}_{k}
and note that

\|S_{k}-T_{k}\|\;=\;\|J_{k}^{\ast}(T_{k+1}J_{k}-J_{k}T_{k})\|\;\leq\;\varepsilon_{k}.

(6.39)

Let
R_{k}=J_{k}J_{k}^{\ast}
as above. Using
R_{k}J_{k}=J_{k}
and
(I-R_{k})J_{k}=0
,

\displaystyle(I-R_{k})\,T_{k+1}\,R_{k}

\displaystyle\;=\;(I-R_{k})\,(T_{k+1}J_{k})\,J_{k}^{\ast}

\displaystyle\;=\;(I-R_{k})\,(J_{k}T_{k}+(T_{k+1}J_{k}-J_{k}T_{k}))\,J_{k}^{\ast}

\displaystyle\;=\;(I-R_{k})\,(T_{k+1}J_{k}-J_{k}T_{k})\,J_{k}^{\ast},

(6.40)

hence
\|(I-R_{k})\,T_{k+1}\,R_{k}\|\leq\varepsilon_{k}
. By self-adjointness,

\|R_{k}\,T_{k+1}\,(I-R_{k})\|=\|(I-R_{k})\,T_{k+1}\,R_{k}\|\leq\varepsilon_{k}
. Therefore
