P_{\sigma}(t;U)\;=\;\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-s\,\Delta_{A^{\,h}(t)}}\,d\nu_{\sigma}(s).

(10.8)

Since
e^{-s\Delta_{A^{\,h}(t)}}
has a nonnegative integral kernel and is positivity preserving on functions
[
4
]
, the kernel of
P_{\sigma}(t;U)
is entrywise nonnegative and decays exponentially off-diagonal uniformly in
U
restricted to the slice fundamental modular region. Reflection covariance
P_{\sigma}(t;\theta U)=P_{\sigma}(t;U)
holds by construction.

Lemma 10.1

(Slice-wise FMR selection and positivity)
.

There exists a measurable, reflection-covariant slice selector
h:U(\Lambda)\to G(\Lambda)
such that for each time slice
t
the transformed configuration
U^{h}
lies in the slice FMR, and the Faddeev-Popov operator has strictly positive spectrum on the complement of constants. For any Gevrey cutoff
\chi_{\sigma}
with support in
[0,2\sigma]
, the associated horizon projector

P_{\sigma}(t;U)=\chi_{\sigma}\!\big({\Delta_{A^{\,h}(t)}}\big)

is a bounded positive contraction with an entrywise nonnegative, exponentially decaying kernel, and is reflection covariant.

Proof.

Measurability and reflection covariance of
h
follow from slice-wise Landau minimization with a reflection-invariant lexicographic tie-breaker. The heat-kernel representation

P_{\sigma}(t)=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-s\Delta_{A^{\,h}(t)}}\,d\nu_{\sigma}(s)

with
d\nu_{\sigma}
finite positive and supported in
(0,\infty)
implies positivity and exponential locality of the kernel, as
e^{-s\Delta_{A^{\,h}(t)}}
has a nonnegative kernel with Gaussian off-diagonal bounds. Positivity of the FP determinant on the complement of constants is standard on FMR slices and is inherited by the Jacobian factor entering the projected measure.
∎

We define the
horizon-projected weight
by a slice-wise positive-type insertion

\mathcal{Q}_{\sigma}(U)\;=\;\prod_{t\in\mathbb{Z}/L_{0}\mathbb{Z}}\Gamma_{\sigma}\bigl(P_{\sigma}(t;U)\bigr),\qquad\Gamma_{\sigma}(P)\;=\;\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\exp\bigl(-\langle\phi,(\mathbf{1}-P)\phi\rangle\bigr)\,d\gamma(\phi),

(10.9)

where
d=\dim\bigl(\ell^{2}(\mathbb{Z}/L_{1}\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}/L_{2}\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}/L_{3}\mathbb{Z};\,\mathfrak{su}(N))\bigr)
,
d\gamma
is the centered Gaussian probability measure with covariance
\mathbf{1}
, and
\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle
is the
\ell^{2}
inner product on the slice. The map
P\mapsto\Gamma_{\sigma}(P)
is continuous and satisfies
0<c_{-}\leq\Gamma_{\sigma}(P)\leq c_{+}<\infty
uniformly in
P
because
0\leq\mathbf{1}-P\leq\mathbf{1}
. Moreover,
\Gamma_{\sigma}(P)
is of positive type in the sense required for reflection positivity (it is a Laplace transform of a positive quadratic form in the fields). The projected Gibbs measure is

d\nu_{\beta,\sigma}(U)\;=\;Z_{\beta,\sigma}^{-1}\,\mathcal{Q}_{\sigma}(U)\,e^{-S_{W}(U)}\,d\mu_{\rm Haar}(U),

(10.10)

with normalization
Z_{\beta,\sigma}
. Gauge invariance and reflection covariance are immediate from (
10.9
).

Let
\mathscr{A}_{+}
be the
∗
-algebra of bounded, gauge-invariant cylinder functions on
\mathcal{U}(\Lambda)
depending only on links in
\mathcal{B}_{+}\cup\mathcal{B}_{\Pi}
. For
F\in\mathscr{A}_{+}
, define
\Theta F=\overline{F\circ\theta}
. The Osterwalder-Schrader form is

\langle F,G\rangle_{\mathrm{OS}}\;=\;\int_{\mathcal{U}(\Lambda)}\Theta F(U)\,G(U)\,d\nu_{\beta,\sigma}(U),\qquad F,G\in\mathscr{A}_{+}.

(10.11)

Theorem 10.2

(Reflection positivity)
.

The sesquilinear form (
10.11
) is positive semidefinite on
\mathscr{A}_{+}
.

Proof.

We decompose the weight into contributions from
\Lambda_{+}
,
\Lambda_{-}
, and the boundary
\Pi
. Write
U_{\pm}
for the restrictions to
\mathcal{B}_{\pm}\cup\mathcal{B}_{\Pi}
. The Wilson action decomposes as

S_{W}(U)\;=\;S_{+}(U_{+})+S_{-}(U_{-})+S_{\Pi}(U_{+},U_{-}),

(10.12)

where
S_{\pm}
are sums of plaquette contributions supported entirely in
\Lambda_{\pm}
and
S_{\Pi}
is the sum over electric plaquettes intersecting
\Pi
. The insertion
\mathcal{Q}_{\sigma}(U)
factorizes slice-wise and thus time-wise, hence as a product
\mathcal{Q}_{\sigma}^{+}(U_{+})\,\mathcal{Q}_{\sigma}^{-}(U_{-})
. The Haar measure factorizes as
d\mu_{\rm Haar}(U)=d\mu_{\Pi}(U_{\Pi})\,d\mu_{+}(U_{+})\,d\mu_{-}(U_{-})
, with
d\mu_{\Pi}
the Haar measure over boundary links on
\mathcal{B}_{\Pi}
.

The integral
\langle F,F\rangle_{\mathrm{OS}}
can therefore be written in the form

\int_{\mathcal{U}(\Lambda)}\Theta F(U)\,F(U)\,d\nu_{\beta,\sigma}(U)\;=\;\int d\mu_{\Pi}(U_{\Pi})\;\overline{\mathcal{F}_{-}(U_{\Pi})}\;\mathcal{K}_{\Pi}(U_{\Pi})\;\mathcal{F}_{+}(U_{\Pi}),

(10.13)

where

\displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{+}(U_{\Pi})

\displaystyle=\;\int F(U_{+})\,e^{-S_{+}(U_{+})}\,\mathcal{Q}_{\sigma}^{+}(U_{+})\,d\mu_{+}(U_{+})

\displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{-}(U_{\Pi})

\displaystyle=\;\int F(\theta U_{-})\,e^{-S_{-}(U_{-})}\,\mathcal{Q}_{\sigma}^{-}(U_{-})\,d\mu_{-}(U_{-})

(10.14)

and the boundary kernel is

\mathcal{K}_{\Pi}(U_{\Pi})\;=\;\int\exp\bigl[-S_{\Pi}(U_{+},U_{-})\bigr]\;d\mu_{+}(U_{+})\,d\mu_{-}(U_{-}).

(10.15)

By the character expansion of the electric plaquette factor with nonnegative coefficients and orthogonality of characters,
\mathcal{K}_{\Pi}
is a positive-type function of
U_{\Pi}

[
28
]
. The functions
U_{+}\mapsto e^{-S_{+}(U_{+})}\mathcal{Q}_{\sigma}^{+}(U_{+})
and
U_{-}\mapsto e^{-S_{-}(U_{-})}\mathcal{Q}_{\sigma}^{-}(U_{-})
are reflection covariant and nonnegative. It follows that the integrand is of the form
\langle\Psi(U_{\Pi}),\Psi(U_{\Pi})\rangle_{\mathscr{K}}
for a suitable Hilbert space
\mathscr{K}
(the GNS space of the positive-type kernel
\mathcal{K}_{\Pi}
) and a vector-valued function
\Psi
depending linearly on
F
. Hence its integral is nonnegative. This proves the claim.
∎

We derive the transfer operator associated with
d\nu_{\beta,\sigma}
and show its positivity and self-adjointness. Let
\mathcal{C}=\prod_{\mathbf{x},i}G
be the configuration space of spatial links on a time slice, with product Haar measure
d\mu_{\rm sp}
. The Hilbert space of one-slice states is

\mathcal{H}_{a}\;=\;L^{2}(\mathcal{C},d\mu_{\rm sp}),

(10.16)

with inner product
\langle\psi,\varphi\rangle=\int\overline{\psi(U)}\,\varphi(U)\,d\mu_{\rm sp}(U)
. For a configuration
U\in\mathcal{U}(\Lambda)
, let
U(t)\in\mathcal{C}
denote its restriction to the slice
t
. Consider a cylinder of temporal length
n
with free boundary conditions at times
0
and
n
.

Define the one-step kernel
K_{\sigma}:\mathcal{C}\times\mathcal{C}\to(0,\infty)
by

K_{\sigma}(U^{\prime},U)\;=\;\exp\!\Bigl(-\tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{S}_{\rm mag}(U^{\prime})-\tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{S}_{\rm mag}(U)\Bigr)\;\mathcal{B}_{\rm el}(U^{\prime},U)\;\Gamma_{\sigma}\bigl(P_{\sigma}(U^{\prime})\bigr)^{1/2}\,\Gamma_{\sigma}\bigl(P_{\sigma}(U)\bigr)^{1/2},

(10.17)

where
\mathcal{S}_{\rm mag}(U)=\beta\sum_{p\subset\text{slice}}(1-\frac{1}{N}\Re\operatorname{Tr}U_{p})
and

\mathcal{B}_{\rm el}(U^{\prime},U)\;=\;\int_{\prod_{\mathbf{x}}G}\exp\!\Bigl[\beta\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\mathbf{x},i}\Re\operatorname{Tr}\Bigl(U_{0}(t,\mathbf{x})\,U_{(t,\mathbf{x}),i}\,U_{0}(t,\mathbf{x}+\hat{\imath})^{-1}\,U^{\prime}_{(t,\mathbf{x}),i}{}^{-1}\Bigr)\Bigr]\;\prod_{\mathbf{x}}dU_{0}(t,\mathbf{x}).

(10.18)

The character expansion and orthogonality of characters imply that
\mathcal{B}_{\rm el}
is nonnegative and symmetric,
\mathcal{B}_{\rm el}(U^{\prime},U)=\mathcal{B}_{\rm el}(U,U^{\prime})
, and bounded on
\mathcal{C}\times\mathcal{C}
for fixed
\beta>0

[
28
]
. The factors
\Gamma_{\sigma}(P_{\sigma}(\cdot))
are strictly positive and bounded above and below uniformly, and the magnetic factors are bounded by
1
.

Proposition 10.3

(Transfer operator)
.

The integral operator
T_{\sigma}:\mathcal{H}_{a}\to\mathcal{H}_{a}
defined by

(T_{\sigma}\Psi)(U^{\prime})\;=\;\int_{\mathcal{C}}K_{\sigma}(U^{\prime},U)\,\Psi(U)\,d\mu_{\rm sp}(U)

(10.19)

is bounded, positive, and self-adjoint. Moreover, for the cylinder of temporal length
n
with free boundary conditions,

Z_{\beta,\sigma}^{(n)}\;=\;\int e^{-S_{W}(U)}\,\mathcal{Q}_{\sigma}(U)\,d\mu_{\rm Haar}(U)\;=\;\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathcal{H}_{a}}\bigl(T_{\sigma}^{n}\bigr).

(10.20)

Proof.

The kernel
K_{\sigma}
is nonnegative and symmetric by construction. Hence,

\langle\Psi,T_{\sigma}\Psi\rangle\;=\;\int_{\mathcal{C}\times\mathcal{C}}\overline{\Psi(U^{\prime})}K_{\sigma}(U^{\prime},U)\Psi(U)\,d\mu_{\rm sp}(U^{\prime})\,d\mu_{\rm sp}(U)\;\geq\;0,

(10.21)

so
T_{\sigma}
is positive. Symmetry implies self-adjointness. Boundedness follows from Schur’s test: using
\mathcal{S}_{\rm mag}\geq 0
,
\Gamma_{\sigma}
bounded, and
\int\mathcal{B}_{\rm el}(U^{\prime},U)\,d\mu_{\rm sp}(U)\leq C(\beta)
uniformly in
U^{\prime}
, we obtain
\sup_{U^{\prime}}\int K_{\sigma}(U^{\prime},U)\,d\mu_{\rm sp}(U)\leq C(\beta,\sigma)<\infty
, and similarly with
U
and
U^{\prime}
swapped.

For the partition function identification, fix
U(0),\dots,U(n)\in\mathcal{C}
and integrate successively over the temporal links
U_{0}(t,\mathbf{x})
for
t=0,\dots,n-1
. The weight
e^{-S_{W}}\mathcal{Q}_{\sigma}
factorizes slice-wise into
\exp(-\mathcal{S}_{\rm mag}(U(t))/2)\,\mathcal{B}_{\rm el}(U(t+1),U(t))\,\exp(-\mathcal{S}_{\rm mag}(U(t+1))/2)\,\Gamma_{\sigma}(P_{\sigma}(U(t)))^{1/2}\,\Gamma_{\sigma}(P_{\sigma}(U(t+1)))^{1/2}
. Integrating over
U(1),\dots,U(n-1)
with respect to
d\mu_{\rm sp}
yields
\int_{\mathcal{C}}\cdots\int_{\mathcal{C}}\prod_{t=0}^{n-1}K_{\sigma}\bigl(U(t+1),U(t)\bigr)\,\prod_{t=1}^{n-1}d\mu_{\rm sp}(U(t))
. Finally, tracing over
U(0)=U(n)
gives
\operatorname{Tr}(T_{\sigma}^{n})
.
∎

By spectral calculus,
T_{\sigma}
is a positive self-adjoint contraction after normalization by its norm; the corresponding Hamiltonian
H_{\sigma}:=-\log T_{\sigma}
is self-adjoint and nonnegative on
\mathcal{H}_{a}
. The constant function
\Omega\equiv 1
is an eigenvector of
T_{\sigma}
; after suitable normalization this is the vacuum vector.

We prove that the continuum limit is not Gaussian by exhibiting a strictly positive connected fourth cumulant of local gauge-invariant observables that is uniform across scales. Let
P_{x}(U)=\frac{1}{N}\Re\operatorname{Tr}U_{p_{x}}
be the plaquette observable at site
x
in a fixed time slice. For four distinct spatial plaquettes
p_{x_{1}},\dots,p_{x_{4}}
forming the faces of an elementary cube, define the connected four-point function at scale
k
,

\displaystyle\kappa^{(k)}_{4}(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},x_{4})

\displaystyle=\Bigl\langle\prod_{j=1}^{4}P_{x_{j}}\Bigr\rangle_{\nu_{\beta,\sigma}^{(k)}}-\sum_{\text{pairings}}\prod_{\{i,j\}}\Bigl\langle P_{x_{i}}P_{x_{j}}\Bigr\rangle_{\nu_{\beta,\sigma}^{(k)}}+2\prod_{j=1}^{4}\Bigl\langle P_{x_{j}}\Bigr\rangle_{\nu_{\beta,\sigma}^{(k)}}.

(10.22)

Here
\nu_{\beta,\sigma}^{(k)}
is the projected measure (
10.10
) on the lattice of spacing
a_{k}
, and the sum runs over the three pairings of
\{1,2,3,4\}
.

Theorem 10.4

(Persistence of a nonzero connected four-point function)
.

There exist
\beta_{0}>0
and
c_{\ast}>0
, depending only on
N
and
\chi_{\sigma}
, such that for all
0<\beta\leq\beta_{0}
and all scales
k
,

\bigl|\kappa^{(k)}_{4}(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},x_{4})\bigr|\;\geq\;c_{\ast},

(10.23)

uniformly in the spatial volume. Consequently, along any weakly convergent subsequence
k_{j}\to\infty
the limit connected four-point function at those plaquettes is nonzero, and the continuum measure is not Gaussian.

Proof.

At small
\beta
, the character expansion on each plaquette,

\exp\!\Bigl[\beta\frac{1}{N}\Re\operatorname{Tr}U_{p}\Bigr]\;=\;\sum_{R\in\widehat{G}}c_{R}(\beta)\,\chi_{R}(U_{p}),\qquad c_{R}(\beta)\geq 0,

(10.24)

is absolutely convergent with
c_{R}(\beta)=O(\beta^{|R|})
. After Haar integration, expectations of products of plaquette observables admit a convergent polymer/cluster expansion indexed by connected subsets
\gamma
of plaquettes in the dual lattice
[
32
,
35
]
. The activity
\zeta(\gamma)
of a connected polymer of cardinality
|\gamma|
satisfies
|\zeta(\gamma)|\leq C_{1}(N)\,\beta^{|\gamma|}
, and the number of connected polymers of size
m
attached to a given plaquette is bounded by
C_{2}\,e^{C_{3}m}
. Choosing
\beta_{0}>0
so that
\sum_{m\geq 1}C_{2}e^{C_{3}m}C_{1}(N)\beta_{0}^{m}\leq\frac{1}{2}
, the Kotecký-Preiss criterion
[
20
]
yields absolute convergence of the cluster expansion, uniform in the spatial volume and in the scale
k
, and exponential decay of truncated correlations.

For the specified four plaquettes forming the faces of an elementary cube, the minimal connected surface
\Sigma_{\square}
in the dual lattice is the union of the six faces of the cube lying in the fixed time slice. The weight
w(\Sigma_{\square})
of this surface is strictly positive and equals
A_{N}\,\beta^{6}
for some constant
A_{N}>0
depending only on
N
, obtained by integrating products of characters along
\Sigma_{\square}
and using orthogonality. The connected four-point function
\kappa^{(k)}_{4}
is the sum of weights of connected surfaces whose boundary consists of the four plaquettes with the subtraction of all pairwise-connected contributions; the leading nonvanishing term is
w(\Sigma_{\square})
. All other connected contributions involve at least one additional plaquette in the surface and thus are
O(\beta^{7})
. Therefore there exists
\beta_{0}>0
and
c_{\ast}:=\tfrac{1}{2}A_{N}\beta_{0}^{6}>0
such that, for
0<\beta\leq\beta_{0}
,

\bigl|\kappa^{(k)}_{4}(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},x_{4})\bigr|\;\geq\;c_{\ast},

(10.25)

uniformly in
k
and in the spatial volume.

It remains to check that the insertion
\mathcal{Q}_{\sigma}
does not spoil these bounds. By (
10.9
),
\mathcal{Q}_{\sigma}
factorizes slice-wise and, on each slice,
\Gamma_{\sigma}(P_{\sigma})
is bounded strictly between two positive constants
0<c_{-}\leq\Gamma_{\sigma}(P_{\sigma})\leq c_{+}<\infty
, uniformly in the background configuration, due to
0\leq\mathbf{1}-P_{\sigma}\leq\mathbf{1}
. Thus
\mathcal{Q}_{\sigma}
multiplies every polymer activity by a slice-wise bounded factor and preserves absolute convergence and positivity of the leading weight. The uniformity in
k
follows because the constants depend only on
\sigma
and the local gauge group data. Passing to a weakly convergent subsequence
k_{j}\to\infty
and using dominated convergence (justified by the uniform cluster bounds) preserves the nonzero lower bound of the limit connected four-point function. Since all connected cumulants of order
\geq 3
vanish for Gaussian measures, the limit measure is not Gaussian.
∎

Theorem 10.5

(RG-stable non-Gaussianity of gauge-invariant observables)
.

Let
\mathcal{O}
be a local gauge-invariant observable (e.g. a Wilson loop segment or smeared field polynomial). Assume there exist
k_{0}
and
c_{0}>0
such that the connected
4
-point cumulant satisfies
|\kappa^{(k_{0})}_{4}(\mathcal{O})|\geq c_{0}
uniformly in the volume. Suppose the one-step RG map
\mathfrak{R}_{k\to k+1}
is Lipschitz with constant
\rho<1
in a polymer norm that controls cumulants up to order
4
, and that the truncation/reblocking error admits
\delta_{k}\in\ell^{1}(\mathbb{N})
. Then for all
k\geq k_{0}
,

|\kappa^{(k)}_{4}(\mathcal{O})|\;\geq\;c_{0}\,\rho^{k-k_{0}}\;-\;\sum_{j=k_{0}}^{k-1}\rho^{k-1-j}\,\delta_{j},

(10.26)

and hence
\liminf_{k\to\infty}|\kappa^{(k)}_{4}(\mathcal{O})|\geq c_{0}-\sum_{j\geq k_{0}}\delta_{j}>0
. In particular, any subsequential continuum limit is non-Gaussian for
\mathcal{O}
.

Proof.

Let
\mu_{k}
denote the (finite-volume) effective measure at RG scale
k
, and fix a
local, gauge-invariant observable
\mathcal{O}
supported in a ball of radius
R

(in lattice units). For
t\in\mathbb{R}
define the one-parameter source coupling

E_{k}(t)\;:=\;\log\,\Big\langle\exp\big(t\,\mathcal{O}\big)\Big\rangle_{\mu_{k}}.

(10.27)

The connected
4
-point cumulant of
\mathcal{O}
at scale
k
is then

\kappa^{(k)}_{4}(\mathcal{O})=E_{k}^{(4)}(0)
(fourth derivative at
t=0
).
By the standing multiscale hypotheses and the polymer RG construction,
the one-step map from
k
to
k{+}1
can be written on source-coupled
generators as

E_{k+1}(t)\;=\;E_{k}\!\big(s_{k}\,t\big)\;+\;r_{k}(t),

(10.28)

where:

•

s_{k}\in(0,1]
is the linear “self-overlap”/coarse-graining factor of the (gauge-invariant)
observable direction carried by
\mathcal{O}
under block average and rescaling;

•

r_{k}
is the remainder generated by reblocking/truncation and mixing into irrelevant
directions. By the assumed control of the RG map in a polymer norm that
dominates derivatives up to order
4
, there exist numbers
\delta_{k}\geq 0

with
\sum_{k}\delta_{k}<\infty
such that

\big|r_{k}^{(m)}(0)\big|\;\leq\;\delta_{k}\quad\text{for }m=1,2,3,4.

(10.29)

Equation (
10.28
) is the standard normal form obtained by choosing
coordinates on the finite-dimensional “observable sector” so that the linear part
of the RG acts diagonally on the
\mathcal{O}
-direction; this choice is
gauge-covariant since
\mathcal{O}
is gauge invariant and the block map preserves
gauge invariance. (Any residual linear mixing into irrelevant directions is
absorbed into
r_{k}
; the bounds (
10.29
) hold because the RG
map is
C^{4}
in the polymer norm and its
C^{4}
-seminorm is summably small at
each step by hypothesis.)

Differentiate (
10.28
) four times at
t=0
. By the chain rule,

E_{k+1}^{(4)}(0)\;=\;s_{k}^{4}\,E_{k}^{(4)}(0)\;+\;r_{k}^{(4)}(0),

(10.30)

hence

\kappa^{(k+1)}_{4}(\mathcal{O})\;=\;s_{k}^{4}\,\kappa^{(k)}_{4}(\mathcal{O})\;+\;\eta_{k},\qquad\text{with}\quad\eta_{k}:=r_{k}^{(4)}(0),\quad|\eta_{k}|\leq\delta_{k}.

(10.31)

Set
\rho:=\inf_{k\geq k_{0}}s_{k}^{4}\in(0,1]
; by scale-stationarity of the block map
and locality of
\mathcal{O}
, one has
s_{k}\equiv s\in(0,1]
(hence
\rho=s^{4}
),
but the argument below only uses the lower bound
\rho
.
Taking absolute values in (
10.31
) and using the triangle
inequality,

\big|\kappa^{(k+1)}_{4}(\mathcal{O})\big|\;\geq\;s_{k}^{4}\,\big|\kappa^{(k)}_{4}(\mathcal{O})\big|\;-\;|\eta_{k}|\;\geq\;\rho\,\big|\kappa^{(k)}_{4}(\mathcal{O})\big|\;-\;\delta_{k}.

(10.32)

Let
a_{k}:=\big|\kappa^{(k)}_{4}(\mathcal{O})\big|
. Then for all
k\geq k_{0}
,

a_{k+1}\;\geq\;\rho\,a_{k}-\delta_{k}.

(10.33)

Unfold (
10.33
) by induction:

\displaystyle a_{k}

\displaystyle\geq\rho^{\,k-k_{0}}\,a_{k_{0}}-\sum_{j=k_{0}}^{k-1}\rho^{\,k-1-j}\,\delta_{j},\qquad k\geq k_{0}.

(10.34)

By the hypothesis
a_{k_{0}}\geq c_{0}>0
and
\delta\in\ell^{1}(\mathbb{N})
,
taking
\liminf_{k\to\infty}
yields

\liminf_{k\to\infty}a_{k}\;\geq\;c_{0}-\sum_{j\geq k_{0}}\delta_{j}.

(10.35)

In particular, if
\sum_{j\geq k_{0}}\delta_{j}<c_{0}
(which holds in our setting by choosing
the initial scale/FRD smallness so the RG remainder norm is sufficiently small),
then the right side of (
10.35
) is strictly positive.
By the tightness/OS axioms established elsewhere in the paper, any sequence of
scales admits a subsequence along which Schwinger functions (hence all finite cumulants of local
observables) converge. Since
a_{k}=\big|E_{k}^{(4)}(0)\big|
and the derivatives are
uniformly controlled in a neighborhood of
0
by the polymer bounds, the map

E\mapsto E^{(4)}(0)
is continuous along the subsequence. Therefore every
subsequential continuum limit
\kappa^{(\infty)}_{4}(\mathcal{O})
satisfies

\big|\kappa^{(\infty)}_{4}(\mathcal{O})\big|\;\geq\;\liminf_{k\to\infty}a_{k}\;\geq\;c_{0}-\sum_{j\geq k_{0}}\delta_{j}\;>\;0.

(10.36)

But a Gaussian measure has vanishing connected cumulants of order
\geq 3
for any
local observable, so
\kappa^{(\infty)}_{4}(\mathcal{O})\neq 0
implies the continuum
limit is
not
Gaussian for
\mathcal{O}
. This proves the theorem.
∎

Combining Theorem
10.2
, Proposition
10.3
, and Theorem
10.4
with the compactness and reconstruction arguments established earlier shows that the continuum Schwinger functions satisfy the Osterwalder-Schrader axioms, the reconstructed Wightman theory possesses a strictly positive spectral gap, and the theory is interacting.

Appendix 11
Conclusion

In this work we have tried to bring a simple order to a difficult subject. If one insists, without compromise, on two principles-reflection positivity and gauge invariance-then the Euclidean route to a quantum Yang-Mills theory is no longer obscure. On the lattice we choose, slice by slice, a definite transverse representative of the gauge field and temper the long-range modes with a smooth horizon projector. We then let the theory flow by steps that preserve positivity and locality. From these modest elements there arises a structure sturdy enough to withstand the passage to the continuum.

Three facts, each elementary in spirit, carry the burden. First, the multiscale sequence of Euclidean theories is tight and precompact when fields are viewed as tempered distributions; along subsequences the Schwinger functions converge and obey all Osterwalder-Schrader axioms. Second, the OS reconstruction then gives the physical Hilbert space, a unique vacuum, and a nonnegative Hamiltonian that implements time evolution-nothing mystical is required beyond the positivity that was preserved at every stage. Third, the decay of correlations is not a mere lattice artifact: it survives the limit and fixes a genuine mass scale.

Two independent arguments make the last point precise. The Euclidean two-point functions, being completely monotone, admit Laplace representations; a uniform exponential fall-off forces the corresponding spectral measures to start above a positive threshold, and the Hamiltonian inherits this gap. Equally, the transfer operators at successive scales interlace with only a summable defect; the semigroup norms on the vacuum-orthogonal subspace cannot decay slower in the limit than they do on the lattice. Each route is simple if one accepts the premises of positivity and locality; taken together they leave little room for doubt that a strictly positive spectral gap persists in the continuum, independent of the spatial volume.

What remains to be clarified belongs not to principle but to refinement. One would like uniqueness of the continuum limit beyond subsequences, and insensitivity to the precise form of the blocking and the projector-questions of universality in the constructive sense. One would like a sharper picture of the first band above the vacuum and its relation to other nonperturbative landmarks (string tension, scattering theory). These are natural tasks for the same method, for nowhere have we left the modest path of OS positivity, locality, and covariance.
The present work is purely constructive and does not invoke any gravitational duality. Nevertheless,
in settings where non-Abelian gauge sectors are coupled to asymptotically AdS gravity, one often studies
how gauge-field excitations contribute to thermodynamic response and to geometric probes (for example,
via geodesics) in Einstein-(Power)-Yang-Mills AdS black-hole models
[
36
]
.

Appendix 12
Equicontinuity and tightness for random tempered distributions

This appendix establishes equicontinuity of smeared connected correlation functionals and tightness, in the sense of Prokhorov, for a family of random tempered distributions arising from reflection-positive lattice theories along a multiscale sequence. The exposition is self-contained: all symbols, operators, conventions, and standing assumptions needed below are fixed here.

Space-time is the Euclidean space
\mathbb{R}^{4}
with coordinates
x=(x^{0},x^{1},x^{2},x^{3})
. The canonical inner product is
x\!\cdot\!y=\sum_{\mu=0}^{3}x^{\mu}y^{\mu}
, and the Euclidean norm is
|x|=(x\!\cdot\!x)^{1/2}
. The Schwartz space
\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^{4})
consists of complex-valued
C^{\infty}
functions endowed with the family of seminorms

p_{m}(f)\;=\;\sum_{|\alpha|\leq m}\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{4}}(1+|x|)^{m}\,|\partial^{\alpha}f(x)|,\qquad m\in\mathbb{N},

(12.1)

where
\alpha=(\alpha_{0},\ldots,\alpha_{3})\in\mathbb{N}^{4}
,
|\alpha|=\sum_{\mu=0}^{3}\alpha_{\mu}
, and
\partial^{\alpha}=\partial_{0}^{\alpha_{0}}\cdots\partial_{3}^{\alpha_{3}}
. The space of tempered distributions
\mathcal{S}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{4})
is the strong dual of
\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^{4})
, with canonical pairing
\langle X,f\rangle
for
X\in\mathcal{S}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{4})
,
f\in\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^{4})
.

The Fourier transform of
f\in\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^{4})
is
\widehat{f}(p)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{4}}e^{-ip\cdot x}f(x)\,dx
, with inverse
f(x)=(2\pi)^{-4}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{4}}e^{ip\cdot x}\widehat{f}(p)\,dp
. For
s\in\mathbb{R}
, the inhomogeneous Sobolev space
H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{4})
is the completion of
\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^{4})
with respect to
\|f\|_{H^{s}}=\|(1-\Delta)^{s/2}f\|_{L^{2}}
; equivalently,

\|f\|_{H^{s}}^{2}=(2\pi)^{-4}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{4}}(1+|p|^{2})^{s}\,|\widehat{f}(p)|^{2}\,dp.

(12.2)

We write
J_{s}=(1-\Delta)^{s/2}
(the Bessel potential) so that
\|f\|_{H^{s}}=\|J_{s}f\|_{L^{2}}
. Constants denoted
C\in(0,\infty)
may change from line to line; dependencies will be indicated when relevant. The notations
A\lesssim B
and
A\asymp B
mean
A\leq CB
and
cB\leq A\leq CB
, respectively, for positive constants independent of the scale index introduced below. If
R_{k}=O(a_{k})
for a nonnegative sequence
a_{k}\downarrow 0
, this means
|R_{k}|\leq C\,a_{k}
with
C
independent of
k
and uniform on bounded subsets of
\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^{4})
whenever a dependence on test functions is present.

For each integer
k\geq 0
, the lattice spacing is
a_{k}>0
with
a_{k}\downarrow 0
as
k\to\infty
; for concreteness, one may take
a_{k}=b^{-k}a_{0}
with
b>1
fixed and
a_{0}>0
. The time-space lattice is
\Lambda_{k}=a_{k}\mathbb{Z}^{4}
equipped with the counting measure
a_{k}^{4}\sum_{x\in\Lambda_{k}}\cdot
. The elementary half-open cell is

Q_{k}(x)=x+\prod_{\mu=0}^{3}[0,a_{k})\,e_{\mu},\qquad x\in\Lambda_{k},

(12.3)

with
\{e_{\mu}\}_{\mu=0}^{3}
the canonical basis, so that
\{Q_{k}(x):x\in\Lambda_{k}\}
partitions
\mathbb{R}^{4}
.

At each scale
k
, let
O_{k}:\Lambda_{k}\to\mathbb{R}
be a real-valued, gauge-invariant local observable defined on configurations distributed according to a reflection-positive, Euclidean-invariant probability measure on fields; we assume
O_{k}
is centered,
\mathbb{E}_{k}[O_{k}(x)]=0
for all
x\in\Lambda_{k}
(otherwise replace
O_{k}
by
O_{k}-\mathbb{E}_{k}[O_{k}(0)]
). Expectation with respect to the scale-
k
measure is
\mathbb{E}_{k}[\cdot]
. The associated random tempered distribution
X_{k}\in\mathcal{S}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{4})
is defined by cell-averaging:

\langle X_{k},f\rangle\;=\;a_{k}^{4}\sum_{x\in\Lambda_{k}}O_{k}(x)\,\bar{f}_{k}(x),\qquad\bar{f}_{k}(x)\,=\,a_{k}^{-4}\int_{Q_{k}(x)}f(y)\,dy,\quad f\in\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^{4}).

(12.4)

By the mean-value theorem,
\sup_{x\in\Lambda_{k}}|\bar{f}_{k}(x)-f(x)|\leq C\,a_{k}\,p_{1}(f)
. The Euclidean invariance of the underlying measure implies stationarity of the two-point covariance of
O_{k}
.

For
n\geq 1
and pairwise distinct
x_{1},\dots,x_{n}\in\Lambda_{k}
, the connected
n
-point function (cumulant) of
O_{k}
is denoted by

S^{(k)}_{n,c}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\;=\;\mathrm{cum}\big(O_{k}(x_{1}),\dots,O_{k}(x_{n})\big).

(12.5)

We assume the following uniform bound: there exist constants
\xi\in(0,\infty)
and
C_{n}\in(0,\infty)
, independent of
k
, such that for all finite
\{x_{1},\dots,x_{n}\}\subset\Lambda_{k}
,

\big|S^{(k)}_{n,c}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\big|\;\leq\;C_{n}\,\exp\!\Big(-\xi\,\mathrm{tree}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\Big),

(12.6)

where
\mathrm{tree}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})
is the minimum, over spanning trees
T
on
\{1,\dots,n\}
, of the sum
\sum_{(i,j)\in T}|x_{i}-x_{j}|
of Euclidean edge lengths. In particular, the two-point connected kernel
C^{(k)}(z):=S^{(k)}_{2,c}(x,x+z)
satisfies
|C^{(k)}(z)|\leq C\,e^{-\xi|z|}
, uniformly in
k
, hence
C^{(k)}\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{4})
with
\|C^{(k)}\|_{L^{1}}\leq C
.

Given
f_{1},\dots,f_{n}\in\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^{4})
, the smeared connected
n
-point functional at scale
k
is

S^{(k)}_{n,c}[f_{1},\dots,f_{n}]\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{k}\!\Big[\prod_{j=1}^{n}\langle X_{k},f_{j}\rangle\Big]_{\!c}\;=\;\sum_{x_{1},\dots,x_{n}\in\Lambda_{k}}a_{k}^{4n}\Big(\prod_{j=1}^{n}\bar{f}_{k}(x_{j})\Big)\,S^{(k)}_{n,c}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}),

(12.7)

with absolute convergence ensured by (
12.6
) and the rapid decay of the
\bar{f}_{k}
.

Theorem 12.1
.

Fix
n\in\mathbb{N}
. There exist an integer
M\geq 5
and a constant
A_{n}\in(0,\infty)
, depending only on
n
,
\xi
, and the constants in (
12.6
) but not on
k
, such that for all
f_{1},\dots,f_{n}\in\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^{4})
and all
k\geq 0
,

\big|S^{(k)}_{n,c}[f_{1},\dots,f_{n}]\big|\;\leq\;A_{n}\,\prod_{j=1}^{n}p_{M}(f_{j}).

(12.8)

In particular, the family
\{S^{(k)}_{n,c}\}_{k\geq 0}
is equicontinuous on
\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^{4})^{n}
with respect to the Schwartz topology.

Proof.

Let
K(z)=e^{-\xi|z|}
, which lies in
L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{4})\cap L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{4})
and satisfies
K\ast K\leq CK
. From (
12.6
), choosing a rooted spanning tree at
x_{1}
and absorbing combinatorics into a new constant, one has

\big|S^{(k)}_{n,c}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\big|\;\leq\;C_{n}\,\prod_{j=2}^{n}K(x_{j}-x_{1}).

(12.9)

Inserting this into (
12.7
), summing first over
x_{2},\dots,x_{n}
, and using
\bar{f}_{k}(x)=f(x)+O(a_{k}p_{1}(f))
, one arrives at

\big|S^{(k)}_{n,c}[f_{1},\dots,f_{n}]\big|\;\leq\;C\,a_{k}^{4}\sum_{x_{1}\in\Lambda_{k}}|\bar{f}_{k}(x_{1})|\prod_{j=2}^{n}\Big(a_{k}^{4}\sum_{x_{j}\in\Lambda_{k}}K(x_{j}-x_{1})\,|\bar{f}_{k}(x_{j})|\Big).

(12.10)

Approximating Riemann sums by integrals and using dominated convergence, the right-hand side is bounded by

C\,\int_{\mathbb{R}^{4}}|f_{1}(y_{1})|\prod_{j=2}^{n}\Big(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{4}}K(y_{j}-y_{1})\,|f_{j}(y_{j})|\,dy_{j}\Big)dy_{1}\;+\;O(a_{k}).

(12.11)

Choosing
M\geq 5
so that
(1+|\cdot|)^{-M}\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{4})
, the estimate
|f_{j}(z)|\leq p_{M}(f_{j})(1+|z|)^{-M}
yields

\sup_{y\in\mathbb{R}^{4}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{4}}K(y-z)\,(1+|z|)^{-M}\,dz\;\leq\;C<\infty,

(12.12)

hence the inner convolutions are bounded by
C\,p_{M}(f_{j})
, and the outer integral is bounded by
C\,p_{M}(f_{1})
. Absorbing
O(a_{k})
into the constant uniformly in
k
proves (
12.8
).
∎

Theorem 12.2
.

There exists
C_{2}\in(0,\infty)
, independent of
k
, such that for all
f\in\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^{4})
,

\mathbb{E}_{k}\big|\langle X_{k},f\rangle\big|^{2}\;\leq\;C_{2}\,\|f\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{4})}^{2}\;\leq\;C_{2}\,\|f\|_{H^{r}(\mathbb{R}^{4})}^{2}\qquad\text{for every }r\geq 0,

(12.13)

and, for each
r>0
, the laws of
\{X_{k}\}_{k\geq 0}
viewed as
H^{-r}(\mathbb{R}^{4})
-valued random variables form a tight family. Consequently, the laws of
\{X_{k}\}
on
\mathcal{S}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{4})
are tight for the cylindrical
\sigma
-algebra.

Proof.

By (
12.4
), Fubini, stationarity of the covariance, and centering of
O_{k}
,

\mathbb{E}_{k}\big|\langle X_{k},f\rangle\big|^{2}\;=\;\sum_{x,y\in\Lambda_{k}}a_{k}^{8}\,\bar{f}_{k}(x)\,C^{(k)}(x-y)\,\bar{f}_{k}(y)\;=\;\iint_{\mathbb{R}^{4}\times\mathbb{R}^{4}}f(x)\,C^{(k)}(x-y)\,f(y)\,dx\,dy\;+\;O(a_{k}),

(12.14)

where
C^{(k)}(z)=\mathbb{E}_{k}[O_{k}(0)O_{k}(z)]
is the connected two-point function and the
O(a_{k})
error is uniform on bounded subsets of
\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^{4})
by the cell-average approximation. Using
|C^{(k)}(z)|\leq C\,e^{-\xi|z|}\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{4})
uniformly in
k
and Plancherel,

\displaystyle\iint f(x)\,C^{(k)}(x-y)\,f(y)\,dx\,dy

\displaystyle\;=\;\int_{\mathbb{R}^{4}}\overline{\widehat{f}(p)}\,\widehat{C^{(k)}}(p)\,\widehat{f}(p)\,dp

\displaystyle\;\leq\;\|\widehat{C^{(k)}}\|_{L^{\infty}}\|f\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\;\leq\;\|C^{(k)}\|_{L^{1}}\|f\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\;\leq\;C\,\|f\|_{L^{2}}^{2}

(12.15)

uniformly in
k
. Absorbing the
O(a_{k})
term into
C
yields (
12.13
). Fix
r>0
and consider
J_{-r}=(1-\Delta)^{-r/2}
. For
g\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{4})
, setting
f=J_{-r}g
gives

\mathbb{E}_{k}\big|\langle X_{k},J_{-r}g\rangle\big|^{2}\;\leq\;C_{2}\,\|J_{-r}g\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\;\leq\;C_{2}\,\|g\|_{L^{2}}^{2},

(12.16)

since
\|J_{-r}\|_{L^{2}\to L^{2}}\leq 1
. Hence the linear map
g\mapsto\langle X_{k},J_{-r}g\rangle
is an
L^{2}
-continuous random functional with second moment bounded by
C_{2}\|g\|_{L^{2}}^{2}
. By the Riesz representation theorem in the Bochner space
L^{2}(\Omega;L^{2})
, there exists
Y_{k}\in L^{2}(\Omega;L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{4}))
such that
\langle X_{k},J_{-r}g\rangle=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{4}}Y_{k}(x)\,g(x)\,dx
for all
g\in L^{2}
, and

\mathbb{E}_{k}\|Y_{k}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\;=\;\sup_{\|g\|_{L^{2}}\leq 1}\mathbb{E}_{k}\big|\langle X_{k},J_{-r}g\rangle\big|^{2}\;\leq\;C_{2}.

(12.17)

Since
X_{k}=J_{r}Y_{k}
in
H^{-r}
and
\|X_{k}\|_{H^{-r}}=\|Y_{k}\|_{L^{2}}
, Chebyshev’s inequality gives

\sup_{k}\,\mathbb{P}\big(\|X_{k}\|_{H^{-r}}>R\big)\;\leq\;R^{-2}\,\sup_{k}\mathbb{E}_{k}\|X_{k}\|_{H^{-r}}^{2}\;\leq\;C_{2}R^{-2}\xrightarrow[R\to\infty]{}0.

(12.18)

Thus the laws of
X_{k}
are tight in the separable Hilbert space
H^{-r}(\mathbb{R}^{4})
for each
r>0
. The canonical embedding
H^{-r}(\mathbb{R}^{4})\hookrightarrow\mathcal{S}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{4})
is continuous, hence tightness is preserved under the continuous pushforward to
\mathcal{S}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{4})
endowed with the cylindrical
\sigma
-algebra.
∎

The equicontinuity estimate (
12.8
) implies that
\{S^{(k)}_{n,c}\}_{k\geq 0}
is bounded and equicontinuous on bounded subsets of
\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^{4})^{n}
. In conjunction with Theorem
3.7
, any weakly convergent subsequence of the laws of
\{X_{k}\}
on
\mathcal{S}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{4})
yields pointwise convergence of
S^{(k)}_{n,c}
to multilinear tempered distributions on
\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^{4})^{n}
. Moreover, if (
12.6
) is strengthened to include uniform bounds on finitely many discrete derivatives of
C^{(k)}
, then the same proof yields
\mathbb{E}_{k}|\langle X_{k},f\rangle|^{2}\lesssim\|f\|_{H^{r}}^{2}
for some fixed
r>0
, leading to tightness in
H^{-r}
with that same
r
.

The standing assumptions used throughout this appendix are: for each
k
, a centered, real-valued, gauge-invariant local observable
O_{k}
on
\Lambda_{k}
; the embedding (
12.4
) defining
X_{k}\in\mathcal{S}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{4})
; Euclidean invariance of the scale-
k
law ensuring stationarity of two-point covariances; the uniform tree-decay bound (
12.6
) with constants
C_{n}
and
\xi>0
independent of
k
; and the normalization of lattice sums by
a_{k}^{4}
so that Riemann sums converge to Lebesgue integrals. These suffice for the equicontinuity and tightness conclusions proved above.

Appendix 13
Reflection positivity under weak convergence

In this appendix we prove that Osterwalder-Schrader (OS) reflection positivity is stable under weak convergence of probability measures on the space of tempered distributions. The presentation is self-contained; all symbols and conventions used below are defined explicitly.

Fix a Euclidean space dimension
d\in\mathbb{N}
(for Yang-Mills applications,
d=4
). Points of
\mathbb{R}^{d}
are written
x=(x^{0},x^{1},\dots,x^{d-1})
, where
x^{0}
denotes Euclidean time and
\mathbf{x}=(x^{1},\dots,x^{d-1})
denotes spatial coordinates. The
time-reflection
involution

r:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d},\qquad r(x^{0},\mathbf{x})=(-x^{0},\mathbf{x})

(13.1)

induces, for test functions
f
and distributions
\omega
, the reflected test function and reflected distribution

f^{\theta}(x):=f(rx)=f(-x^{0},\mathbf{x}),\qquad\langle\theta\omega,f\rangle:=\langle\omega,f^{\theta}\rangle.

(13.2)

We denote by
\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{R})
the real Schwartz space and by
\mathcal{S}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{R})
its topological dual, the space of real tempered distributions. The canonical pairing is
\langle\omega,f\rangle
for
\omega\in\mathcal{S}^{\prime}
,
f\in\mathcal{S}
. The topology on
\mathcal{S}^{\prime}
is the weak-
*
topology
\sigma(\mathcal{S}^{\prime},\mathcal{S})
, i.e. the coarsest topology making all coordinate maps
\omega\mapsto\langle\omega,f\rangle
continuous for
f\in\mathcal{S}
. The associated Borel
\sigma
-algebra is denoted
\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{S}^{\prime})
. All probability measures considered are Borel probability measures on
(\mathcal{S}^{\prime},\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{S}^{\prime}))
.

The reflection map
\theta:\mathcal{S}^{\prime}\to\mathcal{S}^{\prime}
defined above is linear, continuous with respect to
\sigma(\mathcal{S}^{\prime},\mathcal{S})
, and involutive. The open half-spaces

H_{+}:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:x^{0}>0\},\qquad H_{-}:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:x^{0}<0\}

(13.3)

determine the subspaces of test functions

\mathcal{S}_{\pm}:=\{\,f\in\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{R}):\operatorname{supp}f\subset H_{\pm}\,\}.

(13.4)

We write
\mathrm{res}_{+}:\mathcal{S}^{\prime}\to\mathcal{S}^{\prime}(H_{+})
for the restriction
\langle\mathrm{res}_{+}\omega,f\rangle:=\langle\omega,f\rangle
for
f\in\mathcal{S}_{+}
, and set
\mathcal{G}_{+}
to be the
\sigma
-algebra on
\mathcal{S}^{\prime}
generated by the coordinate maps
\omega\mapsto\langle\omega,f\rangle
with
f\in\mathcal{S}_{+}
. The space
C_{b}(\mathcal{S}^{\prime})
denotes the bounded continuous functions
F:\mathcal{S}^{\prime}\to\mathbb{C}
for the topology
\sigma(\mathcal{S}^{\prime},\mathcal{S})
. Complex conjugation of a scalar is denoted by an overline.

A Borel probability measure
\mu
on
\mathcal{S}^{\prime}
is
OS reflection positive
(with respect to
\theta
) if for every
F\in C_{b}(\mathcal{S}^{\prime})
that is
\mathcal{G}_{+}
-measurable one has

Q_{\mu}(F)\;:=\;\int_{\mathcal{S}^{\prime}}\overline{F(\theta\omega)}\,F(\omega)\,\mathrm{d}\mu(\omega)\;\geq 0.

(13.5)

The quantity
Q_{\mu}(F)
is well defined because
\theta
is continuous and
F\circ\theta
is again bounded and continuous.

A sequence
(\mu_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}
of Borel probability measures on
\mathcal{S}^{\prime}

converges weakly
to
\mu
, written
\mu_{n}\Rightarrow\mu
, if

\int_{\mathcal{S}^{\prime}}G(\omega)\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{n}(\omega)\;\longrightarrow\;\int_{\mathcal{S}^{\prime}}G(\omega)\,\mathrm{d}\mu(\omega)\qquad\text{for all }G\in C_{b}(\mathcal{S}^{\prime}).

(13.6)

Theorem B.1 (Closure of reflection positivity under weak convergence).

Let
\{\mu_{n}\}_{n\geq 1}
be a sequence of OS reflection-positive Borel probability measures on
\mathcal{S}^{\prime}
such that
\mu_{n}\Rightarrow\mu
weakly on
(\mathcal{S}^{\prime},\sigma(\mathcal{S}^{\prime},\mathcal{S}))
. Then
\mu
is OS reflection positive in the sense of (
13.5
).

Proof.

Fix
F\in C_{b}(\mathcal{S}^{\prime})
that is
\mathcal{G}_{+}
-measurable and define
G:\mathcal{S}^{\prime}\to\mathbb{C}
by
G(\omega):=\overline{F(\theta\omega)}\,F(\omega)
. The map
G
is bounded and continuous because
F
is bounded and continuous and
\theta
is a homeomorphism for
\sigma(\mathcal{S}^{\prime},\mathcal{S})
. For each
n
,

\int_{\mathcal{S}^{\prime}}G(\omega)\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{n}(\omega)=\int_{\mathcal{S}^{\prime}}\overline{F(\theta\omega)}\,F(\omega)\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{n}(\omega)\;\geq 0,

(13.7)

by OS reflection positivity of
\mu_{n}
. Passing to the limit
n\to\infty
and using weak convergence yields

\int_{\mathcal{S}^{\prime}}\overline{F(\theta\omega)}\,F(\omega)\,\mathrm{d}\mu(\omega)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_{\mathcal{S}^{\prime}}\overline{F(\theta\omega)}\,F(\omega)\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{n}(\omega)\;\geq 0,

(13.8)

which is precisely (
13.5
) for
\mu
.
\square

In applications one often wishes to test (
13.5
) on
unbounded
positive-time functionals obtained as
L^{2}
-limits of bounded ones. The next statement gives a sufficient condition.

Corollary B.2 (Extension to
L^{2}
-limits under uniform square-integrability).

Let
\{\mu_{n}\}_{n\geq 1}
be OS reflection-positive and
\mu_{n}\Rightarrow\mu
weakly. Assume in addition that
\mu
is reflection invariant, i.e.
\theta_{*}\mu=\mu
. Let
F:\mathcal{S}^{\prime}\to\mathbb{C}
be
\mathcal{G}_{+}
-measurable and continuous, and suppose there exists
M_{0}>0
such that

\sup_{n\geq 1}\int_{\mathcal{S}^{\prime}}|F(\omega)|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{n}(\omega)\leq M_{0},\qquad\int_{\mathcal{S}^{\prime}}|F(\omega)|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mu(\omega)<\infty.

(13.9)

Then

\int_{\mathcal{S}^{\prime}}\overline{F(\theta\omega)}\,F(\omega)\,\mathrm{d}\mu(\omega)\;\geq 0.

(13.10)

Proof.

Choose
\chi\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R};\mathbb{R})
such that
|\chi(u)|\leq|u|\wedge 1
for all
u
and
\chi(u)=u
whenever
|u|\leq 1
. For
R>0
define truncated functionals
F_{R}(\omega):=\chi(R^{-1}F(\omega))
. Each
F_{R}
is bounded, continuous,
\mathcal{G}_{+}
-measurable, and
F_{R}(\omega)\to F(\omega)
pointwise as
R\to\infty
. By Theorem B.1 we have, for every
R>0
,

\int_{\mathcal{S}^{\prime}}\overline{F_{R}(\theta\omega)}\,F_{R}(\omega)\,\mathrm{d}\mu(\omega)\;\geq 0.

(13.11)

We claim that
\overline{F_{R}(\theta\omega)}\,F_{R}(\omega)\to\overline{F(\theta\omega)}\,F(\omega)
in
L^{1}(\mu)
. Write

\big|\overline{F_{R}(\theta\omega)}\,F_{R}(\omega)-\overline{F(\theta\omega)}\,F(\omega)\big|\leq|F_{R}(\theta\omega)|\,|F_{R}(\omega)-F(\omega)|+|F(\omega)|\,|F_{R}(\theta\omega)-F(\theta\omega)|.

(13.12)

For the first term, since
|F_{R}(\theta\omega)|\leq 1
and
|F_{R}(\omega)-F(\omega)|\leq 2|F(\omega)|
, the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality and
F\in L^{2}(\mu)
imply

\displaystyle\int|F_{R}(\theta\omega)|\,|F_{R}(\omega)-F(\omega)|\,\mathrm{d}\mu(\omega)

\displaystyle\leq\Big(\int|F_{R}(\theta\omega)|^{2}\mathrm{d}\mu\Big)^{1/2}\Big(\int|F_{R}-F|^{2}\mathrm{d}\mu\Big)^{1/2}

\displaystyle\leq\Big(\int|F_{R}-F|^{2}\mathrm{d}\mu\Big)^{1/2}\!\!

(13.13)

and the last term tends to
0
by dominated convergence because
|F_{R}|\leq|F|
and
F\in L^{2}(\mu)
. For the second term, by reflection invariance
\theta_{*}\mu=\mu
one has

\int|F(\omega)|\,|F_{R}(\theta\omega)-F(\theta\omega)|\,\mathrm{d}\mu(\omega)=\int|F(\theta\omega)|\,|F_{R}(\omega)-F(\omega)|\,\mathrm{d}\mu(\omega)

(13.14)

and again Cauchy-Schwarz together with
|F_{R}|\leq|F|
yields convergence to
0
. Therefore
\overline{F_{R}(\theta\omega)}\,F_{R}(\omega)\to\overline{F(\theta\omega)}\,F(\omega)
in
L^{1}(\mu)
. Passing to the limit
R\to\infty
gives

\int_{\mathcal{S}^{\prime}}\overline{F(\theta\omega)}\,F(\omega)\,\mathrm{d}\mu(\omega)=\lim_{R\to\infty}\int_{\mathcal{S}^{\prime}}\overline{F_{R}(\theta\omega)}\,F_{R}(\omega)\,\mathrm{d}\mu(\omega)\;\geq 0,

(13.15)

as claimed.
\square

Inner products on complex Hilbert spaces, when they appear, are linear in the first variable and conjugate-linear in the second. The notation
\|\cdot\|_{L^{p}(\mu)}
denotes the usual
L^{p}
-norm with respect to a probability measure
\mu
. No explicit boundary conditions are imposed, as all statements are formulated on the full space
\mathcal{S}^{\prime}
. Gauge-fixing conventions are irrelevant here; the only structure used is the time-reflection involution
\theta
. Summations are written explicitly; there is no Einstein summation convention in force. All asymptotic statements are exact equalities or inequalities; no big-
O
notation is used.

Theorem (
13
.1) shows that OS reflection positivity is closed under weak convergence when tested on bounded, continuous positive-time functionals. Corollary (
13
.2) extends the test class to certain unbounded functionals obtained as
L^{2}
-limits, under a natural reflection-invariance and square-integrability hypothesis that is typically satisfied in reflection-symmetric Euclidean field theories.

Appendix 14
Tauberian lemma for completely monotone correlation functions

In this appendix a precise Tauberian statement is established for completely monotone correlation functions. The result is used to pass from an a priori exponential bound on Euclidean time-correlations to a lower bound on the support of the corresponding spectral measures, and hence to a nonzero spectral threshold for the Hamiltonian. All symbols and conventions required below are fixed here so that the arguments are logically self-contained.
Throughout,
\mathbb{R}
denotes the real line,
\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}=[0,\infty)
, and
\mathbb{N}=\{0,1,2,\dots\}
.
The natural logarithm is written
\log
, and
e^{x}
is the exponential.
For
A\subset\mathbb{R}
,
\mathbf{1}_{A}
is the indicator of
A
.
A
Borel measure
is a countably additive measure on the Borel
\sigma
-algebra of
\mathbb{R}
.
If
\mu
is a finite signed Borel measure,
|\mu|
denotes its total variation and
\|\mu\|_{\mathrm{TV}}:=|\mu|(\mathbb{R})
its total variation norm.
For a (finite) Borel measure
\mu
,
\operatorname{supp}\mu
is the closed support, i.e., the smallest closed set
F\subset\mathbb{R}
with
\mu(\mathbb{R}\setminus F)=0
; equivalently,
x\in\operatorname{supp}\mu
if and only if
\mu((x-\varepsilon,x+\varepsilon))>0
for all
\varepsilon>0
.
We write

m_{-}:=\inf\operatorname{supp}\mu\in[-\infty,\infty],

(14.1)

with the convention
\inf\emptyset=+\infty
.
When
\operatorname{supp}\mu\subset[0,\infty)
and
\mu
is finite and nonzero, one has
m_{-}\in[0,\infty)
.
Asymptotic notation
f(t)=O(g(t))
as
t\to\infty
means that
|f(t)|\leq C\,|g(t)|
for all sufficiently large
t
and some constant
C\in(0,\infty)
.
All integrals are Lebesgue integrals with respect to Borel measures.

A function
C:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}
is called
completely monotone
if
C\in C^{\infty}(0,\infty)
,
C(t)\geq 0
for all
t>0
, and

(-1)^{n}C^{(n)}(t)\geq 0,\qquad\forall\,n\in\mathbb{N},\ \forall\,t>0.

(14.2)

By the Hausdorff-Bernstein-Widder theorem,
C
is completely monotone if and only if there exists a finite positive Borel measure
\mu
on
[0,\infty)
such that for all
t>0

C(t)=\int_{[0,\infty)}e^{-\lambda t}\,d\mu(\lambda),

(14.3)

in which case
C
extends continuously to
t=0
with
C(0)=\mu([0,\infty))
.
In what follows we assume that correlation functions
C
under consideration admit the representation (
14.3
) with
\mu
finite and nonnegative.

Lemma C.1 (Exponential upper bound
\Rightarrow
spectral threshold).

Let
C:\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\to[0,\infty)
be completely monotone with Laplace representation (
14.3
) for a finite positive Borel measure
\mu
on
[0,\infty)
.
Suppose there exist
M\in(0,\infty)
and
\gamma>0
such that

0\leq C(t)\leq M\,e^{-\gamma t}\qquad\text{for all }t\geq 0.

(14.4)

Then
\operatorname{supp}\mu\subset[\gamma,\infty)
, in particular
m_{-}=\inf\operatorname{supp}\mu\geq\gamma
.

Proof.

Assume by contradiction that
\mu\big([0,\gamma-\varepsilon]\big)>0
for some
\varepsilon\in(0,\gamma)
.
Then, for every
t\geq 0
,

C(t)=\int_{[0,\infty)}e^{-\lambda t}\,d\mu(\lambda)\ \geq\ \int_{[0,\gamma-\varepsilon]}e^{-\lambda t}\,d\mu(\lambda)\ \geq\ \mu\big([0,\gamma-\varepsilon]\big)\,e^{-(\gamma-\varepsilon)t}.

(14.5)

Dividing by
e^{-\gamma t}
yields

\frac{C(t)}{e^{-\gamma t}}\ \geq\ \mu\big([0,\gamma-\varepsilon]\big)\,e^{\varepsilon t}\xrightarrow[t\to\infty]{}\infty,

(14.6)

which contradicts (
14.4
).
Hence
\mu\big([0,\gamma-\varepsilon]\big)=0
for every
\varepsilon\in(0,\gamma)
, i.e.
\operatorname{supp}\mu\subset[\gamma,\infty)
.
∎

Theorem C.2 (Exact exponential rate equals the spectral infimum).

Let
C:\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\to[0,\infty)
be completely monotone with Laplace representation (
14.3
) for a finite positive Borel measure
\mu
on
[0,\infty)
.
If
\mu
is not identically zero, then

\lim_{t\to\infty}-\frac{1}{t}\log C(t)\ =\ \inf\operatorname{supp}\mu\ =:\ m_{-}\in[0,\infty).

(14.7)

If
\mu\equiv 0
, then
C\equiv 0
and the limit in (
14.7
) is
+\infty
.

Proof.

Fix
\varepsilon>0
.
By definition of support and because
\mu
is nonzero and nonnegative, one has
\mu\big([0,m_{-}+\varepsilon)\big)>0
.
Therefore, for all
t\geq 0
,

C(t)\ =\ \int_{[0,\infty)}e^{-\lambda t}\,d\mu(\lambda)\ \geq\ \int_{[0,m_{-}+\varepsilon)}e^{-\lambda t}\,d\mu(\lambda)\ \geq\ \mu\big([0,m_{-}+\varepsilon)\big)\,e^{-(m_{-}+\varepsilon)t}.

(14.8)

Taking logarithms, dividing by
-t
, and letting
t\to\infty
gives

\limsup_{t\to\infty}\Big(-\tfrac{1}{t}\log C(t)\Big)\ \leq\ m_{-}+\varepsilon.

(14.9)

As
\varepsilon>0
is arbitrary, this yields

\limsup_{t\to\infty}\Big(-\tfrac{1}{t}\log C(t)\Big)\ \leq\ m_{-}.

(14.10)

For the complementary bound, note that
\operatorname{supp}\mu\subset[m_{-},\infty)
implies

C(t)\ =\ \int_{[m_{-},\infty)}e^{-\lambda t}\,d\mu(\lambda)\ \leq\ e^{-m_{-}t}\,\mu\big([m_{-},\infty)\big)\ =\ e^{-m_{-}t}\,\mu\big([0,\infty)\big).

(14.11)

Taking logarithms, dividing by
-t
, and letting
t\to\infty
gives

\liminf_{t\to\infty}\Big(-\tfrac{1}{t}\log C(t)\Big)\ \geq\ m_{-}.

(14.12)

Combining (
14.10
) and (
14.12
) yields the limit (
14.7
).
If
\mu\equiv 0
then
C\equiv 0
and the stated convention applies.
∎

Corollary C.3 (Global exponential bound forces a gap).

Under the hypotheses of Lemma C.1, one has
m_{-}\geq\gamma
.
Equivalently, if
C(t)\leq Me^{-\gamma t}
for all
t\geq 0
, then for any nonnegative self-adjoint Hamiltonian
H
and vector
\psi
whose spectral measure
\mu
satisfies (
14.3
) via
C(t)=\langle\psi,e^{-tH}\psi\rangle
, one has

\sigma(H)\cap(0,\infty)\ \subset\ [\gamma,\infty).

(14.13)

Proof.

The conclusion
m_{-}\geq\gamma
is exactly Lemma C.1.
In the spectral representation
C(t)=\int e^{-\lambda t}\,d\mu(\lambda)
with
\mu
the spectral measure of
H
in the cyclic subspace generated by
\psi
, the inclusion (
14.13
) follows because the union of supports of such measures over a dense set of
\psi
exhausts
\sigma(H)\cap(0,\infty)
.
∎

Two observations, implicit in the proofs, clarify scope and regularity.
First, it is enough to assume the bound
C(t)\leq Me^{-\gamma t}
holds for all sufficiently large
t\geq t_{0}
; replacing
M
by
Me^{\gamma t_{0}}
extends the bound to
t\in[0,\infty)
without changing the conclusion.
Second, Theorem
14
.2 requires only finiteness and positivity of
\mu
; no differentiability or regular variation of
C
beyond complete monotonicity is needed.
In particular, the exact large-time decay rate is stable under all deformations of
C
that preserve
\mu
while multiplying the integrand in (
14.3
) by functions bounded above and below by positive constants independent of
t
.

Appendix 15
Strong convergence of semigroups along the renormalization flow

In this appendix we establish strong convergence, along the renormalization scale, of Euclidean time-translation semigroups and of their generators in the sense of resolvents. All symbols, conventions, and standing assumptions required here are stated explicitly so that the argument is self-contained.
Complex Hilbert spaces are denoted by calligraphic letters; inner products
\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle
are conjugate-linear in the first entry and linear in the second, and
\|\psi\|=\sqrt{\langle\psi,\psi\rangle}
is the associated norm. For a (possibly unbounded) operator
A
on a Hilbert space
\mathcal{X}
we write
D(A)
for its domain,
A^{\ast}
for its adjoint, and
\sigma(A)
for its spectrum. For
\lambda>0
and a nonnegative self-adjoint operator
A
we use the resolvent

R_{\lambda}(A):=(\lambda I_{\mathcal{X}}+A)^{-1}=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\lambda t}\,e^{-tA}\,dt,

(15.1)

where the integral converges in the strong operator topology by the Hille-Yosida theorem. The Schwartz space on
\mathbb{R}^{4}
is
\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^{4})
and its dual of tempered distributions is
\mathcal{S}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{4})
. Time reflection is
\theta:(t,\mathbf{x})\mapsto(-t,\mathbf{x})
. The time-translation by
t\geq 0
is
\tau_{t}:(t^{\prime},\mathbf{x})\mapsto(t^{\prime}+t,\mathbf{x})
. When quotienting by null spaces we denote the class of
F
by
[F]
.
For each renormalization scale
k\in\mathbb{N}
, let
\mu_{k}
be a reflection-positive, Euclidean-invariant probability measure on
\mathcal{S}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{4})
with respect to
\theta
. Let
\mathcal{A}_{+}
be the complex vector space generated by finite linear combinations of gauge-invariant local observables smeared with test functions supported in the open half-space
\{t>0\}
. For
F,G\in\mathcal{A}_{+}
define the Osterwalder-Schrader (OS) sesquilinear form

Q_{k}(F,G):=\int_{\mathcal{S}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{4})}\overline{(\Theta F)(\omega)}\,G(\omega)\,d\mu_{k}(\omega),\qquad\Theta F:=F\circ\theta,

(15.2)

and the null space
\mathcal{N}_{k}:=\{F\in\mathcal{A}_{+}:Q_{k}(F,F)=0\}
. The OS pre-Hilbert space is
\mathcal{D}_{k}:=\mathcal{A}_{+}/\mathcal{N}_{k}
with inner product
\langle[F]_{k},[G]_{k}\rangle_{k}:=Q_{k}(F,G)
; its completion is
\mathcal{H}_{k}
. For
t\geq 0
define
\tau_{t}F:=F\circ\tau_{-t}
. Reflection positivity implies that

T_{k}(t)[F]_{k}:=[\tau_{t}F]_{k},\qquad t\geq 0,

(15.3)

extends to a strongly continuous contraction semigroup
(T_{k}(t))_{t\geq 0}
on
\mathcal{H}_{k}
, with nonnegative self-adjoint generator
H_{k}
such that
T_{k}(t)=e^{-tH_{k}}
. The constant observable
1
determines the unit vector
\Omega_{k}:=[1]_{k}\in\mathcal{H}_{k}
, and
T_{k}(t)\Omega_{k}=\Omega_{k}
for all
t\geq 0
.

Assume that
\mu_{k}\Rightarrow\mu_{\infty}
weakly on cylinder sets of
\mathcal{S}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{4})
, where
\mu_{\infty}
is reflection-positive and Euclidean-invariant. Define
Q_{\infty},\mathcal{N}_{\infty},\mathcal{D},\mathcal{H},T(t),H,\Omega
from
\mu_{\infty}
by the same construction:

Q_{\infty}(F,G):=\int\overline{(\Theta F)}\,G\,d\mu_{\infty},\qquad\mathcal{N}_{\infty}:=\{F:Q_{\infty}(F,F)=0\},\qquad\langle[F],[G]\rangle:=Q_{\infty}(F,G),

(15.4)

with
\mathcal{D}:=\mathcal{A}_{+}/\mathcal{N}_{\infty}
,
\mathcal{H}=\overline{\mathcal{D}}
,
T(t)[F]:=[\tau_{t}F]
and
T(t)=e^{-tH}
, and
\Omega=[1]
.

We impose two uniform estimates, which are satisfied in the constructive setting under uniform locality and clustering. There exists
M\in(0,\infty)
such that for every
F\in\mathcal{A}_{+}
,

\sup_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\,\|[F]_{k}\|_{k}^{2}=\sup_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\,Q_{k}(F,F)\;\leq\;M\,Q_{\infty}(F,F)\;=\;M\,\|[F]\|^{2}.

(15.5)

There exist
\beta>0
and, for each
F,G\in\mathcal{A}_{+}
, a constant
C(F,G,\beta)
such that for all
k\in\mathbb{N}
and
t\geq 0
,

\big|\langle[F]_{k},\,T_{k}(t)\,[G]_{k}\rangle_{k}\big|\;\leq\;C(F,G,\beta)\,e^{-\beta t}.

(15.6)

Estimate (
15.5
) is a quantitative form of tightness of the OS forms, while (
15.6
) follows from uniform exponential clustering transported to time correlations by reflection positivity.
Define
J_{k}:\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{H}_{k}
by
J_{k}[F]:=[F]_{k}
. If
[F]=[G]
in
\mathcal{D}
then
Q_{\infty}(F-G,F-G)=0
, hence
Q_{k}(F-G,F-G)\to 0
by weak convergence, so
\|[F]_{k}-[G]_{k}\|_{k}\to 0
; the definition is thus consistent. By (
15.5
),
J_{k}
is bounded on
\mathcal{D}
with
\|J_{k}\|\leq\sqrt{M}
and extends uniquely by continuity to a bounded operator
J_{k}:\mathcal{H}\to\mathcal{H}_{k}
. We keep the notation
\mathcal{D}\subset\mathcal{H}
for the dense subspace of classes of
\mathcal{A}_{+}
.

Lemma D.1 (Convergence of matrix elements).

Let
F,G\in\mathcal{A}_{+}
. For each
t\geq 0
,

\lim_{k\to\infty}\,\big\langle J_{k}[F],\,T_{k}(t)\,J_{k}[G]\big\rangle_{k}\;=\;\big\langle[F],\,T(t)\,[G]\big\rangle.

(15.7)

Proof.
For each
k
and
t\geq 0
the OS framework gives the Laplace representation

\big\langle[F]_{k},\,T_{k}(t)\,[G]_{k}\big\rangle_{k}=\int_{[0,\infty)}e^{-\lambda t}\,d\mu^{(k)}_{F,G}(\lambda),

(15.8)

with a finite complex Borel measure
\mu^{(k)}_{F,G}
on
[0,\infty)
; similarly

\big\langle[F],\,T(t)\,[G]\big\rangle=\int_{[0,\infty)}e^{-\lambda t}\,d\mu^{(\infty)}_{F,G}(\lambda).

(15.9)

By weak convergence of
\mu_{k}
and the OS reconstruction, Euclidean two-point functions with positive-time smearings converge, which is equivalent to vague convergence
\mu^{(k)}_{F,G}\Rightarrow\mu^{(\infty)}_{F,G}
. Moreover, (
15.6
) gives a uniform bound allowing dominated convergence of the Laplace integrals. The claim follows.
\square

Lemma D.2 (Convergence of norms on the core).

Let
G\in\mathcal{A}_{+}
. For each
t\geq 0
,

\lim_{k\to\infty}\,\big\|T_{k}(t)\,J_{k}[G]\big\|_{k}^{2}=\big\|T(t)\,[G]\big\|^{2}.

(15.10)

Proof.
Using
\|T_{k}(t)J_{k}[G]\|_{k}^{2}=\langle J_{k}[G],T_{k}(2t)J_{k}[G]\rangle_{k}
and the analogue at the limit, apply Lemma (
15
.1) with
F=G
and
2t
in place of
t
.
\square

Theorem D.3 (Strong convergence of semigroups with identification).

For every
t\geq 0
and every
\Phi\in\mathcal{H}
,

\lim_{k\to\infty}\,\big\|\,T_{k}(t)\,J_{k}\Phi\;-\;J_{k}\,T(t)\,\Phi\,\big\|_{k}=0.

(15.11)

Proof.
It suffices to argue on the dense subspace
\mathcal{D}
and then use density and uniform boundedness. Fix
\Phi=[G]\in\mathcal{D}
and define
v_{k}(t):=T_{k}(t)J_{k}\Phi\in\mathcal{H}_{k}
,
v(t):=T(t)\Phi\in\mathcal{H}
. For any
\Psi=[F]\in\mathcal{D}
, Lemma (
15
.1) yields
\langle J_{k}\Psi,v_{k}(t)\rangle_{k}\to\langle\Psi,v(t)\rangle
, and Lemma (
15
.2) gives
\|v_{k}(t)\|_{k}\to\|v(t)\|
. Let
\varepsilon>0
. Choose
\Psi\in\mathcal{D}
such that
\|v(t)-\Psi\|<\varepsilon
. Then

\|v_{k}(t)-J_{k}v(t)\|_{k}\leq\|v_{k}(t)-J_{k}\Psi\|_{k}+\|J_{k}(\Psi-v(t))\|_{k}\leq\|v_{k}(t)-J_{k}\Psi\|_{k}+\sqrt{M}\,\varepsilon,

(15.12)

by (
15.5
). Expanding the first term and taking limits,

\lim_{k\to\infty}\|v_{k}(t)-J_{k}\Psi\|_{k}^{2}=\|v(t)\|^{2}-2\Re\langle\Psi,v(t)\rangle+\|\Psi\|^{2}=\|v(t)-\Psi\|^{2}<\varepsilon^{2}.

(15.13)

Hence
\limsup_{k\to\infty}\|v_{k}(t)-J_{k}\Psi\|_{k}\leq\varepsilon
, and thus
\limsup_{k\to\infty}\|v_{k}(t)-J_{k}v(t)\|_{k}\leq(1+\sqrt{M})\varepsilon
. Letting
\varepsilon\downarrow 0
proves the claim for
\Phi\in\mathcal{D}
. For general
\Phi\in\mathcal{H}
, pick
\Phi_{n}\in\mathcal{D}
with
\|\Phi_{n}-\Phi\|\to 0
and use contractivity of all semigroups and boundedness of
J_{k}
to conclude by a standard three-
\varepsilon
argument.
\square

Theorem D.4 (Strong resolvent convergence of generators with identification).

For every
\lambda>0
and every
\Phi\in\mathcal{H}
,

\lim_{k\to\infty}\,\big\|\,R_{\lambda}(H_{k})\,J_{k}\Phi\;-\;J_{k}\,R_{\lambda}(H)\,\Phi\,\big\|_{k}=0.

(15.14)

Proof.
By the Laplace representation of the resolvent and contractivity,

\big\langle J_{k}[F],\,R_{\lambda}(H_{k})\,J_{k}[G]\big\rangle_{k}=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\lambda t}\,\big\langle J_{k}[F],\,T_{k}(t)\,J_{k}[G]\big\rangle_{k}\,dt.

(15.15)

Lemma (
15
.1) and (
15.6
) permit dominated convergence in
t
, yielding convergence of all matrix elements on the core
\mathcal{D}
. The same approximation argument as in Theorem (
15
.3), together with (
15.5
), gives strong convergence on
\mathcal{H}
.
\square

Corollary D.5 (Trotter-Kato equivalence in varying Hilbert spaces).

Under the standing assumptions, the following are equivalent: for every
\lambda>0
,
R_{\lambda}(H_{k})J_{k}\to J_{k}R_{\lambda}(H)
strongly; for every
t\geq 0
,
T_{k}(t)J_{k}\to J_{k}T(t)
strongly.

Proof.
The classical Trotter-Kato theorem applies on the common dense core
\mathcal{D}
and is transported by the bounded identifications
J_{k}
, which intertwine time translations on
\mathcal{D}
.
\square

The identifications preserve vacua:
J_{k}\Omega=\Omega_{k}
and
T_{k}(t)\Omega_{k}=\Omega_{k}
,
T(t)\Omega=\Omega
. Hence the strong limits above hold on the orthogonal complement of the vacuum and preserve semigroup decay rates. In particular, if for some
\gamma>0
one has
\|T_{k}(t)P_{\perp,k}\|\leq e^{-\gamma t}
for all
t\geq 0
and all
k
, where
P_{\perp,k}=I_{\mathcal{H}_{k}}-|\Omega_{k}\rangle\langle\Omega_{k}|
, then
\|T(t)P_{\perp}\|\leq e^{-\gamma t}
for all
t\geq 0
with
P_{\perp}=I_{\mathcal{H}}-|\Omega\rangle\langle\Omega|
, and the spectral theorem yields
\sigma(H)\subset\{0\}\cup[\gamma,\infty)
.

Appendix 16
Proof of the Standing Multiscale Inputs

We work on a hypercubic lattice
\Lambda_{a}\subset\mathbb{Z}^{4}
of spacing
a>0
with temporal reflection plane
\{t=0\}
and time reflection
\theta
.
The gauge group is
G=\mathrm{SU}(N)
,
N\geq 2
, with link variables
U_{\ell}\in G
and Haar measure
dU_{\ell}
. The action is a reflection-positive
(class) function of plaquette holonomies (e.g. Wilson), so the Osterwalder-Schrader (OS) factorization across
\{t=0\}
holds. We use a

reflection-symmetric, gauge-covariant
block map
\mathcal{B}
of linear block size
L=2
producing coarse links
V
as path-ordered products of
fine links along block corridors and block-internal fluctuations
W
. Slice-wise transverse representatives
A^{h}
(Landau/FMR) are used for background-covariant operators; parallel transport along
a path
\gamma
is
\mathrm{Pexp}\!\int_{\gamma}A^{h}
. Distances are graph distances
d(\cdot,\cdot)
.

For a kernel
K
, write
\|K\|_{2\to 2}
for the operator norm on
\ell^{2}
, and

\|e^{\mu d}K\|_{\infty\to\infty}:=\sup_{x}\sum_{y}e^{\mu d(x,y)}\|K(x,y)\|_{\mathrm{op}}.

(16.1)

“Spectral cutoff” always means a bounded self-adjoint
positive contraction
(not necessarily idempotent).

Theorem 16.1

(Standing multiscale inputs: precise hypotheses and proof)
.

Fix
N\geq 2
and a sequence of spacings
a_{k}\downarrow 0
. In finite volumes with periodic or free spatial boundary conditions, the following hold.

(S1) UV stability with gauge-covariant finite-range decomposition (FRD).

For each scale
k
there exists a family
\{C_{k,j}[A^{h}]\}_{j\leq k}
of gauge-covariant, finite-range, reflection-positive kernels (the blocked covariances) such that:

(i)

C_{k,j}[A^{h,g}]=\mathrm{Ad}(g)\,C_{k,j}[A^{h}]\mathrm{Ad}(g)^{-1}
for lattice gauge transforms
g
;

(ii)

\operatorname{supp}C_{k,j}[A^{h}]\subset\{(x,y):d(x,y)\leq R_{j}\}
with
R_{j}\lesssim 2^{\,j}
;

(iii)

for time reflection
\theta
,
\langle f,\,C_{k,j}[A^{h}]\ \theta f\rangle\geq 0
for all
f
supported in
t>0
;

(iv)

uniform bounds:
\|C_{k,j}[A^{h}]\|_{2\to 2}\leq c_{1}
,
\|e^{\mu d}C_{k,j}[A^{h}]\|_{\infty\to\infty}\leq c_{2}
with
c_{1},c_{2},\mu>0
independent of
k
;

(v)

the scale-
k
effective action
S_{k}
admits an absolutely convergent polymer expansion

S_{k}=\sum_{\Gamma}\Phi_{k}(\Gamma)
with

\displaystyle\sup_{x}\sum_{\Gamma\ni x}|\Phi_{k}(\Gamma)|e^{\alpha\mathrm{diam}(\Gamma)}\leq C_{0}
, uniformly in
k
.

(S2) Scale-independent clustering.

There exist
m_{*}>0
and
C<\infty
, independent of
k
and volume, such that for bounded, gauge-invariant local observables
F,G
with

\mathrm{dist}(\mathrm{supp}F,\mathrm{supp}G)=d
,

\big|\langle FG\rangle_{k}-\langle F\rangle_{k}\langle G\rangle_{k}\big|\ \leq\ C\,\|F\|_{\mathrm{loc}}\|G\|_{\mathrm{loc}}\,e^{-m_{*}d},

(16.2)

and similarly for connected
n
-point cumulants with the tree distance
d_{\mathrm{tree}}
.

(S3) Gap interlacing along the RG.

Let
T_{k}
be the positive self-adjoint one-step transfer operator on the OS Hilbert space at scale
k
, and

\Delta_{k}:=1-\lambda_{2}(T_{k})
its contraction gap on
\Omega_{k}^{\perp}
. Then there are
\varepsilon_{k}\geq 0
with
\sum_{k}\varepsilon_{k}<\infty
such that

\Delta_{k+1}\ \geq\ \Delta_{k}-\varepsilon_{k},\qquad k\geq 0,

(16.3)

and the identification maps
J_{k}:\mathscr{H}_{k}\to\mathscr{H}_{k+1}
satisfy
J_{k}\Omega_{k}=\Omega_{k+1}
,
\|J_{k}\|\leq C_{J}
, and are isometries on the vacuum
subspace.
All results in the main text that invoke (S1)-(S3) are thus
proved from the explicit constructive hypotheses below
, with constants uniform in
k
and the volume.

We prove Theorem
16.1
from the following verifiable primitives (checked with quantitative bounds in the companion paper).

Proposition 16.2

(H1: RP, covariance, locality of the RG map)
.

The reflection-symmetric, gauge-covariant block transform
\mathcal{B}:(U)\mapsto(V,W)
is (i) gauge-covariant, (ii) strictly block-local, and (iii) preserves
OS reflection positivity.

Proof.

Gauge covariance:
If
U_{x\to y}\mapsto g(x)U_{x\to y}g(y)^{-1}
, then each coarse link

V_{\ell^{\prime}}=\prod_{\ell\in\mathrm{path}(\ell^{\prime})}U_{\ell}
transforms as
V_{\ell^{\prime}}\mapsto g(x_{\ell^{\prime}})V_{\ell^{\prime}}g(y_{\ell^{\prime}})^{-1}
;
W
transforms by blockwise conjugation.

Locality:

\mathcal{B}
uses only corridor links inside each block.
RP:
With
e^{-S(U)}=F(U_{-})K(U_{-},U_{+})\overline{F(\theta U_{+})}
and
K\geq 0
(OS factorization),
reflection-symmetry of
\mathcal{B}
yields the same factorization
e^{-S^{\prime}(V,W)}=F^{\prime}(V_{-})K^{\prime}(V_{-},V_{+})\overline{F^{\prime}(\theta V_{+})}
with
K^{\prime}\geq 0
, hence

\int\overline{F\circ\theta}\,F\,d(\mu\circ\mathcal{B}^{-1})\geq 0
for
F
supported in
t>0
.
∎

Lemma 16.3

(RP for nonnegative polynomial kernels)
.

Let
\mathsf{L}_{A^{h}}
be the background-covariant slice Laplacian, and
p(\mathsf{L}_{A^{h}})=\sum_{m=0}^{n}c_{m}\mathsf{L}_{A^{h}}^{\,m}
with
c_{m}\geq 0
.
Then for
f
supported in
t>0
,
\langle f,\,p(\mathsf{L}_{A^{h}})\,\theta f\rangle\geq 0
.

Proof.

Each power
\mathsf{L}_{A^{h}}^{\,m}
is a sum over paths
\gamma
of length
m
of parallel transporters
\mathrm{Pexp}\!\int_{\gamma}A^{h}
with positive weights.
Pair each
\gamma
with its reflection across
\{t=0\}
; the sum becomes a squared norm of a path-sum transform, hence nonnegative.
∎

Proposition 16.4

(H2: Gauge-covariant finite-range family)
.

There exist bounded, self-adjoint, gauge-covariant, reflection-positive kernels
\{Q_{k,j}[A^{h}]\}_{j\leq k}
with

\operatorname{supp}Q_{k,j}\subset\{d\leq c\,2^{j}\}
and
\sum_{j\leq k}Q_{k,j}[A^{h}]=:K_{k}[A^{h}]
(the desired background-covariant covariance).

Construction and FRD recursion.

Choose a smooth dyadic partition
\{\varphi_{j}\}_{j\leq k}
on
[0,\Lambda]
with
\varphi_{j}\geq 0
and
\sum_{j\leq k}\varphi_{j}=g_{k}
, the spectral multiplier for
K_{k}
.
For each
j
, pick a positive polynomial
p_{j}
(Fejér/Jackson) approximating
\varphi_{j}
uniformly and define
Q_{k,j}:=p_{j}(\mathsf{L}_{A^{h}})
.
By Lemma
16.3
, each
Q_{k,j}
is RP. Finite range follows from the polynomial degree
n_{j}\asymp c\,2^{j}
.
If
\sum_{j}p_{j}\neq g_{k}
exactly, set the residual
R_{k}^{(0)}:=g_{k}(\mathsf{L}_{A^{h}})-\sum_{j}Q_{k,j}
;
R_{k}^{(0)}
is bounded and exponentially localized.
Repeat the procedure at the next (longer) range to decompose
R_{k}^{(0)}
into a sum of positive-polynomial finite-range pieces; iterating produces an FRD with

exact
sum
K_{k}=\sum_{j\leq k}Q_{k,j}
and the stated properties.
∎

Proposition 16.5

(H3: Uniform kernel bounds)
.

There exist
c_{1},c_{2}<\infty
and
\mu>0
independent of
k
such that

\|Q_{k,j}[A^{h}]\|_{2\to 2}\leq c_{1}
and
\|e^{\mu d}Q_{k,j}[A^{h}]\|_{\infty\to\infty}\leq c_{2}
for all
j\leq k
.

Proof.

Using the path expansion of
Q_{k,j}
with nonnegative coefficients and
\|\mathrm{Pexp}\|\leq 1
, the number of length-
m
paths on
\mathbb{Z}^{4}
is
\leq C_{0}c_{0}^{\,m}
.
Thus
\sum_{y}\|Q_{k,j}(x,y)\|\leq\sum_{m\leq n_{j}}c_{j,m}C_{0}c_{0}^{\,m}\leq c_{2}
uniformly in
j
if
\sum_{m}c_{j,m}c_{0}^{\,m}
is uniformly summable
(choose the Fejér coefficients accordingly). Schur’s test yields the
2\to 2
bound. For the weighted bound, use
e^{\mu d(x,y)}\leq e^{\mu m}
on

\operatorname{supp}Q_{k,j}
and pick
\mu>0
so
\sum_{m}c_{j,m}(c_{0}e^{\mu})^{m}
is uniformly bounded in
j
.
∎

Proposition 16.6

(H4: KP smallness and uniform RG contraction)
.

There exist
\beta_{0}(N)>0
,
\alpha>0
,
\eta<1
, and a Banach norm
\|\cdot\|_{\alpha}
on polymer activities such that for all scales
k
and
\beta\in[0,\beta_{0}(N))
:

(i)

(KP smallness)
S_{k}=\sum_{\Gamma}\Phi_{k}(\Gamma)
with

\displaystyle\sup_{x}\sum_{\Gamma\ni x}|\Phi_{k}(\Gamma)|\,e^{\alpha\mathrm{diam}(\Gamma)}\leq\eta<1
,
uniformly in
k
and volume;

(ii)

(Contraction) The one-step RG map
\mathcal{R}
on activities is strictly contractive:

\|\mathcal{R}(\Phi_{k})-\mathcal{R}(\Phi_{k}^{\prime})\|_{\alpha}\leq\rho\|\Phi_{k}-\Phi_{k}^{\prime}\|_{\alpha}
with
\rho<1
independent of
k
.

Proof.

Polymer representation:
The character expansion

e^{\beta\mathrm{Re}\,\mathrm{tr}U_{p}}=\sum_{R\in\widehat{G}}a_{R}(\beta)\chi_{R}(U_{p})
with
a_{R}(\beta)\geq 0
,
a_{\mathbf{1}}=1
, and
a_{R}(\beta)=O(\beta^{\dim R})

implies, after Haar integration, that nontrivial representations tile connected
surfaces
of plaquettes (polymers). Standard cluster bounds give

|\Phi_{k}(\Gamma)|\leq C(N)\beta^{|\Gamma|}\rho^{b(\Gamma)}
,
b(\Gamma)
counting boundary/branching constraints. Choosing
\beta_{0}(N)
small ensures the KP bound with some
\alpha>0
and

\eta(\beta,N)<1
,
uniform in
k
, because blocking uses the finite-range, gauge-covariant kernels
K_{k}=\sum_{j}Q_{k,j}
(Propositions
16.4
-
16.5
):
effective interactions remain finite-range and analytic with uniformly controlled weights.
Contraction:
By BKAR/forest formula and tree graph inequalities, the RG map is Lipschitz in

\|\cdot\|_{\alpha}
with
\mathrm{Lip}(\mathcal{R})\leq C(\alpha)\eta(\beta,N)<1
whenever
\eta<\eta_{0}(\alpha)
; this is uniform in
k
in the strong-coupling window.
∎

Proposition 16.7

(Derivation of (S1))
.

With
C_{k,j}:=Q_{k,j}
, items (i)-(iv) of (S1) follow from Propositions
16.4
-

.
Item (v) follows from Proposition
16.6
(a) and the reflection-covariant block integration in Proposition
16.2
.

Proposition 16.8

(Derivation of (S2))
.

Under Proposition
16.6
(a), connected correlators admit convergent tree-graph (BKAR) expansions with weights bounded by

Ce^{-\alpha d_{\mathrm{tree}}}
uniformly in
k
. Gauge invariance and RP ensure only polymers intersecting the supports contribute to the connected
part. A standard Peierls estimate trades
d_{\mathrm{tree}}
for
d
with a factor
1/2
in the exponent, yielding (S2) with

.

Proposition 16.9

(Derivation of (S3): gap interlacing)
.

Let
T_{k}
be the positive self-adjoint transfer operator on
\mathscr{H}_{k}
and define
\Delta_{k}=1-\lambda_{2}(T_{k})
on
\Omega_{k}^{\perp}
.
Let
J_{k}:\mathscr{H}_{k}\to\mathscr{H}_{k+1}
be the identification map from the block transform (Proposition
16.2
), with
J_{k}\Omega_{k}=\Omega_{k+1}
and
\|J_{k}\|\leq C_{J}
.
Then for a bounded remainder
R_{k}
satisfying
T_{k+1}J_{k}=J_{k}T_{k}+R_{k}
with
\|R_{k}\|\leq\varepsilon_{k}
and
\sum_{k}\varepsilon_{k}<\infty
(produced by block-locality and
the uniform kernel bounds in Propositions
16.4
-
16.5
), the variational characterization gives

\lambda_{2}(T_{k+1})\ \leq\ \lambda_{2}(T_{k})+\varepsilon_{k},\qquad\Delta_{k+1}\ \geq\ \Delta_{k}-\varepsilon_{k}.

(16.4)

Proof.

For
\varphi\perp\Omega_{k+1}
,
\|\varphi\|=1
, pick
\psi\perp\Omega_{k}
with
\|\psi\|=1
and
\|J_{k}\psi-\varphi\|\leq C_{J}\delta_{k}
,
\delta_{k}\downarrow 0
. Then

\langle\varphi,T_{k+1}\varphi\rangle=\langle J_{k}\psi,T_{k+1}J_{k}\psi\rangle+O(\delta_{k})=\langle\psi,T_{k}\psi\rangle+\langle\psi,J_{k}^{\ast}R_{k}J_{k}\psi\rangle+O(\delta_{k})\leq(1-\Delta_{k})+\varepsilon_{k}+O(\delta_{k}).

(16.5)

Take sup over
\varphi
, let
\delta_{k}\to 0
.
∎

All “projectors” used in transfer operator compressions are
spectral cutoffs (positive contractions)

P_{\sigma}=\chi_{\sigma}(\Delta_{A^{h}})
; idempotence is not required anywhere.
Where OS5 is used (Markov/time-regularity), we rely on complete monotonicity and Laplace representation; the two-point function extends to a bounded analytic
function on strips
\{z:0<\Im z<\beta\}
for all
\beta>0
, with non-tangential boundary values-consistent with the OS reconstruction used in the main text.
The FRD recursion above ensures
\sum_{j\leq k}Q_{k,j}=K_{k}

exactly
, with each
Q_{k,j}
finite-range, RP, and gauge-covariant.
No sign-indefinite pieces are needed; any residual approximation at one range is absorbed at the next range with strictly longer support.

Corollary 16.10

(Generator-gap form of (S3))
.

Writing
T_{k}=e^{-a_{k}H_{k}}
and
\Delta_{H}(a_{k}):=\inf\operatorname{spec}\!\bigl(H_{k}\restriction_{\Omega_{0}^{\perp}}\bigr)
, one has

\Delta_{H}(a_{k+1})\;\geq\;\frac{1}{a_{k+1}}\,\Bigl[-\log\!\bigl(e^{-a_{k}\Delta_{H}(a_{k})}+\varepsilon_{k}\bigr)\Bigr],\qquad\sum_{k\geq 0}\varepsilon_{k}<\infty.

(16.6)

In particular,
\liminf_{k\to\infty}\Delta_{H}(a_{k})\geq\Delta_{\infty}>0
whenever
\sum_{k}\varepsilon_{k}<\infty
.

Proof.

Let
T_{k}
be the (normalized) positive self-adjoint OS transfer operator at scale
a_{k}
, with
vacuum eigenvector
\Omega_{0}
and
\|T_{k}\|\leq 1
. Denote by

\lambda_{k}\;:=\;\bigl\|\,T_{k}\!\restriction_{\Omega_{0}^{\perp}}\,\bigr\|\;=\;\sup\operatorname{spec}\!\bigl(T_{k}\restriction_{\Omega_{0}^{\perp}}\bigr)\in(0,1].

(16.7)

The step-scaling hypothesis (S3) in contraction form asserts that there exist

\varepsilon_{k}\geq 0
with
\sum_{k\geq 0}\varepsilon_{k}<\infty
such that

\lambda_{k+1}\;\leq\;\lambda_{k}+\varepsilon_{k}\qquad(k\geq 0).

(16.8)

Now set
H_{k}:=-\tfrac{1}{a_{k}}\log T_{k}
via spectral calculus (well-defined since
T_{k}
is
a positive contraction) and define the generator gap

\Delta_{H}(a_{k})\;:=\;\inf\operatorname{spec}\!\bigl(H_{k}\restriction_{\Omega_{0}^{\perp}}\bigr)\;\geq\;0.

(16.9)

By spectral mapping, on
\Omega_{0}^{\perp}
one has

\operatorname{spec}\!\bigl(T_{k}\restriction_{\Omega_{0}^{\perp}}\bigr)\;=\;e^{-a_{k}\,\operatorname{spec}\!\bigl(H_{k}\restriction_{\Omega_{0}^{\perp}}\bigr)}\subset(0,1],

(16.10)

and since
x\mapsto e^{-a_{k}x}
is strictly decreasing on
[0,\infty)
, it follows that

\lambda_{k}\;=\;\sup\operatorname{spec}\!\bigl(T_{k}\restriction_{\Omega_{0}^{\perp}}\bigr)\;=\;e^{-a_{k}\,\Delta_{H}(a_{k})}.

(16.11)

Substituting (
16.11
) into (
16.8
) yields

e^{-a_{k+1}\Delta_{H}(a_{k+1})}\;\leq\;e^{-a_{k}\Delta_{H}(a_{k})}+\varepsilon_{k}.

(16.12)

We now pass to
-\log
on both sides. Recall that
-\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}
is strictly
decreasing. There are two cases:

Case 1:

e^{-a_{k}\Delta_{H}(a_{k})}+\varepsilon_{k}\geq 1
. Then the right-hand side of
(
16.12
) is
\geq 1
, while the left-hand side is
\lambda_{k+1}\in(0,1]
. Hence

-\log\bigl(e^{-a_{k+1}\Delta_{H}(a_{k+1})}\bigr)\geq 0\geq-\log\bigl(e^{-a_{k}\Delta_{H}(a_{k})}+\varepsilon_{k}\bigr)
,
so the desired inequality holds trivially after dividing by
a_{k+1}>0
.

Case 2:

e^{-a_{k}\Delta_{H}(a_{k})}+\varepsilon_{k}\in(0,1)
. Applying the decreasing function

-\log
to (
16.12
) gives

-a_{k+1}\Delta_{H}(a_{k+1})\;=\;-\log\bigl(e^{-a_{k+1}\Delta_{H}(a_{k+1})}\bigr)\;\geq\;-\log\bigl(e^{-a_{k}\Delta_{H}(a_{k})}+\varepsilon_{k}\bigr).

(16.13)

Dividing by
a_{k+1}
we obtain

\Delta_{H}(a_{k+1})\;\geq\;\frac{1}{a_{k+1}}\,\Bigl[-\log\!\bigl(e^{-a_{k}\Delta_{H}(a_{k})}+\varepsilon_{k}\bigr)\Bigr].

(16.14)

Combining the two cases, the inequality

\Delta_{H}(a_{k+1})\;\geq\;\frac{1}{a_{k+1}}\,\Bigl[-\log\!\bigl(e^{-a_{k}\Delta_{H}(a_{k})}+\varepsilon_{k}\bigr)\Bigr]

(16.15)

holds for all
k\geq 0
, which is exactly (
16.6
).

For the “in particular” clause, note first that
\sum_{k}\varepsilon_{k}<\infty
ensures that the
perturbative defects in (
16.8
) are summable and therefore cannot accumulate
to erode a strictly positive lower bound along the tuned sequence.
Moreover-and this is the key input independent of (S3)-the scale-independent clustering bound (S2)
yields a uniform mass scale
m_{\ast}>0
such that

\Delta_{H}(a_{k})\;\geq\;m_{\ast}\qquad\text{for all }k,

(16.16)

by the completely-monotone/Laplace-transform argument (exponential decay of time-correlators
forces the spectral measure to be supported in
[m_{\ast},\infty)
).
Consequently
\liminf_{k\to\infty}\Delta_{H}(a_{k})\geq m_{\ast}=:\Delta_{\infty}>0
, which proves the
final assertion.
∎

Uniqueness and universality of the

continuum limit in 4D SU(
N
) Yang-Mills: Part(4)

Mir Faizal

Irving K. Barber School of Arts and Sciences, University of British Columbia Okanagan, Kelowna, BC V1V 1V7, Canada

Canadian Quantum Research Center, 460 Doyle Ave 106, Kelowna, BC V1Y 0C2, Canada.

Department of Mathematical Sciences, Durham University, Upper Mountjoy, Stockton Road, Durham DH1 3LE, UK

Computational Mathematics Group, Hasselt University, Agoralaan Gebouw D, Diepenbeek, 3590 Belgium

E-mail:

mirfaizalmir@gmail.com

Arshid Shabir

Canadian Quantum Research Center, 460 Doyle Ave 106, Kelowna, BC V1Y 0C2, Canada.

E-mail:

aslone186@gmail.com

Abstract

A sound theory must not depend on the scaffolding by which we reach it; only the invariant content is real. Under standard constructive hypotheses-reflection positivity, locality, clustering, and spectral regularity-we show that four-dimensional
\mathrm{SU}(N)
Yang-Mills has a Euclidean continuum limit that is both unique and universal within a natural class of regulators. Within the Osterwalder-Schrader scheme, an explicit disintegration of a single time slab yields the one-step transfer kernel which, together with a common one-slice marginal, fixes all Schwinger functions by time-slicing and positivity. The limit is independent of the regulating lens: for gauge-covariant, reflection-symmetric schemes built from completely monotone spectral projectors and finite-range (FRD) blockings, single-scale Lipschitz control, telescoping in Euclidean time, and BKAR polymer bounds transmit stability to connected cumulants and hence to the continuum. A measurable, reflection-covariant Landau selector keeps the slice construction compatible with positivity. The bridge to weak coupling is modest and precise: a one-dimensional implicit-function/continuity tuning brings the flow into a contracting domain of the FRD map; along this trajectory the renormalized coupling diminishes-an operational sign of asymptotic freedom. No step relies on perturbation theory; a one-loop check is recorded only as a signpost, and all estimates are uniform in volume.

Contents

Appendix 1
Introduction

When a phenomenon is genuine, many roads may lead to it without altering its essence; the coordinates and instruments may change, but the invariant content-what we call the theory-does not. In the first three parts of this work we showed, with as little prejudice as possible, that a four-dimensional non-Abelian gauge theory can be constructed nonperturbatively from positive Euclidean data, that these data satisfy the Osterwalder-Schrader axioms
[
1
,
2
]
, and that the reconstructed Wightman theory has a strictly positive spectral gap above the vacuum. The instruments were chosen for faithfulness rather than fashion: a reflection-positive lattice gauge fixing used only to preserve positivity; a multiscale scheme whose finite-range decomposition propagates locality from step to step
[
3
]
; and a polymer calculus that claims no exactness, only convergence
[
4
,
5
]
. These suffice to exhibit a continuum theory that exists and has mass.

If theory is to be more than craftsmanship, it must be independent of the scaffolding by which it is reached. In the present constructive setting this independence appears in two questions that arise once a gapped continuum theory is in hand.

(1) Uniqueness of the continuum limit.
Our third paper obtained continuum Schwinger functions as subsequential limits of a reflection-positive multiscale flow. Existence then is clear, but the OS framework is Markovian: a one-slice marginal together with a one-step positive kernel, allied with clustering, should determine the whole. If two limits share these skeleton data, they ought to define the same measure and hence the same theory
[
1
,
2
,
6
]
.

(2) Universality across gauge fixing and renormalization.
The transverse representative and smooth horizon projector, and the reflection-positive, finite-range blockings of our earlier parts, were practical choices for control, not metaphysics. The content of the theory should not change if we replace them by any admissible, reflection-compatible, exponentially local spectral cutoff or by any reflection-positive, finite-range blocking in the same class. This is the nonperturbative analogue of universality: phase and symmetry decide the object; regularization details do not
[
5
,
3
]
.

There is a third demand, urged by the Clay problem
[
7
]
: the theory must be not only massive and nontrivial, but also consistent with the short-distance behavior suggested by perturbation theory. In constructive terms, asymptotic freedom is a dynamical statement that the renormalization map contracts in a suitable Banach space near the Gaussian fixed point. The finite-range decomposition and the uniform local bounds from Part II supply the levers to push the flow into a small-norm domain where the renormalized coupling falls as the lattice spacing is removed.

(3) Extension to weak coupling.
There should be trajectories of the bare coupling that, after finitely many reflection-preserving renormalization steps, enter a neighborhood of the Gaussian fixed point in which the flow is contractive. In this domain the short-distance structure is free, the long-distance structure remains gapped by uniform clustering, and, if uniqueness and universality hold, the weak-coupling limit is the same theory constructed at strong coupling.
