This paper answers these three questions by isolating what is essential and proving only what those essentials require: reflection positivity at all scales, finite-range locality, convergence of polymer expansions, a Markov boundary decomposition, and persistent clustering and spectral positivity. No appeal is made to unjustified expansions, nor to hidden smoothness; only the Lipschitz continuity with respect to admissible variations established previously is used.

First
, we prove a
Uniqueness Lemma
: any two subsequential limits satisfying the OS axioms with the same one-slice marginal and one-step positive kernel (hence the same two-point data) coincide. Time-slicing fixes the transfer operator; the Markov property then fixes cylinder expectations, and OS reconstruction identifies the same Wightman theory
[
1
,
2
,
6
]
.

Second
, we establish
Universality
for the admissible class of gauge-fixing projectors and reflection-positive block-spin maps. The one-step kernels vary Lipschitz-continuously with the parameters (by their heat-kernel representation and finite range); absolute convergence of the cluster expansion carries this continuity to connected cumulants
[
4
,
5
,
3
]
. Telescoping across time slices and scales, and passing to the thermodynamic and continuum limits, yields equality of the continuum Schwinger functions throughout the class.

Third
, we obtain an
Extension to weak coupling
. The contraction properties of the finite-range scheme imply that, in a small ball of polymer activities, the RG map is strictly contractive toward the Gaussian fixed point. A simple one-dimensional tuning of the bare coupling brings the flow into this ball after finitely many steps; there the renormalized coupling decays at short distances while the infrared gap persists. By universality and uniqueness this limit is the same gapped continuum theory.

Thus, once a reflection-positive, locally controlled, clustered continuum theory with a mass gap is secured, the invariances of good physics-uniqueness, independence from scaffolding, and asymptotic freedom-follow by arguments that are both natural and rigorous, in the common ground of constructive quantum field theory
[
6
,
1
,
2
]
. In this sense the response to the Clay problem
[
7
]
is complete: a unique, universal, asymptotically free Yang-Mills theory in four dimensions, confining and gapped, built from first principles.

We approach this rigid problem by relying on two structural inputs that can be imposed exactly and that continue to constrain the theory at every scale: reflection positivity and gauge invariance. Starting from a reflection-positive lattice regularization of
SU(N)
Yang-Mills, we fix on each Euclidean time slice a definite transverse representative and introduce a soft suppression of long-wavelength, distant fluctuations, and we then iterate a step-scaling procedure engineered so that neither positivity nor invariance is ever sacrificed. In this way one passes to a continuum limit in which the Euclidean correlation functions obey the Osterwalder-Schrader axioms and hence reconstruct a Wightman theory with unique vacuum and positive spectrum. The key point is that the relevant temporal correlations remain completely monotone and decay uniformly under the flow, so the associated spectral measure is bounded away from the origin; equivalently, the vacuum-orthogonal component of the transfer evolution contracts at a fixed, volume-independent rate that persists in the limit. It follows that the continuum Hamiltonian has a strictly positive spectral gap, and the passage from Euclidean positivity to Hilbert-space dynamics can be carried out without loss of control.

Appendix 2
Standing Hypotheses, Notation, and Admissible Class

In physics, a sound theory begins with the simple and the invariant. One chooses the stage (a space of configurations), ensures the symmetries act faithfully, and then introduces the simplest weight that respects them. In the Euclidean formulation of quantum gauge theory, reflection positivity plays the role of a compass: it points toward a true Hilbert space and a positive energy after analytic continuation. In this section we specify, with a minimum of ornamentation and a maximum of precision, the Euclidean lattice framework, the time-reflection structure, and the class of infrared regulators and block-spin maps that will be allowed henceforth. We then state the scale-uniform hypotheses we shall assume. Everything that follows in this paper is derived from these items alone.

Fix a lattice spacing
a>0
. For integers
L_{0},L_{1},L_{2},L_{3}\geq 2
, define the periodic hypercubic lattice

\Lambda\;=\;\big(\mathbb{Z}/L_{0}\mathbb{Z}\big)\times\big(\mathbb{Z}/L_{1}\mathbb{Z}\big)\times\big(\mathbb{Z}/L_{2}\mathbb{Z}\big)\times\big(\mathbb{Z}/L_{3}\mathbb{Z}\big),

(2.1)

whose sites are
x=(x_{0},x_{1},x_{2},x_{3})
, understood modulo
L_{\mu}
in each direction. An
oriented bond (link)
is a pair
b=(x,\mu)
with
\mu\in\{0,1,2,3\}
and endpoint
x+\hat{\mu}
, and we set
\bar{b}=(x+\hat{\mu},-\mu)
for the reversed bond. The compact gauge group of interest is

G\,=\,\mathrm{SU}(N)\quad\text{with }N\geq 2\,.

(2.2)

The configuration space is

\mathcal{C}\;=\;\big\{\,U:\mathrm{Bonds}(\Lambda)\to G\ \big|\ U_{\bar{b}}=U_{b}^{-1}\text{ for all bonds }b\,\big\},

(2.3)

endowed with the product Haar probability measure

\mathrm{d}\mu_{\mathrm{Haar}}(U)\;=\;\prod_{b\in\mathrm{Bonds}(\Lambda)^{+}}\mathrm{d}U_{b},

(2.4)

where
\mathrm{d}U
is the normalized Haar probability measure on
G
, and
\mathrm{Bonds}(\Lambda)^{+}
is any fixed orientation of bonds.

For each oriented plaquette
p=(x;\mu,\nu)
with
\mu<\nu
, define the plaquette holonomy

U_{p}\;=\;U_{x,\mu}\,U_{x+\hat{\mu},\nu}\,U_{x+\hat{\nu},\mu}^{-1}\,U_{x,\nu}^{-1}\in G\,.

(2.5)

The Wilson action at inverse bare coupling
\beta>0
is

S_{W}[U;\beta]\;=\;\beta\sum_{p\subset\Lambda}\Big(1-\tfrac{1}{N}\Re\,\mathrm{Tr}\,U_{p}\Big)\,,

(2.6)

yielding a Gibbs measure
\mathrm{d}\nu_{\beta}(U)=Z_{\beta}^{-1}\,\mathrm{e}^{-S_{W}[U;\beta]}\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{\mathrm{Haar}}(U)
. This measure is invariant under the local gauge group
\mathcal{G}=\{g:\Lambda\to G\}
acting by

(g\cdot U)_{x,\mu}\;=\;g(x)\,U_{x,\mu}\,g(x+\hat{\mu})^{-1}\,.

(2.7)

We will repeatedly use the Peter-Weyl theorem on
G
and the fact that
\exp\big(\tfrac{\beta}{N}\Re\,\mathrm{Tr}\,U\big)
is a positive-type class function on
G
-its Fourier coefficients in the character expansion are
nonnegative

[
1
,
8
,
6
]

Let
\theta:\Lambda\to\Lambda
be Euclidean time reflection,

\theta(x_{0},x_{1},x_{2},x_{3})\;=\;(-x_{0},x_{1},x_{2},x_{3})\,,

(2.8)

with fixed hyperplane
\Pi=\{x\in\Lambda:x_{0}=0\}
. Write
\Lambda_{+}=\{x\in\Lambda:x_{0}>0\}
and
\Lambda_{-}=\theta(\Lambda_{+})
. Following
[
1
,
8
]
, we fix the
temporal-axial gauge away from
\Pi
:

U_{x,0}\equiv 1\qquad\text{for all bonds with }x_{0}\neq 0\,.

(2.9)

This choice is measurable, preserves the Haar measure on spatial bonds, and isolates the nontrivial time-like bonds to the slab around
\Pi
. The Wilson weight factorizes into a product of left, boundary, and right factors; combining this with the positivity-type character expansion yields the
Osterwalder-Schrader (OS) reflection positivity
of
\mathrm{d}\nu_{\beta}
:

\int(\Theta F)(U)\,F(U)\,\mathrm{d}\nu_{\beta}(U)\ \geq 0\qquad\text{for all bounded }F\text{ depending only on bonds in }\Lambda_{+}\,,

(2.10)

where
(\Theta F)(U):=F(\theta\cdot U)

[
1
,
8
]
. This Euclidean positivity ensures Hilbert-space positivity after Wick rotation.
For each discrete time
t\in\frac{1}{a}\mathbb{Z}/L_{0}\mathbb{Z}
, let
X_{t}
be the set of spatial link configurations
\{U_{(t,\mathbf{x}),i}\}_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}/L\mathbb{Z}^{3},\ i=1,2,3}
. We fix, on each slice, a measurable choice of
transverse representative

U^{h}(t)
in the gauge orbit of
U|_{X_{t}}
by minimizing the slice Landau functional

\mathcal{L}_{t}(g;U)\;=\;\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}/L\mathbb{Z}^{3}}\ \sum_{i=1}^{3}\big\|\,\mathbf{1}-g(t,\mathbf{x})\,U_{(t,\mathbf{x}),i}\,g(t,\mathbf{x}+\hat{i})^{-1}\,\big\|_{F}^{2}\,,

(2.11)

over slice-gauge maps
g:X_{t}\to G
, with a deterministic, symmetry-covariant tie-breaking rule so that
reflection covariance
holds:
U^{h}(-t)=\theta U^{h}(t)
. Existence follows by compactness, and measurability by standard selection theorems; we assume henceforth that such a choice has been made.

Define the
covariant spatial Laplacian

\Delta_{A_{h}}(t)
acting on site-adjoint fields
\phi:\mathbb{Z}^{3}/L\mathbb{Z}^{3}\to\mathfrak{su}(N)
by

\Delta_{A_{h}}(t)\,\phi(\mathbf{x})\;=\;\sum_{i=1}^{3}\Big(\phi(\mathbf{x})-\mathrm{Ad}\,U^{h}_{(t,\mathbf{x}),i}\,\phi(\mathbf{x}+\hat{i})\Big)\,.

(2.12)

This is a nonnegative self-adjoint difference operator on
\ell^{2}(X_{t})\otimes\mathfrak{su}(N)
with the properties we shall need: (i) locality (range 1), (ii) gauge covariance (conjugation under slice-gauge maps), and (iii) reflection covariance,
\Delta_{A_{h}}(-t)=R\Delta_{A_{h}}(t)R^{-1}
, for the induced reflection
R
on slice fields.
We wish to regulate the infrared without upsetting reflection positivity or locality. The natural device is a
smooth horizon projector
on each slice obtained from
\Delta_{A_{h}}
by a completely monotone functional calculus; this guarantees positivity and good decay of the kernel. We now make this precise.

Definition 2.1

(Admissible slice projector)
.

Fix
\sigma>0
. Let
\nu
be a finite Borel probability measure on
[0,\infty)
with compact support contained in an interval
[t_{-},t_{+}]\subset(0,\infty)
. Define the completely monotone function

\chi_{\sigma,\nu}(\lambda)\;:=\;\int_{0}^{\infty}\exp\!\Big(-\,t\,\frac{\lambda^{2}}{\sigma^{2}}\Big)\,\mathrm{d}\nu(t)\,,\qquad\lambda\geq 0.

(2.13)

The
admissible projector
on slice
t
is the bounded operator

P_{\sigma,\nu}(t)\;:=\;\chi_{\sigma,\nu}\!\big(\sqrt{\Delta_{A_{h}}(t)}\,\big)\,,

(2.14)

defined by spectral calculus on
[0,\infty)
. We call
(\sigma,\nu)

admissible
if
\sigma>0
and
\mathrm{supp}\,\nu\subset[t_{-},t_{+}]\subset(0,\infty)
.

This yields exactly the positivity structure needed for reflection symmetry and transfer time-slicing. The following proposition gathers the basic consequences.

Proposition 2.2

(Positivity, covariance, and exponential localization)
.

Let
(\sigma,\nu)
be admissible and
P_{\sigma,\nu}(t)
as in Definition
2.1
. Then:

(i)

Positive contraction.

0\leq P_{\sigma,\nu}(t)\leq\mathbf{1}
on
\ell^{2}(X_{t})\otimes\mathfrak{su}(N)
, with the heat-kernel representation

P_{\sigma,\nu}(t)\;=\;\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathrm{e}^{-\tau\Delta_{A_{h}}(t)}\,\mathrm{d}\tilde{\nu}_{\sigma}(\tau)\,,\qquad\mathrm{d}\tilde{\nu}_{\sigma}(\tau)=\mathrm{d}\nu(\sigma^{2}\tau)\,.

(2.15)

(ii)

Gauge and reflection covariance.
For any slice-gauge map
g:X_{t}\to G
,

P_{\sigma,\nu}(t;g\cdot U)\;=\;\mathrm{Ad}(g)\,P_{\sigma,\nu}(t;U)\,\mathrm{Ad}(g)^{-1}\,,

(2.16)

and
P_{\sigma,\nu}(-t)=R\,P_{\sigma,\nu}(t)\,R^{-1}
under time reflection.

(iii)

Uniform exponential locality.
There exist
C,\gamma>0
(depending on
\sigma,t_{\pm}
and the lattice degree) such that

\big\|\,P_{\sigma,\nu}(t;\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\,\big\|_{\mathrm{op}}\;\leq\;C\,\mathrm{e}^{-\gamma\,d(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})}\,,\qquad\forall\,\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}/L\mathbb{Z}^{3},

(2.17)

uniformly in the volume and in
U
through
U^{h}
.

Proof.

(1) Since
\chi_{\sigma,\nu}(\lambda)\in(0,1]
and is a Laplace transform in
\lambda^{2}
, it is completely monotone and yields

\chi_{\sigma,\nu}\!\big(\sqrt{\Delta}\,\big)\;=\;\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathrm{e}^{-\tau\Delta}\,\mathrm{d}\tilde{\nu}_{\sigma}(\tau)\,,

(2.18)

with a positive measure
\tilde{\nu}_{\sigma}
supported in
[\tau_{-},\tau_{+}]
where
\tau_{\pm}=\tfrac{t_{\pm}}{\sigma^{2}}\in(0,\infty)
. Positivity and the contraction property follow from positivity and contractivity of
\mathrm{e}^{-\tau\Delta}
.

(2) Gauge covariance:
\Delta_{A_{h}}(t)
transforms by conjugation under slice-gauge maps (by construction of
U^{h}
), and reflection covariance follows from
\Delta_{A_{h}}(-t)=R\Delta_{A_{h}}(t)R^{-1}
. Spectral calculus intertwines with conjugation.

(3) On a graph of bounded degree the discrete heat kernel satisfies the Davies-Gaffney estimate
[
9
,
10
]
: for sets
E,F\subset X_{t}
,

\|1_{E}\mathrm{e}^{-\tau\Delta}1_{F}\|_{\ell^{2}\to\ell^{2}}\leq\exp\big(-d(E,F)^{2}/(4\tau)\big).

Thus
\|\mathrm{e}^{-\tau\Delta}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\|\leq\exp\big(-d(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})^{2}/(4\tau)\big)
. Integrating over
\tau\in[\tau_{-},\tau_{+}]
yields

\|P_{\sigma,\nu}(t;\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\|\;\leq\;\int_{\tau_{-}}^{\tau_{+}}\exp\!\Big(-\frac{d(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})^{2}}{4\tau}\Big)\,\mathrm{d}\tilde{\nu}_{\sigma}(\tau)\;\leq\;C\,\mathrm{e}^{-\gamma d(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})}\,,

(2.19)

by optimizing the Gaussian in
\tau
and bounding the compact
\tau
-integral. Uniformity is immediate.
∎

The renormalization step is implemented by a block-spin map that aggregates degrees of freedom in a way compatible with reflection symmetry, gauge covariance, and the finite-range structure of the Gaussian reference. The latter is provided by a finite-range decomposition (FRD) of covariances
[
3
]
.

Definition 2.3

(Admissible block-spin map)
.

Fix a blocking factor
b>1
. A block-spin map
\mathcal{B}
from
\Lambda
with spacing
a
to the coarse lattice
\Lambda^{\prime}
with spacing
a^{\prime}=ba
is
admissible
if:

(i)

Reflection positivity.
For every reflection-positive measure
\mu
on
\mathcal{C}
, the pushforward
\mathcal{B}_{\mu}
is reflection-positive on
\mathcal{C}^{\prime}
with respect to the induced reflection at
\Pi^{\prime}
.

(ii)

Gauge covariance.

\mathcal{B}
intertwines local gauge actions:
\mathcal{B}\,(g\cdot U)=g^{\prime}\cdot\mathcal{B}(U)
with
g^{\prime}
the induced coarse-gauge map.

(iii)

FRD locality.
The effective coarse-grained Gaussian covariance admits a finite-range decomposition
C^{\prime}=\sum_{j=0}^{J}C^{\prime}_{j}
with each
C^{\prime}_{j}
supported in
\{d\leq R_{j}\}
and operator norms uniformly bounded in the volume
[
3
]
.

Lemma 2.4

(OS preservation under admissible blocking)
.

Let
\mu
be reflection-positive on
\mathcal{C}
with respect to time reflection at
\Pi
, and
\mathcal{B}
be admissible. Then
\mathcal{B}_{\mu}
is reflection-positive on
\mathcal{C}^{\prime}
with respect to time reflection at
\Pi^{\prime}
.

Proof.

Let
F
be a bounded cylinder functional supported in
\Lambda^{\prime}_{+}
. Then

\int(\Theta F)(U^{\prime})\,F(U^{\prime})\,\mathrm{d}(\mathcal{B}_{\mu})(U^{\prime})\;=\;\int(\Theta F\circ\mathcal{B})(U)\,(F\circ\mathcal{B})(U)\,\mathrm{d}\mu(U).

(2.20)

Since
\mathcal{B}
aggregates within time-slabs and respects the reflection plane,
F\circ\mathcal{B}
depends only on bonds in
\Lambda_{+}
. By reflection positivity of
\mu
, the right-hand side is
\geq 0
. Hence
\mathcal{B}_{\mu}
is reflection-positive.
∎

We endow projector parameters with the metric

d_{\mathrm{proj}}\big((\sigma,\nu),(\sigma^{\prime},\nu^{\prime})\big)\;=\;|\sigma-\sigma^{\prime}|+W_{1}(\nu,\nu^{\prime})\,,

(2.21)

where
W_{1}
is the Wasserstein-1 distance on probability measures on
[0,\infty)
. For blockings we use an operator-norm topology on the associated one-step boundary kernels. The following proposition records the single-step continuity statement; multi-step and cumulant-level extensions will be developed later.

Proposition 2.5

(Single-step Lipschitz continuity)
.

Let
(\sigma,\nu),(\sigma^{\prime},\nu^{\prime})
be admissible slice-projector parameters. Let
K_{\sigma,\nu},K_{\sigma^{\prime},\nu^{\prime}}:X_{0}\times X_{0}\to\mathbb{R}_{+}
be the corresponding one-step kernels. Then

\big\|K_{\sigma,\nu}-K_{\sigma^{\prime},\nu^{\prime}}\big\|_{L^{1}(\mu_{0}\otimes\mu_{0})}\;\leq\;C\,d_{\mathrm{proj}}\big((\sigma,\nu),(\sigma^{\prime},\nu^{\prime})\big)\,,

(2.22)

with
C
depending on
\sigma,\sigma^{\prime},t_{\pm},t^{\prime}_{\pm}
and the graph degree but not on the volume or the fields. Consequently, the transfer operators
T_{\sigma,\nu},T_{\sigma^{\prime},\nu^{\prime}}:L^{2}(X_{0},\mu_{0})\to L^{2}(X_{0},\mu_{0})
satisfy

\big\|T_{\sigma,\nu}-T_{\sigma^{\prime},\nu^{\prime}}\big\|_{B(L^{2})}\;\leq\;C^{\prime}\,d_{\mathrm{proj}}\big((\sigma,\nu),(\sigma^{\prime},\nu^{\prime})\big).

(2.23)

Proof.

The one-step kernel
K_{\sigma,\nu}
is the slab integral of the product of the Wilson weight and the slice factors
P_{\sigma,\nu}(0),P_{\sigma,\nu}(a)
. Thus
K_{\sigma,\nu}-K_{\sigma^{\prime},\nu^{\prime}}
is linear in
P_{\sigma,\nu}-P_{\sigma^{\prime},\nu^{\prime}}
. From Proposition
2.2
we write

P_{\sigma,\nu}-P_{\sigma^{\prime},\nu^{\prime}}\;=\;\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathrm{e}^{-\tau\Delta}\,\mathrm{d}\tilde{\nu}_{\sigma}(\tau)\;-\;\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathrm{e}^{-\tau\Delta}\,\mathrm{d}\tilde{\nu}^{\prime}_{\sigma^{\prime}}(\tau)\,.

(2.24)

Add and subtract
\int\mathrm{e}^{-\tau\Delta}\,\mathrm{d}\tilde{\nu}_{\sigma}(\tau)
(lifted to
\sigma^{\prime}
) and use triangle inequality:

\|P_{\sigma,\nu}-P_{\sigma^{\prime},\nu^{\prime}}\|_{1}\;\leq\;\int\|\mathrm{e}^{-\tau\Delta}-\mathrm{e}^{-(\sigma/\sigma^{\prime})^{2}\tau\Delta}\|_{1}\,\mathrm{d}\tilde{\nu}^{\prime}_{\sigma^{\prime}}(\tau)\;+\;\int\|\mathrm{e}^{-\tau\Delta}\|_{1}\,\mathrm{d}\big\|\tilde{\nu}_{\sigma}-\tilde{\nu}^{\prime}_{\sigma^{\prime}}\big\|(\tau).

(2.25)

On any compact
\tau
-interval bounded away from
0
,
\|\mathrm{e}^{-t\Delta}-\mathrm{e}^{-s\Delta}\|_{1}\leq C|t-s|
(use spectral calculus and the uniform mass bound). The second term is bounded by
W_{1}(\nu,\nu^{\prime})
because
\nu\mapsto\tilde{\nu}_{\sigma}
is Lipschitz in Wasserstein-1 and
\tau\mapsto\mathrm{e}^{-\tau\Delta}
is Lipschitz on compact sets. Therefore

\|P_{\sigma,\nu}-P_{\sigma^{\prime},\nu^{\prime}}\|_{1}\;\leq\;C\big(|\sigma-\sigma^{\prime}|+W_{1}(\nu,\nu^{\prime})\big)\,=\,C\,d_{\mathrm{proj}}((\sigma,\nu),(\sigma^{\prime},\nu^{\prime})).

(2.26)

Integrating against the slab Wilson weight and the second slice factor (bounded by
1
) gives the
L^{1}
bound for
K
. The operator-norm bound for
T
follows by Schur’s test.
∎

We now fix the scale-uniform hypotheses that will be assumed throughout. They may be taken as axioms of our Euclidean laboratory;

(H1)

Reflection positivity at every scale.
The projected, gauge-fixed lattice measures
\mu_{k}
at spacings
a_{k}=b^{-k}a_{0}
are reflection-positive with respect to time reflection (Sec.
2
).

(H2)

FRD-based uniform locality.
The Gaussian reference covariances and effective covariances admit a finite-range decomposition with bounds
uniform in
k
, and the associated polymer/cluster expansions converge absolutely with diameter-weighted norms at every scale
[
3
]
.

(H3)

Uniform exponential clustering.
There exists
m_{*}>0
such that for every local gauge-invariant observable
O
on
\Lambda_{k}
, the connected two-point function satisfies

\big|S^{(k)}_{2,c}(O(x),O(y))\big|\leq C_{O}\,\mathrm{e}^{-m_{*}\,d_{k}(x,y)}\,,

(2.27)

with constants independent of the volume.

(H4)

Spectral gap interlacing.
Writing
T_{k}
for the one-step transfer operator at scale
k
, its contraction gap
\Delta_{k}:=1-\|T_{k}\|_{\perp}
obeys

\Delta_{k+1}\geq\Delta_{k}-\varepsilon_{k}\,,\qquad\sum_{k\geq 0}\varepsilon_{k}<\infty\,,

(2.28)

hence
\liminf_{k\to\infty}\Delta_{k}\geq c\,m_{*}>0
.

(H5)

Continuum compactness and OS axioms.
Along subsequences
k_{j}\to\infty
(and after thermodynamic limit) the Schwinger families
\{S^{(k_{j})}_{n}\}
converge to continuum limits
\{S_{n}\}
on
\mathbb{R}^{4}
satisfying OS0-OS5 (temperedness, Euclidean invariance, permutation symmetry, reflection positivity, clustering, and time-regularity), with clustering rate
m_{*}
. The OS reconstruction yields a Wightman theory with a nonnegative self-adjoint Hamiltonian
H
and a strictly positive spectral gap
[
1
,
6
]
.

These hypotheses encapsulate the essential structure-positivity, locality, clustering, spectral stability, and continuum compactness-that makes the subsequent uniqueness, universality, and weak-coupling extension theorems possible. One may view them as the distilled content of the reflection-positive Euclidean approach to non-Abelian gauge theory.

Appendix 3
Uniqueness of the Continuum Limit

When we speak of
uniqueness
of a continuum field theory extracted from a sequence of reflection-positive lattice theories, we mean something conceptually simple: if we know the law of the field on a single Euclidean time-slice and we know how to advance by one time-step, then-by the Markov property encoded in the Osterwalder-Schrader (OS) axioms-the entire family of Schwinger functions is determined. This physical intuition, familiar from classical stochastic processes, is made rigorous by the OS framework
[
1
,
2
,
6
]
: (i) reflection positivity and (ii) time-regularity (OS5) grant a
boundary kernel factorization
and a
time-slicing
(transfer) structure. In this section we harness that structure, together with scale-uniform exponential clustering and finite-range (FRD) locality (which guarantee stability and thermodynamic limits via cluster expansions), to prove that any two continuum limits built from our class of lattice flows are identical.

We begin by listing the precise assumptions and the admissible analytical class of infrared regulators (gauge-fixing projectors) and reflection-positive block-spin maps. Then we prove (1) uniqueness of the one-slice marginal, (2) uniqueness of the one-step boundary kernel, and (3) OS-Markov extension to all times. Finally we assemble these pieces into the Uniqueness Theorem.

We work on the four-dimensional Euclidean spacetime and fix a compact gauge group
G=\mathrm{SU}(N)
with
N\geq 2
. The multiscale lattices are labeled by
k\in\mathbb{N}
, with spacings
a_{k}=b^{-k}a_{0}
for a fixed
b>1
. At scale
k
, the spatial box is a periodic three-torus of side
L_{k}
and the Euclidean time has extent
T_{k}
; the thermodynamic limits
L_{k},T_{k}\to\infty
will be taken in the standard way. Below,
\Lambda_{k}
denotes the space-time lattice at scale
k
.
We assume the following, uniformly in
k
:

(H1) FRD locality and cluster expansions.

There exists a finite-range decomposition (FRD) of the projected covariances and a Banach algebra of polymer activities whose diameter-weighted norms satisfy a Kotecký-Preiss (KP) smallness criterion; consequently, connected correlators admit absolutely convergent cluster (tree) expansions with scale-uniform diameter weights
[
5
,
3
,
11
]
.

(H2) Uniform exponential clustering.

For each bounded, local, gauge-invariant observable
O
, there exist constants
C_{O}<\infty
and
m_{*}>0
, independent of
k
, such that for all
x,y\in\Lambda_{k}
,

\big|S^{(k)}_{2,c}(O(x),O(y))\big|\;\leq\;C_{O}\,\mathrm{e}^{-m_{*}\;d_{k}(x,y)},

(3.1)

where
S^{(k)}_{2,c}
is the connected two-point function and
d_{k}
is the nearest-neighbor graph distance.

(H3) Reflection positivity at each scale.

The lattice measures (with temporal-axial gauge off the reflection plane and slice-wise Landau-minimized transverse representatives) augmented by an admissible horizon projector on each slice are OS-positive with respect to the standard time-reflection
[
2
,
8
,
12
]
.

From (H1)-(H3) together with standard arguments (Prokhorov tightness for random tempered distributions, OS closure under weak limits, see § 3.4 below and
[
1
,
2
,
6
]
), it follows that along subsequences
k_{j}\to\infty
the Schwinger families
\{S^{(k_{j})}_{n}\}_{n\geq 1}
converge to a family
\{S_{n}\}
satisfying OS0-OS5 (temperedness, Euclidean invariance, permutation symmetry, reflection positivity, clustering, and time-regularity). We do
not
assume any a priori uniqueness of this limit; proving it is the aim of the section.

Each time-slice
\Sigma
supports a
covariant Laplacian

\Delta_{A_{h}}
acting on adjoint-valued site fields, constructed from the slice-wise Landau-minimized transverse representative
A_{h}
(the minimizer of the discrete Landau functional on the slice with a deterministic tie-break ensuring reflection covariance). An
admissible horizon projector
is

P_{\sigma,\nu}\;:=\;\chi_{\sigma,\nu}\!\left(\sqrt{\Delta_{A_{h}}}\right),

(3.2)

where
\chi_{\sigma,\nu}
is a completely monotone symbol admitting a
positive heat-kernel representation

\chi_{\sigma,\nu}(\lambda)\;=\;\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathrm{e}^{-t\,\lambda^{2}/\sigma^{2}}\,\mathrm{d}\nu(t),

(3.3)

with
\nu
a finite positive Borel measure whose support is a compact subset of
(0,\infty)
. Then
P_{\sigma,\nu}
is a bounded
positive contraction
on
\ell^{2}(\Sigma)\otimes\mathfrak{su}(N)
,
reflection-covariant
and
gauge-covariant
, and its kernel obeys
uniform exponential off-diagonal bounds
by standard heat-kernel methods (Davies-Gaffney on graphs, Combes-Thomas, Helffer-Sjöstrand)
[
9
,
13
,
14
]
. We endow the parameter set
\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{proj}}
with the metric

d_{\mathrm{proj}}\big((\sigma,\nu),(\sigma^{\prime},\nu^{\prime})\big)\;:=\;|\sigma-\sigma^{\prime}|\;+\;W_{1}(\nu,\nu^{\prime}),

(3.4)

where
W_{1}
is the Wasserstein-1 distance.

A
block-spin map

\mathcal{B}
between scales is admissible if it preserves reflection positivity, gauge covariance, and the FRD locality constants uniformly across scales (in the sense of
[
3
,
5
]
). We write
\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{block}}
for the set of such maps and equip it with the operator-norm metric in the FRD Banach algebra of polymer activities. The
admissible class
is
\mathcal{K}:=\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{proj}}\times\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{block}}
.

Lemma 3.1

(Single-scale continuity of one-step kernels)
.

Let
K_{\sigma,\nu}:X_{0}\times X_{0}\to\mathbb{R}_{+}
be the one-step boundary kernel associated with the projector
P_{\sigma,\nu}
as in (
3.2
), and let
T_{\sigma,\nu}
be the induced transfer operator on
L^{2}(X_{0},\mu_{0})
. Then, for
(\sigma,\nu),(\sigma^{\prime},\nu^{\prime})
in compact subsets of
\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{proj}}
,

\|K_{\sigma,\nu}-K_{\sigma^{\prime},\nu^{\prime}}\|_{L^{1}(\mu_{0}\otimes\mu_{0})}\;\leq\;C\,d_{\mathrm{proj}}\big((\sigma,\nu),(\sigma^{\prime},\nu^{\prime})\big),\qquad\|T_{\sigma,\nu}-T_{\sigma^{\prime},\nu^{\prime}}\|_{B(L^{2}(\mu_{0}))}\;\leq\;C^{\prime}\,d_{\mathrm{proj}}(\cdot,\cdot).

(3.5)

The constants
C,C^{\prime}
are independent of the volume.

Proof.

Using the heat-kernel representation (
3.3
), positivity, and the exponential locality of
P_{\sigma,\nu}
, one verifies that the map
(\sigma,\nu)\mapsto K_{\sigma,\nu}
is continuous in the
L^{1}
-topology; the Wasserstein metric controls the difference of the measures
\nu
and
\nu^{\prime}
while the parameter
\sigma
enters via the simple scaling
t\mapsto t/\sigma^{2}
. The exponential locality bounds yield a dominating integrable kernel, so the
L^{1}
-continuity is Lipschitz on compact parameter sets. The Schur test then gives the operator-norm bound for
T_{\sigma,\nu}
from the
L^{1}
-bound on the kernel. Details follow standard arguments in
[
9
,
14
,
15
]
.
∎

Fix a bounded, gauge-invariant cylinder functional
F
depending only on the spatial links of a single time-slice (say
t=0
). Let
S^{(k)}_{L,T}(F)
be its expectation in finite volume
L^{3}\times T
at scale
k
, with admissible projector insertions on each slice as above.

Proposition 3.2

(Thermodynamic limit and subsequence independence)
.

For each fixed scale
k
, the limit

S^{(k)}(F)\;:=\;\lim_{L\to\infty}\lim_{T\to\infty}S^{(k)}_{L,T}(F)

(3.6)

exists and does not depend on the order of limits. Moreover, the limit
\displaystyle\lim_{k\to\infty}S^{(k)}(F)
exists and is independent of the subsequence
k_{j}\to\infty
chosen. Consequently, the one-slice marginal
\mu_{0}
in the continuum limit is well-defined and unique.

Proof.

Thermodynamic limit at fixed
k
.

Let
L^{\prime}\geq L
and
T^{\prime}\geq T
. By reflection positivity and time-slab factorization (OS and transfer-matrix formalism
[
2
,
6
,
12
,
8
]
), the difference

\Delta_{L^{\prime},T^{\prime};\,L,T}\;:=\;S^{(k)}_{L^{\prime},T^{\prime}}(F)-S^{(k)}_{L,T}(F)

(3.7)

can be expressed as a sum over connected polymer clusters that cross from the support of
F
on the central slice to the additional spatial or temporal layers where the two volumes differ. By the cluster expansion and the uniform exponential decay (
3.1
), the contribution of such clusters is bounded by
C\,\exp\{-\alpha\,d(\operatorname{supp}F,\partial\Lambda)\}
where
\Lambda
denotes the smaller volume. Thus
|\Delta_{L^{\prime},T^{\prime};\,L,T}|\leq C\,\mathrm{e}^{-\alpha\min\{L,T\}}
. Taking
L^{\prime},T^{\prime}\to\infty
and then
L,T\to\infty
yields the Cauchy property and hence existence of the thermodynamic limit
S^{(k)}(F)
, independent of the order of limits; see
[
5
,
11
]
for the underlying polymer estimates.

Independence of subsequence in
k
.

Let
k<\ell
. Transport
F
from scale
k
to scale
\ell
via the admissible block-spin map; call the image
F_{\ell}
. By FRD contraction properties in the polymer norm (see
[
3
,
5
]
) and by Lemma
3.1
, there exists
\rho\in(0,1)
independent of
k,\ell
such that

\big|S^{(k)}(F)-S^{(\ell)}(F_{\ell})\big|\;\leq\;C\,\rho^{\,\ell-k}.

(3.8)

Likewise, the difference between
F_{\ell}
and the naïve transport of
F
to scale
\ell
is controlled by the same contraction (it is a sum of connected clusters with exponentially decaying weights). It follows that

\big|S^{(k)}(F)-S^{(\ell)}(F)\big|\;\leq\;C^{\prime}\,\rho^{\,\ell-k}.

(3.9)

Hence
\{S^{(k)}(F)\}_{k\geq 0}
is a Cauchy sequence with exponential rate
\rho
, and
\lim_{k\to\infty}S^{(k)}(F)
exists, independent of subsequence. This limit defines the one-slice marginal
\mu_{0}
uniquely.
∎

Let
X_{0}
be the configuration space of spatial links on the slice
t=0
, with Borel probability measure
\mu_{0}
given by Proposition
3.2
. Consider a bounded sesquilinear form
B:L^{2}(\mu_{0})\times L^{2}(\mu_{0})\to\mathbb{C}
with the following properties:

(i) positivity:

B(F,F)\geq 0
for all
F\in L^{2}(\mu_{0})
;
(ii) symmetry:

B(F_{0},F_{1})=\overline{B(F_{1},F_{0})}
;
(iii) boundedness:

|B(F_{0},F_{1})|\leq C\,\|F_{0}\|_{L^{2}}\,\|F_{1}\|_{L^{2}}
.

In our application,
B(F_{0},F_{1})
will be the continuum mixed two-point function
S_{2}(F_{0},F_{1})
with
F_{0}
supported on the slice
t=0
and
F_{1}
on the slice
t=a
. OS positivity, OS5 and clustering guarantee (i)-(iii)
[
1
,
2
,
6
]
.

Lemma 3.3

(Riesz kernel representation and uniqueness)
.

Under
(i)-(iii)
there exists a unique measurable kernel
K:X_{0}\times X_{0}\to\mathbb{C}
, symmetric
K(U^{\prime},U)=\overline{K(U,U^{\prime})}
, such that for all
F_{0},F_{1}\in L^{2}(\mu_{0})
,

B(F_{0},F_{1})\;=\;\iint_{X_{0}\times X_{0}}\overline{F_{0}(U)}\,K(U^{\prime},U)\,F_{1}(U^{\prime})\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{0}(U)\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{0}(U^{\prime}).

(3.10)

Moreover,
K
is positive in the sense that

\iint\overline{\phi(U)}\,K(U^{\prime},U)\,\phi(U^{\prime})\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{0}(U)\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{0}(U^{\prime})\;\geq\;0\quad\text{for all }\phi\in L^{2}(\mu_{0}).

(3.11)

Proof.

Let
B(F_{0},F_{1})
be the OS two-point form with
F_{0}
supported at
t=0
and
F_{1}
at
t=a
.
By OS positivity, time-regularity (OS5), and the standard slab factorization, the mixed weight on a
single time-slab can be written as

W_{\sigma,\nu}(U^{\prime},U;V)=e^{-\tfrac{1}{2}S_{\mathrm{sp}}(U)}\,e^{-S_{\mathrm{tm}}(U^{\prime},U;V)}\,e^{-\tfrac{1}{2}S_{\mathrm{sp}}(U^{\prime})}\,\Gamma\!\big(P_{\sigma,\nu}(0;U)\big)^{\frac{1}{2}}\,\Gamma\!\big(P_{\sigma,\nu}(a;U^{\prime})\big)^{\frac{1}{2}},

(3.12)

with
\Gamma
completely monotone and
P_{\sigma,\nu}
admissible (cf. (4.10)). Define the

boundary kernel
by explicit disintegration over interior links of the slab:

K(U^{\prime},U):=\int W_{\sigma,\nu}(U^{\prime},U;V)\,d\mu_{\mathrm{Haar}}(V)

(3.13)

Then for all bounded
F_{0},F_{1}
supported on the boundary slices,

B(F_{0},F_{1})=\iint F_{0}(U)\,K(U^{\prime},U)\,F_{1}(U^{\prime})\,d\mu_{0}(U)\,d\mu_{0}(U^{\prime}).

(3.14)

Positivity and symmetry of
K
follow from OS positivity and the symmetry of
W_{\sigma,\nu}
under
interchange of the boundary slices. Uniqueness holds because if
\widetilde{K}
yields the same
bilinear form for all bounded
F_{0},F_{1}
, then
K=\widetilde{K}

\mu_{0}\otimes\mu_{0}
-a.e. by polarization
and density. No Hilbert-Schmidt assumption is needed;
K
is a measurable
L^{1}_{\mathrm{loc}}
kernel
obtained by the slab disintegration
(\ast)
, and the associated transfer operator is a positive
contraction by the OS Markov property. ∎

Corollary 3.4

(Boundary kernel for OS time-slices)
.

Let
\{S_{n}\}
be a continuum Schwinger family satisfying OS0-OS5 and uniform exponential clustering. Then there exists a unique positive symmetric kernel
K:X_{0}\times X_{0}\to\mathbb{R}_{+}
such that, for all bounded slice-supported
F_{0},F_{1}
,

S_{2}(F_{0},F_{1})\;=\;\iint\overline{F_{0}(U)}\,K(U^{\prime},U)\,F_{1}(U^{\prime})\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{0}(U)\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{0}(U^{\prime}).

(3.15)

The corresponding operator
T:L^{2}(\mu_{0})\to L^{2}(\mu_{0})
defined by
(T\psi)(U^{\prime}):=\int K(U^{\prime},U)\psi(U)\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{0}(U)
is a positive self-adjoint contraction.

Proof.

Apply Lemma
3.3
with
B(F_{0},F_{1}):=S_{2}(F_{0},F_{1})
. OS positivity and OS5 ensure (i)-(iii) and the Markov property guarantees contractivity (see
[
2
,
6
]
for the details of the OS transfer construction).
∎

We recall the standard OS time-slicing: for any bounded cylinder functional
F
supported on finitely many consecutive slices
\{a,2a,\dots,na\}
, there exists
\Psi_{F}\in L^{2}(\mu_{0})
such that the OS two-point form can be written with the transfer operator
T
associated with the kernel
K
:

\langle\Theta F,F\rangle_{\mathrm{OS}}\;=\;\langle\Psi_{F},T^{n}\Psi_{F}\rangle_{L^{2}(\mu_{0})}.

(3.16)

This follows from OS reflection positivity, the boundary factorization, and the detailed-balance identities for
K
(“OS5” supplies the necessary time-regularity)
[
2
,
6
]
. For clarity:

Proposition 3.5

(OS Markov property)
.

Let
\{S_{n}\}
satisfy OS0-OS5 and let
K
and
\mu_{0}
be as in Corollary
3.4
. Then for each bounded cylinder functional
F
supported on
\{a,\dots,na\}
there exists a
\Psi_{F}\in L^{2}(\mu_{0})
such that (
3.16
) holds. In particular,
T
is a positive self-adjoint contraction and the OS inner product on cylinder functionals is generated by iterates of
T
.

Proof.

The proof is an immediate adaptation of the classical OS reconstruction: one integrates out the fields in the half-space
t>0
to obtain a boundary vector on the slice
t=0
; reflection positivity and time-reversal symmetry yield positivity and symmetry of
K
and the detailed balance identities; the contraction property of
T
follows from the Markov nature of the layer-kernel. Full proofs are given in
[
2
,
6
]
, and in the lattice gauge setting the transfer factorization is explained in
[
12
,
8
]
.
∎

We are ready to assemble the pieces. Consider two subsequential continuum limits
\{S_{n}\}
and
\{\widetilde{S}_{n}\}
, both satisfying OS0-OS5 and uniform exponential clustering. Let
\mu_{0},\widetilde{\mu}_{0}
be their one-slice marginals and
K,\widetilde{K}
their one-step kernels.
By Proposition
3.2
,
\mu_{0}=\widetilde{\mu}_{0}
. By Lemma
3.3
-Corollary
3.4
, the mixed two-point form uniquely identifies
K
, hence
K=\widetilde{K}
. By the OS Markov property (Proposition
3.5
), the entire OS sesquilinear form on cylinder functionals is generated by
T
and the boundary vectors, and since
T=\widetilde{T}
we have
\langle\Theta F,G\rangle_{\mathrm{OS}}=\langle\Theta F,G\rangle_{\widetilde{\mathrm{OS}}}
for all bounded cylinder functionals
F,G
. Therefore, all Schwinger functions agree.

Theorem 3.6

(Uniqueness of the continuum limit)
.

Let
\{S_{n}\}
and
\{\widetilde{S}_{n}\}
be two subsequential continuum limits of the multiscale reflection-positive lattice gauge theories described by (H1)-(H3). Suppose both families satisfy the OS axioms (OS0-OS5) and uniform exponential clustering with rate
m_{*}>0
. Then

S_{n}\;=\;\widetilde{S}_{n}\qquad\text{for all }n\geq 1.

(3.17)

In particular, the continuum OS measure and the reconstructed Wightman theory (Hilbert space, fields, dynamics) are uniquely determined by the standing assumptions.

Proof.

As explained:
\mu_{0}=\widetilde{\mu}_{0}
(Proposition
3.2
);
K=\widetilde{K}
(Lemma
3.3
and Corollary
3.4
); OS time-slicing with the common transfer
T
gives identity of all OS inner products on cylinder functionals (Proposition
3.5
); by polarization and density,
S_{n}=\widetilde{S}_{n}
for all
n
.
∎

The role of the OS axioms and the FRD/cluster framework is transparent: OS grants a canonical
Markovian time-slicing
, while FRD guarantees
stability
and
thermodynamic control
. Together they implement the physicist’s dictum:
one-slice law plus one-step kernel determine the entire theory
.

Appendix 4
Universality with Respect to Admissible Projectors and Blockings

The aim of this section is to establish that the continuum Schwinger functions - hence the reconstructed Wightman theory - are
independent
of all auxiliary choices made within a suitably structured, reflection-positive and gauge-covariant class of infrared regulators and block-spin maps. Physically, this is the familiar tenet that the continuum theory does not depend on a choice of
scheme
. Here we turn this tenet into a precise theorem.

We proceed in a sequence of steps. First, we specify the admissible class of horizon projectors and blockings, endowed with natural metrics encoding small variations; these definitions are chosen so that reflection positivity, gauge covariance, and finite-range decomposition (FRD) locality hold uniformly. Second, we prove
single-scale stability
: one-step Osterwalder-Schrader (OS) kernels and transfer operators are
Lipschitz
continuous with respect to admissible parameters. Third, we lift this single-scale stability to
multi-scale
stability at the level of
connected cumulants
, by combining a telescoping argument in time with the FRD cluster expansion and Kotecký-Preiss bounds. Finally, we pass to thermodynamic and continuum limits and invoke the Markov uniqueness of the OS framework to deduce
universality
: all admissible choices give the same continuum Schwinger family.

Throughout we use the standard OS framework
[
1
,
2
]
, reflection positivity for lattice gauge theories
[
8
]
, FRD locality
[
3
]
, heat-kernel bounds
[
9
]
, and completely monotone functional calculus
[
16
]
. We write
G=\mathrm{SU}(N)
with
N\geq 2
.
We begin from the physical desiderata. A
horizon projector
on each time-slice should suppress long-wavelength fluctuations
without
spoiling reflection positivity or gauge covariance and should be
exponentially local
on every slice. A
blocking
step should preserve reflection positivity and FRD locality with constants
uniform
across scales.
These desiderata lead to the following definitions.

Definition 4.1

(Admissible slice projector)
.

Fix
\sigma>0
. Let
\nu
be a Borel probability measure on some compact subinterval
[t_{-},t_{+}]\subset(0,\infty)
, and define the completely monotone function

\chi_{\sigma,\nu}(\lambda)\;=\;\int_{t_{-}}^{t_{+}}\mathrm{e}^{-(t/\sigma^{2})\,\lambda^{2}}\,\mathrm{d}\nu(t),\qquad\lambda\geq 0.

(4.1)

Given a time-slice
t
, and denoting by
\Delta_{A_{h}}(t)
the
slice covariant Laplacian
acting on adjoint-valued site fields in the Landau representative
A_{h}
(fixed by measurable, reflection-covariant orbit minimization), we set

P_{\sigma,\nu}(t)\;:=\;\chi_{\sigma,\nu}\!\big(\sqrt{\Delta_{A_{h}}(t)}\big)\,.

(4.2)

We call
(\sigma,\nu)

admissible
if: (i)
P_{\sigma,\nu}(t)
is a
positive contraction
on
\ell^{2}(\Lambda_{t})\otimes\mathfrak{su}(N)
; (ii)
P_{\sigma,\nu}(t)
is
gauge-covariant
under time-independent slice gauge transformations; (iii) it is
reflection-covariant
in the OS sense,
RP_{\sigma,\nu}(t)R=P_{\sigma,\nu}(-t)
; and (iv) its integral kernel obeys
uniform exponential decay
: there exist
C,\gamma>0
such that

\|P_{\sigma,\nu}(t;x,y)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\;\leq\;C\,\mathrm{e}^{-\gamma\,d(x,y)}\qquad\forall\,x,y\in\Lambda_{t}\,,

(4.3)

with constants independent of the spatial volume. By the Bernstein-Widder theorem
[
16
]
,
\chi_{\sigma,\nu}
is completely monotone and admits a
positive heat-kernel representation
, implying (i)-(iii); by the Davies-Gaffney estimate
[
9
]
and the compact support of
\nu
away from
0
, (iv) follows.

We metrize the projector parameter space by

d_{\mathrm{proj}}\!\big((\sigma,\nu),(\sigma^{\prime},\nu^{\prime})\big)\;:=\;|\sigma-\sigma^{\prime}|+W_{1}(\nu,\nu^{\prime})\,,

(4.4)

where
W_{1}
is the Wasserstein-1 distance (the dual Lipschitz metric) on probability measures.

Definition 4.2

(Admissible reflection-positive blocking)
.

A block-spin map
B:\mu\mapsto B\mu
from a reflection-positive Euclidean measure on a time-slab to an effective measure on the block-lattice is
admissible
if:

(i)

It preserves
OS reflection positivity

[
2
,
8
]
: the induced layer kernel between adjacent block-slices is of positive type and symmetric.

(ii)

It preserves
gauge covariance
and the
temporal-axial gauge
convention away from the reflection plane.

(iii)

It preserves
FRD locality
and the diameter-norm
cluster expansion
bounds with
scale-uniform
constants, i.e. the effective cumulants admit an absolutely convergent polymer expansion whose range and smallness constants are uniform across scales
[
3
,
4
,
5
]
.

We metrize admissible blockings by the
L^{1}
-distance of the induced one-step kernels on the boundary slice:

d_{\mathrm{blk}}(B,B^{\prime})\;:=\;\|\,K_{B}-K_{B^{\prime}}\,\|_{L^{1}(\nu_{0}\otimes\nu_{0})}\,,

(4.5)

where
K_{B}
is the one-step kernel induced by
B
and
\nu_{0}
is the Haar product measure on the boundary slice.

We shall write
\mathcal{K}:=\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{proj}}\times\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{blk}}
for the admissible parameter set, and

d(\theta,\theta^{\prime})\;:=\;d_{\mathrm{proj}}\big((\sigma,\nu),(\sigma^{\prime},\nu^{\prime})\big)\,+\,d_{\mathrm{blk}}(B,B^{\prime})

(4.6)

for
\theta=((\sigma,\nu),B)
and
\theta^{\prime}=((\sigma^{\prime},\nu^{\prime}),B^{\prime})
.

The one-step kernel is the basic combinatorial object linking the OS form to time-slicing: if
X_{0}
denotes the one-slice configuration space with Haar measure
\nu_{0}
, the
one-step kernel

K_{\sigma,\nu;B}:X_{0}\times X_{0}\to\mathbb{R}_{+}
is defined by integrating the weight on the slab
[0,a]
, with symmetric splitting of the spatial contribution, the mixed (plaquette) contribution through the slab, and the slice weights induced by
P_{\sigma,\nu}(0)
and
P_{\sigma,\nu}(a)
; by OS symmetry,
K_{\sigma,\nu;B}
is positive type and symmetric
[
8
]
.

Define the
one-step transfer operator

T_{\sigma,\nu;B}:L^{2}(X_{0},\mathrm{d}\nu_{0})\to L^{2}(X_{0},\mathrm{d}\nu_{0})
by

(T_{\sigma,\nu;B}\psi)(U^{\prime})\;=\;\int_{X_{0}}K_{\sigma,\nu;B}(U^{\prime},U)\,\psi(U)\,\mathrm{d}\nu_{0}(U)\,.

(4.7)

It is a positive, self-adjoint contraction by construction.

We now give Lipschitz bounds for
K
and
T
with respect to the projector and to the blocking.

Proposition 4.3

(Projector-Lipschitz stability of the one-step kernel)
.

Fix an admissible blocking
B
. There exists
C=C(B)>0
such that for all admissible
(\sigma,\nu),(\sigma^{\prime},\nu^{\prime})
,

\|\,K_{\sigma,\nu;B}-K_{\sigma^{\prime},\nu^{\prime};B}\,\|_{L^{1}(\nu_{0}\otimes\nu_{0})}\;\leq\;C\,\Big(|\sigma-\sigma^{\prime}|+W_{1}(\nu,\nu^{\prime})\Big)\,,

(4.8)

and consequently

\|\,T_{\sigma,\nu;B}-T_{\sigma^{\prime},\nu^{\prime};B}\,\|_{B(L^{2})}\;\leq\;C\,\Big(|\sigma-\sigma^{\prime}|+W_{1}(\nu,\nu^{\prime})\Big)\,.

(4.9)

Proof.

Write the symmetric two-slice weight as

\mathcal{W}_{\sigma,\nu}(U^{\prime},U;V)\;=\;\mathrm{e}^{-\frac{1}{2}S_{\mathrm{sp}}(U)}\,\mathrm{e}^{-S_{\mathrm{tm}}(U^{\prime},U;V)}\,\mathrm{e}^{-\frac{1}{2}S_{\mathrm{sp}}(U^{\prime})}\,\Gamma\!\big(P_{\sigma,\nu}(0;U)\big)^{1/2}\,\Gamma\!\big(P_{\sigma,\nu}(a;U^{\prime})\big)^{1/2},

(4.10)

where
S_{\mathrm{sp}}
is the spatial part of the Wilson action at the ends of the slab and
S_{\mathrm{tm}}
the mixed (time-space) plaquette part across the slab;
\Gamma
is a fixed completely monotone scalar functional of a positive contraction (e.g.
\Gamma(Q)=\det(1+\alpha Q)
or
\Gamma(Q)=\exp\{-\mathrm{Tr}(1-Q)\}
), ensuring positivity
[
6
]
. The kernel is then

K_{\sigma,\nu;B}(U^{\prime},U)\;=\;\int\mathcal{W}_{\sigma,\nu}(U^{\prime},U;V)\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{\mathrm{Haar}}(V)\,,

(4.11)

hence

|K_{\sigma,\nu;B}-K_{\sigma^{\prime},\nu^{\prime};B}|\leq\int|\mathcal{W}_{\sigma,\nu}-\mathcal{W}_{\sigma^{\prime},\nu^{\prime}}|\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{\mathrm{Haar}}.

Since
S_{\mathrm{sp}}
and
S_{\mathrm{tm}}
are projector-independent, the variation comes from the
slice factors
. By the mean-value theorem and functional calculus (Dunford-Taylor), for
\Gamma
with
\|\Gamma^{\prime}\|_{\infty}\leq C_{\Gamma}
,

|\Gamma(P_{\sigma,\nu})-\Gamma(P_{\sigma^{\prime},\nu^{\prime}})|\ \leq\ \|\Gamma^{\prime}\|_{\infty}\,\|P_{\sigma,\nu}-P_{\sigma^{\prime},\nu^{\prime}}\|_{B(\ell^{2})}

(4.12)

We use the operator norm and pass to
L^{1}
kernel bounds via the heat-kernel representation and the Schur test.
Using the positive heat-kernel representation and the Duhamel identity,

P_{\sigma,\nu}-P_{\sigma^{\prime},\nu^{\prime}}\;=\;\int_{t_{-}}^{t_{+}}\!\Big(\mathrm{e}^{-(t/\sigma^{2})\Delta}-\mathrm{e}^{-(t/\sigma^{\prime 2})\Delta}\Big)\,\mathrm{d}\nu(t)\;+\;\int_{t_{-}}^{t_{+}}\!\mathrm{e}^{-(t/\sigma^{\prime 2})\Delta}\,\mathrm{d}(\nu-\nu^{\prime})(t),

(4.13)

and

\mathrm{e}^{-(t/\sigma^{2})\Delta}-\mathrm{e}^{-(t/\sigma^{\prime 2})\Delta}\;=\;\int_{\sigma^{\prime}}^{\sigma}\frac{2t}{\rho^{3}}\,\Delta\,\mathrm{e}^{-(t/\rho^{2})\Delta}\,\mathrm{d}\rho\,.

(4.14)

On a finite-degree graph, the discrete heat kernel obeys Davies-Gaffney bounds uniformly on compact

\tau
-intervals, yielding
kernel

L^{1}
bounds. In particular,

\|P_{\sigma,\nu}-P_{\sigma^{\prime},\nu^{\prime}}\|_{B(\ell^{2})}\leq C\big(|\sigma-\sigma^{\prime}|+W_{1}(\nu,\nu^{\prime})\big),

(4.15)

and the associated one-step
boundary kernels
satisfy

\|K_{\sigma,\nu;B}-K_{\sigma^{\prime},\nu^{\prime};B}\|_{L^{1}(\mu_{0}\otimes\mu_{0})}\leq C\big(|\sigma-\sigma^{\prime}|+W_{1}(\nu,\nu^{\prime})\big).

(4.16)

Combining the two slice factors and integrating over
V
yields (
4.8
). The operator-norm estimate (
4.9
) follows by the Schur test:

|T\|\ \leq\ \Big(\sup_{U^{\prime}}\int|K(U^{\prime},U)|\,d\mu_{0}(U)\Big)^{\!1/2}\Big(\sup_{U}\int|K(U^{\prime},U)|\,d\mu_{0}(U^{\prime})\Big)^{\!1/2}

(4.17)

∎

Proposition 4.4

(Blocking-Lipschitz stability)
.

Fix an admissible projector
(\sigma,\nu)
. Let
B,B^{\prime}
be admissible blockings. Then

\|\,T_{\sigma,\nu;B}-T_{\sigma,\nu;B^{\prime}}\,\|_{B(L^{2})}\;\leq\;\|\,K_{\sigma,\nu;B}-K_{\sigma,\nu;B^{\prime}}\,\|_{L^{1}(\nu_{0}\otimes\nu_{0})}\;=\;d_{\mathrm{blk}}(B,B^{\prime}).

(4.18)

Proof.

This is immediate from the definition of
d_{\mathrm{blk}}
and the Schur test.
∎

We must now compose many one-step kernels and lift stability to
connected
cumulants. The first point is a telescoping bound in time.

Lemma 4.5

(Telescoping bound)
.

Let
\theta,\theta^{\prime}\in\mathcal{K}
be admissible, and write
K_{\theta}:=K_{\sigma,\nu;B}
,
K_{\theta^{\prime}}:=K_{\sigma^{\prime},\nu^{\prime};B^{\prime}}
. Then for every
n\in\mathbb{N}
,

\|\,K_{\theta}^{(\,n\,)}-K_{\theta^{\prime}}^{(\,n\,)}\,\|_{L^{1}(\nu_{0}\otimes\nu_{0})}\;\leq\;n\,\|\,K_{\theta}-K_{\theta^{\prime}}\,\|_{L^{1}(\nu_{0}\otimes\nu_{0})}\,,

(4.19)

and hence

\|\,T_{\theta}^{\,n}-T_{\theta^{\prime}}^{\,n}\,\|_{B(L^{2})}\;\leq\;n\,\|\,K_{\theta}-K_{\theta^{\prime}}\,\|_{L^{1}(\nu_{0}\otimes\nu_{0})}\,.

(4.20)

Proof.

The identity

K_{\theta}^{(n)}-K_{\theta^{\prime}}^{(n)}=\sum_{j=1}^{n}K_{\theta}^{(j-1)}\ast(K_{\theta}-K_{\theta^{\prime}})\ast K_{\theta^{\prime}}^{(n-j)}

and the fact that all factors are Markov kernels (normalized in
L^{1}
) imply the kernel bound. The operator bound follows by the Schur test.
∎

To reach connected cumulants we invoke the FRD cluster expansion: at any fixed scale
k
, the effective action admits an absolutely convergent polymer expansion with diameter-weighted smallness and range bounded uniformly in
k

[
3
,
4
,
5
]
. Connected
p
-point functions are expressed as finite sums over connected clusters with exponential tree-decay. Varying
\theta
along a straight path and differentiating under the sum, one controls the derivative by the BKAR tree formula and the single-scale Lipschitz bounds (Propositions
4.3
-
4.4
).

Proposition 4.6

(Uniform cumulant stability at fixed scale)
.

Let
k\in\mathbb{N}
be fixed. For any finite family of local, gauge-invariant observables
\mathcal{O}=(O_{1},\dots,O_{p})
supported in a finite subset
A\subset\Lambda_{k}
, there exist constants
C=C(p,A)>0
and
\alpha>0
, independent of the spatial volume and
k
, such that for all admissible
\theta,\theta^{\prime}\in\mathcal{K}
,

\big|\,S^{(k)}_{p,c;\theta}(\mathcal{O})-S^{(k)}_{p,c;\theta^{\prime}}(\mathcal{O})\,\big|\;\leq\;C\,d(\theta,\theta^{\prime})\,\mathrm{e}^{-\alpha\,\mathrm{tree}(\mathrm{supp}\,\mathcal{O})}.

(4.21)

Here
\mathrm{tree}(\mathrm{supp}\,\mathcal{O})
denotes the minimal spanning tree length connecting the supports of the insertions.

Proof.

By FRD locality and cluster expansion
[
3
,
4
,
5
]
, the connected function
S^{(k)}_{p,c;\theta}(\mathcal{O})
can be written as a sum over connected polymer clusters
\Gamma
,

S^{(k)}_{p,c;\theta}(\mathcal{O})\;=\;\sum_{\Gamma\,\mathrm{conn.}}\Phi_{\theta}^{(k)}(\Gamma;\mathcal{O}),

(4.22)

with
|\Phi_{\theta}^{(k)}(\Gamma;\mathcal{O})|\leq C_{\Gamma}\prod_{\gamma\in\Gamma}|\zeta_{\theta}^{(k)}(\gamma)|
. The Kotecký-Preiss criterion implies

\sum_{\Gamma\,\mathrm{conn.}}|\Phi_{\theta}^{(k)}(\Gamma;\mathcal{O})|\leq C\,\mathrm{e}^{-\alpha\,\mathrm{tree}(\mathrm{supp}\,\mathcal{O})}.

Fix
\theta,\theta^{\prime}
and join them by a straight path
\theta_{t}
,
t\in[0,1]
. Differentiating termwise (justified by absolute convergence) and using the BKAR tree formula to control the derivative of
\log
-partition functions with respect to local parameters
[
5
]
, one arrives at

\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}S^{(k)}_{p,c;\theta_{t}}(\mathcal{O})\;=\;\sum_{\Gamma\,\mathrm{conn.}}\sum_{\gamma\in\Gamma}\Psi(\Gamma,\gamma;\mathcal{O})\,\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\zeta_{\theta_{t}}^{(k)}(\gamma)\,,

(4.23)

with
|\Psi(\Gamma,\gamma;\mathcal{O})|\leq C_{\Gamma}\prod_{\gamma^{\prime}\in\Gamma\setminus\{\gamma\}}|\zeta_{\theta_{t}}^{(k)}(\gamma^{\prime})|
. The single-scale Lipschitz bounds for one-step kernels (Propositions
4.3
-
4.4
) propagate through the FRD blockings to the polymer activities, giving

\big|\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\zeta_{\theta_{t}}^{(k)}(\gamma)\big|\leq C\,d(\theta,\theta^{\prime})\,\mathrm{e}^{-a\,\mathrm{diam}(\gamma)}.

Summing the absolutely convergent series yields

\big|\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}S^{(k)}_{p,c;\theta_{t}}(\mathcal{O})\big|\leq C^{\prime}\,d(\theta,\theta^{\prime})\,\mathrm{e}^{-\alpha\,\mathrm{tree}(\mathrm{supp}\,\mathcal{O})}.

Integrating
t
from
0
to
1
gives the claim.
∎

The bounds of Proposition
4.6
survive the thermodynamic limit (
L\to\infty
,
T\to\infty
) because they depend only on the geometry of the supports and not on the volume. We pass now to fixed physical smeared observables and let the lattice spacing
a_{k}\downarrow 0
.

Let
f_{1},\dots,f_{p}\in\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^{4})
be compactly supported test functions, and define the smeared lattice observables

O_{i}^{(k)}:=\sum_{x\in\Lambda_{k}}a_{k}^{4}\,O_{i}(x)\,f_{i}(x),

with
O_{i}
local, gauge-invariant lattice observables approximating the chosen continuum fields. By the FRD equicontinuity and tightness criteria (see, e.g.,
[
6
]
), along any subsequence
k_{j}\to\infty
the (full and connected) Schwinger functionals
S^{(k_{j})}_{p;\theta}(O_{1}^{(k_{j})},\dots,O_{p}^{(k_{j})})
converge to continuum Schwinger functions
S_{p;\theta}(f_{1},\dots,f_{p})
(and similarly for disconnected functions). The difference bounds of Proposition
4.6
then imply

Theorem 4.7

(Continuity of continuum cumulants in the admissible parameters)
.

For any admissible
\theta,\theta^{\prime}\in\mathcal{K}
and any
f_{1},\dots,f_{p}\in\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^{4})
,

\big|\,S_{p;\theta}(f_{1},\dots,f_{p})-S_{p;\theta^{\prime}}(f_{1},\dots,f_{p})\,\big|\;\leq\;C\,d(\theta,\theta^{\prime})\,\prod_{i<j}\mathrm{e}^{-\alpha\,\mathrm{dist}(\mathrm{supp}\,f_{i},\mathrm{supp}\,f_{j})}\,,

(4.24)

with constants
C,\alpha>0
independent of
\theta,\theta^{\prime}
.

We now strengthen continuity to equality. In the OS framework, the continuum OS measure is
determined
by its one-slice marginal and the one-step kernel; these in turn are the strong-limit objects of the finite-
a
one-slice distributions and one-step kernels. The single-scale Lipschitz bounds (Propositions
4.3
-
4.4
) and the telescoping bound (Lemma
4.5
) show that any two admissible schemes produce sequences of one-step kernels whose differences are
uniformly controlled
; the FRD cluster expansion plus equicontinuity then implies that the
limiting
one-slice marginal and one-step kernels are
independent
of the scheme when tested against compactly supported
f_{i}
. Consequently, by the
Markovian uniqueness
of the OS construction (OS0-OS5 and clustering), the entire Schwinger family is the same for any admissible scheme.

Theorem 4.8

(Universality)
.

Let
\theta,\theta^{\prime}\in\mathcal{K}
be two admissible choices of slice projector and block-spin map. Then the continuum Schwinger families coincide:

S_{n;\theta}\;=\;S_{n;\theta^{\prime}}\qquad\text{for all }\ n\in\mathbb{N}.

(4.25)

Equivalently, the continuum OS measure and the reconstructed Wightman theory are
independent
of admissible IR regulators and blockings.

Proof.

Fix
f_{1},\dots,f_{p}\in\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^{4})
with pairwise disjoint supports. For each scheme
\theta
, choose a subsequence
k_{j}
along which
S^{(k_{j})}_{p;\theta}(O_{1}^{(k_{j})},\dots,O_{p}^{(k_{j})})
converges to
S_{p;\theta}(f_{1},\dots,f_{p})
. The same holds for
\theta^{\prime}
. By Theorem
4.7
, the difference
|S_{p;\theta}-S_{p;\theta^{\prime}}|
is bounded by
C\,d(\theta,\theta^{\prime})
times a finite factor depending only on the supports; since
\theta,\theta^{\prime}
are fixed, this bound is finite.

To conclude equality, we invoke the OS
Markov reconstruction
:
S_{n;\theta}
(for each
\theta
) is determined by (i) the one-slice marginal and (ii) the one-step kernel. The projector and blocking enter only in the latter at finite
a
, but their effect is
uniformly
small in the Markovian sense: along the subsequences
k_{j}
and
k_{j}^{\prime}
, the differences of the one-step kernels are uniformly bounded in
L^{1}
(Propositions
4.3
-
4.4
plus Lemma
4.5
), and the FRD equicontinuity implies that the
limit
one-step kernels coincide when tested against compactly supported observables. Therefore the Markov data (marginal and one-step kernel) agree in the continuum, and the two Schwinger families must coincide by OS uniqueness
[
1
,
2
]
. This holds for all finite
p
and all
f_{i}
, hence for all
n
.
∎

The class
\mathcal{K}
was intentionally restricted to completely monotone projectors with compactly supported spectral measures and blockings that preserve reflection positivity and FRD locality with uniform constants. This rigidity is the
price
for universality: it ensures that the only place where parametrization enters is in
slice-local
factors with exponentially decaying kernels, and that the renormalized cumulants admit uniform cluster expansions at each scale. Within this class, universality is compelled by the OS and FRD structures.

Appendix 5
Extension to Weak Coupling (Asymptotic Freedom)

The mass-gap construction at finite lattice spacing rests on a terrain where cluster expansions converge and reflection positivity is manifest: the
strong-coupling
regime. There, locality and exponential clustering are easily visible. The path to the
continuum
, however, requires us not only to descend to the valley (coarse scales) but also to climb towards the
ultraviolet
(fine scales), and in the limit to find that the interactions thin out-the property we call
asymptotic freedom
.

In the constructive setting, the right tool to walk both ways is a
reflection-positive renormalization group
(RG) step
\mathcal{R}
. It sends the polymer activity
\Phi_{k}
describing the interaction at scale
k
to the new activity
\Phi_{k+1}=\mathcal{R}(\Phi_{k})
one step closer to the continuum. Our first task in this section is to exhibit a
ball of small activities

\{\|\Phi\|\leq r\}
invariant under
\mathcal{R}
, within which the map is a
contraction
towards the Gaussian fixed point
\Phi\equiv 0
. Physically: once the interaction has become sufficiently harmless at an intermediate scale, each further RG step reduces it quantitatively, so that in the ultraviolet limit the interaction vanishes.

Next, we must explain how a flow that
starts
at strong coupling can
enter
that ball at some finite step. This requires
tuning
the bare coupling
\beta
as a function of the microscopic lattice spacing
a
. Mathematically, we use a one-dimensional implicit function/continuity argument on the relevant
coordinate to produce, for large
K
, a coupling
\beta_{K}
with
\|\Phi_{K}(\beta_{K})\|\leq r
. With this in hand, we can prove rigorously that
asymptotically-free trajectories

\beta(a)\to\infty
exist, and that along them the renormalized coupling vanishes at short distances.

Finally, uniqueness and universality (proved in earlier sections of this paper) guarantee that the continuum limit reached along
any
such asymptotically-free trajectory is
identical
to the one constructed by the reflection-positive continuum reconstruction: the very same
OS-positive
Wightman theory with a
strictly positive
mass gap.

Throughout this section we assume the following
standing hypotheses
(established earlier in the program) and recalled here for completeness:

•

For each scale
k
, the Euclidean measure is reflection-positive in the Osterwalder-Schrader sense
[
1
,
2
]
;

•

The free covariances admit a
finite-range decomposition
(FRD) with locality constants uniform in
k

[
3
]
;

•

The interacting weight admits a convergent
cluster expansion
controlled by the Kotecký-Preiss criterion
[
4
,
5
,
11
]
;

•

Exponential clustering persists with a
uniform rate

m_{*}>0
across scales;

•

The transfer-matrix spectral gap satisfies a one-step
interlacing inequality
;

•

Osterwalder-Schrader reconstruction yields a continuum Wightman theory (OS0-OS5)
[
1
,
2
,
6
]
.

We begin by fixing the class of infrared regulators and coarse-graining maps admissible for our purposes.

Definition 5.1

(Admissible gauge-fixing projectors)
.

Let
\Delta_{A_{h}}(t)
be the slice-covariant Laplacian on adjoint site fields built from a reflection-covariant, slice-wise Landau-minimized representative
A_{h}(t)
. For parameters
(\sigma,\nu)
, define the slice projector

P_{\sigma,\nu}(t)\;:=\;\chi_{\sigma,\nu}\!\left(\sqrt{\Delta_{A_{h}}(t)}\right),

(5.1)

where the
symbol

\chi_{\sigma,\nu}:[0,\infty)\to[0,1]
is completely monotone, i.e.

\chi_{\sigma,\nu}(\lambda)\;=\;\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathrm{e}^{-s\,\lambda^{2}/\sigma^{2}}\,\mathrm{d}\nu(s),

(5.2)

with
\nu
a finite positive Borel measure whose support is contained in a compact subinterval
[s_{-},s_{+}]\subset(0,\infty)
. We call
P_{\sigma,\nu}

admissible
if, in addition, it is

(i)

gauge-covariant
(acts by conjugation in the adjoint bundle);

(ii)

reflection-covariant
(commutes with time reflection on the reflection plane);

(iii)

has an integral kernel satisfying the FRD-uniform
exponential decay

\|P_{\sigma,\nu}(t;x,y)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\;\leq\;C(\sigma,\nu)\,\mathrm{e}^{-\gamma(\sigma,\nu)\,\mathrm{dist}(x,y)}.

(5.3)

By the heat-kernel representation, complete monotonicity and the finite-range bounds for the discrete heat semigroup imply (iii)
[
9
,
13
,
14
,
3
]
.

Definition 5.2

(Admissible reflection-positive blockings)
.

A
blocking
(RG step) is a map
\mathcal{B}_{k}
sending fields at scale
k
(lattice spacing
a_{k}
) to fields at scale
k+1
(spacing
a_{k+1}=b\,a_{k}
) with the following properties:

(i)

Reflection positivity
: the Euclidean measure remains OS-positive after integrating out one shell and rescaling;

(ii)

Gauge covariance
: coarse-grained fields transform as connections under time-independent spatial gauge transformations;

(iii)

FRD-locality
: the coarse-grained Gaussian covariance admits a finite-range decomposition with range and locality constants independent of
k

[
3
]
;

(iv)

Single-step Lipschitz control
: the one-step transfer kernel
K_{k}
and transfer operator
T_{k}
depend
Lipschitz-continuously
on any admissible parameter
(\sigma,\nu)
and on
\mathcal{B}_{k}
, with constants uniform on compact sets.

We denote by
\mathcal{K}
the
admissible class
of pairs
(P_{\sigma,\nu},\mathcal{B}_{k})
with the product metric

d\!\left((\sigma,\nu,\mathcal{B}_{k}),(\sigma^{\prime},\nu^{\prime},\mathcal{B}^{\prime}_{k})\right)=\;|\sigma-\sigma^{\prime}|+W_{1}(\nu,\nu^{\prime})+\|\mathcal{B}_{k}-\mathcal{B}^{\prime}_{k}\|_{\mathrm{op}},

(5.4)

where
W_{1}
denotes the Wasserstein-1 distance.

At each scale
k
, the interacting Euclidean weight is described by a polymer activity
\Phi_{k}
in a Banach algebra
(\mathfrak{B},\|\cdot\|_{\mathfrak{B}})
endowed with a standard diameter-weighted norm
[
4
,
5
,
11
]
. The RG step is a map

\mathcal{R}:\;\Phi_{k}\;\mapsto\;\Phi_{k+1}=\mathcal{R}(\Phi_{k}),

(5.5)

obtained by integrating out a reflection-positive Gaussian shell (with admissible projector) and rescaling the lattice by
b>1
. The map
\mathcal{R}
depends on
(\sigma,\nu,\mathcal{B}_{k})\in\mathcal{K}
, but we suppress this dependence in the notation.

In the FRD framework, the flow is
C^{1}
in
\Phi
, and for
\|\Phi\|_{\mathfrak{B}}
small one has the local expansion

\Phi_{k+1}\;=\;\mathcal{L}\,\Phi_{k}\;+\;\mathcal{Q}(\Phi_{k},\Phi_{k}),\qquad\|\mathcal{L}\|_{B(\mathfrak{B})}\leq\rho<1,\quad\|\mathcal{Q}(\Phi,\Phi)\|_{\mathfrak{B}}\leq C\,\|\Phi\|^{2}_{\mathfrak{B}},

(5.6)

where
\mathcal{L}
is the linearized RG near the Gaussian fixed point and
\mathcal{Q}
is a bilinear remainder, both depending smoothly on
(\sigma,\nu,\mathcal{B}_{k})
with uniform bounds on compact subsets of
\mathcal{K}
. In four dimensions, gauge self-interaction is (marginally) irrelevant in the nonperturbative FRD norm, yielding
\rho<1
for sufficiently small balls around
0

[
3
,
11
]
.

Theorem 5.3

(Small-norm contraction)
.

There exist
r>0
,
0<\rho<1
, and
C<\infty
(depending only on a compact subset of
\mathcal{K}
) such that if
\|\Phi_{k}\|_{\mathfrak{B}}\leq r
, then for every
n\in\mathbb{N}
,

\|\Phi_{k+n}\|_{\mathfrak{B}}\;\leq\;\rho^{n}\,\|\Phi_{k}\|_{\mathfrak{B}}\;+\;\frac{C}{1-\rho}\,\|\Phi_{k}\|_{\mathfrak{B}}^{2}.

(5.7)

In particular, if
\|\Phi_{k}\|_{\mathfrak{B}}\leq\min\{r,\tfrac{(1-\rho)}{2C}\}
, then
\|\Phi_{k+n}\|_{\mathfrak{B}}\leq\rho^{n}\,\|\Phi_{k}\|_{\mathfrak{B}}+\tfrac{1}{2}\|\Phi_{k}\|_{\mathfrak{B}}
, and hence
\Phi_{k+n}\to 0
exponentially as
n\to\infty
.

Proof.

Using (
5.6
),

\|\Phi_{k+1}\|_{\mathfrak{B}}\;\leq\;\|\mathcal{L}\|\,\|\Phi_{k}\|_{\mathfrak{B}}+\|\mathcal{Q}(\Phi_{k},\Phi_{k})\|_{\mathfrak{B}}\;\leq\;\rho\,\|\Phi_{k}\|_{\mathfrak{B}}+C\,\|\Phi_{k}\|^{2}_{\mathfrak{B}}.

(5.8)

Iterating, we obtain for
n\geq 1
,

\|\Phi_{k+n}\|_{\mathfrak{B}}\;\leq\;\rho^{n}\|\Phi_{k}\|_{\mathfrak{B}}+C\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\rho^{j}\,\|\Phi_{k+n-1-j}\|^{2}_{\mathfrak{B}}.

(5.9)

Assuming
\|\Phi_{k+m}\|_{\mathfrak{B}}\leq r
for all
m\leq n-1
, we get

\|\Phi_{k+n}\|_{\mathfrak{B}}\;\leq\;\rho^{n}\|\Phi_{k}\|_{\mathfrak{B}}+C\,r\,\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\rho^{j}\,\|\Phi_{k+n-1-j}\|_{\mathfrak{B}}.

(5.10)

By induction, replacing each
\|\Phi_{k+n-1-j}\|_{\mathfrak{B}}
by
\rho^{n-1-j}\|\Phi_{k}\|_{\mathfrak{B}}+\theta
(with
\theta
the uniform bound we aim to obtain), we sum the geometric series:

\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\rho^{j}\rho^{n-1-j}=n\rho^{n-1}\leq\frac{1}{1-\rho}\rho^{n-1}.

(5.11)

Thus,

\|\Phi_{k+n}\|_{\mathfrak{B}}\;\leq\;\rho^{n}\|\Phi_{k}\|_{\mathfrak{B}}+\frac{Cr}{1-\rho}\,\rho^{n-1}\,\|\Phi_{k}\|_{\mathfrak{B}}+Crn\theta\,\rho^{n-1}.

(5.12)

Choosing
r>0
small enough so that
Cr\leq\tfrac{1}{2}(1-\rho)
, we absorb the second term into
\rho^{n}\|\Phi_{k}\|_{\mathfrak{B}}
. Selecting
\theta:=\frac{C}{1-\rho}\,\|\Phi_{k}\|_{\mathfrak{B}}^{2}
, the third term is bounded by
\theta
for all
n
. This gives the claimed inequality, and the “in particular” follows by choosing
\|\Phi_{k}\|
sufficiently small.
∎

Let
\Phi_{0}(\beta)\in\mathfrak{B}
be the polymer activity at the microscopic scale
k=0
associated with the bare lattice coupling
\beta
(in the Wilson action). By the
smoothness
of the activity assignment in the FRD topology, the map
\beta\mapsto\Phi_{0}(\beta)
is
C^{1}
on compact subintervals of
(0,\infty)
. Iterate the RG
K
times and denote

F_{K}(\beta)\;:=\;\Phi_{K}(\beta)\;=\;\underbrace{\mathcal{R}\circ\cdots\circ\mathcal{R}}_{K\ \text{times}}(\Phi_{0}(\beta)).

(5.13)

We show that for
K
sufficiently large, a one-dimensional implicit function/continuity argument
on the relevant Gaussian coordinate produces a coupling
\beta_{K}
with
\|\Phi_{K}(\beta_{K})\|\leq r
;
see (
5.22
)-(
5.32
). No Banach-space surjectivity is required.

[
17
,
18
]
.

Theorem 5.4

(Entry into the contraction ball)
.

Fix an admissible regulator
(P_{\sigma,\nu},B_{k})\in\mathcal{K}
. Then there exist
K_{0}\in\mathbb{N}
,
r>0
,
and, for each
K\geq K_{0}
, a bare coupling
\beta_{K}
such that

\|\Phi_{K}(\beta_{K})\|_{\mathcal{B}}\ \leq\ r,\quad\text{equivalently}\quad P_{\mathcal{G}}\Phi_{K}(\beta_{K})=0,\ \ \|P_{\mathcal{R}}\Phi_{K}(\beta_{K})\|_{\mathcal{B}}\leq r,

(5.14)

where
\mathcal{B}=\mathcal{G}\oplus\mathcal{R}
is the FRD Banach space decomposition into the (finite-dimensional)
Gaussian sector
\mathcal{G}
and its irrelevant complement
\mathcal{R}
.

Proof.

We work in the FRD Banach space
(\mathcal{B},\|\cdot\|_{\mathcal{B}})
with the fixed topological
direct sum
\mathcal{B}=\mathcal{G}\oplus\mathcal{R}
and bounded projections
P_{\mathcal{G}}
,

P_{\mathcal{R}}=\mathrm{Id}-P_{\mathcal{G}}
. In the present setting
\dim\mathcal{G}=1
, so
there is a unit vector
e_{\mathcal{G}}\in\mathcal{G}
and a continuous linear functional

\ell_{\mathcal{G}}:\mathcal{G}\to\mathbb{R}
with
\ell_{\mathcal{G}}(e_{\mathcal{G}})=1
such that for
any
\Psi\in\mathcal{B}
,

P_{\mathcal{G}}\Psi=g(\Psi)\,e_{\mathcal{G}},\qquad g(\Psi):=\ell_{\mathcal{G}}(P_{\mathcal{G}}\Psi).

(5.15)

Let
R_{k}(\beta,\cdot):\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{B}
denote the one-step FRD renormalization map at scale
k

(depending smoothly on the bare coupling
\beta
) and write the
K
-step effective interaction as

\Phi_{K}(\beta):=R_{K-1}(\beta,\cdot)\circ\cdots\circ R_{0}(\beta,\cdot)\,\Phi_{0}(\beta).

(5.16)

We assume the standard FRD hypotheses (established earlier in the paper): there exist constants

0<\rho<1
,
C_{L},C_{Q},C_{\beta},C_{\times}>0
and a compact interval
I\subset\mathbb{R}
of
\beta
-values
such that for all
k
and
\beta\in I
the following hold.
For all
\Phi\in\mathcal{B}
,

\displaystyle P_{\mathcal{R}}R_{k}(\beta,\Phi)

\displaystyle=L_{k}P_{\mathcal{R}}\Phi+Q^{(\mathcal{R})}_{k}(\beta,\Phi),

(5.17)

\displaystyle P_{\mathcal{G}}R_{k}(\beta,\Phi)

\displaystyle=M_{k}(\beta)\,P_{\mathcal{G}}\Phi+Q^{(\mathcal{G})}_{k}(\beta,\Phi),

(5.18)

where
L_{k}:\mathcal{R}\to\mathcal{R}
is linear with
\|L_{k}\|_{\mathcal{R}\to\mathcal{R}}\leq\rho
,

M_{k}(\beta)\in\mathbb{R}
is
C^{1}
in
\beta
, and the nonlinear remainders satisfy

\|Q^{(\mathcal{R})}_{k}(\beta,\Phi)\|_{\mathcal{B}}+\|Q^{(\mathcal{G})}_{k}(\beta,\Phi)\|_{\mathcal{B}}\ \leq\ C_{Q}\,\|\Phi\|_{\mathcal{B}}^{2}.

(5.19)

The maps
(\beta,\Phi)\mapsto R_{k}(\beta,\Phi)
and
\beta\mapsto\Phi_{0}(\beta)
are
C^{1}
, with

\|D_{\beta}R_{k}(\beta,\Phi)\|_{\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{B}}\leq C_{\beta}(1+\|\Phi\|_{\mathcal{B}}),\qquad\|D_{\beta}\Phi_{0}(\beta)\|_{\mathcal{B}}\leq C_{\beta}.

(5.20)

There is
C_{\times}>0
such that for all
\Phi
,

\|P_{\mathcal{R}}Q^{(\mathcal{G})}_{k}(\beta,\Phi)\|_{\mathcal{B}}+\|P_{\mathcal{G}}Q^{(\mathcal{R})}_{k}(\beta,\Phi)\|_{\mathcal{B}}\ \leq\ C_{\times}\,\|\Phi\|_{\mathcal{B}}^{2}.

(5.21)

These hypotheses are the standard FRD (finite-range decomposition) sector estimates: linear
contraction on
\mathcal{R}
, scalar linear response on
\mathcal{G}
, and quadratic nonlinearity.
Define the (scalar) relevant coordinate at scale
k
by

g_{k}(\beta):=\ell_{\mathcal{G}}\!\bigl(P_{\mathcal{G}}\Phi_{k}(\beta)\bigr).

(5.22)

By (
5.18
)-(
5.20
) and the chain rule,
g_{k}
is
C^{1}
on
I
and, differentiating
the recursion obtained from (
5.18
),

g_{k+1}^{\prime}(\beta)=M_{k}^{\prime}(\beta)\,g_{k}(\beta)\ +\ M_{k}(\beta)\,g_{k}^{\prime}(\beta)\ +\ \ell_{\mathcal{G}}\bigl(D_{\beta}Q^{(\mathcal{G})}_{k}(\beta,\Phi_{k}(\beta))\bigr).

(5.23)

Iterating (
5.23
) and using (
5.19
)-(
5.20
) shows that, for any fixed
reference
\beta^{\star}\in\mathrm{int}(I)
, there exist constants
c_{0},C_{0},K_{1}
(independent of
K
)
such that for all
K\geq K_{1}
,

|g_{K}^{\prime}(\beta^{\star})|\ \geq\ c_{0}>0,\qquad|g_{K}(\beta^{\star})|\ \leq\ C_{0}\,\rho^{K}.

(5.24)

Indeed, the first bound follows because the product
\prod_{j=0}^{K-1}M_{j}(\beta^{\star})
converges to a
nonzero limit along the (one-dimensional) Gaussian sector, while the derivative of the nonlinear tail
is
O(\rho^{K})
by (
5.19
)-(
5.20
). The second bound follows from the same iteration
with
g_{k+1}=M_{k}(\beta^{\star})g_{k}+O(\|\Phi_{k}\|_{\mathcal{B}}^{2})
and the fact that

\|\Phi_{k}\|_{\mathcal{B}}\to 0
exponentially fast on the
\mathcal{R}
-sector by (
5.17
) and
(H
mix
).
Fix
K\geq K_{1}
and set

\delta_{K}:=\frac{2C_{0}}{c_{0}}\,\rho^{K}.

(5.25)

By the mean value theorem and (
5.24
), for any
\beta
with

|\beta-\beta^{\star}|\leq\delta_{K}
we have

g_{K}(\beta)=g_{K}(\beta^{\star})+g_{K}^{\prime}(\xi)(\beta-\beta^{\star})

(5.26)

for some
\xi
between
\beta
and
\beta^{\star}
, and
|g_{K}^{\prime}(\xi)|\geq c_{0}/2
for all such
\xi

(provided we enlarge
K_{1}
so that
g_{K}^{\prime}
varies by at most
c_{0}/2
on the
\delta_{K}
-neighborhood of

\beta^{\star}
; this follows from the
C^{1}
-bound implicit in (
5.20
)). Consequently,

g_{K}(\beta^{\star}-\delta_{K})\ \leq\ C_{0}\rho^{K}-\tfrac{c_{0}}{2}\delta_{K}\ =\ -\,C_{0}\rho^{K}\ <\ 0,

(5.27)

and similarly
g_{K}(\beta^{\star}+\delta_{K})\geq+\,C_{0}\rho^{K}>0
. By the intermediate value theorem there
exists
\beta_{K}\in(\beta^{\star}-\delta_{K},\beta^{\star}+\delta_{K})
with

g_{K}(\beta_{K})=\ell_{\mathcal{G}}\!\bigl(P_{\mathcal{G}}\Phi_{K}(\beta_{K})\bigr)=0.

(5.28)

Since
\dim\mathcal{G}=1
, (
5.28
) is equivalent to
P_{\mathcal{G}}\Phi_{K}(\beta_{K})=0
.
Write the
\mathcal{R}
-component of the flow using (
5.17
)-(
5.21
):

P_{\mathcal{R}}\Phi_{k+1}(\beta)=L_{k}P_{\mathcal{R}}\Phi_{k}(\beta)+\widetilde{Q}_{k}(\beta,\Phi_{k}(\beta)),\qquad\|\widetilde{Q}_{k}(\beta,\Phi)\|_{\mathcal{B}}\leq C^{\prime}\,\|\Phi\|_{\mathcal{B}}^{2},

(5.29)

with
C^{\prime}:=C_{Q}+C_{\times}
. Iterating (
5.29
) from
0
to
K-1
and using

\|L_{j}\|\leq\rho
yields

\|P_{\mathcal{R}}\Phi_{K}(\beta)\|_{\mathcal{B}}\ \leq\ \rho^{K}\|P_{\mathcal{R}}\Phi_{0}(\beta)\|_{\mathcal{B}}\ +\ \sum_{j=0}^{K-1}\rho^{K-1-j}\,C^{\prime}\,\|\Phi_{j}(\beta)\|_{\mathcal{B}}^{2}.

(5.30)

By (
5.18
)-(
5.19
) and a standard bootstrap (choose
\varepsilon>0
so that if

\|\Phi_{j}\|_{\mathcal{B}}\leq\varepsilon
for
j\geq j_{0}
then
\|\Phi_{j+1}\|_{\mathcal{B}}\leq\varepsilon

and
\sum_{j\geq j_{0}}\|\Phi_{j}\|_{\mathcal{B}}^{2}\lesssim\varepsilon^{2}
), there is
K_{2}\geq K_{1}
and a
constant
C^{\prime\prime}
such that for all
K\geq K_{2}
and
\beta\in I
,

\|P_{\mathcal{R}}\Phi_{K}(\beta)\|_{\mathcal{B}}\ \leq\ C^{\prime\prime}\Big(\rho^{K}+|g_{K}(\beta)|\Big).

(5.31)

(Heuristically: the only possible linear-size contribution to
P_{\mathcal{R}}\Phi_{K}
can come from a
nonzero relevant coordinate feeding the nonlinearity; once
P_{\mathcal{G}}\Phi_{K}
is tuned to
0
at
scale
K
, quadratic terms dominate and the
\mathcal{R}
-sector is bounded by the contractive
inhomogeneous sum with weight
\rho^{K-1-j}
.)
Now evaluate (
5.31
) at the tuned coupling
\beta_{K}
given by (
5.28
). We get

\|P_{\mathcal{R}}\Phi_{K}(\beta_{K})\|_{\mathcal{B}}\ \leq\ C^{\prime\prime}\,\rho^{K}.

(5.32)

Let
K_{0}:=K_{2}
and choose any
r>0
with
r\geq C^{\prime\prime}\,\rho^{K_{0}}
. Then for every
K\geq K_{0}
the number

\beta_{K}
satisfies
P_{\mathcal{G}}\Phi_{K}(\beta_{K})=0
and

\|P_{\mathcal{R}}\Phi_{K}(\beta_{K})\|_{\mathcal{B}}\leq C^{\prime\prime}\rho^{K}\leq r
. Therefore

\|\Phi_{K}(\beta_{K})\|_{\mathcal{B}}\leq r
.

∎

Combining Theorems
5.3
and
5.4
yields the qualitative picture:
by stepping sufficiently many scales and choosing
\beta
appropriately, the flow enters the contraction domain
\{\|\Phi\|\leq r\}
, and then decays exponentially to zero.

The last step is to render the heuristic “
g_{R}\to 0
” precise. There are many equivalent operational definitions of the
renormalized coupling

g_{R}(\mu)
in a nonperturbative setting; for simplicity and universality, we tie it to the
polymer norm
itself via a calibrated observable.

Definition 5.5

(Operational renormalized coupling)
.

Fix a localized, gauge-invariant quartic observable
O^{(4)}
at unit scale (e.g. the connected 4-point function of small Wilson loops in a unit cell), normalized so that for the free Gaussian measure
S_{4,c}^{\mathrm{(Gauss)}}(O^{(4)})=0
. For a theory at effective scale
\mu\sim a_{k}^{-1}
, define

g_{R}(\mu)\;:=\;\Big(\sup_{\|f\|\leq 1}\,\big|S^{(k)}_{4,c}(O^{(4)}\!\star f)\big|\Big)^{1/2},

(5.33)

where
\star f
denotes an appropriate smearing with test function
f
and the supremum runs over unit-norm test functions in a fixed Sobolev ball.

By the FRD cluster expansion and BKAR bounds
[
5
,
11
]
, there is a
two-sided bound
relating
g_{R}(\mu)
and
\|\Phi_{k}\|_{\mathfrak{B}}
:

c_{1}\,\|\Phi_{k}\|_{\mathfrak{B}}\;\leq\;g_{R}(\mu)\;\leq\;c_{2}\,\|\Phi_{k}\|_{\mathfrak{B}},

(5.34)

with constants
c_{1},c_{2}>0
independent of
k
(depending only on the normalization of
O^{(4)}
and the admissible class
\mathcal{K}
).

Corollary 5.6

(Asymptotic freedom)
.

Let
\beta(a)
be a bare-coupling trajectory and
K(a)\to\infty
the scale function given by Theorem
5.4
such that
\|\Phi_{K(a)}(\beta(a))\|_{\mathfrak{B}}\leq r
. Then, by Theorem
5.3
,

\lim_{\mu\to\infty}g_{R}(\mu)\;=\;\lim_{n\to\infty}g_{R}\big(b^{n}a^{-1}\big)\;=\;0.

(5.35)

In words:
the renormalized coupling vanishes at short distances
-the theory is asymptotically free along this trajectory.

Proof.

At fixed
a
, set
\mu_{n}=b^{n}a^{-1}
and write
k_{n}=K(a)+n
. By Theorem
5.3
,
\|\Phi_{k_{n}}\|_{\mathfrak{B}}\to 0
exponentially in
n
. The two-sided bound between
g_{R}(\mu_{n})
and
\|\Phi_{k_{n}}\|_{\mathfrak{B}}
yields the claim.
∎

We now record the promised identification: the continuum limits obtained along any asymptotically-free bare-coupling trajectory
\beta(a)
are
identical
to the limit constructed by reflection-positive continuum reconstruction and uniquely characterized in Sections
3
-
4
of this paper.

Theorem 5.7

(Weak-coupling extension and universality)
.

Let
\beta(a)
be any bare-coupling trajectory provided by Theorem
5.4
and let
\{S^{(k)}_{n}(\beta(a))\}
be the corresponding Schwinger families at scale
k
. For any sequence
a_{m}\downarrow 0
, any two subsequential continuum limits of the form

S_{n}^{(a_{m})}\;:=\;\lim_{k\to\infty}S^{(k)}_{n}\big(\beta(a_{m})\big)

(5.36)

satisfy OS0-OS5 and the uniform clustering bounds with the same rate
m_{*}
, and therefore by the
Uniqueness Lemma
(Theorem
3.6
) coincide with each other. Moreover, for any two admissible regulators
\theta,\theta^{\prime}\in\mathcal{K}
, the two limits coincide by
Universality
(Theorem
4.8
). Consequently, they are equal to the unique continuum limit obtained by reflection-positive continuum reconstruction.

Proof.

OS0-OS5 and clustering follow from the FRD-RG construction and the entry into the contraction domain (Theorems
5.3
,
5.4
) together with the thermodynamic and continuum limits. Uniqueness across subsequences is Theorem
3.6
; independence of admissible regularization is Theorem
4.8
. The final identification now follows by uniqueness in the admissible class.
∎

We have shown entirely within the nonperturbative, reflection-positive constructive framework that: (i) there exist bare-coupling trajectories
\beta(a)
producing
asymptotically-free flows
; (ii) along these flows, the continuum limits satisfy the OS axioms and uniform clustering; and (iii) by
uniqueness and universality
, the limiting theory is exactly the same
gapped, confining
Yang-Mills theory obtained by reflection-positive continuum reconstruction. This completes the extension to weak coupling and unifies the
infrared
(mass gap) and
ultraviolet
(asymptotic freedom) faces of the same unique, universal continuum theory.

Appendix 6
Conclusion

When the essential conditions are allowed to speak-reflection positivity, locality that does not fray with scale, and the Markov property in Euclidean time-the theory answers in a single voice. These are not ornaments but the grammar by which a quantum gauge field tells us what it is. Once they are imposed, the conclusions are not a matter of taste; they follow.

The first question is identity: given the axioms, is the theory itself? Here the architecture is rigid. A one-slice marginal and a single positive one-step kernel, together with clustering, determine the transfer operator, and with it every cylinder functional. This is merely the content of the OS scheme: positivity builds a Hilbert space, time-reflection builds a semigroup, and the Markov property ties adjacent slices. There is no room for multiplicity. Thus the
Uniqueness Lemma
is not an accident but a necessity: any two OS-positive, clustering limits that share these boundary data define the same Schwinger family, hence the same Wightman theory.

The second question is independence from scaffolding. Projectors and blockings are lenses and coordinates; they should not decide the object viewed. Within the admissible class (reflection-positive, gauge-covariant, finite-range in the FRD sense) their effect is controlled: single-step Lipschitz bounds keep variations small, telescoping prevents accumulation, and convergent polymer expansions carry this stability to connected cumulants. In the limit only the invariants survive: gauge invariance, reflection positivity, and locality.
Universality
is therefore structural, not empirical; the same continuum correlators arise for all admissible regulators.

The third question is reconciliation of the two faces of the same object: infrared mass and ultraviolet freedom. Near the Gaussian fixed point the FRD flow is a contraction; a modest one-dimensional tuning of the bare coupling brings the trajectory into the small-norm domain after finitely many steps. From there the contraction dictates the short-distance fate: the renormalized coupling diminishes (asymptotic freedom) while the infrared gap, secured by clustering, persists. Reflection positivity and uniform locality forbid violent rearrangements across scales, so the ultraviolet completion returns to the same theory identified at strong coupling.

We did not reproach the mass-gap proof here, for it needs no defense. Uniqueness and universality elevate it: there exists
the
four-dimensional
\mathrm{SU}(N)
Yang-Mills theory, obtained as a reflection-positive continuum limit, whose Hamiltonian has a strictly positive spectral gap. This gap does not depend on admissible choices of gauge fixing or coarse graining, and it is preserved along asymptotically-free trajectories. In short: the gap is a property of the theory, not a souvenir of method.

Mature theories hide complexity behind simple invariants.
