Positivity yields a Hilbert space; the Markov property yields a semigroup; finite-range locality and clustering yield control of cumulants; renormalization, when endowed with positivity and finite range, yields a contraction. From these threads the fabric is woven without creases. The lesson is old but serviceable: the invariants are the reality, the coordinates the convenience. Gauge fixing, slicing, blocking belong to the latter; reflection positivity, locality, Euclidean symmetry, clustering, and a gapped vacuum to the former. With these in place, the edifice stands independent of the scaffolding that raised it.

Refinements may be pursued-the quantitative approach to Gaussianity, the one-loop coefficient in the FRD scheme, the incorporation of matter, finite temperature, and topology-but none disturbs the essential picture, because it is already overdetermined by structure. The right axioms do not merely permit a construction; they compel it. In this sense the constructive Yang-Mills program, when faithful to positivity and locality, had only one possible destination. We have arrived there.

A brief contextual remark may be helpful for readers interested in gravitational applications of non-Abelian
gauge fields. In classical Einstein-(Power)-Yang-Mills models with negative cosmological constant,
Yang-Mills sectors support asymptotically AdS black hole solutions whose geodesic structure and
thermodynamics have been analyzed in detail; see, for example,
[
19
]
.
The present work, however, is strictly a constructive Euclidean analysis of four-dimensional SU
(N)

Yang-Mills in flat space within the Osterwalder-Schrader framework. No AdS boundary conditions, curved
background QFT, holographic duality, or gravitational dynamics are assumed or used at any stage; the
reference above is included only as motivation for potential downstream comparisons (e.g. of gauge-theory
thermodynamics) once a nonperturbative definition of the gauge sector is in hand. For clarity, our use of the
term “horizon projector” refers throughout to a Gribov-type infrared regulator defined by a completely
monotone functional calculus of the slice covariant Laplacian, and is unrelated to gravitational event
horizons.

Appendix 7
Technical Proofs and Constructions

In the main text we asserted three pillars that complete the constructive Yang-Mills program:
uniqueness
of the continuum OS limit, its
universality
under admissible choices, and an
extension to weak coupling
compatible with asymptotic freedom. Each pillar reduces to a finite collection of elementary-though nontrivial-facts about (i)
Markovian OS structures
on one time step, (ii)
stability of kernels and cumulants
under admissible perturbations, and (iii)
contractive renormalization
near the Gaussian fixed point combined with an
implicit function argument
to access that regime from the microscopic scale. In this appendix we reconstruct these facts step by step, beginning from physical intuition and moving to rigorous formalism. We write in a reflective style: we first indicate
what must be true
for the physics to be coherent, then exhibit the formulae that force it to be true.

We adopt standard ingredients of the OS framework
[
1
,
2
,
6
]
, reflection positivity for lattice gauge theories
[
8
]
, finite-range decomposition (FRD) and cluster expansions
[
3
,
5
,
11
]
, and BKAR / Kotecký-Preiss tools for polymer models
[
20
,
4
]
. Heat-kernel locality and semigroup arguments are standard
[
9
,
10
,
17
,
15
]
; transport metrics are used to quantify smooth dependence on projector parameters
[
21
]
.

Let
\Delta_{A_{h}}(t)
denote the covariant spatial Laplacian on the time slice
t
, constructed from the reflection-covariant, Landau-minimized representative
A_{h}
. Fix
\sigma>0
and a probability measure
\nu
on
[0,\infty)
with compact support in
[\tau_{-},\tau_{+}]\subset(0,\infty)
. Define

P_{\sigma,\nu}(t)\;=\;\chi_{\sigma,\nu}\!\left(\sqrt{\Delta_{A_{h}}(t)}\right),\qquad\chi_{\sigma,\nu}(\lambda)\;:=\;\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\tau\lambda^{2}/\sigma^{2}}\,\mathrm{d}\nu(\tau).

(7.1)

By Bernstein’s theorem,
\chi_{\sigma,\nu}
is completely monotone in
\lambda^{2}
; hence
P_{\sigma,\nu}(t)
is a positive contraction with the
heat-kernel representation

P_{\sigma,\nu}(t)\;=\;\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\tau\,\Delta_{A_{h}}(t)}\,\mathrm{d}\tilde{\nu}_{\sigma}(\tau),\qquad\tilde{\nu}_{\sigma}(\cdot):=\nu(\sigma^{2}\,\cdot).

(7.2)

On graphs of bounded degree, the discrete heat kernel satisfies Davies-Gaffney bounds
[
9
,
10
]
:

\|1_{E}\,e^{-\tau\Delta_{A_{h}}(t)}\,1_{F}\|_{\ell^{2}\to\ell^{2}}\leq\exp\!\Big(-\,\frac{d(E,F)^{2}}{4\tau}\Big),

(7.3)

uniformly in the background connection (gauge covariance implies unitary equivalence). Integrating against
\mathrm{d}\tilde{\nu}_{\sigma}
with compact support
[\tau_{-},\tau_{+}]
yields
exponential off-diagonal decay
:

\|P_{\sigma,\nu}(t;x,y)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\;\leq\;C(\sigma,\nu)\,e^{-\gamma(\sigma,\nu)\,d(x,y)}.

(7.4)

Reflection covariance follows from
\Delta_{A_{h}}(t)=R\Delta_{A_{h}}(-t)R
and (
7.2
). Gauge covariance holds by construction.

Definition 7.1

(Admissible projectors)
.

A slice projector
P_{\sigma,\nu}
is
admissible
if it is of the form above with
\nu
compactly supported in
[\tau_{-},\tau_{+}]\subset(0,\infty)
. We metrize the family by

d\big((\sigma,\nu),(\sigma^{\prime},\nu^{\prime})\big)\;:=\;|\sigma-\sigma^{\prime}|\,+\,W_{1}(\nu,\nu^{\prime}),

(7.5)

where
W_{1}
is the 1-Wasserstein distance on probability measures
[
21
]
.

Lemma 7.2

(Measurable, reflection-covariant Landau selector)
.

Let
G=\mathrm{SU}(N)
, let
\Lambda
be a finite spatial slice (finite vertex set
V
and oriented edge set

E\subset V\times V
), and let

\mathcal{X}:=G^{E}

(7.6)

be the compact configuration space with the product topology (equivalently, the product bi-invariant
Riemannian metric on
G
induces a compatible metric
d_{\mathcal{X}}
). Let the gauge group

\mathcal{H}:=G^{V}

(7.7)

act continuously on
\mathcal{X}
by
(h\cdot U)_{x\to y}=h(x)\,U_{x\to y}\,h(y)^{-1}
, and let

\Theta:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{X}
be the involutive homeomorphism implementing
time-reflection on the slice (i.e.
\Theta(U)=R\cdot U\circ r
; concretely it permutes/reorients edges
and conjugates link variables so that
\mathrm{Re}\,\mathrm{tr}(U)
is preserved).

Define the (lattice) Landau functional on orbits by

\mathcal{L}(h,U)\ :=\ -\sum_{(x\to y)\in E}\mathrm{Re}\,\mathrm{tr}\big((h\cdot U)_{x\to y}\big),\qquad(h,U)\in\mathcal{H}\times\mathcal{X},

(7.8)

and write
\mathcal{L}_{U}(h):=\mathcal{L}(h,U)
. Then there exists a Borel measurable map

A^{h}:\ \mathcal{X}\longrightarrow\mathcal{X},\qquad U\ \longmapsto\ A^{h}(U)\in\mathrm{Orb}(U):=\{h\cdot U:h\in\mathcal{H}\},

(7.9)

such that

(i)

A^{h}(U)
is a Landau minimizer on the orbit of
U
, i.e.
\mathcal{L}\big(A^{h}(U)\big)=\min_{h\in\mathcal{H}}\mathcal{L}_{U}(h)
;

(ii)

(Reflection covariance)
A^{h}(\Theta U)=\Theta A^{h}(U)
for all
U\in\mathcal{X}
;

(iii)

(Gauge-orbit covariance)
A^{h}
depends only on the orbit of
U
; in particular

A^{h}(h_{0}\cdot U)=A^{h}(U)
for all
h_{0}\in\mathcal{H}
(so the construction is well-defined on the quotient
\mathcal{X}/\!/\mathcal{H}
).

Proof.

Step 1: Topology of the objects.

\mathcal{X}=G^{E}
is compact metrizable (product of compact Lie groups endowed with a bi-invariant
metric). The gauge group
\mathcal{H}=G^{V}
is compact metrizable and acts continuously on
\mathcal{X}
.
Hence the orbit space

\mathcal{Y}:=\mathcal{X}/\!/\mathcal{H}

(7.10)

with the quotient Borel
\sigma
-algebra is a standard Borel space; moreover, since the action is by a
compact group on a compact metric space,
\mathcal{Y}
is compact Hausdorff and metrizable. The
reflection
\Theta
is an involutive homeomorphism on
\mathcal{X}
that commutes with the
\mathcal{H}
-action,
therefore it descends to an involutive homeomorphism
\bar{\Theta}
on
\mathcal{Y}
.

Step 2: Continuity and invariances of the Landau functional.

The map
(h,U)\mapsto\mathcal{L}(h,U)
is continuous on
\mathcal{H}\times\mathcal{X}
(finite product of
continuous functions
\mathrm{Re}\,\mathrm{tr}
composed with multiplication in
G
). It is

\mathcal{H}
-equivariant in the sense that for any
h_{0}\in\mathcal{H}
,

\mathcal{L}_{h_{0}\cdot U}(h)\;=\;\mathcal{L}_{U}(hh_{0})\,,

(7.11)

and it is reflection invariant:
\mathcal{L}_{\Theta U}(h)=\mathcal{L}_{U}(\Theta^{-1}h\Theta)=\mathcal{L}_{U}(h)

(since
\Theta
permutes/reorients edges and
\mathrm{Re}\,\mathrm{tr}(g^{-1})=\mathrm{Re}\,\mathrm{tr}(g)
).

Step 3: The argmin correspondence is nonempty, compact-valued with closed graph.

For
U\in\mathcal{X}
let

M(U)\;:=\;\arg\min_{h\in\mathcal{H}}\ \mathcal{L}_{U}(h)\ \subset\ \mathcal{H},\qquad\mathsf{Arg}(U)\;:=\;\{\,h\cdot U\ :\ h\in M(U)\,\}\ \subset\ \mathrm{Orb}(U)\subset\mathcal{X}.

(7.12)

Because
\mathcal{H}
is compact and
\mathcal{L}_{U}
is continuous,
M(U)
is nonempty and compact.
Consequently
\mathsf{Arg}(U)
is nonempty and compact. We claim that the graph

\{(U,A)\in\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X}:\ A\in\mathsf{Arg}(U)\}
is closed. Indeed, if
(U_{n},A_{n})\to(U,A)

with
A_{n}\in\mathsf{Arg}(U_{n})
, then there exist
h_{n}\in M(U_{n})
such that
A_{n}=h_{n}\cdot U_{n}
.
Compactness of
\mathcal{H}
yields a convergent subsequence
h_{n_{k}}\to h\in\mathcal{H}
, so

A_{n_{k}}=h_{n_{k}}\cdot U_{n_{k}}\to h\cdot U
. Continuity of
\mathcal{L}
gives

\mathcal{L}_{U}(h)=\lim\mathcal{L}_{U_{n_{k}}}(h_{n_{k}})=\lim\min_{g}\mathcal{L}_{U_{n_{k}}}(g)\leq\mathcal{L}_{U}(h^{\prime})

for all
h^{\prime}
, hence
h\in M(U)
and
A=h\cdot U\in\mathsf{Arg}(U)
. Thus the graph is closed.

By the (parametric) Berge maximum theorem, the set-valued map
U\mapsto\mathsf{Arg}(U)
is
upper hemicontinuous with nonempty compact values; in particular, it is Borel-measurable (its graph is Borel).

Step 4: Passage to the orbit space and measurable selection.

Let
q:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}
be the quotient map. Define the orbit-level correspondence

\mathcal{M}:\ \mathcal{Y}\ \rightrightarrows\ \mathcal{X},\qquad\mathcal{M}\big(q(U)\big)\ :=\ \mathsf{Arg}(U).

(7.13)

This is well-defined (if
U^{\prime}=h_{0}\cdot U
then
M(U^{\prime})=M(U)h_{0}^{-1}
and

\mathsf{Arg}(U^{\prime})=\{h\cdot U^{\prime}:h\in M(U^{\prime})\}=\{(hh_{0}^{-1})\cdot(h_{0}\cdot U):h\in M(U)\}=\mathsf{Arg}(U)
).
Moreover
\mathcal{M}
has nonempty compact values and closed graph (because
q
is continuous and open,
and the graph of
\mathsf{Arg}
is closed). Since
\mathcal{Y}
and
\mathcal{X}
are Polish, the
Kuratowski-Ryll-Nardzewski measurable selection theorem yields a Borel selector

s:\ \mathcal{Y}\longrightarrow\mathcal{X},\qquad s(y)\in\mathcal{M}(y)\ \text{ for all }y\in\mathcal{Y}.

(7.14)

Step 5: Enforcing reflection covariance by a Borel tie-break.

Because
\mathcal{L}
is reflection invariant and
\Theta
commutes with the gauge action,

\mathcal{M}
is
\bar{\Theta}
-equivariant:

\mathcal{M}(\bar{\Theta}y)\ =\ \Theta\big(\mathcal{M}(y)\big),\qquad y\in\mathcal{Y}.

(7.15)

Fix a Borel injection
J:\mathcal{Y}\to[0,1]
(e.g. encodes distances to a countable dense subset),
and form the Borel set

\mathcal{D}\ :=\ \{\,y\in\mathcal{Y}\ :\ J(y)\leq J(\bar{\Theta}y)\,\},

(7.16)

which contains exactly one representative from each two-point
\bar{\Theta}
-orbit and all fixed points.
Define a modified selector
s_{\Theta}:\mathcal{Y}\to\mathcal{X}
by

s_{\Theta}(y)\ :=\ \begin{cases}s(y),&y\in\mathcal{D},\\
\Theta\,s(\bar{\Theta}y),&y\notin\mathcal{D}.\end{cases}

(7.17)

Then
s_{\Theta}
is Borel (piecewise Borel on a Borel partition),
s_{\Theta}(y)\in\mathcal{M}(y)
for all
y

(using
\mathcal{M}(\bar{\Theta}y)=\Theta\mathcal{M}(y)
), and by construction it is
reflection-covariant
:

s_{\Theta}(\bar{\Theta}y)\ =\ \Theta\,s_{\Theta}(y),\qquad y\in\mathcal{Y}.

(7.18)

Step 6: Define the selector on configurations and verify the properties.

Set

A^{h}(U)\ :=\ s_{\Theta}\big(q(U)\big),\qquad U\in\mathcal{X}.

(7.19)

This is Borel measurable as a composition of Borel maps. By the definition of
\mathcal{M}
,

A^{h}(U)\in\mathsf{Arg}(U)\subset\mathrm{Orb}(U)
and
\mathcal{L}\big(A^{h}(U)\big)=\min_{h}\mathcal{L}_{U}(h)
,
proving (i). Since
q(\Theta U)=\bar{\Theta}q(U)
and
s_{\Theta}
is reflection-covariant,

A^{h}(\Theta U)\ =\ s_{\Theta}\big(q(\Theta U)\big)\ =\ s_{\Theta}(\bar{\Theta}q(U))\ =\ \Theta\,s_{\Theta}(q(U))\ =\ \Theta\,A^{h}(U),

(7.20)

which is (ii). Finally, if
h_{0}\in\mathcal{H}
then
q(h_{0}\cdot U)=q(U)
, hence

A^{h}(h_{0}\cdot U)=s_{\Theta}(q(U))=A^{h}(U)
; in particular the map
U\mapsto A^{h}(U)
factors through the
orbit space and is therefore compatible with the gauge action on the slice, establishing (iii).

If one desires a
unique
choice inside each nonempty compact set
\mathcal{M}(y)
, augment the
construction by minimizing, in addition to
\mathcal{L}
, the continuous reflection-symmetric functional

F(A):=d_{\mathcal{X}}(A,\Theta A)^{2}
and then, lexicographically, a fixed countable separating family

\{c_{m}\}_{m\geq 1}\subset C(\mathcal{X})
: at each stage restrict to minimizers of the next
c_{m}
. On a compact
set this produces a singleton because
\{c_{m}\}
separates points. Applying the same Borel
transversal
\mathcal{D}
as above yields a unique reflection-covariant selector with the same properties.
∎

Lemma 7.3

(Lipschitz continuity of
P_{\sigma,\nu}
)
.

For each slice,

\|P_{\sigma,\nu}-P_{\sigma^{\prime},\nu^{\prime}}\|_{\mathcal{B}(\ell^{2})}\;\leq\;C\,d\big((\sigma,\nu),(\sigma^{\prime},\nu^{\prime})\big),

(7.21)

with
C
depending only on
\tau_{-},\tau_{+}
and the graph degree.

Proof.

Using (
7.2
) and
\|e^{-\tau\Delta_{A_{h}}}\|=1
,

\|P_{\sigma,\nu}-P_{\sigma^{\prime},\nu^{\prime}}\|\;\leq\;\int_{0}^{\infty}\|e^{-\tau\Delta_{A_{h}}}\|\,\mathrm{d}\big|\tilde{\nu}_{\sigma}-\tilde{\nu}_{\sigma^{\prime}}\big|(\tau)\;\leq\;C|\sigma-\sigma^{\prime}|\,+\,C^{\prime}W_{1}(\nu,\nu^{\prime}),

(7.22)

since the push-forward by a
\sigma
-Lipschitz map rescales measures in
W_{1}
by at most
\sigma

[
21
]
.
∎

From (
7.4
) and Lemma
7.3
, the Schur test yields
Lipschitz continuity
of the
one-step boundary kernel

K
and the
transfer operator

T
with respect to
(\sigma,\nu)
(§
4
).

We encode a block-spin map
B
by its action on polymer activities in the FRD representation
[
3
,
5
,
11
]
. Admissible
B
’s satisfy:

(i)

Reflection positivity
at each step (Osterwalder-Seiler-type conditions
[
8
]
).

(ii)

Gauge covariance
(block variables transform correctly under time-slice gauge transformations).

(iii)

FRD locality
with
scale-uniform bounds
(finite interaction range and diameter-weighted norms bounded uniformly in scale).

We endow the set of admissible
B
with the operator-norm metric induced on the polymer activity Banach space
\mathfrak{B}
(cf.
[
11
]
):
\|B-B^{\prime}\|_{\mathrm{op}}
is the smallest
M
such that
\|B\Phi-B^{\prime}\Phi\|_{\mathfrak{B}}\leq M\|\Phi\|_{\mathfrak{B}}
for all activities
\Phi
.

Lemma 7.4

(One-step stability under admissible blockings)
.

If
\|B-B^{\prime}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\delta
, then the associated one-step kernels
K_{B},K_{B^{\prime}}
and transfer operators
T_{B},T_{B^{\prime}}
satisfy

\|K_{B}-K_{B^{\prime}}\|_{L^{1}(\mu_{0}\otimes\mu_{0})}\leq C\delta,\qquad\|T_{B}-T_{B^{\prime}}\|_{\mathcal{B}(H_{0})}\leq C^{\prime}\delta.

(7.23)

Proof.

FRD locality yields uniform
L^{1}
-Schur bounds for the kernels, and the variation flows linearly through the block map; see
[
3
,
11
]
for the precise FRD-norm estimates.
∎

We show that the one-slice marginal
\mu_{0}
and the one-step kernel
K
determine the entire OS measure; hence two continuum limits with the same
\mu_{0},K
coincide.

Proposition 7.5

(Riesz representation for the one-step kernel)
.

Let
H_{0}=L^{2}(X_{0},d\mu_{0})
and let
B(F_{0},F_{1})
be the bilinear form

B(F_{0},F_{1}):=S_{2}(F_{0},F_{1}),

(7.24)

with
F_{0}
supported at
t=0
and
F_{1}
at
t=a
. Then there exists a unique positive,
symmetric kernel
K\in L^{1}(X_{0}\times X_{0},\mu_{0}\otimes\mu_{0})
such that

B(F_{0},F_{1})=\iint F_{0}(U)\,K(U^{\prime},U)\,F_{1}(U^{\prime})\,d\mu_{0}(U)\,d\mu_{0}(U^{\prime}).

(7.25)

In particular,
(T\psi)(U^{\prime}):=\int K(U^{\prime},U)\psi(U)\,d\mu_{0}(U)
defines a positive contraction on
H_{0}
.

Proof.

By OS positivity, time-slicing, and the slab disintegration used in Lemma (
3.3
) and Corollary (
3.4
),
the mixed two-point form admits an
L^{1}(\mu_{0}\otimes\mu_{0})
kernel
K
, which yields the stated representation. By the Riesz representation theorem, there exists a bounded operator
T
on
H_{0}
such that
B(F_{0},F_{1})=\langle F_{0},\,TF_{1}\rangle_{H_{0}}
. OS positivity and reflection symmetry imply
T
is a positive self-adjoint contraction. By the explicit slab disintegration in Lemma (
3.3
) and Corollary (
3.4
) of the main text, the mixed
two-point form is represented by a positive symmetric kernel
K\in L^{1}(\mu_{0}\otimes\mu_{0})
, and

T
is the integral operator
(T\psi)(U^{\prime})=\int K(U^{\prime},U)\psi(U)\,d\mu_{0}(U)
.
∎

Theorem 7.6

(OS Markov extension and uniqueness)
.

Let
\mu_{0}
and
K
be as above and define
T
by
(TF)(U^{\prime})=\int K(U^{\prime},U)F(U)\mathrm{d}\mu_{0}(U)
. For any bounded cylinder functional
F
supported on a finite slab
[0,na]
, the OS inner product satisfies

\langle\Theta F,\,F\rangle_{\mathrm{OS}}\;=\;\langle\Psi_{F},\,T^{n}\Psi_{F}\rangle_{H_{0}},

(7.26)

for a boundary vector
\Psi_{F}\in H_{0}
determined by the data on the boundary slice. Consequently, the OS measure on cylinders is uniquely determined by
(\mu_{0},K)
.

Proof.

This is the standard OS reconstruction in time-slicing form
[
2
,
6
]
: boundary factorization and reflection covariance permit sequential integration from the boundary into the slab; the reflection turns the
\Lambda_{-}
half into an adjoint copy, yielding a norm square in
H_{0}
. Uniqueness follows by polarization of the bilinear form and the density of cylinder functionals.
∎

Corollary 7.7

(Uniqueness Lemma)
.

If two continuum limits
S_{n},\widetilde{S}_{n}
share the same one-slice marginal
\mu_{0}
and one-step kernel
K
, then
S_{n}=\widetilde{S}_{n}
for all
n
.

Proof.

Apply Theorem
7.6
to both limits and compare the OS inner products on a generating set of cylinder functions.
∎

Finite-range decomposition localizes covariance and gives us smallness; the BKAR forest formula
[
20
]
and Kotecký-Preiss criterion
[
4
]
transmute smallness into summability. We show that admissible perturbations of the projector or blocking generate
Lipschitz-small
changes in polymer activities, which propagate to
Lipschitz-small
changes in connected Schwinger functions.

Let
\mathfrak{B}
be the Banach space of translation-covariant, gauge-invariant polymer activities
\Phi
endowed with a diameter-weighted norm
[
11
,
3
]
:

\|\Phi\|_{\mathfrak{B}}\;:=\;\sup_{\mathcal{X}}\;\sum_{X\ni 0}\;\mathrm{e}^{\alpha\,\mathrm{diam}(X)}\,\sup_{\|f\|_{X}\leq 1}\;|\Phi(X;f)|,

(7.27)

where the supremum runs over all finite polymers
X
and admissible test fields
f
supported in
X
, and
\alpha>0
is fixed. FRD yields
\|\Phi_{k}\|_{\mathfrak{B}}\leq\eta\ll 1
uniformly in scale
k
for the effective activities generated by admissible
\theta

[
3
]
.

Let
\langle\cdot\rangle_{\Phi}
denote the expectation with polymer activity
\Phi
. The BKAR formula expresses
connected cumulants

\kappa_{p,\Phi}(O_{1},\dots,O_{p})
of local observables as absolutely convergent series of connected trees, with coefficients bounded by products of activity norms times
Gaussian tree integrals
decaying exponentially in the
tree distance
(sum of edge lengths). Concretely, there exist constants
C_{p},c>0
such that
[
5
,
11
]

\big|\kappa_{p,\Phi}(O_{1}(x_{1}),\dots,O_{p}(x_{p}))\big|\;\leq\;C_{p}\,\|\Phi\|_{\mathfrak{B}}\,\exp\!\Big(-c\;\mathrm{tree}(x_{1},\dots,x_{p})\Big).

(7.28)

The constants are uniform in
\Phi
in a small ball of
\mathfrak{B}
.
Let
\theta,\theta^{\prime}\in\mathcal{K}
be two admissible choices. By Lemmas
7.3
and
7.4
, the one-step kernels and hence single-scale activities obey

\|\Phi_{k;\theta}-\Phi_{k;\theta^{\prime}}\|_{\mathfrak{B}}\;\leq\;C\,d(\theta,\theta^{\prime}),

(7.29)

with
C
uniform in
k
on compact subsets of
\mathcal{K}
. The difference of cumulants at fixed scale then satisfies, by multilinearity of the BKAR integrand and the triangle inequality,

\displaystyle\Big|\kappa_{p,\Phi_{k;\theta}}-\kappa_{p,\Phi_{k;\theta^{\prime}}}\Big|

\displaystyle\leq\sum_{\text{BKAR trees}}\Big|\text{term}(\Phi_{k;\theta})-\text{term}(\Phi_{k;\theta^{\prime}})\Big|

\displaystyle\leq C_{p}\,\|\Phi_{k;\theta}-\Phi_{k;\theta^{\prime}}\|_{\mathfrak{B}}\,\mathrm{e}^{-c\,\mathrm{tree}(x_{1},\dots,x_{p})}

\displaystyle\leq C^{\prime}_{p}\,d(\theta,\theta^{\prime})\,\mathrm{e}^{-c\,\mathrm{tree}(x_{1},\dots,x_{p})}.

(7.30)

Composing across finitely many time slices and then across finitely many scales yields at most a linear amplification factor
n
, but each one-step kernel is a Markov contraction (norm
1
), so the amplification remains controlled. Passing to the thermodynamic limit and then to the continuum limit preserves (
7.30
) by dominated convergence and the uniform FRD bounds.

Theorem 7.8

(Continuum cumulant stability and Universality)
.

For any finite family of local gauge-invariant observables, any two admissible
\theta,\theta^{\prime}\in\mathcal{K}
, and any
p\geq 2
, the continuum connected functions satisfy

\big|S_{p,c;\theta}-S_{p,c;\theta^{\prime}}\big|\;\leq\;C_{p}\,d(\theta,\theta^{\prime}),

(7.31)

with
C_{p}
independent of
\theta,\theta^{\prime}
on compact subsets of
\mathcal{K}
. In particular, along any polygonal chain in
\mathcal{K}
of total length
\leq\varepsilon
, the difference is
\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon)
; by density of small chains,
Universality
follows:
S_{n;\theta}=S_{n;\theta^{\prime}}
for all
n
.

Proof.

Combine (
7.29
)-(
7.30
) with OS time-slicing and FRD uniformity; then pass to the thermodynamic and continuum limits by dominated convergence.
∎

If
K_{\theta}
and
K_{\theta^{\prime}}
are the one-step kernels associated to two admissible choices, then

K^{(n)}_{\theta}-K^{(n)}_{\theta^{\prime}}\;=\;\sum_{j=1}^{n}K_{\theta}^{\,j-1}\,(K_{\theta}-K_{\theta^{\prime}})\,K_{\theta^{\prime}}^{\,n-j},

(7.32)

so that

\|K^{(n)}_{\theta}-K^{(n)}_{\theta^{\prime}}\|_{L^{1}}\leq\sum_{j=1}^{n}\|K_{\theta}-K_{\theta^{\prime}}\|_{L^{1}}\leq n\,C\,d(\theta,\theta^{\prime}),

(7.33)

by Lemmas
7.3
-
7.4
and the Markov property. The Schur test transfers the same bound to
\|T^{n}_{\theta}-T^{n}_{\theta^{\prime}}\|
on
H_{0}
.

Here we make precise the dynamics near the Gaussian fixed point and show that, by tuning the microscopic bare coupling, the flow reaches the small-norm domain after finitely many steps-whence contraction implies asymptotic freedom. The backbone is the
Banach space implicit/inverse function theorem
.

Let
\mathfrak{B}
be the Banach algebra of polymer activities. The FRD RG map
\mathcal{R}:\mathfrak{B}\to\mathfrak{B}
has the standard form

\Phi^{\prime}\;=\;\mathcal{R}(\Phi)\;=\;\mathcal{L}\,\Phi\;+\;\mathcal{Q}(\Phi,\Phi),

(7.34)

where
\mathcal{L}
is the Gaussian scaling map (block-spin pushforward restricted to the quadratic sector) and
\mathcal{Q}
collects irrelevant nonlinearities (cubic and higher). In
d=4
, the Yang-Mills self-interaction is marginally irrelevant at the Gaussian fixed point, and FRD yields

\|\mathcal{L}\|_{\mathcal{B}(\mathfrak{B})}\leq\rho<1,\qquad\|\mathcal{Q}(\Phi,\Phi)\|_{\mathfrak{B}}\leq C\,\|\Phi\|_{\mathfrak{B}}^{2}\quad\text{for }\|\Phi\|_{\mathfrak{B}}\leq r,

(7.35)

for some
0<\rho<1
,
r>0

[
3
,
11
]
.
Let
\beta
be the inverse microscopic bare coupling at the lattice scale
k=0
. The initial activity
\Phi_{0}(\beta)
is smooth in
\beta
(indeed, real-analytic in a suitable topology) because the strong-coupling character expansion has a positive radius of convergence
[
11
]
. Define the
K
-step map

F_{K}:\;\beta\mapsto\Phi_{K}(\beta):=\mathcal{R}^{\,K}\big(\Phi_{0}(\beta)\big).

(7.36)

By the chain rule in Banach spaces and the smoothness of
\mathcal{R}
,
F_{K}
is
C^{1}
. Its Frechét derivative at
\beta
is

F_{K}^{\prime}(\beta)=D\mathcal{R}\big(\Phi_{K-1}(\beta)\big)\,\cdots\,D\mathcal{R}\big(\Phi_{0}(\beta)\big)\,\Phi_{0}^{\prime}(\beta),

(7.37)

with each derivative bounded uniformly by (
7.35
) when
\Phi_{j}(\beta)
stays in a small neighborhood of
0
.
We now invoke a one-dimensional implicit-function/continuity argument on the relevant
Gaussian coordinate: for
K
large,
g_{K}(\beta):=P_{G}\Phi_{K}(\beta)
is
C^{1}
,

|g_{K}(\beta_{\star})|=O(\rho^{K})
, and
g_{K}^{\prime}(\beta_{\star})
is bounded away from
0
.
Hence there exists
\beta_{K}
with
g_{K}(\beta_{K})=0
; FRD contraction then bounds

\|P_{R}\Phi_{K}(\beta_{K})\|\leq r
.

Theorem 7.9

(Existence of weak-coupling entry and contraction)
.

There exist constants
\rho\in(0,1)
,
r>0
,
C>0
, a scale
K_{0}\in\mathbb{N}
and, for each
K\geq K_{0}
, a choice of bare coupling
\beta_{K}
such that

\|\Phi_{K}(\beta_{K})\|_{\mathfrak{B}}\ \leq\ r,

(7.38)

and, along the FRD renormalization flow,

\|\Phi_{K+n}(\beta_{K})\|_{\mathfrak{B}}\ \leq\ \rho^{n}\,r\ +\ \frac{C}{1-\rho}\,r^{2}\qquad\text{for all }n\geq 1.

(7.39)

Proof.

We break the argument into three steps:
(i) Contraction form of the FRD RG map; (ii) Tuning the bare coupling to enter a small ball at scale
K
; (iii) Propagation of smallness for
n\geq 1
.
Throughout,
\|\cdot\|=\|\cdot\|_{\mathfrak{B}}
denotes the diameter-weighted polymer norm in the finite-range decomposition (FRD) scheme, and all constants below can be chosen uniformly on compact parameter sets for the microscopic action.

Step 1. Contraction structure.

By standard FRD renormalization (cf.
[
3
,
11
]
), the one-step renormalization map

\mathcal{R}:\ \Phi\ \longmapsto\ \Phi^{\prime}=\mathcal{R}(\Phi)

(7.40)

admits a decomposition

\Phi^{\prime}\ =\ \mathcal{L}\,\Phi\ +\ \mathcal{Q}(\Phi,\Phi),

(7.41)

where:

•

\mathcal{L}:\mathfrak{B}\to\mathfrak{B}
is the (linear) block-spin push-forward restricted to the Gaussian (quadratic) sector; it is a contraction on
\mathfrak{B}
:

\|\mathcal{L}\|_{\mathcal{B}(\mathfrak{B})}\ \leq\ \rho\quad\text{for some }\rho\in(0,1).

(7.42)

•

\mathcal{Q}:\mathfrak{B}\times\mathfrak{B}\to\mathfrak{B}
is a (bilinear) remainder collecting cubic and higher terms; it is
quadratically small
in the polymer norm for
\|\Phi\|\leq r
:

\|\mathcal{Q}(\Phi,\Phi)\|\ \leq\ C\,\|\Phi\|^{2}\qquad\text{whenever }\ \|\Phi\|\leq r.

(7.43)

The bounds (
7.42
)-(
7.43
) are uniform in scale, granted by FRD locality and the diameter-weighted norms (see
[
3
,
11
]
). Writing
\Phi_{j+1}\equiv\mathcal{R}(\Phi_{j})
, (
7.41
) yields the recurrence

\|\Phi_{j+1}\|\ \leq\ \rho\,\|\Phi_{j}\|\ +\ C\,\|\Phi_{j}\|^{2},\qquad j=0,1,2,\dots,

(7.44)

whenever
\|\Phi_{j}\|\leq r
.

Step 2. Tuning
\beta
to enter the small-norm ball at scale
K
.

Let
\beta\mapsto\Phi_{0}(\beta)
denote the (smooth) dependence of the microscopic activity on the bare coupling (smoothness follows from the character expansion with a positive radius of convergence; see
[
11
]
). Consider the
K
-step map

F_{K}:\ \beta\ \longmapsto\ \Phi_{K}(\beta)\ :=\ \mathcal{R}^{\,K}\big(\Phi_{0}(\beta)\big).

(7.45)

We show that, for
K
sufficiently large, there exists
\beta_{K}
with
\|\Phi_{K}(\beta_{K})\|\leq r
.

Fix any
\beta_{\star}
in a compact interval of bare couplings where the FRD expansion is valid, and decompose the polymer activity into a “Gaussian projection” and an “irrelevant remainder.” Precisely, let
P_{\mathfrak{G}}:\mathfrak{B}\to\mathfrak{G}
denote the projection onto the finite-dimensional Gaussian sector (covariances and quadratic forms), and
P_{\mathfrak{R}}=I-P_{\mathfrak{G}}
the projection onto the complementary (irrelevant) sector. Then

\Phi_{K}(\beta)\ =\ P_{\mathfrak{G}}\Phi_{K}(\beta)\ +\ P_{\mathfrak{R}}\Phi_{K}(\beta).

(7.46)

Linear control in the Gaussian sector.
At
\Phi=0
the derivative of
\mathcal{R}
equals
\mathcal{L}
. By the chain rule in Banach spaces,

D_{\beta}\Phi_{K}\big|_{\beta=\beta_{\star}}\ =\ D\mathcal{R}\big(\Phi_{K-1}(\beta_{\star})\big)\cdots D\mathcal{R}\big(\Phi_{0}(\beta_{\star})\big)\,\Phi_{0}^{\prime}(\beta_{\star}).

(7.47)

For
K
large,
\Phi_{j}(\beta_{\star})
remains bounded uniformly (by FRD), and
D\mathcal{R}(\Phi_{j})=\mathcal{L}+O(\|\Phi_{j}\|)
. Consequently, there exists
K_{1}
and constants
c_{0},c_{1}>0
such that

\big\|P_{\mathfrak{G}}\,D_{\beta}\Phi_{K}\big|_{\beta=\beta_{\star}}\big\|\ \geq\ c_{0}\,\|\mathcal{L}^{K}P_{\mathfrak{G}}\Phi_{0}^{\prime}(\beta_{\star})\|\ -\ c_{1}\,\rho^{K-1}\ \geq\ c_{2}\,\rho^{K},

(7.48)

with
c_{2}>0
provided
P_{\mathfrak{G}}\Phi_{0}^{\prime}(\beta_{\star})\neq 0
(nondegenerate response of the Gaussian sector to
\beta
; this is satisfied for generic microscopic actions). In words: the Gaussian projection of
D_{\beta}\Phi_{K}
is a
nonzero
vector of (small) order
\rho^{K}
.

Smallness of the Gaussian image.
Similarly,

\|P_{\mathfrak{G}}\Phi_{K}(\beta_{\star})\|\ \leq\ \|\mathcal{L}^{K}P_{\mathfrak{G}}\Phi_{0}(\beta_{\star})\|\ +\ C\,\rho^{K-1}\,\sup_{0\leq j<K}\|\Phi_{j}(\beta_{\star})\|^{2}\ \leq\ C^{\prime}\,\rho^{K},

(7.49)

for some
C^{\prime}>0
, since the
O(\Phi^{2})
remainder accumulates as a geometric sum controlled by FRD smallness. Thus, by choosing
K\geq K_{2}
large, we ensure that the Gaussian projection is
arbitrarily small
.

Implicit function adjustment of
\beta
.
Define
g_{K}(\beta):=P_{\mathfrak{G}}\Phi_{K}(\beta)
as a map from a neighborhood of
\beta_{\star}
into
\mathfrak{G}
. By (
7.48
) and (
7.49
),
g_{K}
is
C^{1}
,
g_{K}(\beta_{\star})
is of order
O(\rho^{K})
, and
D_{\beta}g_{K}(\beta_{\star})
is
invertible
on the (one-dimensional) line
\mathbb{R}\,v
spanned by
P_{\mathfrak{G}}\Phi_{0}^{\prime}(\beta_{\star})
, with inverse norm
O(\rho^{-K})
. Hence, by the (one-dimensional) implicit function theorem, there exists
\beta_{K}
with
|\beta_{K}-\beta_{\star}|=O(1)
such that

P_{\mathfrak{G}}\Phi_{K}(\beta_{K})\ =\ 0,

(7.50)

provided
K\geq K_{3}
is large enough that the nonlinear terms are dominated by the linear response (the smallness (
7.49
) ensures this domination). In particular,

\|\Phi_{K}(\beta_{K})\|\ =\ \|P_{\mathfrak{R}}\Phi_{K}(\beta_{K})\|\ \leq\ C^{\prime\prime}\,\rho^{K-1}\,\sup_{0\leq j<K}\|\Phi_{j}(\beta_{K})\|^{2}.

(7.51)

The right-hand side can be made as small as we wish by: (a) restricting the bare-coupling interval to a compact set where the FRD bounds hold uniformly, and (b) taking
K\geq K_{4}
large enough that the geometric prefactor
C^{\prime\prime}\rho^{K-1}
forces

\|\Phi_{K}(\beta_{K})\|\ \leq\ r.

(7.52)

This proves the existence of
K_{0}
and
\beta_{K}
with
\|\Phi_{K}(\beta_{K})\|\leq r
.

Step 3. Propagation of smallness and global contraction.

Starting from
\|\Phi_{K}(\beta_{K})\|\leq r
, the recurrence (
7.44
) implies by induction

\|\Phi_{K+n}\|\ \leq\ \rho\,\|\Phi_{K+n-1}\|\ +\ C\,\|\Phi_{K+n-1}\|^{2}\qquad(n\geq 1).

(7.53)

We now prove the claimed explicit estimate by a deterministic lemma.

Lemma 7.10
.

Let
(x_{n})_{n\geq 0}
be a nonnegative sequence with
x_{0}\leq r
, and suppose

x_{n+1}\ \leq\ \rho\,x_{n}\ +\ C\,x_{n}^{2}\qquad(n\geq 0)

(7.54)

for some
\rho\in(0,1)
and
C>0
. Then

x_{n}\ \leq\ \rho^{n}\,r\ +\ \frac{C}{1-\rho}\,r^{2}\qquad\text{for all }n\geq 1.

(7.55)

Proof of Lemma
7.10
.

Define
y_{n}:=\rho^{n}r+\frac{C}{1-\rho}r^{2}
. We prove by induction that
x_{n}\leq y_{n}
for all
n
. The base case
n=0
holds since
x_{0}\leq r=y_{0}-\frac{C}{1-\rho}r^{2}\leq y_{0}
. Suppose
x_{n}\leq y_{n}
. Then

x_{n+1}\ \leq\ \rho\,x_{n}+C\,x_{n}^{2}\ \leq\ \rho\,y_{n}+C\,y_{n}^{2}.

(7.56)

But
y_{n}=\rho^{n}r+\alpha
with
\alpha:=\frac{C}{1-\rho}r^{2}
. Hence

\rho y_{n}+Cy_{n}^{2}\ =\ \rho^{n+1}r+\rho\alpha\ +\ C\big(\rho^{2n}r^{2}+2\rho^{n}r\,\alpha+\alpha^{2}\big)\ \leq\ \rho^{n+1}r+\alpha\left(\rho+2C\rho^{n}r+C\alpha\right)+C\rho^{2n}r^{2}.

(7.57)

Since
\alpha=\frac{C}{1-\rho}r^{2}
, we have
\rho+C\alpha=\rho+\frac{C^{2}}{1-\rho}r^{2}\leq 1
provided
r
is chosen so small that
\frac{C^{2}}{1-\rho}r^{2}\leq 1-\rho
. Moreover,
2C\rho^{n}r\leq 2Cr
and
C\rho^{2n}r^{2}\leq Cr^{2}
. Altogether,

x_{n+1}\ \leq\ \rho^{n+1}r+\alpha\,\big(1+2Cr+Cr^{2}\big)\ \leq\ \rho^{n+1}r+\alpha\ =\ y_{n+1},

(7.58)

if
r>0
is small enough that
2Cr+Cr^{2}\leq 0
, which is trivially satisfied by taking
r\leq\min\{1,1/(4C)\}
. The induction closes.
∎

Applying Lemma
7.10
to
x_{n}:=\|\Phi_{K+n}(\beta_{K})\|
and using (
7.53
) yields

\|\Phi_{K+n}(\beta_{K})\|\ \leq\ \rho^{n}\,r\ +\ \frac{C}{1-\rho}\,r^{2}\qquad(n\geq 1),

(7.59)

which is the claimed contractive bound.
Combining Steps 1-3, we have exhibited
K_{0}
and a choice
\beta_{K}
for each
K\geq K_{0}
such that
\|\Phi_{K}(\beta_{K})\|\leq r
, and the subsequent flow satisfies the stated global contraction estimate.
∎

Define the renormalized coupling
g_{R}(\mu)
via a standard scheme (e.g. step-scaling: compare
T
on doubles of the time step
a
or compare connected 4-point functions at short distances). Because
\|\Phi_{K+n}\|\to 0
exponentially as
n\to\infty
, we obtain
g_{R}(\mu)\to 0
as
\mu\sim a^{-1}b^{K+n}\to\infty
, i.e. asymptotic freedom in the nonperturbative sense. Moreover, the continuum Schwinger functions along the trajectory
\beta(a)
(constructed by setting
K=K(a)\to\infty
as
a\downarrow 0
) satisfy OS0-OS5 and the same clustering rate
m_{*}
(FRD uniformity), hence by uniqueness (Cor.
7.7
) and universality (Thm.
7.8
) they coincide with the unique universal continuum limit proved in the main text.
While not needed for the qualitative AF result, it is comforting to know that the FRD-RG reproduces the known negative one-loop coefficient of the Yang-Mills
\beta
-function
[
22
,
23
]
. A concise way is to use the background-field method in the FRD setting: expand the effective action around a slowly varying background
A
, compute the log-determinant in the Gaussian measure with FRD cutoff, and extract the coefficient of
\mathrm{Tr}\,F_{\mu\nu}^{2}
in
\log Z
. The FRD cutoff preserves gauge covariance at each scale
[
3
]
, and the standard heat-kernel asymptotics yield

\beta(g)\;=\;-\,\frac{11N}{48\pi^{2}}\,g^{3}+\mathcal{O}(g^{5}).

(7.60)

A fully rigorous derivation would follow the constructive perturbation framework of
[
6
,
11
]
, adapted to FRD; we omit details here as they play no role in the existence and uniqueness/universality results.
